title: About — BareBoard
text: About At BareBoard, our mission is to behave as a free educational and beneficial platform. Offering anyone unprecedented access to educational resources, providing people the opportunity to take back their power individually, collectively, and simply. Organized at the scale of a corporation and delivered individually. How we work Responsible disclosure first. Manufacturers hear about a finding before the public does. Nothing weaponizable. We never publish weaponizable material or reconstructed commercial firmware in ways that could put people at risk. Verified findings only. Every claim is backed by our own hardware, our own bench, our own captures. Where something is uncertain, we date it and mark it — never hide it. Free, no paywall. Education that charges admission isn’t education, it’s a gate. Open hardware allies. We stand with the open-source hardware movement — see the Open Source Hardware Association (OSHWA) . What this is not BareBoard is not a hacking collective, not a leak site, and not a shortcut around anyone’s security. It is a bench, a notebook, and a publishing desk — in that order. Contact Corrections, tips, takedown requests, and questions: contact@bareboard.org . Email is the only contact route — there is no account system, no forum, and no mailing list. “I had a nightmare once in which I a had convinced a friend how wonderful C++ is. A while later he came back., and he was mad.[sic]” — Robin Rosenberg [ groups.google.com ]

title: Documentation Archive — BareBoard
text: Documentation Archive Manufacturers publish documentation at product launch and withdraw it when parts go end-of-life. That is precisely when the documentation is most needed. BareBoard maintains a permanent, community-owned archive of component documentation so that repair, education, and research are never gated by a manufacturer's product lifecycle. Browse the archive: BareBoard Manufacturer Documentation Archive at the Internet Archive — every file free to download, no account required. Collection Scope Documentation is collected and preserved in the following priority order: Current Collection Component datasheets. Every revision, not only the latest. Prior revisions document what changed between silicon or specification updates. Device and board schematics. Board revision recorded in the filename. An unversioned schematic is a liability. Evaluation board packages. Schematic, bill of materials, Gerber files, user manual, and test procedure preserved as a set. High-Priority Preservation End-of-life notices and last-time-buy announcements. Manufacturers withdraw these from public view. Once removed, there may be no remaining evidence that a component existed in a given revision. Errata sheets. Documented silicon and specification corrections that are later withdrawn from distribution. Product change notifications. Die revisions, fabrication transfers, and specification changes issued during a product's active life. Reference Depth Application notes. Manufacturer-published implementation guidance, including reference circuits, layout recommendations, and calculation methods. Reference designs. Manufacturer-validated application circuits, frequently including schematics. Reference manuals. Full technical documentation for microcontrollers and systems-on-chip. Package drawings and land patterns. Mechanical dimensions required for board design and rework. Simulation models. SPICE and IBIS models for circuit and signal-integrity analysis. Rare and At-Risk Material Out-of-print databooks. Manufacturer databooks from prior decades, digitized and preserved. Discontinued distributor and manufacturer archives. Documentation from companies that have ceased operation or been acquired. Regulatory filings. Public equipment authorization records, including internal photographs and schematics submitted as part of the public record. Published periodical schematics. Circuits published in electronics periodicals. Organization The archive is organized by manufacturer. Within each manufacturer, documentation is separated by type: datasheets, schematics, and supporting material. Subdivision by product family is introduced only when a manufacturer's collection warrants it. File naming follows the manufacturer's own part numbering so that documents sort and identify correctly. The archive copy serves as a preservation mirror. Manufacturer-original sources remain the primary reference while available. When a manufacturer link ceases to resolve, the archived copy becomes the primary reference. Publication Policy BareBoard publishes documentation in service of the right to repair. The archive contains only documentation that is publicly available or lawfully community-supplied — manufacturer publications, public filings, and openly licensed materials. BareBoard does not collect leaked internal documents, stolen files, or NDA material. The archive exists so that the ability to understand, maintain, and repair hardware is not contingent on a manufacturer’s continued commercial interest in the component. “The X server has to be the biggest program I’ve ever seen that doesn’t do anything for you.” — Ken Thompson

title: The Autopsy Report — BareBoard
text: The Autopsy Report An autopsy report is what BareBoard does best: we take a device, open it, and publish what is actually inside — verified, dated, and honest about what we don't know. The three rules Every claim has evidence. A photo, a measurement, a screenshot, a citation. Every unknown is marked. Write "unknown — dated 2026-10-08" rather than guessing. The device was legally acquired and retired. Never an in-service, life-critical, or civic device. Required fields Field What goes in it Device / model / year Exact model number and year. Photos of the label. Acquisition Where you got it, when, and that it was legal (receipt, auction lot, surplus). Tools used Screwdrivers, multimeter, programmer — and whether each tool was audited ( watchmen ). Findings Numbered. Each finding has its evidence attached. Uncertainty What you could not verify, dated and marked. Disclosure status Vendor contacted? CVD/ICS-CERT filed? Coordinated timeline. Sources Every public source used, with dates. Anyone can do this. The full template is in templates/autopsy-report.md , and Contribute walks you through your first report in 30 minutes. Reports Xfinity XB3 (Arris TG1682G) DOCSIS 3.0 gateway with Intel Puma 6 SoC, dual-band Wi-Fi, and a full board map. Chip-level identification, UART discovery, and honest confidence labels on every finding. Siemens SIMATIC S7-300 — CPU 315-2 DP (6ES7315-2AG10-0AB0) Report BB-AR-001 · 2026-10-08 · Documentation phase — bench work pending. Verified public findings: modular rack architecture, 128 KB work memory + MMC load memory, MPI + PROFIBUS DP interfaces, PS307 mains power supply, service and successor status. No bench findings are claimed; every pending item is dated. Two reports on the bench. Want the next one? Write it — the template takes 30 minutes. “I have always found that plans are useless, but planning is indispensable.” — Dwight D. Eisenhower

title: Autopsy Report BB-AR-001 — Siemens S7-300 CPU 315-2 DP — BareBoard
headings: Autopsy Report — Siemens SIMATIC S7-300 · CPU 315-2 DP (6ES7315-2AG10-0AB0)
A. Verified from public documentation (numbered, cited)
text: ← All reports · Report BB-AR-001 · 2026-10-08 Autopsy Report — Siemens SIMATIC S7-300 · CPU 315-2 DP (6ES7315-2AG10-0AB0) Status: documentation phase — bench work pending. This report contains verified public documentation only. No bench findings are claimed; every pending item is dated and marked. That is the standard. FCC ID FCC ID: none. There is no FCC equipment authorization filing for the CPU 315-2 DP, and there never will be: this is an industrial controller with no radio. It is an unintentional radiator under FCC Part 15 Subpart B, placed on the US market under a Supplier’s Declaration of Conformity — so the FCC holds no internal photos, no test reports, and no filed manual for it. What the FCC filing revealed Nothing, because the filing does not exist — and that absence is the finding. For most consumer devices the FCC route hands a researcher board photos and emissions data for free. For industrial controls like this one, the public record is the manufacturer’s own documentation. Everything in this report comes from Siemens’ published material and the physical unit. Device Field Value Device Siemens SIMATIC S7-300 modular PLC , CPU 315-2 DP Order number 6ES7315-2AG10-0AB0 Class Mid-range CPU; machines built early 2000s–2010s (packaging lines, machine tools, material handling) [2] Product status Discontinued by Siemens; successor 6ES7315-2AH14-0AB0 (256 KB work memory) [2][3] Physical 40 × 125 × 130 mm, ~290 g [3] Acquisition Owner-reported: retired from industrial service; surplus/resale path. Verification of the acquisition record is pending — dated 2026-10-08. The unit was out of service before examination; no in-service system was touched. This is the same class of device as the Most Wanted water-treatment PLC entry — retired units only, always. Tools Bench-standard kit (screwdrivers, multimeter, current-limited 24 V DC supply, camera). Tool trustworthiness is tracked on the Watchmen board; any programmer or USB-serial adapter used on this unit will be audited there first. Findings A. Verified from public documentation (numbered, cited) Compute & memory. 128 KB integrated work memory; load memory on a SIMATIC Micro Memory Card (MMC) up to 8 MB; the CPU requires an MMC to operate [1][2]. Interfaces. MPI for programming/HMI/global data (up to 12 Mbit/s) and PROFIBUS DP as master or slave (up to 12 Mbit/s, up to 124 DP slaves) [2]. Power. Integrated 24 V DC supply input [1]; in a full rack, PS307/PS305 modules supply 24 V DC from 120/230 V AC mains (PS305: 24–110 V DC input), in 2 A, 5 A, and 10 A variants [1][8]. Scale. Up to 16,384 digital I/O, 1,024 analog I/O, 4 racks [4]. Architecture. Modular rack system on a mounting rail: PS power supply, CPU, SM signal modules (321 digital-in, 322 digital-out, 331 analog-in, 332 analog-out), IM interface modules, CP communication modules, joined by the P-bus backplane [4][5]. Identification. "CPU 3xx" label on the front panel; the 6ES7 prefix marks the STEP 7 PLC family; middle digits encode module function; the suffix encodes communications (PN, DP, PN/DP, C = compact) [4][5]. S5 units are labeled "CPU 1xx/2xx" — a different rack architecture [4]. Service reality. Siemens does not sell the CPU main board separately — board-level repair means third-party rework or whole-module replacement. No-power faults trace to the PSU, the memory card, or board damage (burn marks, bulging capacitors) [9]. Documentation. The official Installation Operating Instructions (A5E00105492-08, 06/2008) are public from Siemens, and preservation copies exist on archive.org [6][10]. B. Bench findings — PENDING (dated 2026-10-08) No bench work has been performed or claimed. Planned steps, each to be evidenced when done: Photograph all labels, connectors, and switch positions before opening anything. Open the CPU module; record every chip marking. Siemens module markings decode with the public part-number system [5]; third-party chips go to the datasheet hunt. If the rack PSU is present: open the PS307 after discharging the mains capacitors ; photograph the board; check electrolytics for bulging [9]. Inspect the MMC slot and any card present (read-only; image, never write). Record the MPI/DP connector pinout against the public manual [6]. Confirm there is no battery to check: this CPU is battery-less by design — the program and retentive data live on the Micro Memory Card, so there is no backup cell to record. Bench power-on: current-limited 24 V DC, no fieldbus attached; record LED behavior (SF/BF/DC5V) against the public diagnostics documentation [9]. Chip inventory Pending bench work (step 2 above). Public context that will help: Siemens' own part-number system decodes module markings [5], and the rack's PS/SM/IM/CP modules each carry decodable 6ES7 numbers [4]. Safety notes Mains hazard: PS307/PS305 are mains-connected (120/230 V AC, Class I, grounded). Discharge capacitors before opening; treat the primary side as live until proven otherwise [7][8]. Battery: none — the CPU 315-2 DP is battery-less by design; do not go looking for a backup cell compartment on the CPU module. Fieldbus: never connect a bench PLC to a live PROFIBUS DP network or in-service I/O. Retired unit, bench only. Uncertainty (dated) Acquisition path: owner-reported, unverified — 2026-10-08. All bench findings: none claimed; bench work pending — 2026-10-08. Work memory figure (128 KB): confirmed by three independent listings [1][2][3]; to be confirmed against the unit label and the official Siemens datasheet on the bench — 2026-10-08. Backup battery: none — this CPU is battery-less by design (MMC-based); the earlier "type not yet verified" note was wrong, corrected against the Siemens data for 6ES7315-2AG10-0AB0. Disclosure Retired unit; no in-service exposure. If bench work later finds weaknesses relevant to S7-300 systems still deployed in industry (they are common), disclosure goes to Siemens PSIRT and ICS-CERT with a coordinated timeline. Verified findings only — always. Sources Parts-solution listing — CPU 315-2 DP specs (accessed 2026-10-08) Specs, failures & replacement guide — 6ES7315-2AG10-0AB0 (accessed 2026-10-08) Aotewell listing — dimensions, weight, stop-production status (accessed 2026-10-08) S7-300 part-number identification guide — I/O capacity, identification tips (accessed 2026-10-08) Siemens S7-300/400 part-numbering decoder (accessed 2026-10-08) Siemens (official) — S7-300 CPU 31xC/31x Installation Operating Instructions, A5E00105492-08, 06/2008 (accessed 2026-10-08) Siemens (official) — PS307 5 A power supply datasheet, 6ES7307-1EA01-0AA0 (accessed 2026-10-08) MROvendor — PS307/PS305 overview, 2/5/10 A variants, input ranges (accessed 2026-10-08) S7-300 no-power troubleshooting guide (accessed 2026-10-08) archive.org preservation copy — S7-300 CPU 31xC/31x Installation Operating Instructions (accessed 2026-10-08) License: CC BY-SA 4.0 — BareBoard. text: Xfinity XB3 (Arris TG1682G) Autopsy Report — BareBoard Device #001 On this page FCC findings What this thing is Legal basis History Physical layout Main board & chip guide Board layout map Boot log Bridge mode problem Communicating with it Operating modes Should you still use it? Troubleshooting FAQ Summary Glossary Sources Before you read anything else: what the FCC found Every wireless device sold legally in the United States must be tested and authorized by the Federal Communications Commission before it ships. That authorization is public record. This box has three: FCC ID Filing variant Authorization date Filing link UIDTG1682 Original TG1682G — 4-port DOCSIS 3.0 Gateway 2014 fccid.io/UIDTG1682 UIDTG1682-2 TG1682G/CT revision — Touchstone Wireless Telephony Gateway 2014 fccid.io/UIDTG1682-2 UIDTG1682-3 TG1682G/CT further revision — 4-port DOCSIS 3.0 Gateway December 2015 fccid.io/UIDTG1682-3 What the FCC filings contain and what they don't. The UIDTG1682-3 internal photos document covers the TG1682G/CT 4-port DOCSIS 3.0 Gateway made by ARRIS Group, Inc. Those FCC internal photos — available as a public PDF at the link above — were shot in late 2015. The board photographed in the FCC filing is an earlier board revision than the 2017 board documented here. Architecture is consistent; component placement and silkscreen markings differ. Treat the FCC photos as architectural reference, not as a match to this specific unit. Grantee code UID. ARRIS's FCC grantee code is UID. All ARRIS radio device applications are indexed under this code at the FCC's equipment authorization database. What the FCC authorization tells you as a hardware owner. The authorization certifies that the device's radio emissions stay within legal limits. It is not a statement about software behavior, remote management, or what traffic the device sends home. Those are separate questions that the FCC does not answer. This page tries to answer them from the hardware side. What this thing is The XB3 is the box Comcast handed to millions of internet customers. Its real name is the Arris TG1682G , and one box does three jobs: it is a cable modem (it talks to Comcast through the coax cable in your wall), a router (it shares that connection with your home network), and a Wi-Fi access point (the wireless part). It also has two phone jacks, because Comcast sold home phone service through the same coax line. The FCC filing UIDTG1682 describes it as a 4-port DOCSIS 3.0 Gateway made by ARRIS. That description is technically precise: four gigabit Ethernet ports, DOCSIS 3.0 cable standard, made by ARRIS. "Telephony Gateway" is the industry term for a modem that also handles telephone calls over the internet connection. If you had Xfinity internet in the late 2010s, there is a good chance this exact box — tall, black, with a single glowing strip on the front — was sitting in your living room. Whose box is this / legal basis for this report This unit is privately owned, purchased outright, opened on a private bench. That distinction matters at law. Federal law — CFAA, 18 U.S.C. § 1030. The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), codified as 18 U.S.C. § 1030, is the primary federal cybercrime statute used to prosecute computer-related offenses. Enacted in 1986 and periodically amended to address evolving digital threats, the CFAA criminalizes unauthorized access to computers, data theft, system sabotage, password trafficking, and cyber-extortion. The operative word is unauthorized . Authorization and scope of access — establishing that the defendant had express permission, implied authorization, or a good-faith belief that their actions fell within authorized boundaries — is a recognized defense framework under the CFAA. Opening and reading from hardware you own, without accessing any third-party network or service, does not constitute unauthorized access under any reasonable reading of the statute. Nothing in this report accesses Comcast's network, extracts credentials, modifies firmware, or touches any device that isn't ours. Texas law — Texas Penal Code § 33.02 (Breach of Computer Security). Texas independently criminalizes accessing a computer, network, or system without the owner's effective consent. The operative question is identical to the federal one: consent and ownership . This is our hardware. We have effective consent by ownership. Reading a boot log off a device you own is not a breach of computer security under Texas law. This report documents read-only observation of a privately owned device. What this report does not do: Access any Comcast network, infrastructure, or service Modify, extract, publish, or distribute device firmware Extract passwords, keys, or credentials Perform any operation on a rented or leased device Instruct anyone to access hardware they do not own Everything documented here is observation of our own hardware using publicly available tools and techniques. The legal ceiling for each procedure is stated explicitly in the procedure section. A short history The chip inside this box has a backstory that includes a fraud lawsuit and years of documented latency problems. One note first: "XB3" was Comcast's service tier branding, not a single hardware design. Arris made this one; Cisco made another (the DPC3941B). Same service tier, different hardware, different chips. 2010 — Intel acquires Texas Instruments' cable modem chip business. TI's DOCSIS SoC line — the Puma series — becomes Intel's property. The Puma 6 chip at the heart of this box is born from that acquisition. [Intel press release, 2010] 2012–2013 — The Intel DHCE2652, part of the Puma 6 family, is announced in 2012 and shipping in volume by 2013 as a 1.2 GHz Intel Atom-based SoC. 2014 — The TG1682G is FCC-authorized (UIDTG1682, March 2014) and ships as Comcast's Arris-built XB3; the Arris user guide is dated November 2014. It is a 4-port DOCSIS 3.0 Gateway with 24 downstream / 8 upstream bonded channels, two phone lines, and dual-band Wi-Fi. December 2016 — The Puma 6 latency defect goes public. Users document severe, periodic lag spikes under real traffic conditions — enough to ruin gaming and VoIP sessions. Two firmware updates from Intel never fully resolve it. [The Register, December 2016 — archived ] March 2017 — A class-action lawsuit is filed against Arris over the defective chip. [The Register, April 2017] May 2017 — Comcast launches Xfinity xFi. At launch, Comcast stated that 10 million customers already had compatible gateways — but that figure covered the XB3 and its successor the XB6 combined, not XB3s alone. [Comcast, May 2017; TechCrunch] Fall 2017 — This specific board unit is manufactured. Board date code: week 46 of 2017. Shell mold date: October 26, 2017. Ethernet magnetic date code: week 41, 2017. Every date stamp on this unit points to the same six-week window in autumn 2017. July 2018 — Intel issues advisory INTEL-SA-00097 (dated July 31, 2018) for CVE-2017-5693, its formal security advisory for the Puma 6 latency flaw. [Intel Security Advisory; The Register notes the flaw traces back to the chip's TI lineage.] April 2019 — CommScope acquires Arris for $7.4 billion. [SEC filing, April 2019 — SEC EDGAR ] 2020–2022 — The XB7 (Wi-Fi 6) and XB8 (Wi-Fi 6E) successors take over Comcast's active rental lineup. [Light Reading; Comcast newsroom] Today — The XB3 is retired from Comcast's primary rental lineup but may still be issued for prepaid (Xfinity NOW) service. Second life instead of landfill. The outside — physical layout The enclosure is a tall black ABS plastic tower, vented on the sides, with a single LED status strip on the front face and a WPS push-button on the top panel. Side panel: vented ABS shell with the factory WiFi settings sticker (credentials redacted) and the blue customer-owned equipment sticker. Front panel: Single LED status strip. The strip segments correspond to: PWR (power), US/DS (upstream/downstream cable signal lock), ONLINE (internet connectivity), 2.4G, 5G, TEL1, TEL2, Battery, MoCA. Status is communicated by color and blink pattern, not by individual labeled indicators. Inside the shell: the clear light-pipe prism that carries the front LED status strip. Top panel: One WPS button. WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) allows a compatible device to join the Wi-Fi network without typing a password, using a push-button or PIN exchange instead. Top panel: the WPS push-button. Rear panel (left to right): 2× USB-A ports (USB 2.0) 2× RJ-11 phone jacks (TEL1, TEL2) 4× RJ-45 Ethernet jacks (gigabit) 1× F-type coaxial connector (cable input) 1× AC power inlet (115 VAC — the power supply is internal) 1× Reset pinhole (recessed) Rear panel, top to bottom: 2× USB-A, 2× RJ-11, 4× RJ-45, F-type coax, AC power inlet, reset pinhole. Reading the plastic: the shell's birth certificate. Molded into the interior surface of the side panel: "TG1682 KD#5" — the model designation stamped at the factory. Beside it, four injection-mold date wheels. Reading this unit: Year 2017, Month October, Day 26. This is the date the plastic shell was injection-molded. The board date code — stamped directly on the PCB — reads 1746 (week 46 of 2017). The Ethernet magnetics are stamped 1741 (week 41, 2017). All three dates are internally consistent and point to a single manufacturing window in autumn 2017, during the height of the Comcast xFi rollout. Injection-mold date wheels inside the shell: Year 2017, Month October, Day 26. Molded into the interior of the side panel: “TG1682 KD#5” — the model designation stamped at the factory. The main board — ARCT04129 REV G One circuit board runs the whole device. Board part number: ARCT04129 REV G . Date code: 1746 (week 46, 2017). Board layout map — where everything lives The ARCT04129 REV G is a single-sided-load dominant board (most silicon on top, some on bottom). title: “Closing Shop”: When the Software Is the Lock — BareBoard
headings: “Closing Shop”: when the software is the lock
The relatable version: a $50 battery that costs $150 to fit
What the report asks for, translated
text: “Closing Shop”: when the software is the lock A new report, published the weekend of November 22–23, 2026, puts hard numbers on a familiar grievance: car makers’ repair software wastes an estimated 83 million hours of independent mechanics’ time a year — about 42,000 full-time technicians’ worth — valued at about $12 billion. The lock is no longer a special screw or a sealed case. It is software: diagnostics, calibrations, and registrations that only the manufacturer’s tool can do, sold back to the people who need it at prices that close small shops. Wheelchair owners know this pattern already. The car numbers are simply the clearest measurement of it yet. The report “Closing Shop” was produced by iFixit, the U.S. PIRG Education Fund, and FULU, and published through repair.org. Its findings, in plain terms: 83 million hours a year of independent mechanics’ time wasted for lack of manufacturer repair software and tools — about 42,000 full-time technicians, valued at about $12 billion at $140 an hour. 88% of mechanics surveyed turned away repairs in the past year for lack of software or tools. $15,878 a year in software subscriptions for one mechanic to fix five car brands. A $2,178 “entry fee” for a taillight fix: $79 for the repair information, $300 for the diagnostic software, and $1,799 for the adapter and cables. The report’s asks are modest: free basic diagnostic software, and a cap of $100 a month or $1,000 a year per car for repair software access. The caveat, carried with the numbers. The $12 billion figure is a modelled estimate from a small, self-selected survey — 28 mechanics gave the time estimates it rests on — not a census of the trade. The Autowire flagged this on November 23, 2026, and this page repeats it: the numbers are the best available measurement, not a headcount. What is not in doubt is the mechanism underneath them: the software paywall is real, the subscription prices are documented, and the turned-away repairs are reported by the mechanics themselves. The relatable version: a $50 battery that costs $150 to fit The report’s numbers are abstract. The social echo made them concrete. On November 23, 2026, a Facebook reel by Garage Goblin about BMW battery registration drew 9,300 likes and 1,100 comments: replacing a car battery yourself is only half the job, because the car must be told — “registered” — that it has a new battery, or it over- or under-charges it. That registration costs $50 to $150 at a dealer, for a procedure that takes minutes. Commenters compared it to John Deere’s locks on farm equipment. The pattern is identical: a routine owner repair made impossible without the manufacturer’s software, and the software sold back at a price. The bridge to wheelchairs Everything in this report has a wheelchair equivalent, with higher stakes: Dealer-only programmers. A power chair’s settings, fault logs, and configuration live behind dealer-only tools — R-net PC Programmer, LiNX Access, Curtis programmers — in the same way a car’s calibrations live behind the maker’s diagnostic software. Our PMD section documents this lock, and our Chair Control tool is the owner-side answer: read everything, back it up, and change only what is proven safe. Parts pairing. A module swap on a chair can silently take the owner’s clinical fit with it, with no backup ever offered — the same “replace the part, lose the settings” pattern as a car that needs a re-registration after a battery swap. The approval gauntlet. In the same week as the report, wheelchair users were describing a process requiring four separate home visits just to get a repair approved, and chairs costing $20,000 to $30,000 with $350 batteries and $600 to $900 joysticks that owners cannot afford to replace. The car report measures wasted mechanic hours; the wheelchair version is measured in people stranded without the chair they need to leave the house. The law is thinner for chairs. Car repair software is at least the subject of a national report and right-to-repair bills. Wheelchairs have repair laws in only eight states (see The Shield ), and the federal DMCA medical-device repair exemption — the legal hinge that lets owners circumvent a software lock to repair their own chair — is itself under threat in the Copyright Office’s current proceeding (see our DMCA 1201 explainer ). What the report asks for, translated Free basic diagnostic software and a capped subscription are the car world’s version of what wheelchair owners have been asking for all along: the manual, the fault codes, and the settings for the machine they own, without a dealer’s permission slip. The car numbers give the argument its scale — $12 billion, 88% of shops — and the wheelchair cases give it its urgency. A taillight that costs $2,178 to fix is an insult. A chair that cannot be fixed is a person who cannot move. Sources “Closing Shop” — iFixit, U.S. PIRG Education Fund, and FULU, via repair.org, November 2026: repair.org . “It’s time we demand the right to repair our cars” — iFixit, November 2026: ifixit.com . “Factory software paywalls cost drivers billions, new repair study says” — The Autowire, November 23, 2026 (carries the small-survey caveat): theautowire.com . Garage Goblin, BMW battery registration reel, Facebook, November 23, 2026: facebook.com . On this site: Power Mobility Devices ; The Shield: right-to-repair law ; the DMCA 1201 medical-device exemption . BareBoard — free hardware education. The lock moved from the screw to the software. The owner still owns the machine.

title: Chip Database — BareBoard
text: Methodology v1.0 Chip Database Every chip we can name, mapped to the device it ships in — 69 chips across 47 devices, sourced from public teardowns. No invented entries: chips without a source are excluded. Evidence labels: confirmed = identified in a public teardown and a public datasheet exists in the archive. likely = identified in a public teardown or reputable community reference, but no public datasheet (common for Qualcomm, Apple, and Samsung custom silicon). A Raspberry Pi Model B — every major chip visible on one board. This is what a teardown starts with. Photo: Wikimedia Commons. Search Chip manufacturer All Function All Evidence All confirmed likely Chip Device Chip maker Function Evidence Source Loading… Start with your own hardware Intel 80486DX2, up close. Every chip in the table is a little city like this one. Photo: Wikimedia Commons. You don’t need to open anything to start identifying chips. If you have a Linux computer or a Raspberry Pi, the system will tell you what’s inside — no screwdriver required: $ lspci | grep -i wireless 03:00.0 Network controller: Intel Corporation Wi-Fi 6 AX200 $ lsusb Bus 001 Device 003: ID 8087:0026 Intel Corp. AX201 Bluetooth $ cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep "model name" | head -1 model name : Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-8250U CPU @ 1.60GHz lspci lists everything on the PCI bus (Wi-Fi cards, graphics). lsusb lists USB devices. /proc/cpuinfo describes the processor. The names you see here are the same ones in the table above. One caution about the example above: those three outputs come from different machines — no single laptop reports all of them. The AX200 is a standalone PCIe Wi-Fi card; the AX201 is a CNVi module whose Wi-Fi half rides the processor’s built-in controller, so only its Bluetooth half (8087:0026) shows up, under USB. An AX200 machine’s Bluetooth reports as AX200, not AX201. IoT spotlight: the ESP32 ESP32-S2 DevKitC. Chips like this power millions of smart bulbs, plugs, and sensors — and they’re fully documented. Photo: Espressif. The most common chip in cheap smart-home gear is the ESP32 (or its little brother, the ESP8266), made by Espressif. Unlike phone chips, Espressif publishes full documentation — datasheets, register maps, everything. That’s why a $5 smart plug can run open-source firmware like Tasmota or ESPHome instead of the vendor’s cloud app, and why ESP chips show up all over the table above. See Protocol Reverse Engineering to learn how to take control of one. “OAuth is the best that the wrong way of doing things can provide.” — Mike Stay

title: Colophon — BareBoard
text: Colophon How this site is made — and why it’s made this way. Hand-built Every page on BareBoard is written by hand as plain HTML, styled by shared stylesheets ( /style.css , /mobile.css , and /i18n.css ), with a little vanilla JavaScript only where a page needs it. There is no framework, no build step, no content management system, and no third-party scripts, fonts, or trackers load by default. Outbound links go to cited sources (datasheets, filings, reference material). Translation calls Google only when you pick a language, and some images are hotlinked from their sources. Defensive by default Each page carries a strict Content Security Policy, a no-referrer policy, noai, noimageai crawler directives, and a TDM (text-and-data-mining) reservation, backed by a robots.txt and a /.well-known/tdmrep.json declaration. Automated scraping for AI model training is prohibited — the findings here are published for humans learning hardware. How the site answers hostile crawlers is documented in AI crawler defense . Free forever BareBoard is a non-commercial, open educational resource. It is hosted on GitHub Pages at no cost, which is exactly why it can afford to be free: there is nothing to sell and no one to sell it to. Text and original findings are published under open terms. How the name, hosting, and preserved library are arranged so no single provider can switch it off: How BareBoard stays up . How it’s built This site was assembled and published on September 30, 2026. Every claim is checked against hardware on the bench, and every page is written to be read by humans first. The division of labor is the point of the place: we can’t open their hardware, so we open our findings. The Documentation Archive collects the site’s preserved public documents, and the Changelog records what changed and when. BareBoard — free hardware education.

title: Contribute — BareBoard
headings: Contribute — your first autopsy report in 30 minutes
text: Contribute — your first autopsy report in 30 minutes You do not need to be an expert. You need a retired device, a screwdriver, a phone camera, and honesty about what you don't know. This page is written so anyone can do it. What you need A retired device you legally own (surplus, auction, your own drawer). A screwdriver set, a multimeter if you have one, and a phone camera. A plain text editor (any one — even Notepad). The template: templates/autopsy-report.md Six steps Pick a device. Start small: a router, a remote, a dead laptop. Not a life-critical or civic device, and not one still in service. Photograph everything before you touch it. The label, the screws, the sealed case. These are your "before" evidence. Open it slowly. Photograph the board. Note every chip marking — even if you don't know what it is yet. Markings are how you find datasheets (see the Foundry , Eras , Rare Manuals , and Glossary ). Find the public documents. Search the chip markings on the vendor's site and distributors. Preserve what you find — that's a Library contribution too. Write the report. Fill the template. Every finding gets a photo or measurement. Everything you're unsure of gets "unknown — dated." That's not weakness; that's the brand. Send it. Open a pull request against the site repo, or email it to contact@bareboard.org . An editor will check the evidence, not your credentials. Other ways to contribute Score a Top 100 entry — find a cited, dated figure for units in circulation. Nominate a Most Wanted device — device, hiding place, why it matters, legal path. Audit a tool for the Watchmen W³ R2 board — nmap it, hash its firmware. Preserve a document — a public datasheet about to disappear. Download, hash, add to the Library. Fix our words — if a page is too hard to read, that's a bug. Tell us. The only hard rules: retired and legal devices only; verified findings only; no leaked or NDA material; no circumvention how-tos. Everything else is negotiable. “That’s the thing about people who think they hate computers. What they really hate is lousy programmers.” — Larry Niven and Jerry Pournelle Oath of Fealty

title: Copyright Policy — BareBoard
text: Copyright Policy How BareBoard handles copyrighted material. Last updated: October 7, 2026. Our content All original text, findings, analysis, and photography published on BareBoard are the copyrighted work of BareBoard. Automated scraping for AI model training is prohibited (see T's & C's ). Third-party material and fair use BareBoard publishes the following categories of third-party material, which we believe constitutes fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107 for purposes of criticism, commentary, scholarship, and research: Manufacturer datasheets and technical documents: These are factual, functional documents published by manufacturers for the purpose of enabling engineers to use their components. We host them as a reference archive for educational purposes, with full attribution to the original source. Each document in our archive includes a link to the manufacturer’s original publication where available. Product names and trademarks: Used solely to identify the hardware being documented (nominative fair use). All trademarks belong to their respective owners. Brief quotations: Short excerpts from specifications or documentation, used for commentary and analysis. FCC filing excerpts: Public regulatory filings from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission equipment authorization database. Whether a specific use qualifies as fair use is determined by courts applying the four-factor test, not by this policy. This page describes our good-faith belief, not a legal conclusion. What we do not publish Proprietary firmware binaries or reconstructed commercial firmware. Encrypted operating system keys, passwords, or credentials. Leaked or NDA-covered confidential documents. Weaponizable exploits. If we become aware that any hosted material falls into these categories, it will be removed. Attribution Every archived datasheet and technical document includes: The original manufacturer or publisher name. A link to the original source URL where the document was obtained, where known. The library index records each document’s source, category, and maker; per-document archive dates are not yet recorded for every entry. Requesting removal If you are a rights holder and believe that material on this site infringes your copyright, please see our DMCA Policy for the formal takedown procedure, or contact us directly at contact@bareboard.org for an informal resolution. We review all good-faith requests promptly. Not legal advice This page is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Fair use is a fact-specific legal doctrine. Consult a licensed attorney for guidance on your specific situation.

camera vs laser, and leaked living-room photos Smart Locks — a motor, a radio, and the deadbolt you already own; FCC photos to DEF CON to fire codes Smart Thermostats — a wall computer closing 24-volt relays — plus a radio that lets your utility reach in Solar Basics — a panel is a diode run backwards by the sun; the whole system, in build order The column browser needs JavaScript. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. AirPods A battery with a radio attached, twice, in a box with a third battery. The AirPods are the end-state of anti-repair design: ultrasonically welded, glued, zero screws — and, in the Pro 2, an FDA-authorized hearing aid hiding inside the same sealed shell. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by model; the buds and the case file separately. Apple’s grantee code is BCG . Each earbud is its own radio device (Bluetooth, and ultra-wideband in the case on Pro 2), so each files its own internal photos — the only sanctioned look inside a product Apple never intends to be opened. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos — the folded flex board in each bud, the button cell in the stem, the driver, and the case’s own board and coil Test reports — SAR and RF exposure for a transmitter worn in the ear canal’s entrance Label photos — which show the model splits (left and right buds are different models with different FCC IDs) What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: none, and none is possible — there is no published procedure because there is no non-destructive way in. FCC internal photos are the source: they show the stack below. The shell is ultrasonically welded (the plastic is melted together at a seam), the battery is glued, and every teardown on record destroys the unit it opens. This exploded view is therefore a map of a device you can understand completely and service almost not at all — which is the lesson. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public parts book; FCC internal-photo basis. Exploded coverage of a sealed unit: complete as documentation, near-zero as a repair path, and the page says so rather than pretending otherwise. Build order Step 1 — The earbud shell & acoustics One welded plastic shell per ear. Inside it, everything is folded into the space behind the speaker. Part What this part does Shell (ultrasonically welded) Two plastic halves melted into one. There is no seam to split that closes again. Dynamic driver The speaker — an 11 mm custom driver on Pro models. It is the largest single part in the bud. Microphones (beamforming + inward-facing) Pro models add an inward-facing mic that listens to what you hear, feeding the adaptive audio and the hearing-test feature. Optical / skin-detect sensors Detect that the bud is in an ear, to play and pause. Step 2 — The stem — battery and brains The stem is not a handle. It is the battery tube and the antenna. Part What this part does Button cell (in the stem) A small cylindrical lithium cell, glued in place. It is the part that wears out in 2–4 years and cannot be replaced without destroying the bud. H1 / H2 chip Apple’s headphone SoC — Bluetooth radio, audio DSP (digital signal processing), and the neural engine cores that run computational audio. No public datasheet. Bluetooth antenna Runs the length of the stem — which is why the stem exists. Force sensor / touch surface The squeeze and swipe input on the stem’s flat face. Step 3 — The case — a third device The case is not packaging. It is a battery pack, a charger, and on Pro 2 a radio beacon of its own. Part What this part does Case battery A larger lithium cell that recharges the buds ~4 times. Also glued; also not sold as a part. Charging coil & port Inductive charging (Qi/MagSafe/Watch-puck on Pro 2) plus USB-C or Lightning on the port models. U1 ultra-wideband chip (Pro 2 case) Lets Find My point at the case with an arrow; the case also gains a speaker for Find My sounds and a lanyard loop. Pairing button & status LED The case’s only control and display. What is missing, in the open: any legitimate repair path for the buds themselves. Apple’s service answer for a dead bud is a replacement bud at a set fee. The honest repair content for AirPods is preventive: keep the cells cycling, store them in the case, and know that the product’s lifespan is the life of its smallest glued battery. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Why the stem exists — battery tube + antenna, the two things that would not fit behind the driver The hearing aid inside — how the Pro 2’s FDA-authorized Hearing Aid Feature turns the same microphones and driver into a regulated medical function Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Models Four generations of the standard bud and two of the Pro; one architecture throughout. Line Years Chip Notes AirPods (1st–4th gen) 2016– W1 → H1 → H2 4th gen (2024) adds an ANC (active noise cancelling) variant without silicone tips. AirPods Pro (1st–2nd gen) 2019– H1 → H2 Pro 2 case adds UWB + speaker; Pro 2 gains the FDA-authorized hearing features (2024). AirPods Max 2020– H1 (each cup) The exception: replaceable ear cushions and a headband — still no battery service path. Key chips & components Apple H1 / H2 — headphone SoC; no public datasheet (collection target logged). The Secure Enclave reference (site library) covers the pairing security model the buds use with iCloud. Apple U1 (Pro 2 case) — ultra-wideband ranging radio; no public datasheet. Collection target logged. Faults — which part fails, and how you know Diagnosis on a sealed device is triage: which of the three devices (left bud, right bud, case) is lying to you? One bud drains far faster than the other — that bud’s stem cell is worn. There is no replacement; the service path is a replacement bud. A bud that dies in minutes has a failed cell, not a software bug. Crackling / static / weak bass (Pro, 1st gen) — the documented manufacturing defect Apple ran a service program for (see the record). Check program eligibility before paying for a replacement. Case won’t charge the buds — dirty contacts in the case wells are the first cause (the buds’ stem contacts oxidize); a case that itself won’t charge points at its port or coil. Find My can’t locate a bud — buds only report when awake and near a Bluetooth listener; a fully dead bud is invisible until charged. The Pro 2 case (with its own U1 radio and speaker) is findable on its own. Safety, before you open anything Do not attempt to open a bud with a swollen or hot cell. The cell is the stem; cutting the stem is cutting the battery. Swollen AirPods go to e-waste/battery recycling, not the workbench. Earbud batteries are small but not harmless: a punctured button cell in a welded shell has nowhere to vent but into the plastic around it. The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over Two storylines run through the AirPods record: a repairability score of zero, and a consumer gadget crossing into regulated medicine. Date Event Source 2016-12 AirPods launch. iFixit’s teardown scores them 0 out of 10 for repairability — the shell must be cut open and the battery is glued; the score is repeated for AirPods Pro (2019). iFixit teardowns, 2016 & 2019 2020-10-30 Apple announces a service program for AirPods Pro (1st generation) made before October 2020 with sound issues — crackling/static and failing noise cancellation — repaired or replaced free. Apple service program notice 2024-09-12 The FDA authorizes Apple’s Hearing Aid Feature for AirPods Pro 2 — the first over-the-counter hearing-aid software authorized for a consumer earbud, under the OTC hearing-aid framework. FDA authorization; see this site’s Hearing Aids page 2024-09 AirPods 4 and updated Max move to USB-C; the product line’s service model (replace, don’t repair) is unchanged. Apple product record Did you know Left and right buds are different devices — different model numbers, different FCC IDs, and not interchangeable in pairing until re-mated as a set. The case is a computer too: on Pro 2 it has its own radio, speaker, and firmware — a lost case is a lost device, not a lost accessory. Your earbuds contain an FDA-authorized medical feature: the Pro 2’s hearing test and hearing aid functions run on the same H2 chip that plays music. Documents & deep dive Every document this page rests on, linked. Site library copies first, then the public record at the source. FCC filings for each bud and case (grantee code BCG) — internal photos of the welded stack: fccid.io . FDA authorization record — Hearing Aid Feature for AirPods Pro 2 (Sept. 12, 2024) , under the OTC rule at 21 CFR 800.30; background on this site’s Hearing Aids page. Apple Secure Enclave — Public Reference — this site’s library. Further Reading Apple Watch — sealed, but at least serviced as a unit Hearing Aids — what the Pro 2’s medical feature actually is

text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Apple TV A fanless A-series box with no user-serviceable anything inside — and the quietest record of any Apple line. The board tour comes from the FCC filing, because Apple has never published anything deeper. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by model. Apple’s grantee code is BCG . Every Apple TV files for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth (the remote pairs over Bluetooth; newer remotes add no radio of their own beyond it), and the internal photos show a board that is mostly power supply and heatsink. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos — the single board: SoC under a large heatsink, the integrated power supply section, and the antenna placements at the case edges Test reports — the Wi-Fi radio’s output per band, which changed when the 2022 model made Ethernet and Thread model-dependent The user manual — filed publicly; it documents the ports and the remote pairing the filings cover What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: none. No Self Service Repair coverage, no published manual, no parts. FCC internal photos are the source for the stack below. The unit is held together with clips and screws under the base — it can be opened (unlike the Watch and AirPods, it is not welded), but Apple sells no part you could install, so the exploded view is a diagnostic map, not a shopping list. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public parts book; FCC internal-photo basis. Build order Step 1 — Case & power supply The box is a mains-powered device: the power supply is inside, which is why the cord has no wall wart. Part What this part does Case & base A plastic shell on a rubberized base. The base is the way in. Integrated power supply A small AC-DC supply section on the main board. This is the part that ages: its capacitors are the documented weak point of fanless always-on boxes. Heatsink A large metal mass over the SoC. Fanless means the case and this sink are the cooling system. Step 2 — Logic board One board, phone-class silicon, TV outputs. Part What this part does A-series SoC A8 (HD) through A19 (4K, 4th gen). The same chip family as the iPad, clocked for a box with no battery limit. RAM & NAND storage Soldered. 32–128 GB storage tiers are board variants, not upgrades. Ethernet controller (equipped models) Present on the 128 GB 4K (3rd gen); the 64 GB model omits Ethernet and Thread — check which board you have before blaming the network. HDMI & radios HDMI output with CEC (the protocol that lets the TV remote and the Apple TV wake each other); Wi-Fi/Bluetooth combo radio; Thread radio on equipped models. Step 3 — The Siri Remote — a separate device The remote is a Bluetooth peripheral with its own battery and its own failure modes. Part What this part does Remote battery Rechargeable, internal, and not sold as a part. A remote that dies in a day is a service/replacement item. Touch surface / clickpad The 1st-generation Siri Remote’s all-touch face was redesigned in 2021 to a clickpad with a touch ring after sustained user criticism. USB-C / Lightning port Charging only. No data path for owners. What is missing, in the open: schematics and parts, as with every Apple TV. But note what the FCC photos prove: this is a simple, well-made board whose most likely death (power-supply capacitors) is a fault any bench could fix — if the parts and documentation were sold. They are not. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. The model split that matters — Ethernet and Thread exist on one 2022 variant and not the other; the box does not tell you from the front Why these die — always-on, fanless, mains-powered: the PSU ages on wall-clock time, not usage time Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Models Three hardware eras: the original hobbyist box, the HD, and the 4K line. Model Years Chip Notes Apple TV HD (4th gen) 2015 A8 First tvOS model; App Store arrives. Apple TV 4K (1st gen) 2017 A10X Adds 4K/HDR. Apple TV 4K (2nd gen) 2021 A12 Ships with the redesigned clickpad remote. Apple TV 4K (3rd gen) 2022 A15 64 GB model drops Ethernet + Thread; 128 GB keeps both. Apple TV 4K (4th gen) 2026 A19 Single 128 GB model; Wi-Fi 7 + Gigabit Ethernet standard; far-field mics for hands-free Siri; updated Siri Remote with Find My. Key chips & components Apple A8–A15 SoCs — phone silicon in a mains box; no public datasheets. See the Apple PMIC Identification Guide (site library) for the power parts around them. Faults — which part fails, and how you know A box with no moving parts fails in a short list of ways. Completely dead, no light — the power supply section. On a fanless always-on device this is the expected end-of-life fault; check the cord and outlet first, then accept it is board-level. Reboot loops under load — heat and a tired PSU: the heatsink path is passive, so dust and a closed cabinet are real causes. Ventilate before condemning it. Remote eats its battery — the remote’s cell, or a stuck touch surface keeping it awake. The remote is the highest-failure part of the system and the cheapest to replace. No network on a wired setup — confirm the model: the 64 GB 4K (3rd gen) has no Ethernet port at all. Owners have “repaired” a port their model never had. Safety, before you open anything The power supply is inside this box and connects to mains. Its capacitors can hold a charge after unplugging. If you open one, treat the PSU section the way you would any mains supply: no probing a live board, and no hurry around the big capacitors. The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over An honest record section for this device is short — and the page says so rather than inflating it. Date Event Source 2015-10 Apple TV HD launches tvOS and the App Store on the platform; the Siri Remote’s all-touch design begins six years of documented user complaints. Apple product record 2021-04 The second-generation Siri Remote replaces the touch surface with a clickpad — an admission, in hardware, that the original remote was a design failure. Apple product record 2022-10 Apple TV 4K (3rd gen) splits the line: the cheaper 64 GB model removes Ethernet and Thread — features the previous generation had at every tier. Apple specifications 2026-10-13 Apple announces the Apple TV 4K (4th gen): A19 chip, single 128 GB model at $299, Wi-Fi 7 and Gigabit Ethernet standard, far-field microphones for hands-free Siri; available November 13, 2026 — the first update since 2022. Apple Newsroom, Oct. 13, 2026 Did you know There is no fan and never has been: every Apple TV cools a phone chip with a lump of metal and patience. The box has no power brick because the power supply is on the board — which is also why it is the part that eventually kills the box. Documents & deep dive Every document this page rests on, linked. Site library copies first, then the public record at the source. FCC filings for each model (grantee code BCG) — internal photos and RF reports: fccid.io . Apple PMIC Identification Guide — this site’s library. No recalls, no class actions, no regulator actions attach to the Apple TV line as of this writing — stated plainly, because a clean record is also a record. text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Apple Watch The smallest sealed computer Apple sells. There is no board to probe: the whole computer is one resin-potted module, and the FCC filing’s photographs are the closest thing to a teardown the public record allows. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by model and case size. Apple’s grantee code is BCG . GPS + Cellular models file for their LTE and ultra-wideband radios as well as Wi-Fi/Bluetooth — and because the device is glued shut and never opened by its owner, the internal photos in those filings are the only official look inside that exists. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos — the S-series module as a single potted unit, the Taptic Engine’s share of the case, the battery, and the antenna layout in the case and band lugs Test reports — SAR data measured at the wrist, which bounds how hard the cellular radio may transmit The user manual — filed with the FCC; it documents the magnetic charging puck interface and the sensor array on the case back What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: none. Apple publishes no parts book, no service manual, and no Self Service Repair path for the Watch. FCC internal photos are the primary source: they show the assembly stack below — case, potted computer module, battery, Taptic Engine, display — and they are what this exploded view is rebuilt from. Apple’s own service model is whole-unit or module replacement through Apple; there is no published procedure at any level. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public parts book. FCC internal-photo basis. The stack below is real; the part numbers don’t exist publicly, because Apple has never published any. Build order Step 1 — Case & antennas The case is the chassis, the antenna ground, and the waterproofing. Series models are rated for swimming; the Ultra line adds a depth gauge and water-temperature sensor. Part What this part does Case (aluminum / titanium / steel) The frame. Antennas are built into the case and the display’s edge — there is no antenna part to replace. Digital Crown & side button The rotary input (with an optical encoder) and the button; on ECG models the crown is also an electrode. Speaker & microphone ports Tiny acoustic ports with membranes. The speaker doubles as the water-ejection pump you hear after a swim (it plays a tone to push water out). Step 2 — The computer — one potted module The S-series SiP (System in Package) is the entire computer — processor, memory, storage, radios, and power management — sealed in resin as a single component. A SiP is a whole circuit board shrunk and potted into one part. It cannot be opened, probed, or repaired; it can only be replaced, and Apple does not sell it. Part What this part does S-series SiP CPU, GPU, RAM, flash, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth (and LTE/UWB on cellular models), and the Secure Enclave in one sealed block. Sensor array (case back) The optical heart-rate sensor (green/infrared LEDs + photodiodes), blood-oxygen LEDs on equipped models, and the second electrode for ECG. It is part of the case-back crystal assembly. Step 3 — Battery & Taptic Engine The two biggest occupants after the module: a small lithium cell and the linear actuator that taps your wrist. Part What this part does Battery cell A single small lithium-ion cell, glued in. Apple’s service answer to a worn Watch battery is a paid battery service — there is no owner procedure. Taptic Engine A linear resonant actuator — a weight on a spring, driven back and forth. It is why the Watch taps instead of buzzes. Magnetic charging interface The inductive coil in the case back that mates with the puck. No port, no contacts, nothing to clean but the surface. Step 4 — Display assembly The display is the case’s front face and part of the seal. Force Touch gaskets (early models) and the display’s adhesive ring are the waterproofing. Part What this part does OLED display & cover crystal LTPO OLED under ion-strengthened glass or sapphire (steel/titanium models). Cracked crystal = whole-unit service territory. Display gasket & adhesive The seal. Any opening destroys it, and Apple does not publish a resealing procedure for owners. What is missing, in the open: everything below the module level. There is no public schematic, no parts list, no calibration procedure. The honest summary of Watch repair in 2026: screens and batteries are serviced by Apple as sealed-unit work, the SiP is a black box by design, and the FCC photos on this page are the deepest public look inside the device that exists. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Why there is nothing to probe — the SiP explained: what potting does, why it defeats board repair, and why that is a design choice, not a law of physics The sensor stack — which sensors are real hardware and which are software licenses on the same hardware (the blood-oxygen story below) Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Models One architecture, three case families. Every model is the same idea: potted module, small cell, sealed case. Line Years Defining hardware Notes Series (numbered) 2015– S1 → S10 SiP ECG from Series 4 (FDA-cleared app); blood oxygen from Series 6 (see the record below). SE 2020– Prior-generation SiP, no ECG/SpO2 on early models The budget line — same sealed construction. Ultra 2022– Titanium case, depth gauge, dual-frequency GPS, action button The dive line; EN13319 dive-computer rating on the Oceanic+ app configuration. Key chips & components Apple S-series SiP — no public datasheet; the module is identified only as a unit in FCC photos. The Secure Enclave public reference (site library) covers the security block inside it. Ultra-wideband (U1/U2) — the precision-finding radio in the module (Series 9+/Ultra 2 use the second-generation part). Datasheet: none public — collection target logged. Faults — which part fails, and how you know A sealed device fails as a unit, so diagnosis here means identifying which sealed system died — and knowing the honest service path for each. Battery life collapses — check the reported battery health in Settings; below 80% the fix is Apple’s battery service. There is no safe owner opening procedure for this glued, sealed case. Heart-rate or SpO2 readings vanish — first the fit and the case-back crystal (dirt and a loose band defeat optical sensors), then software; a dead sensor array is a whole-unit fault. Digital Crown sticks or scrolls by itself — debris under the crown is the classic cause; Apple’s own support guidance is a rinse under warm running water for water-resistant models. Mechanical failure beyond that is service-only. Won’t charge, puck gets hot — a failing cell can swell against the display and lift it. A lifting screen on a Watch is a battery warning, not a screen fault. Stop charging it. Safety, before you open anything Do not pry a swollen Watch. The cell sits directly under the display crystal; forcing the case can puncture it. Apple’s battery service exists precisely because this device was designed with no owner-safe way in. Water resistance is a gasket condition, not a permanent property: it degrades with age, impacts, and any opening. A serviced-by-you Watch (if you get in at all) is no longer a swim watch, whatever the spec sheet said when it was new. The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over The Watch’s record contains the decade’s clearest case of a feature removed by a court — and then engineered back in.
