text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Chromebooks The school-fleet computer — and the best first full teardown in computing. A million identical boards, firmware documentation Google actually publishes, and a write-protect switch you are allowed to flip. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by manufacturer and model — a Chromebook is built by Acer, HP, Lenovo, ASUS, Samsung, or Dell to Google’s platform designs, and each OEM files under its own grantee code. The filings matter here for the usual reason (internal photos of boards you will genuinely open) and one unusual one: the same reference design appears under many brands, so one filing can document several retail models. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos — small single boards: SoC, soldered or socketed storage (eMMC on most, NVMe on high-end models), one or two RAM configurations, and the battery spanning the chassis Board names in the manual — every Chromebook board has a code name (the Chromium project names boards, not marketing); the filed manual and the project’s public docs use it Test reports — Wi-Fi 6/6E radio configurations by region What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: no single book — something better and worse. Google’s Chromium project publishes board-level documentation openly (board names, firmware design, recovery and write-protect mechanics), and several OEMs publish real service manuals for education models because school districts demanded them. But there is no universal Chromebook parts catalog: screens, keyboards, and batteries are model-specific and sourced by part number off the failed part itself. The exploded view below is the generic education-fleet board layout the FCC photos and Chromium docs agree on. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public universal parts book; firmware and board documentation is unusually public via the Chromium project, and that openness is cited per-step. Assembly coverage from FCC internal photos + published OEM service guides for education models. Build order Step 1 — Base, keyboard & battery A fleet Chromebook is a shallow plastic or aluminum base. The battery is usually the biggest part in it. Part What this part does Battery pack A 2–3 cell lithium pack, screwed (fleet models) or glued (consumer models) to the base. The first part schools replace, and the first to swell. Keyboard deck / palmrest On most fleet models the keyboard is part of the top cover — one spilled drink can mean a whole deck. Some education models make it separately replaceable; check before ordering. Speakers & I/O board USB-C charging + data on both sides on many models; a small daughterboard carries the side ports on some designs. Step 2 — Mainboard One board does everything. Its code name — printed on the board and used throughout the public documentation — is the key to every firmware and parts search you will ever run on the machine. Part What this part does SoC (Intel N-series / Core, MediaTek Kompanio, or Snapdragon) The processor. Fleet models favor low-power Intel (N100-class) or ARM (Kompanio); storage and RAM are soldered on most. eMMC / NVMe storage Soldered eMMC on budget models (32–64 GB is common and is a wear item); socketed NVMe appears on high-end models. Security chip (H1 / Titan C2) Google’s discrete security chip. It enforces verified boot and holds the firmware write-protect state — there is no write-protect screw on modern models; protection is electronic, released through the chip’s debug interface (CCD) or by disconnecting the battery on some designs. Wi-Fi module Usually a socketed M.2 card (Intel AX201-class) — one of the few genuinely swappable parts. Firmware flash (SPI ROM) The chip that holds coreboot — the open-source firmware most Chromebooks boot. Readable and writable with a clip programmer once write-protect is released. Step 3 — Display assembly The lid: panel, webcam, antennas, hinges. Part What this part does LCD panel (30-pin eDP) The panel connector is an industry-standard 30-pin embedded DisplayPort — panels cross between brands more often than any other Chromebook part. The panel’s own part number is the order key. Webcam & microphones A small board at the top bezel; privacy shutters appear on newer fleet models. Wi-Fi antennas Routed into the lid for height — which is why a hinge-area pinched cable presents as a Wi-Fi fault. Hinges The fleet killer. Hinge mounts tear out of plastic lids; the fix is the lid or the deck, not the hinge. What is missing, in the open: schematics. Board documentation, firmware source (coreboot is open source), and recovery images are public; the schematic PDFs are not. That still makes this the most honestly documented mass-market computer line in existence — the floor every other platform on this page is measured against. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. The board code name system — why the name printed on the board, not the name on the lid, is how you find everything Write-protect, honestly — screw (legacy), electronic via the security chip (current), and what each means for firmware freedom AUE — the date printed in software — every model carries an Auto Update Expiration; see the record Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Platform families Chromebooks are reference designs wearing brand badges. The families that matter for parts and firmware: Family Typical chips Hallmarks Notes Intel fleet (Acer/HP/Lenovo education) Intel N100 / N200, Celeron N4xxx eMMC, 4–8 GB RAM, ruggedized cases The school standard. Service guides exist for many models. ARM fleet MediaTek Kompanio 500/800 series Fanless, long battery, soldered everything Lenovo/Duet-style tablets and clamshells. Premium / Chromebook Plus Intel Core i3+, Snapdragon 7c on some NVMe, backlit keyboards, better panels Chromebook Plus is a spec floor (2023), not a model. Detachables & tablets Kompanio / Snapdragon Keyboard is an accessory; board lives behind the screen Different teardown order: screen-first. Key chips & components Intel N-series / Celeron SoCs — Intel publishes datasheets for its embedded lines through its public documentation library; the N100-class is documented at family level. Datasheet status: no Intel N-series datasheet is indexed yet in this site’s Datasheet Index ; model-specific briefs are collection targets. MediaTek Kompanio — product briefs public, full datasheets not. Collection target logged. Google H1 / Titan C2 security chip — documented by the Chromium project’s public CCD (Case Closed Debugging) documentation; the chip is the write-protect authority on modern boards. coreboot + depthcharge — the open-source firmware stack most Chromebooks ship; source and board documentation are public in the Chromium project — the only mass-market computer whose boot firmware you can read. Faults — which part fails, and how you know Fleet machines fail fleet ways. Symptom first: Won’t update / ‘ChromeOS is missing or damaged’ — first check the model’s AUE date (the software end-of-life), then recovery from a USB image (Esc + Refresh + Power), then storage: a worn eMMC presents exactly like corruption. Dead, no charge light — the USB-C charger and cable first (fleet chargers die constantly), then a battery-disconnect reset: on many models, unplugging the internal battery for 30 seconds clears a latched power state. Keyboard rows or columns dead — liquid history. On deck-integrated models the honest fix is the top cover assembly; price it before promising a “keyboard repair.” Screen black, machine clearly boots (sounds, caps light) — backlight or a pinched eDP cable at the hinge; an external monitor separates panel faults from board faults in one minute. Swollen base, trackpad clicking itself — the battery. Stop, replace, recycle. Fleet swelling is the single most common Chromebook hardware failure. Safety, before you open anything The battery is screwed or glued under the palmrest you are leaning on. Punctures happen when a swollen pack is pried against the deck. Discharge first, no metal levers on the pack, and a swelling battery ends the repair until it is out. USB-C charging means the port carries 20 V and the board carries a charge controller that fails shorted on liquid damage. A board that smells burnt near the port is a board to diagnose unpowered, with a meter — not by plugging in chargers until one works. The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over The Chromebook record is the e-waste argument i

title: CPAP Machines — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: Exploded view — the assemblies in build order
Step 1 — The air path — blower, foam, sensors
Step 3 — Electronics, modem & the SD card
Faults — which part fails, and how you know
Safety & the makers’ and FDA’s warnings — read first
The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Medical device — read this first. A CPAP is an FDA Class II prescription medical device that treats sleep apnea, a condition with real cardiovascular stakes. This page teaches the hardware and the public record. It never replaces your clinician: do not change your prescribed pressure, and do not stop therapy because of anything written here — talk to your doctor first, exactly as the FDA instructs. If your machine is a recalled Philips model, the FDA’s guidance is in the record below. CPAP Machines A blower, two sensors, and a prescription — the bedside computer with the largest recall in medical-device history inside it. Your therapy data is written to an SD card in plain files; the machine that makes it was, for one maker, a case study in how not to handle a defect. FCC ID FCC IDs apply to the connected models. CPAPs with cellular or Bluetooth radios (ResMed’s AirSense line carries a cellular modem for its cloud; Philips models carried modems for the Encore/DreamMapper ecosystem) file under each maker’s grantee code. The filings’ internal photos show the blower and flow path — the exact path the Philips recall was about. Non-connected travel models may have no filing; their public record is the FDA’s. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos (connected models) — the blower motor, the foam-lined air path (on Philips designs), the sensor board, and the modem FDA records — this category’s deepest public file: 510(k) clearances, the recall database entries (Z-1974-2021 and siblings), inspection records, and the consent decree — all public, all linked below Test reports — cellular modem characteristics; the modem’s network generation decides when the cloud features die (see Faults) What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: none published to owners or patients by any maker. CPAP service is a DME (durable medical equipment) channel business: machines are supplied, serviced, and swapped by equipment companies under prescription. FDA records + FCC internal photos are the sources for the stack below. The consumables (filters, tubing, masks, water chambers) are owner-handled by design and are marked as such; everything inside the shell is not. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public parts book; FDA-record + FCC-photo basis. Do not open a machine that is your prescribed therapy without a working backup and your clinician’s knowledge — see Safety. Build order Step 1 — The air path — blower, foam, sensors Air enters at the filter, is pressurized by a brushless blower, passes pressure/flow sensors, and leaves for the hose. On Philips’ recalled designs, polyester-based polyurethane (PE-PUR) sound-abatement foam sat in this path to quiet the blower. That foam is the recall. Part What this part does Inlet filter A foam or fine filter at the intake — an owner consumable with a published replacement interval. A clogged filter makes the blower work harder and hotter. Blower (BLDC motor + impeller) The therapy itself: a brushless DC blower whose speed is the pressure. CPAP pressure (4–20 cmH₂O — centimeters of water pressure) is controlled by spinning this motor faster or slower against the sensors’ feedback. Sound-abatement foam (Philips designs) PE-PUR foam pieces placed in the air path to damp blower noise. The foam’s degradation — particles and off-gassed chemicals entering the air path — is FDA recall Z-1974-2021, the largest entry in the record below. Pressure & flow sensors The feedback loop’s eyes: they measure delivered pressure and airflow breath-by-breath, drive auto-adjusting (APAP) algorithms, and generate the therapy data on the card. Step 2 — Humidifier & hose Comfort engineering that decides whether people actually use the machine. Part What this part does Heated humidifier chamber A removable water tub over a heater plate. Owner-handled daily; scale and biofilm are its failure modes, and distilled water is the maker’s instruction for a reason. Heated tube A hose with a heating wire and a temperature sensor at the mask end, fighting ‘rainout’ (condensation). Tubes are consumables with published replacement intervals. Mask (the real interface) Nasal, pillow, or full-face; owned by the patient, replaced on schedule, and the source of most ‘therapy isn’t working’ reports (leaks). Not part of the machine — and most of the therapy. Step 3 — Electronics, modem & the SD card The computer that watches you sleep, and the card that remembers it. Part What this part does Main board + display Controls the blower loop, runs the interface, logs everything. Not sold as a part. Cellular modem / Bluetooth Uploads compliance and therapy summaries to the maker’s cloud (which your clinician and insurer read). Modem generations matter: see the 3G entry in Faults. SD card slot The machine writes detailed flow/pressure data to a standard SD card in documented, readable files. Volunteer-built open-source software (OSCAR — Open Source CPAP Analysis Reporter) reads these cards and shows you everything the summary hides. Your data, in your hands, in plain files: the model this site exists to point at. What is missing, in the open: service manuals, blower assemblies, and boards are not sold to patients. When a CPAP dies out of warranty, the channel’s answer is a new machine at medical-channel prices — while the fault is, as often as not, a blower bearing or a power supply. The exploded view above is documented from the public record precisely because the maker record is closed. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. The SD card is the whole argument — your machine already records everything; OSCAR (free, volunteer-built) reads it. No permission is needed to look at your own therapy data Pressure is motor speed — why the blower is both the therapy and the wear item, and why ‘hours used’ is the machine’s odometer Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. The main lines Two makers dominate the US record, plus the travel class. Line Maker Hallmarks Notes AirSense 10 / 11 ResMed Integrated humidifier, cellular cloud (myAir), SD logging The post-recall US market default. AirSense 10’s modem generation matters (see Faults). DreamStation / System One (recalled) Philips Respironics PE-PUR foam air path The recall line. Philips is barred from US sales of new CPAP/BiPAP under the 2024 consent decree until the FDA confirms compliance. Travel CPAPs (AirMini, Transcend class) ResMed / Somnetics No humidifier (or waterless exchange), small blower Same prescription rules; the size is bought with noise and dryness. Key chips & components BLDC blower + driver — the therapy actuator; driver electronics of the classes indexed in this site’s Datasheet Index . The exact blower assemblies are proprietary and unsold — collection target logged. Pressure/flow sensing — differential-pressure sensor class parts; the same sensor families documented in the site’s index for industrial control (see the S7-300 autopsy’s sensor coverage). Cellular modem modules — bought-in modules (the FCC filings name them per model); their network generation is a lifecycle spec, like a phone’s. Faults — which part fails, and how you know Symptom first — and a hard rule for this category: therapy faults are clinician conversations (pressure, settings, mask fit as prescribed). Hardware faults are these: Machine reports huge leaks / therapy feels weak — mask seal, then hose (a pinhole at the cuff is the classic), then the humidifier tub’s gasket seating. The blower is last on the list and rarely the answer. Loud, rough, or whining blower; error codes for motor faults — the blower’s bearings at end-of-life (hours are the odometer — machines log them). Not an owner part; a DME swap or a new machine is the channel answer, which is the gate this page documents. Cloud/app stopped updating, machine works fine — the modem’s network died, not the machine: AirSense 10 units built on 3G/CDMA modems lost their networks in the 2022 US 3G shutdowns. Therapy and the SD card are unaffected — the card, not the cloud, is the record that matters. Water in the tube (rainout), gurgling — humidity physics: raise tube temperature, lower humidity, insulate the hose, or move the machine below head height per the maker’s guide. Musty smell / visible debris in the air path on a Philips unit — stop and check the recall status of your exact model and serial against the FDA/Philips remediation record before another

title: DJI Drones — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: Exploded view — the assemblies in build order
Faults — which part fails, and how you know
The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. DJI Drones The best-documented consumer aircraft ever sold — and the first product line on this site whose story is a live federal case file. DJI’s FCC filings are a masterclass in public hardware records; as of December 2025, the FCC will not issue new ones. FCC ID FCC ID pattern: SZ DJI Technology files under grantee code SS3. DJI’s filings are famously complete: full internal photos of every board, antenna layouts, and RF reports for the control link (OcuSync-family, in the 2.4/5.8 GHz bands), the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth radios, and the GNSS receiver. For any DJI model already authorized, its filing at fccid.io is the finest public teardown in the industry. What changed on December 22, 2025 is that no new filings can be granted — see the record. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos — the flight-controller board stack, the vision-sensor boards, the gimbal’s three brushless motors, and the smart-battery’s own electronics Antenna documentation — leg/antenna placement for the control link, which explains the range and the orientation sensitivity every pilot learns Test reports — output power per band and the band-edge behavior of a link designed to hold a video feed at kilometers of range What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: DJI does not publish one — but DJI is the rare maker that sells the parts anyway: arms, motors, gimbal assemblies, vision modules, and boards circulate through its service network and a large third-party market, and DJI’s own repair program publishes per-model repair pricing . The stack below is rebuilt from FCC internal photos, in flight-assembly order. DJI’s flyaway/coverage programs (DJI Care Refresh) are service contracts, not documentation — the distinction this page exists to teach. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public parts book or exploded diagram; FCC internal-photo basis (the richest of any platform in this wave). Parts availability is unusually good through service channels; documentation is not. Build order Step 1 — Airframe & propulsion Four arms, four brushless motors, four propellers. The airframe is a set of replaceable arms on most models — the crash economy depends on it. Part What this part does Brushless motors (4) Outrunner motors, one per arm. A motor that feels gritty or notchy after a crash has a bent shaft or damaged bearing — replace the arm/motor unit, don’t fly it ‘to test.’ Propellers (quick-release) Matched CW/CCW pairs. A nicked prop is a vibration source that the flight controller will fight and the gimbal will show you. Props are consumables; treat them that way. Arms & landing gear Designed break points. Carbon or plastic arms fold or snap to save the body — sacrificial structure, like a car’s crumple zone. ESCs (electronic speed controllers) The motor drivers — on the main board or per-arm boards depending on model. A burned ESC presents as one dead motor with a good motor swapped in. Step 2 — Flight controller & sensing The aircraft’s brain and its eyes. This stack is why a DJI flies like it’s on rails. Part What this part does Flight controller (FC) + IMU The autopilot and its inertial measurement unit (gyroscopes + accelerometers, usually redundant). IMU calibration errors after a crash are the board telling you the crash mattered. GNSS module GPS + Galileo/BeiDou/GLONASS positioning. Slow satellite lock after storage is normal; no lock in the open is an antenna/module fault. Vision sensing system Downward and omnidirectional cameras + infrared ToF (time-of-flight) sensors for obstacle avoidance and precision landing. These lenses are exposed: a scratched vision sensor is a blind spot the size of a wall. Main processing board Runs the vision pipeline and the video encoder for the downlink — the hottest, most compute-dense board in the aircraft. Step 3 — Gimbal & camera A 3-axis brushless stabilizer carrying the camera — mechanically the most delicate assembly on the aircraft and the most crashed-into. Part What this part does Gimbal motors (3 axes) Yaw, pitch, and roll brushless motors that counter-rotate the camera against the aircraft’s motion thousands of times a minute. A gimbal that buzzes, droops, or overheats has a damaged motor or a bent axis. Camera + image sensor 1-inch or Micro-Four-Thirds-class sensors on flagships; the camera board and the gimbal are serviced as an assembly in DJI’s network. Ribbon cables The gimbal’s flex ribbons are the classic crash fatality — invisible damage, intermittent video. Connector seating is the first check. Dampening plate Rubber isolation balls between gimbal and frame. Aged/hardened dampers = jello in the footage. Step 4 — Smart battery & downlink The battery is a computer with cells attached; the downlink is the radio the FCC filing is really about. Part What this part does Intelligent Flight Battery Cells + a management board that counts cycles, balances cells, enforces storage charge, and can refuse flight. A swollen DJI battery is retired by the manual’s own rule (see the warnings in Faults) — and the board logs it. OcuSync-family downlink The proprietary control/video link (2.4/5.8 GHz, adaptive). Remote ID broadcast (the FAA’s drone license-plate signal) is part of this radio’s job on current models. Remote controller Its own FCC-filed device: sticks (Hall-effect on newer models — the same drift physics as game controllers), its own battery, and the phone/tablet as display. What is missing, in the open: schematics, boardviews, and any published exploded diagram. DJI’s model is service-network repair with good parts logistics — genuinely better than most of this wave for getting a crashed drone fixed, and still a closed book at the board level. Both halves of that sentence are the finding. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. The filing is the teardown — DJI’s FCC internal photos remain public for every authorized model; nothing in the December 2025 action removes them What the Covered List does and doesn’t do — new authorizations stop; your authorized drone, its parts channel, and (by waiver) its firmware updates continue — dates in the record Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Model families One architecture across the line; size and camera class are the variables. Family Class Defining hardware Notes Mini series Sub-249 g Lightest airframe, 4K camera on current models The 249 g weight class exists to sit under registration thresholds in many jurisdictions (FAA registration still applies to commercial use). Air series Mid-size Dual cameras (wide + medium tele) on current models The prosumer middle. Mavic series Flagship folding Hasselblad camera, omnidirectional sensing The reference design the FCC photos document best. Avata / FPV line Cinewhoop / FPV Ducted props, head-tracking goggles option Most Wanted on this site (Avata 2) before this hub existed. Agras / enterprise Agriculture / industrial Spraying, thermal, docks The lines the tariff and component rules hit hardest; outside this page’s consumer scope. Key chips & components Flight-controller & vision silicon — DJI designs its own boards around a mix of in-house and merchant silicon (image-signal and vision processing has used Ambarella-class parts historically; current models are identified per-board in FCC photos). No public datasheets for the integrated assemblies — collection targets logged. The radio layer is the documented layer: the OcuSync-family link’s filed test reports (via fccid.io , grantee SS3) are the public record of output power and band behavior — more RF documentation than any phone on this site ships with. Faults — which part fails, and how you know Crash first, electronics second — the DJI fault tree is dominated by physics. DJI’s own manuals carry the battery rules quoted in Safety. Gimbal overload / gimbal motor overloaded error — a bent axis, a ribbon fault, or debris in a motor gap. Check for the shipping gimbal clamp left on (the classic), then ribbon seating, then assume mechanical damage. IMU / compass errors after a crash — recalibrate once. Errors that return are the aircraft reporting real sensor damage; DJI’s own guidance is service, not more calibration. One motor stutters or won’t spin up — swap-test the propeller, inspect for hair/debris in the bell, then it’s motor vs. ESC: a known-good motor on the same arm separates them. Battery ‘cell error’ / refusal to charge — the battery’s own board h

title: Kindle & Kobo E-Readers — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: Kobo (Libra Colour, model N428) — front to back, from the manufacturer’s guide
Kindle (Paperwhite, 2024) — the same stack, from FCC internal photos
First, understand the screen: a “frozen” page may be a dead device
Failed E Ink panel — the fractured picture
Kobo: parts and manuals, sold on purpose (2024)
The older Kobos were more open still
Repairability is now a buying difference, not a footnote
Kindle software modification: a community, not a feature
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Kindle & Kobo E-Readers Two e-readers that look almost identical — and give opposite answers to the most basic question an owner can ask: when it breaks, can I fix it? Kobo sells you the parts and the instructions. Amazon sells you a new Kindle. FCC ID Every radio device sold in the United States needs an FCC ID — the code that ties a product to its test filings with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC, the U.S. radio regulator). The first part is the grantee code : the company that filed. The rest identifies the product. FCC IDs vary by model and revision , so the label on your own reader is the one that counts. Device Maker model FCC ID How verified Kindle Paperwhite (2024) SA568B 2A4DH-5688 Amazon’s grantee code is 2A4DH (Amazon.com Services LLC). The ID is printed in the FCC test reports for this model — see the FCC SAR test report for SA568B (SAR: specific absorption rate, a measure of radio energy absorbed by the body). Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2024) SA569P 2A4DH-5698 The same test report names SA569P as the reference model under this ID, and notes the main difference between the two is wireless power transfer (wireless charging). Kobo Clara Colour N367 NOIKBN367 Rakuten Kobo’s grantee code is NOI. The ID is stated in Kobo’s own regulatory and safety document for the Clara Colour (PDF) . Kobo Clara BW (one hardware variant) P365 ARS-P365 This variant was filed under a different grantee code, ARS — a reminder that the same shop product can be built and filed by different manufacturers. See the filed regulatory document for P365 (PDF) . Kobo also sells a Clara BW as model N365, so check your own label. Kobo Libra Colour N428 NOIKBN428 Model number N428 is confirmed on Kobo’s own help page for the Libra Colour ; the FCC ID follows the same NOI grantee pattern and is printed on the device label. How to look yours up: on a Kindle, the FCC ID is printed on the back of the device. On a Kobo, Kobo’s regulatory document says the certification marks are in Settings > About on the device itself. Type the ID into fccid.io and you get the full filing: photos, test reports, and the manual the maker submitted. What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for a device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . What you can typically find: Internal photos — board layout, chip placement, shielding, antenna design. On an e-reader they also show the three things that matter most: how big the battery is, where the mainboard (the one circuit board that runs the device) sits, and how the screen assembly fills the front of the case. Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture (RF: radio frequency, the wireless part). Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which can reveal operating frequencies and power levels. Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the device. What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. One honest limit, specific to these devices: makers can ask the FCC to keep the photos secret for a time after launch. Reporting on the 2024 Paperwhite filing noted that almost everything of note — test photos, external photos, internal photos, and the user manual — was under a 180-day embargo when the filing appeared ( Good e-Reader, September 2024 ). The filing is a teardown on a delay, not on launch day. That delay matters more on an e-reader than on most devices. These readers are thin, sealed slabs with no screws on the outside. For a glued- or clipped-shut reader that the maker will not document, the internal photos in the FCC filing are, for most owners, the only teardown they will ever see. Exploded view Coverage: Partial — no public parts book. A parts book (also called an illustrated parts breakdown) is the manufacturer’s own diagram that names every assembly and its part number. Neither Amazon nor Kobo publishes one for these readers. What follows is the next best thing, and it is labeled by source: for Kobo, the walkthrough follows the manufacturer’s own repair guides, published with iFixit. For Kindle, the same stack is described from the internal photos in Amazon’s FCC filings, because no Amazon guide exists. Nothing below is a fabricated diagram; it is the layer order, in words. Kobo (Libra Colour, model N428) — front to back, from the manufacturer’s guide Source for every step: Kobo’s OEM guide (OEM: original equipment manufacturer — the maker itself), Kobo Libra Colour Screen Replacement, on iFixit , which iFixit labels “OEM Guide — iFixit collaborated with the manufacturer to make this guide.” Read front to back, the reader is five layers: Front cover — the bezel (the frame around the screen) you see and hold. It keeps dust out and gives the thin screen its stiffness. In the guide it is held by clips and adhesive, and it comes off last, after everything behind it is out. Display assembly — the E Ink screen, sold pre-installed in its frame. This is the page itself: the part that shows text, and the part the touch layer reads your taps through. A screen replacement means moving all the internals into a new display assembly — on an e-reader, the screen is not one part among many; the rest of the device is built into it. Mainboard (the guide’s word is motherboard) — the single circuit board carrying the processor, memory, storage, Wi-Fi, and the USB-C port. It thinks, remembers, and connects. In the guide it is held by seven screws, and connects to the screen through flat ribbon cables with ZIF connectors (zero insertion force: a tiny locking flap holds the cable, no soldering). Battery — a flat lithium pouch cell that powers everything. E Ink uses so little power (see Key Chips) that this one cell runs the reader for weeks. In the guide the battery is disconnected first, before any other work, and is held by stretch-release adhesive — pull a tab, and it releases without prying. Back cover — the rear shell. It protects the board and battery and gives the reader its grip. In the guide it is clipped, not glued: an opening pick releases the clips, and it is the first part off and the last part back on. Two smaller boards ride along in the same guide: a power-button board and a page-turn button board, each connected by the same kind of ribbon cable. Everything inside is coated in a thin, plastic-like waterproof coating, which the guide warns is brittle, flakes as you work, and must be picked off connectors before they will open. “Following this guide will remove your eReader’s IP (Ingress Protection) rating, making it susceptible to water damage.” — Warning printed at the top of Kobo’s own iFixit guide, quoted verbatim. In plain words: the reader is waterproof when you buy it; opening it ends that, even if you put it back together perfectly. Safety, in plain words: the guide tells you to drain the battery as much as you can before starting, to unplug everything, and never to use sharp metal tools on or near the battery — a punctured pouch battery can leak dangerous chemicals and catch fire. Do not bend or crease the battery, and never reuse a removed pouch battery. Those are the maker’s own precautions, and they are the right ones. Kindle (Paperwhite, 2024) — the same stack, from FCC internal photos Source label: this walkthrough is built from the internal photos in Amazon’s FCC filing for the device (see FCC ID, above), not from any Amazon repair document — none exists. The photos show the same five-layer sandwich, because physics leaves few other ways to build a thin reader: Front bezel and display assembly — the E Ink screen fills the front, as on the Kobo. It is the largest, most expensive, and most fragile layer. Mainboard — one board with the processor, storage, radios, and the USB-C port, sitting behind the screen. Battery — a flat pouch cell behind or beside the board, taking much of the inside area. Back cover — the sealed rear shell. There are no owner-facing screws and no published opening procedure. Kindle maker warnings: there are none to quote. Amazon publishes no repair guide for any Kindle, so it publishes no repair warnings either — the safety notes above, from Kobo’s guide, are the closest thing to manufacturer guidance that exists for opening a current e-reader, and the battery precautions apply to any pouch cell in any reader. Diagnosis & faults An e-reader fails in fewer ways than a phone, and the most common scare is not a failure at all. Work through these in order before you open anything. First, understand the screen: a “frozen” page may be a dead device E Ink is bistable : the image is made of physical pigment particles that stay where they were put (see Key Chips). The screen uses power to change the picture, not to hold it. So a reader that has crashed, or even run completely flat, keeps showing its last page, looking for all the world like it has merely frozen. Kobo’s guide makes the same point from inside the machine: even after the battery is disconnected, the screen goes on saying Powered off — “this is normal.” A still page tells you nothing about whether the device behind it is alive. Frozen screen, device alive underneath Signs: the page never changes, taps do nothing, but the power light may still respond. Test: the maker’s restart, below. If the screen flashes and redraws, the panel is fine and the software had hung. Kindle

title: E-Bike Controllers — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: Exploded view — the assemblies in build order
Step 1 — Sensors & inputs — how the controller knows you pedaled
Step 2 — The controller — inverter in a finned box
Faults — which part fails, and how you know
Safety — the battery is the story
The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Battery fire warning — read this first. The e-bike battery is the most dangerous energy store most people own: hundreds of lithium cells, often from the least-regulated corner of the industry, charged overnight in apartments. The FDNY counted 268 lithium-ion battery fires and 18 deaths in New York City in 2023 alone . Never charge a damaged, swollen, or water-exposed pack; never charge an uncertified pack unattended; and if a pack hisses, smells sweet/chemical, or gets hot standing still, get it outside and away from anything that burns — and call the fire department, not a repair forum. E-Bike Controllers Pedal, sensor, controller, motor — and between you and the battery, one small box of MOSFETs deciding how much of a 52-volt pack becomes motion. The controller is where an e-bike’s manners, limits, and locks live. It is also the most documented part of the machine, because hobbyists got here first and one flagship design is completely open. FCC ID FCC IDs apply to the connected layers, rarely the controller itself. A plain controller is not a radio and has no filing. Connected e-bike systems (Bosch’s smart system, app-linked displays) file their radios under the makers’ grantee codes. The controller’s public record is instead: the UL 2849 system standard, the CPSC’s warnings and recalls, and — for the open designs — published schematics. This page follows those sources. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Published schematics (open designs) — the VESC project publishes full controller schematics and firmware: the only complete parts-level documentation in this category, and the reference for the stack below UL 2849 / CPSC records — the system-level safety standard (electrical + fire) and the regulator’s battery-warning file: the sources for Safety Maker documentation (varies wildly) — Bafang’s mid-drive ecosystem is documented by a decade of public configuration practice; Bosch’s diagnostic layer is dealer-only (see the record) What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: none from the volume makers. Complete schematics: VESC (Benjamin Vedder’s open-source motor controller project) — board designs, firmware, and the configuration tool are public, and VESC-based controllers are sold by multiple vendors for e-bikes, boards, and robotics. The stack below is the anatomy every brushless e-bike drive shares; the open design is cited because it is the one you can verify line by line. Coverage: FULL for the open design (VESC: published schematics + firmware); PARTIAL for sealed OEM controllers (Bosch/Shimano/Yamaha/Bafang integrated units) — no public parts book. Shared architecture below is standard brushless-drive engineering. Build order Step 1 — Sensors & inputs — how the controller knows you pedaled An e-bike’s legality and feel are decided here: what counts as ‘pedaling,’ and how much help follows. Part What this part does Torque sensor (mid-drives & quality hub systems) Measures how hard you push the pedals and meters assistance proportionally — the part that makes a good e-bike feel like legs, amplified. Lives in the bottom bracket (mid-drive) or rear dropout. Cadence sensor (budget systems) A magnet ring + pickup counting pedal revolutions: assistance as an on/off suggestion. The price-tier tell. Throttle (Class 2) A twist/trigger input asking for power without pedaling — legal class is defined by whether this exists and how fast it goes (Classes, below). Speed sensor & brake cutoffs A spoke magnet tells the controller the wheel’s speed (the 20/28 mph assist cutoff is enforced from this signal); brake-lever switches cut motor power instantly — a safety input, wired in series with everything. Step 2 — The controller — inverter in a finned box The controller is a three-phase inverter: it chops battery DC into rotating AC for the brushless motor, hundreds of times per second, under firmware’s command. Part What this part does MCU + firmware Runs field-oriented control (FOC) on good units (quiet, efficient, sinusoidal) or square-wave commutation on cheap ones (the audible whine and harshness are this choice). Firmware holds the current limits, speed limits, and class behavior — which is why ‘tuning’ is a software act (see the record). MOSFET power stage The switching transistors — the part that burns. Undersized or badly cooled MOSFETs are the #1 controller death: the failure smells of hot electronics and presents as a dead or stuttering motor (Faults). Capacitors & current shunt Bulk capacitors smooth the battery’s delivery; a shunt resistor measures current so firmware can enforce its limits. In VESC’s published design, every one of these is a named, sourced part. DC-DC / 5 V rail & display link Powers sensors, display, and lights from the pack; the display’s UART/CAN chatter with the controller is the system’s nervous system — and, on Bafang’s open UART ecosystem, an owner-accessible configuration port (below). Step 3 — Motor & battery — the endpoints The controller’s two dance partners, each with its own protection brain. Part What this part does Brushless motor — hub or mid-drive Hub motors package the motor (often with planetary gears) in the wheel; mid-drives (Bafang BBS series, Bosch, Shimano) drive the cranks and use the bike’s gears. Hall sensors inside report rotor position to the controller — a failed Hall is a classic stutter/no-start fault. Battery pack + BMS 36/48/52 V packs of 18650/21700 cells under a Battery Management System that balances cells and cuts off over-current/over-temperature. The BMS is the pack’s only conscience: the fire record in Safety is overwhelmingly a story of cheap packs, cheap chargers, and damaged cells — not of the controller. What is missing, in the open: Bosch, Shimano, and Yamaha publish nothing at this level and route diagnosis through dealer software (Bosch’s DiagnosticTool is a licensed channel tool). Bafang sits in the middle: its UART mid-drives are configurable through a public, community-documented programming cable and settings file — the owner-programmable exception among volume systems. VESC is the fully open pole. The spectrum on this page is the industry in one category: open design, owner-configurable, dealer-locked. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Class is firmware — the 20/28 mph lines that define US e-bike classes are enforced by a number in the controller, which is why regulators and dealers fight over who may write it The Bafang cable — a $20 USB-UART lead and a settings file: the most owner-sovereign configuration path on any volume e-bike, documented by its community for a decade Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Classes & systems The legal frame (US three-class system, adopted in most states) and the maker spectrum: Thing What it is Assist limit Notes Class 1 Pedal-assist only (no throttle) 20 mph Welcome almost anywhere bikes are. Class 2 Throttle-equipped 20 mph The throttle is the whole distinction. Class 3 Pedal-assist only, higher limit 28 mph Speedometer required; access rules vary by state/trail. Bafang (BBS02/BBSHD mid-drives, Ultra) DIY/kit ecosystem, UART protocol Owner-configured The tinkerer standard: public configuration practice, swappable controllers, standard connectors (mostly). Bosch / Shimano / Yamaha Integrated OEM systems Dealer-set Torque-sensed, polished, and closed: proprietary batteries, dealer diagnostics, anti-tuning detection that flags modified speed signals. VESC-based Open-source controller platform Owner-defined Schematics and firmware public; the reference for what a controller is. Key chips & components VESC (open design) — an STM32-class MCU + gate-driver + MOSFET stage whose exact parts are published in the project’s schematics (see the Datasheet Index for the STM32 and driver families). The one controller here with a real paper trail. Gate drivers & MOSFETs — commodity power parts of the classes indexed in the Datasheet Index (the same driver families that appear in the site’s NCP302150 datasheet copy (PDF) ’s application class). BMS protection ICs — the pack’s guardians; cell-balancing and protection parts are catalog components, named in better packs’ documentation and absent from the cheap packs’ entirely — which is the point of the fire record. Faults — which part fails, and how you know Symptom first. Battery symptoms live under the fire rules in Safety — a pack fault is a safety event be

title: Amazon Echo Dot (5th Gen) — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: The debug header under the base
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Amazon Echo Dot (5th Gen) Amazon’s spherical smart speaker, rebuilt around the in-house AZ2 Neural Edge processor for on-device speech processing. The best-documented Echo Dot teardown target to date — including a debug header hiding under the rubber base. Amazon Echo Dot. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA). FCC ID FCC ID: 2A4DH-0821 (Grantee: 2A4DH = Amazon.com Services LLC) for the 5th-generation Echo Dot. What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . What you can typically find: Internal photos — board layout, chip placement, shielding, antenna design Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which can reveal operating frequencies and power levels Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the device What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Chip-level identification — every major IC named, with datasheet links where public documentation exists Board mapping — what connects to what, which test pads matter, where the debug interfaces hide What the manufacturer won’t tell you — undocumented features, hidden radios, silent telemetry, repair blockers Key Chips Amazon AZ2 Neural Edge (marked MT8519BAAV) — the main application processor — Amazon’s second-generation on-device ML chip, also used in the Echo Show 15. No public datasheet; marking suggests a MediaTek-fabbed custom part. MediaTek MT7653BSN — Wi-Fi/Bluetooth combo on a small daughterboard, with PCB antennas on both sides. Micron NW942 — NAND flash for OS and data storage. SK Hynix H54926AY — 0.5 GB DRAM. Maxim MAX98396EWB — digital-input mono Class-DG audio amplifier driving the speaker (20 W into 8 Ω). MediaTek MT6398BN — multi-rail DC-DC power management IC. Teardown Notes The fabric-covered sphere opens from the bottom: peel back the non-slip rubber base to find four T5 Torx screws and a recessed nine-pin header that appears to be a debug or programming port. Inside, the main PCB mounts to a cast metal housing — the metal doubles as a heatsink and RF shield. A small ribbon cable links the processor board to the button/microphone/LED board at the top. The speaker connects to the main board through spring-loaded metal prongs touching metalized pads — no wires to desolder, a genuinely serviceable touch. Twelve RGB LEDs ring the perimeter of the main PCB, producing the familiar light ring through the fabric. Simple Entry Points The debug header under the base You need: A 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter (about $3), Dupont wires, and a T5 Torx driver. Remove the rubber base and the four T5 Torx screws to separate the enclosure. Locate the recessed nine-pin header on the bottom of the main PCB — documented by community teardowns as a likely debug/programming port. With the device powered off, connect GND first, then try each remaining pin as TX at 115200 baud while watching for boot output. Never connect VCC from your adapter — let the Echo Dot power itself. A serial console here would show the bootloader and kernel messages, which identify the firmware layout and available recovery options. $ ls /dev/ttyUSB* /dev/ttyUSB0 $ screen /dev/ttyUSB0 115200 # (boot log appears here if the header carries a console) Pin functions on this header are not officially documented; identifying TX/RX/GND requires a multimeter and patience. This is normal reverse-engineering practice on hardware you own. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or Amazon’s own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the Echo Dot is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. Scope note: the Echo Dot (5th Gen) went on sale in October 2022, so most of the record below is the record of the Alexa platform and the Echo line this speaker runs on. Entries are labeled platform-level or Echo line where that is what they are. Year What happened Source 2018 An Echo recorded a private conversation and sent it to a contact (Echo line). A Portland family’s Echo recorded a conversation about hardwood floors and sent it to an employee in the husband’s contact list, who called to warn them. Amazon confirmed the device logs and explained it as an unlikely chain of mishearings: background speech taken for the wake word, then for a “send message” request, then for a contact name, then for the confirmation “right” — a run of misreadings in a row. Amazon called it an extremely rare occurrence and said it was evaluating options to make this case even less likely. TechCrunch — Echo sent a private conversation to a contact 2018 About 1,700 recordings of a stranger sent to the wrong customer (platform-level). A customer in Germany who asked Amazon for his own data under the GDPR (Europe’s privacy law) received a download containing about 1,700 Alexa audio files of a different household — a man who, unlike the recipient, actually owned an Echo. Reporters at the magazine c’t used details in the recordings to identify and contact that man. Amazon called it an unfortunate case of human error and an isolated incident, and said it had resolved the issue with the two customers involved. KNKX / NPR — customer receives 1,700 audio files of a stranger 2019 Human review of Alexa recordings revealed — and confirmed by Amazon (platform-level). Bloomberg reported that Amazon employed thousands of full-time staff and contractors around the world to listen to, transcribe, and annotate a sample of Alexa voice recordings in order to improve speech recognition. Amazon confirmed the program, saying it annotated an “extremely small sample” of recordings to improve the customer experience, and that employees did not have direct access to information identifying the person or account. Bloomberg’s sources said reviewers sometimes encountered recordings in which Alexa did not appear to have been deliberately activated. MacRumors — Amazon employees listen to Alexa recordings (Bloomberg report, Amazon statement) 2023 $25 million FTC/DOJ settlement over children’s Alexa recordings (platform-level). The Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice charged that Amazon kept children’s Alexa voice recordings indefinitely, used them for its own purposes, and undermined parents’ deletion requests — deleting files in some databases while retaining transcripts elsewhere — in violation of the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) Rule. Amazon agreed to a $25 million civil penalty, deletion of inactive child accounts and of certain voice recordings and geolocation data, and a ban on using data subject to deletion requests to create or improve any data product. Amazon said it disagreed with the FTC’s claims and denied violating the law. The FTC announced a separate action against Ring the same day; that case concerns Ring cameras, not Echo devices, and is not part of this device’s record. FTC — Amazon kept kids’ Alexa voice data forever 2025 The local-processing opt-out was switched off (platform-level). On March 28, 2025, Amazon ended the “Do Not Send Voice Recordings” setting, which had let some Echo owners keep Alexa requests from being sent to Amazon’s cloud. Amazon emailed owners of the models that processed audio on the device itself (Echo Dot 4th Gen, Echo Show 10, Echo Show 15); Amazon’s own help page had also listed the Echo Dot (5th Gen) among the supported devices that could use the setting through a local-processing device on the same home network. Amazon said the change supported generative-AI features that rely on its cloud, and told the Associated Press fewer than 0.03% of customers had used the feature. A separate “Don’t save recordings” choice remains, but Alexa voice requests from this speaker are now processed in Amazon’s cloud. Ars Technica — everything you say to your Echo will be sent to Amazon Unverified: “Alexa is recording everything you say, all the time.” No court, regulator, or published technical analysis has shown an Echo continuously recording and uploading room audio. Amazon’s stated design is that the device listens on the device itself for its wake word and streams only after it believes it heard it. Evidence that feeds the belief: the 2018 Portland case began with a word that merely sounded like “Alexa,” and reviewers in the 2019 program reported clips in which Alexa did not appear to have been deliberately activated — mistaken activations are documented. Evidence against the strong version of the claim: every documented case is a mistaken activation or a mishandled file, not continuous capture, and the FTC’s 2023 case was about retention and deletion of recordings, not secret always-on recording. Mistaken activation is fact; always-on recording is not proven. Did you know This speaker is also a thermometer that can act. The 5th-generation Dot added a built-in temperature sensor, and it is not just a readout: Alexa Routines can use it to turn on a fan or adjust a thermostat when the room crosses a temperature you set. Source: MobileSyrup — 5th-gen Echo Dot announcement . It can quietly extend your Wi-Fi. The 5th-gen

title: ESP32 Family — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. ESP32 Family Espressif’s Wi-Fi + Bluetooth microcontroller that ate the IoT world. Cheap, capable, and — unusually for the industry — genuinely well documented. FCC ID FCC ID: 2AC7Z-ESPWROOM32 (Grantee: 2AC7Z = Espressif Systems) for the ESP32-WROOM-32 module. Other variants: 2AC7Z-ESPWROOM32UE, 2AC7Z-ESPWROOM32E (32E variant) Available: Test reports, antenna specs, user manuals, RF exposure docs What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . What you can typically find: Internal photos — board layout, chip placement, shielding, antenna design Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which can reveal operating frequencies and power levels Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the device What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Chip-level identification — every major IC named, with datasheet links where public documentation exists Board mapping — what connects to what, which test pads matter, where the debug interfaces hide What the manufacturer won’t tell you — undocumented features, hidden radios, silent telemetry, repair blockers Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Variants Chip / Module CPU Wireless Notes ESP32 (original) Dual-core Xtensa LX6 @ 240 MHz Wi-Fi 4 + BT 4.2 The classic. Dozens of module variants. ESP32-WROOM-32 ESP32 Wi-Fi + BT Most common module. FCC ID: 2AC7Z-ESPWROOM32 ESP32-WROVER ESP32 Wi-Fi + BT Adds PSRAM. ESP32-S2 Single-core Xtensa LX7 Wi-Fi 4 only USB OTG. No Bluetooth. ESP32-S3 Dual-core Xtensa LX7 Wi-Fi 4 + BT 5 AI acceleration, USB OTG. ESP32-C3 RISC-V @ 160 MHz Wi-Fi 4 + BT 5 Espressif’s RISC-V entry. Cheap. ESP32-C6 RISC-V Wi-Fi 6 + 802.15.4 Newer low-power part. ESP32-H2 RISC-V 802.15.4 only — no Wi-Fi Thread/Zigbee-only part; do not spec it where Wi-Fi is needed. Key Chips ESP32 — the original dual-core Xtensa. The chip that made $3 Wi-Fi possible. ESP32-S3 — current workhorse for new designs. ESP32-C3 — RISC-V, often under $1 in volume. Espressif publishes full technical reference manuals, datasheets, and hardware design guidelines — a stark contrast to most chip vendors. See our datasheet index . Security Research & Notes CVE-2025-27840: Undocumented Bluetooth HCI commands (2025) In March 2025, Tarlogic Security disclosed 29 undocumented vendor-specific HCI commands in the original ESP32’s Bluetooth firmware — including commands that could read/write RAM and flash. Initial coverage called it a “backdoor.” Espressif responded that these are standard debugging and manufacturing-test commands (common across Bluetooth implementations), not intentional backdoors. They require HCI access — meaning physical access or prior firmware compromise — and are not remotely exploitable over Bluetooth alone. Espressif committed to removing them from future firmware. CVSS 6.8 (Medium). This is how responsible disclosure is supposed to work: researchers found it, the vendor acknowledged it, and a fix was committed. Sources: SOC Prime , Espressif security advisories Espressif’s open documentation (positive) Credit where due: Espressif is one of the few chip vendors that publishes comprehensive, public, no-NDA documentation — technical reference manuals, datasheets, hardware design guides, and open-source SDKs (ESP-IDF). This is the model BareBoard wishes every vendor followed. Open docs don’t prevent vulnerabilities, but they let the community find and fix them. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or Espressif’s own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the ESP32 is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. Year What happened Source 2019 Secure Boot bypass by fault injection (CVE-2019-15894). Riscure analysts and, independently, LimitedResults showed that a precisely timed voltage glitch (fault injection — physically disturbing the chip at the right instant) could make the ESP32 skip its Secure Boot digest check and boot unverified code from flash. The attack needs the chip in hand and does not defeat Flash Encryption; Espressif’s fix was firmware that permanently enables Flash Encryption alongside Secure Boot, plus a revised chip with hardened ROM code. NVD — CVE-2019-15894 2019 eFuse key extraction by fault injection (CVE-2019-17391). LimitedResults showed a second glitch, applied just after reset, could corrupt the read-protection bits on the chip’s electronic fuses (eFuses) as they were read out — exposing the Flash Encryption and Secure Boot keys themselves, repeatably, until the full key could be recovered. Chips then in the field could not be patched; Espressif’s answer was the ESP32-D0WD-V3 revision, whose ROM checks block the attack, and a new Secure Boot V2 scheme. Espressif advisory — CVE-2019-17391 2020 Wi-Fi authentication bypass (CVE-2020-12638). Broadcasting forged Wi-Fi beacon frames impersonating an access point could force an ESP32 (and ESP8266) to switch from encrypted to open authentication, effectively disabling its 802.11 encryption for the duration of the attack. It did not break TLS or give access to the real network. Espressif fixed it in ESP-IDF v3.1.8, v3.2.4, v3.3.3, v4.0.2, v4.1, v4.2 and later (advisory AR2020-002). NVD — CVE-2020-12638 2023 Hardened ESP32 V3 bypassed by one EM glitch (CVE-2023-35818). Raelize and the Technology Innovation Institute used electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI — a focused magnetic pulse instead of a voltage glitch) on the ESP32 revision v3.0/v3.1 — the revision built to resist the 2019 attacks — to redirect execution into the ROM UART download mode even with Secure Boot V2 and Flash Encryption enabled and download mode permanently disabled. Espressif advisory AR2023-005 states there is no immediate mitigation; the flaw is in the silicon. Espressif advisory AR2023-005 (PDF) 2025 Undocumented Bluetooth HCI commands (CVE-2025-27840). Tarlogic disclosed 29 undocumented vendor-specific HCI commands in the original ESP32’s Bluetooth controller, including memory read/write; Espressif says they are internal debug commands that cannot be triggered over Bluetooth, radio, or the internet, and shipped a software fix removing access to them (advisory AR2025-004, May 2025). (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Espressif — Clearing the Air Unverified: “The ESP32 has a backdoor.” The 29 undocumented commands are documented fact (above); the backdoor label — a deliberately planted, hidden access route — is not proven. Evidence for the label: Tarlogic’s March 6, 2025 press release used the word “backdoor,” and the commands were undocumented and include direct memory write (opcode 0xFC02). Evidence against: Tarlogic itself replaced “backdoor” with “hidden feature” within days, its own slides never claimed a backdoor, Espressif states the commands are debug commands in the Bluetooth controller IP that require code already running on the chip (or a compromised host) and cannot be triggered remotely, and independent analysis notes that comparable vendor-specific memory commands exist in Bluetooth chips from Broadcom, Cypress, and Texas Instruments. No court, regulator, or CVE record calls it a backdoor; CVE-2025-27840 records undocumented commands, nothing more. Sources: BleepingComputer (updated reporting) , Dark Mentor — “The ESP32 ‘backdoor’ that wasn’t” . Did you know The ESP32 was in over a billion units by 2023. That scale — one low-cost Wi-Fi + Bluetooth chip across an enormous share of the IoT world — is why a set of undocumented debug commands made international news in 2025. Source: BleepingComputer . Only the original ESP32 has the 29 HCI debug commands. Espressif states the ESP32-C, ESP32-S, and ESP32-H series do not have these commands in their Bluetooth controllers at all. Source: Espressif — Clearing the Air . Every silicon break in the timeline above needed the chip in hand. The NVD records for CVE-2019-15894 and CVE-2023-35818 both carry a physical-access attack vector (AV:P): these are lab attacks on a device you already hold, not remote exploits against devices in the field. Sources: NVD — CVE-2019-15894 , Espressif AR2023-005 . The hardened chip fell to a single glitch. The ESP32 V3 was Espressif’s answer to the 2019 fault-injection attacks; the WOOT ’24 paper behind CVE-2023-35818 describes the first successful fault-injection attack bypassing both Secure Boot and Flash Encryption with one electromagnetic glitch, on a target that had fault-injection countermeasures. Source: Delvaux et al., USENIX WOOT ’24 (PDF) .
