text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Lethal voltage — read this before anything else on this page. An EV charger (EVSE) connects your car to a 240 V, 40–80 A circuit — the most powerful circuit in a normal house, running for hours at a time. Installation and any work inside the unit belong to a licensed electrician under NEC Article 625 in the US. This page teaches how the device works and what the record shows. It is not an installation guide, and the fault section is a diagnosis list for conversations with that electrician — not a set of home procedures. EV Chargers The box on the garage wall is not a charger. The charger is in the car; the box is a very careful switch — a switch that negotiates with a one-kilohertz signal, watches for ground faults 20 times more sensitively than your bathroom outlet, and only then closes a relay onto 240 volts. Everything about it is knowable. Some of it is documented in an open-source design you can buy. FCC ID FCC IDs apply to the connected models. Wi-Fi/Bluetooth-equipped EVSEs (ChargePoint Home Flex, Tesla Wall Connector, Emporia, Grizzl-E Smart, JuiceBox when it lived) file under their makers’ grantee codes; dumb EVSEs (the relay-and-pilot boxes with no radio) may have no filing at all — their public record is their UL/ETL listing and the NEC instead. The smart models’ internal photos show the pilot/control board and the contactor plainly. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos (smart models) — the contactor (the big relay), the control board, the current transformers that meter the session, and the radio module UL/ETL listing records — EVSEs are listed to UL 2594 (and the personal-protection system to UL 2231): the listing, not the FCC, is this category’s safety constitution The standards themselves — SAE J1772 (the connector and pilot protocol) and SAE J3400 (the NACS standard, published December 2023) are the public specifications the whole category implements What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: for commercial sealed units, none. For one branch of the family, everything: OpenEVSE is an open-source EVSE project whose schematics, board files, firmware, and parts lists are published — a complete, buildable, standards-compliant charger design that anyone may read. The stack below follows the architecture every J1772/J3400 EVSE shares (and that OpenEVSE documents openly). Sources: the SAE standards’ documented pilot protocol, FCC internal photos for smart units, UL 2594’s requirements, and OpenEVSE’s published design. Coverage: FULL for the open design (OpenEVSE: published schematics and parts); PARTIAL for sealed commercial units — no public parts book, FCC-photo basis. The shared architecture below is standard-defined, not reverse-engineered guesswork. Build order Step 1 — The connector & cable — J1772 / J3400 (NACS) Two connector standards, one protocol family. The connector is a safety device first: no power flows until the car and the box have agreed, in analog, that everything is connected and vented/latched. Part What this part does Power pins (L1/L2 or L/N) Carry the AC. On J1772 these are the two big blades; the connector is rated 80 A in the standard and passively cooled in most home units. Proximity pin & latch switch Tells the car the connector is seated and, when you press the release, tells it to stop drawing before the pins separate — so the connector never breaks a live arc. The little switch in the handle is a safety system. Pilot pin Carries the 1 kHz square wave described in Step 3 — the negotiation wire. Ground pin Longest pin: first to connect, last to break. The whole safety design hangs off this ordering. Step 2 — The contactor & protection — the switch and its conscience Inside the box: a heavy relay and the protection circuits the standards require before that relay may close. Part What this part does Contactor (main relay) The electromechanical switch that connects mains to the car. It closes only when the pilot negotiation succeeds and the protection checks pass. A welded contactor (stuck closed) is the unit’s most dangerous failure — good designs monitor for it (the car-side voltage check) and refuse to start. CCID / ground-fault protection Charge Circuit Interrupting Device: a ground-fault sensor (per UL 2231) tripping at ~20 mA — and EVSEs do not auto-reclose blindly the way a bathroom GFCI might; they latch out per the standard’s rules. Current transformers / metering Smart units meter energy for the app and for load-sharing between multiple EVSEs on one circuit (a J1772 feature: the pilot’s advertised current can be adjusted live). Surge & temperature sensing Plug-face and internal temperature sensors derate or stop a session when a receptacle overheats — the failure that actually starts garage fires is usually a tired 240 V receptacle, not the EVSE. Step 3 — The pilot & control board — a $0.10 negotiation The control board generates the pilot signal and reads the car’s answer. This is the part of the standard anyone can verify with an oscilloscope, and OpenEVSE documents it completely. Part What this part does Pilot generator (1 kHz, ±12 V PWM) A square wave whose duty cycle announces the maximum current the car may draw (roughly: 10% ≈ 6 A, scaling linearly through the home range). The car reads the duty cycle and obeys it — the entire ‘smart charging’ of AC charging is this one wire. State detection (12 V → 9 V → 6 V) The car answers by loading the pilot through resistors/diode: 12 V = no car, 9 V = connected, 6 V = ready/charging. The diode check proves it’s a car and not a short or a child with a paperclip — the box will not energize for anything that can’t answer correctly. Control processor & radio (smart models) Schedules, apps, utility programs, and load management live here — and die here, when a vendor’s cloud dies (see the record). The pilot layer underneath keeps working dumb, which is the saving grace of the standard’s design. What is missing, in the open: for sealed commercial units, boards and contactors are not sold and the exchange is whole-unit. The category’s defense is structural, and it is real: the protocol is a public standard, the safety layer is analog and verifiable, and a complete open design (OpenEVSE) exists as the reference implementation. When a vendor bricks its cloud (below), the standard is why the box still charges. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. The charger is in the car — AC ‘charging’ is negotiated delivery; the car’s onboard charger does the conversion, which is why the same box serves every brand Duty cycle is destiny — read the pilot and you can read any session’s current limit, with a scope, on any EVSE ever made Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Levels & connectors The vocabulary the whole category shares: Thing What it is Power Notes Level 1 EVSE on a 120 V outlet (the cord in the trunk) 1.4–1.9 kW Slow, universal, and the pilot protocol is identical — only the numbers change. Level 2 Hardwired or 240 V plug EVSE (this page) 7.7–19.2 kW NEC Article 625 territory: dedicated circuit, continuous-load sizing (125%), licensed install. DC fast charging The charger really is in the cabinet (off-board DC) 50–350+ kW A different device class (CCS/J3400 DC) — named here so the boundary is explicit; not this page’s subject. J1772 (SAE) The pre-2024 North American AC standard connector — Still the installed base; adapters to J3400 are passive for AC. NACS → SAE J3400 Tesla’s connector, opened as a spec Nov. 2022, standardized as J3400 in Dec. 2023 — The industry’s migration target; the pilot protocol carried over. Key chips & components Pilot/control implementation — in OpenEVSE, a documented ATmega-class design with published firmware; in commercial units, an MCU of the families indexed in this site’s Datasheet Index doing the same documented job. The standard makes the chip boring, which is the highest compliment a standard can earn. Current-sense & metering ICs — commodity energy-metering parts of the classes in the Datasheet Index ; in the open design, every one is named in the published BOM. Faults — which part fails, and how you know Diagnosis only — the interventions belong to a licensed electrician. What each symptom means , so the conversation is informed: Session stops overnight / breaker warm — continuous-load physics: an EVSE is a 3+ hour full-load draw, the harshes

FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits, regulatory actions, and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you are responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This is not legal advice — it is a workbench. Flipper Zero A $169 pocket multi-tool for RFID, NFC, sub-GHz, infrared, iButton, Bluetooth, and GPIO — with open firmware and schematics. Use it on your own systems, or with written authorization. What it is A handheld, microcontroller-based multi-tool, not a phone and not a computer. It reads, stores, and replays low-power radio and contactless signals, and it can act as a USB HID device, a serial terminal, and a GPIO tool. Its strength is also its warning: the same tool that shows a weak access system can be misused on a system you do not own. Use it only on your own equipment or with written authorization. Price, official US store: $169 (launched at $169 in 2022; US store price as of November 2026), microSD card not included in the basic pack. Screen: 128x64, 1.4-inch monochrome LCD, backlit. Battery: LiPo 2100mAh, USB-C charging. Size / weight: 100 x 40 x 25 mm, 102g. Official docs: docs.flipper.net , flipperzero.one , and open firmware on GitHub ( flipperdevices ). FCC filing FCC ID: 2A2V6-FZ , IC 27624-FZ, applicant Flipper Devices Inc, model FZ.1. The radio test report is public record, tested under FCC Part 15 Subpart C. What the filing includes: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual — public record at fccid.io. What it does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality), firmware, bill of materials, or debug documentation. For those, use the official open schematics and firmware below, not the FCC filing. Source: FCC test report for 2A2V6-FZ, and the Flipper Zero filing summary on fccid.io. Every major component — with a datasheet link per part Major ICs are listed here, verified from published specs. A complete passive-component bill of materials (every resistor and capacitor, with values) is not yet transcribed from the official schematic — that list is marked in progress below, not invented. Part Role Datasheet / source STM32WB55RG Main MCU + Bluetooth LE 5.4. ARM Cortex-M4 at 64 MHz + Cortex-M0+ at 32 MHz, 1024KB Flash, 256KB SRAM. ST Microelectronics STM32WB55 datasheet (PDF) TI CC1101 Sub-GHz transceiver. 315 / 433 / 868 / 915 MHz. Texas Instruments CC1101 datasheet (PDF) ST25R3916 family NFC front end, 13.56 MHz, ISO-14443A/B, MIFARE, FeliCa, NFC Forum protocols. ST Microelectronics ST25R3916 product page 125 kHz RFID coil Low-frequency RFID. EM400x, EM410x, EM420x, HIDProx, Indala, T5577. See official schematic and docs.flipper.net RFID section. Infrared RX / TX Infrared capture and replay, 800-950nm. See official docs, infrared section. 128x64 LCD 1.4-inch monochrome display, backlit. See official schematic for the display controller and part number. microSD slot Storage, cards up to 256 GB supported, exFAT (FAT32 also works). See official docs, storage section. LiPo battery, 2100mAh Internal battery, USB-C charging. Official docs, power section In progress, not yet published: full passive BOM, exploded view with every part labelled, and verified SWD pinout. Those will be added only from the official schematic and FCC internal photos, with sources, not from a guessed list. Exploded view — in progress No original BareBoard exploded view exists yet for this device. The view to be added here will be a labelled diagram built from FCC internal photos and the official schematic, with full alt text, in plain HTML, so it works on mobile, on old browsers, and without JavaScript. It will not copy a copyrighted teardown image. Until then, use the Wikimedia CC BY-SA photo of Flipper Zero used in Watchmen §16, and the FCC internal photos linked above, to see the board layout. Manuals and official docs Official documentation: docs.flipper.net — start with the Flipper Zero user guide, then the sub-GHz frequencies page for your region. Official product site: flipperzero.one Open firmware and schematics: github.com/flipperdevices — build from source, or update from the official app, never from a random download. News articles BleepingComputer — Flipper Zero makers respond to Canada’s ‘harmful’ ban proposal (February 2024 announcement, with Flipper Devices response on rolling codes). BleepingComputer / Techmeme — Brazil seizing Flipper Zero shipments (ANATEL, March 2023). Source: BleepingComputer — Brazil seizing Flipper Zero shipments . Restricting Flipper Zero: an accountability approach to security (EFF, March 2024, on the Canadian proposal). Watchmen §16 sources — BleepingComputer Brazil seizure, and XDA on where Flipper Zero is banned , including CBP seizure and Canada / US stance. Lawsuits and discovery No court lawsuit against Flipper Devices was found in Watchmen's check on 2026-10-08, and no court case was found in the public reporting reviewed for this page. The record below is regulatory and marketplace action, not a lawsuit. If a verified court case exists, it belongs here with a citation — do not add one without it. Each event is dated and sourced in The Full Record below. Flipper Devices' response, as reported: the device cannot hijack cars built after the 1990s, because those use rolling codes, and it cannot actively block the owner's signal to catch the original — a point to check against the specific vehicle and system, not as a blanket rule for every car. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or Flipper Devices’ own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the Flipper Zero is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. No court lawsuit against Flipper Devices was found in the public record checked for this page (see Lawsuits and discovery above). The record below is therefore what actually happened: a crowdfunding launch, then regulatory and marketplace actions — seizures, a refused certification, a marketplace ban, and one announced ban that was walked back. Year What happened Source 2020 Kickstarter: $4.8 million. The Flipper Zero campaign closed in September 2020 having raised about $4.8 million from more than 37,000 backers — better than 8,000% of its funding goal. The first devices reached backers about 18 months later, in early 2022. Hackaday — Kickstarter result 2022 U.S. Customs seized 15,000 units — then released them. In late 2022, U.S. Customs and Border Protection seized a shipment of about 15,000 Flipper Zeros; after review, the shipment was released. XDA Developers — where Flipper Zero is banned 2023 Brazil: Anatel seized shipments and refused certification. From early 2023, Brazil’s telecom regulator Anatel redirected incoming Flipper Zero purchases to itself and rejected all homologation (certification) requests, stating in its letters that the device had been used to facilitate crime. The EFF argued the refusal blocks a legitimate security-research tool. BleepingComputer — Brazil seizures 2023 Amazon banned it as a “card skimming device.” In April 2023 Amazon removed Flipper Zero listings, notifying sellers: “This product has been identified as a card skimming device. Amazon policy prohibits the sale or listing of card skimming devices.” Flipper Devices appealed; the device remained on sale through its own store. This was a marketplace policy decision, not a law. Gizmodo — Amazon ban 2023 Gatwick Airport confiscation. On September 27, 2023, airport security staff at London Gatwick confiscated a traveller’s Flipper Zero over security concerns — an individual confiscation, widely reported, not a UK ban. Wikipedia — Flipper Zero, bans and seizures 2024 Canada announced a ban — then walked it back. On February 8, 2024, at a national auto-theft summit, Canada announced it would ban devices used to steal cars by copying keyless-entry signals, naming the Flipper Zero. Flipper Devices responded that the device cannot defeat rolling-code systems used since the 1990s. By March 20, 2024, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada had shifted position: not an outright ban, but measures to restrict such devices to legitimate actors, with details to follow consultations. Malwarebytes — Canada revisits the ban Unverified: “Flipper Zero is stealing modern cars.” That the device is a driver of the recent car-theft surge is asserted but not proven. Evidence for the claim: the Canadian government named the device at its February 2024 auto-theft summit, police bulletins have flagged it, and viral videos show it interacting with vehicles and access systems. Evidence against: modern keyless systems use rolling codes — each press sends a fresh code, so a replayed recording is rejected — and Flipper Devices states the tool cannot hijack cars built after the 1990s; Malwarebytes noted in March 2024 that there had never been an officially confirmed case of a theft committed with a Flipper Zero, and real-world vehicle theft relies on relay and key-programming equipment costing thousands of dollars. No regulator or court record documents a modern car stolen with one. Sources: BleepingComputer — Flipper Devices’ response , Malwarebytes — Canada revisits the ban . Did you know The hacking tool is a pet. The pixel-art dolphin on the screen is a virtual pet in the Tamagotchi mould, and interacting with it is the device’s core game mechanic: using the tools changes the dolphin’s appearance and emotions, and levels it up. The security toolkit is quite literally gamified. Source: Wikipedia — Flipper Zero . It beat its Kickstarter goal by more than 8,000%. The campaign asked for a modest crowdfunding goal and closed at

text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. GoPro A camera built to be crashed — and the one American company that tried to fight DJI in the air and got recalled back to the ground. Inside: a sensor, a stabilization brain, and a battery door that is the whole repair story. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by model. GoPro files under its own grantee code CNF (cameras with Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/GPS); the Karma drone system filed as controller + aircraft + gimbal separately. The filings’ internal photos show the HERO board stack and, on the Karma set, the drone that the CPSC would later recall. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos — the image-sensor board stacked on the main (GP-chip) board, the battery bay’s contacts, and the antenna placement that lets a camera this small stream a live preview Test reports — Wi-Fi/Bluetooth output; GPS models show the receiver’s filed characteristics The manual — filed publicly, including the battery and door instructions that are the extent of sanctioned owner service What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: none. GoPro sells doors, batteries, lenses (protective lens covers), and mounts — the consumable shell — and no internal part at all. FCC internal photos are the source for the stack below. A HERO is a sensor sandwich: lens → sensor board → main board → battery, in a rubberized unibody that is waterproof to 10 m because it is sealed, not because it has serviceable gaskets you can replace. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public parts book; FCC internal-photo basis. Owner-serviceable layer is real but shallow: batteries, doors, lens covers. Build order Step 1 — Housing, lens & doors The waterproofing strategy is a sealed body with exactly one opening — the side door — and its gasket is the camera’s life expectancy. Part What this part does Unibody housing Rubberized polycarbonate shell, waterproof to 10 m (33 ft) bare on current flagships. The rating dies with any cracked door seal. Protective lens cover A twist-off glass cover over the actual lens — the one sacrificial optical part, designed to be replaced after the crash that would otherwise total the camera. Side door & gasket Covers USB-C and the battery/SD bay. A torn gasket or grit in the seal is how ‘waterproof’ cameras drown; the door is sold as a part for this reason. Mounting fingers The folding two-prong mount built into the base — the interface to the entire GoPro mount ecosystem. Step 2 — Imaging stack Sensor on its own board, processor on the main board, joined by a connector that crash forces love to unseat. Part What this part does Image sensor (Sony-class CMOS, 1/1.9″ on recent flagships) The light sensor. Sensor size, not megapixels, is why the footage looks like it does at dusk. GP2 processor (HERO10 onward; GP1 in HERO6–9) GoPro’s in-house SoC: image pipeline, HyperSmooth electronic stabilization (gyro-driven horizon leveling + crop), and the encoder. No public datasheet. Gyroscope / IMU The motion sensor whose data is the stabilization: HyperSmooth is computed from this part, not from a gimbal. microSD slot The only storage. Card speed class is a system spec — a slow card presents as a ‘freezing camera’ fault (see Faults). Step 3 — Battery & boards A removable pack in a sealed camera — the design decision that keeps HEROs repairable at exactly one layer. Part What this part does Enduro battery pack A slide-in lithium pack (1720 mAh class). Removable, swappable, sold everywhere — the correct way to build a sealed device, and the reason a HERO outlives an AirPod. Main board & radios Wi-Fi/Bluetooth (+ GPS on equipped models) on the main board; antennas at the shell edges per the FCC photos. Front & rear displays Two LCDs (status front, touch rear) on flex cables — the rear screen is the most-cracked part on the camera and is not sold separately. What is missing, in the open: any internal part, any diagram, any calibration procedure for the sensor stack. GoPro’s service model is warranty exchange. The parts it does sell (doors, lens covers, batteries) are exactly the parts its design makes sacrificial — a coherent philosophy, documented here because it is the exception in this wave that proves design intent matters. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Stabilization is a sensor + software, not a motor — the IMU’s data, the GP2’s crop: how HyperSmooth actually works The Karma file — what the CPSC recall of GoPro’s drone (below) established about a battery latch, in the regulator’s own record Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. The line One flagship cadence, one small-form experiment, one drone (recalled). Line Years Defining hardware Notes HERO (flagship) 2014– (numbered to 13) GP1 (HERO6) → GP2 (HERO10) in-house silicon Waterproof-without-housing from HERO5; the removable battery survives every redesign. HERO (small / Session line) 2015–2018, Session; mini variants since Sealed, smaller, battery built-in on Session The Session’s built-in battery is the exception that shows the rule. MAX / 360 line 2019– Dual lenses, dual sensors Stitching is compute; the hardware is two HEROs back to back. Karma (drone) 2016–2018 Detachable gimbal (Karma Grip) + quadcopter Recalled (below); GoPro exited drones in January 2018. Key chips & components GoPro GP1 / GP2 — in-house camera SoCs; no public datasheet (collection target logged). Their existence is the documented break from the Ambarella parts earlier HEROs used. Image sensors (Sony CMOS) — identified per model from FCC photos and maker specs; sensor datasheets for the exact SKUs are not public. Collection target logged. Faults — which part fails, and how you know Symptom first. The HERO fault tree is short because the camera is honest about what it is: Freezing / corrupted files — the microSD card, first and almost always: an under-rated or counterfeit card. A card from the maker’s published compatibility list is the fix and the diagnosis in one step. Won’t power on after water exposure — check the door gasket for grit/tears before assuming the board: the seal is the system. Dry the bay fully; a camera that got wet inside is a corrosion clock, not a brick — yet. Overheating shutdowns (static, high-res modes) — documented behavior: a sealed, fanless camera recording 5.3K in still air is a thermal design at its edge. Airflow (the mount on a moving bike is the cooling system) and lower modes are the mitigations; GoPro publishes thermal guidance because this is physics, not defect. GPS never locks / position garbage — the GPS needs sky: first lock after travel or storage can take minutes. A unit that never locks with clear sky has an antenna/board fault. Battery drains in the case, camera warm — a stuck-on radio or a camera that didn’t actually power down (voice control wake is a setting, and a battery cost). Safety, before you open anything Swollen Enduro packs get the lithium rule: out of the camera, into battery recycling, no exceptions for ‘one more shoot.’ The pack is removable precisely so this decision is easy. A HERO that has taken water inside is not made safe by rice or time at the board level — powering a corroding board is how a recoverable camera becomes a dead one. Dry, unpowered, and decide with the board visible or not at all. The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over GoPro’s record is a product record: one famous recall, one exit from a market, one patent war with the rival that replaced it. Date Event Source 2016-11-08 GoPro recalls the Karma drone (~2,500 units sold) after reports of power loss mid-flight; the CPSC record attributes the failures to a battery that could disconnect — a mechanical latch issue. Karma owners are refunded in full. CPSC Recall No. 17-034 (GoPro Karma) 2018-01-08 GoPro discontinues Karma and exits the drone business entirely, citing a hostile regulatory environment and thin margins — the American challenge to DJI ends after one recalled product. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Medical device — read this first. Hearing aids are FDA-regulated medical devices. This page teaches the hardware and the public record. It never replaces your clinician: it cannot diagnose your hearing, fit a device to your ears, or tell you whether a sound you hear is a symptom. Sudden hearing loss is a medical emergency — same-day care, not a shopping trip. Hearing Aids A microphone, an amplifier with a fitted curve, and a speaker the size of a grain of rice — sold for a century through a licensed gate, and since October 17, 2022, also over the counter. The hardware is simple. The gate was the product. FCC ID FCC IDs apply to the wireless models. Bluetooth hearing aids (nearly all current prescription models and most OTC models) file under each maker’s grantee code for their Bluetooth Low Energy radios; some ecosystems add a proprietary 2.4 GHz link (TV streamers, remote mics) that files separately. Non-wireless aids have no FCC filing — their public record lives at the FDA instead (below). The filings’ internal photos show the hybrid circuit and receiver that are the whole device. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos (wireless models) — the amplifier hybrid/DSP board, the receiver’s armature, the battery contacts or rechargeable cell, and the antenna (often the wire that also carries sound to the receiver-in-canal) FDA 510(k) summaries & registration records — prescription aids are Class I/II devices; their FDA listings and, for OTC models, the rule at 21 CFR 800.30 are the category’s real public documents Test reports — Bluetooth output at body-worn range; hearing aids are among the lowest-power radios the FCC certifies What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: none published to owners by any major maker — but the exploded anatomy of a hearing aid is standardized across the industry, because the consumable layer (domes, wax guards, receivers on RIC models, tubes on BTE models) is designed to be owner-handled. The stack below is the dominant modern form, the RIC (receiver-in-canal): the speaker sits in the ear canal on a thin wire; the body sits behind the ear. Sources: FCC internal photos for wireless models, FDA device records, and the makers’ own published care-and-maintenance guides. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public parts book; anatomy from FCC internal photos + FDA records + manufacturers’ published care guides. The owner-serviceable layer (receivers, domes, wax guards, tubes, batteries) is real and is marked as such. Build order Step 1 — Behind the ear — the body The body holds the ears of the system (microphones), the brain (the amplifier), and the power. Part What this part does Microphones (2) Two ports on the body enable directional hearing — the aid compares the pair to favor sound in front of you. A clogged mic port is a ‘dead aid’ that isn’t. Amplifier / DSP chip A digital signal processor running your fitted program: it amplifies frequencies by your audiogram (a graph of your hearing loss), compresses loud sounds, and fights feedback. This chip and its fitting are why an aid is a medical device and not an earbud. Battery — zinc-air button (sizes 10 / 312 / 13 / 675) or sealed Li-ion Disposable zinc-air cells activate when you peel the tab (they breathe air to work) and run days; rechargeable models seal a lithium cell inside — with the service consequences this site documents everywhere else. Push button / rocker & telecoil Program/volume control; the telecoil is a small coil that hears magnetic loop systems (the ‘T’ setting) in theaters and counters — a second, invisible input most owners never learn exists. Step 2 — The wire & the receiver — the part that actually fails On a RIC aid, a thin cable runs from the body into the canal, ending in the receiver — which, confusingly, is the speaker. (In hearing-aid language the ‘receiver’ receives electrical signal and makes sound.) Part What this part does Receiver (speaker) A balanced-armature micro-speaker — the same physics as high-end earphones. It is the most failure-prone part (it lives in earwax and humidity) and, on most RIC models, it is owner-replaceable : it unplugs from the body. This is the category’s one true owner repair, and it fixes the majority of ‘dead aid’ cases. Dome / earmold The silicone tip or custom mold that couples the receiver to your canal. Fit is acoustics: a loose dome leaks bass and causes feedback squeal. Wax guard (cerumen filter) A tiny mesh screen at the receiver’s mouth. It clogs by design so the receiver doesn’t. A clogged wax guard is the #1 cause of a ‘suddenly quiet’ aid — a 60-second owner fix that clinics charge visits for when owners aren’t told. Step 3 — The other forms Same parts, different packaging. Part What this part does BTE (behind-the-ear, with tube) The receiver stays in the body; sound travels down a tube to the mold. Tubes harden and crack — an owner-replaceable consumable. ITE / CIC (in-the-ear / completely-in-canal) Everything, receiver included, is built into a custom shell in the canal. Nothing is owner-serviceable but batteries and wax guards; the deep fit makes wax the whole fault tree. Charging case / dock (rechargeable models) A contact or inductive charger — and, on some models, a UV/drying cycle, because moisture is the category’s chronic disease. What is missing, in the open: fitting software and its documentation. The amplifier’s curve is set by proprietary software (each maker’s fitting suite) through a programming interface, and that software is licensed to clinicians, not sold to owners. The hardware on this page is yours; the adjustment layer is the gate. Self-fitting OTC models move part of that layer into a phone app — which is exactly why the 2022 rule mattered (see the record). What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. The receiver is the repair — the one owner-swappable electronic part, and the industry’s quietest success story The fitting is the moat — why the same hardware costs $200 OTC and $4,000 through a clinic: the amplifier is commodity; the license to tune it is not Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Forms & channels Two independent splits: shape, and how it may legally be sold. Form / channel What it is Owner-serviceable Notes RIC (receiver-in-canal) Body behind ear + wire + in-canal speaker Receiver, domes, wax guards, batteries The dominant prescription form — and the most repairable. BTE (behind-the-ear) Body + tube + earmold Tubes, domes, batteries, wax guards High-power losses; pediatric standard. ITE / CIC Custom shell in the canal Batteries, wax guards only Cosmetic choice with a service cost. OTC (any form) FDA category (21 CFR 800.30), adults 18+, perceived mild-to-moderate loss As per form, plus app self-fitting No prescription, no fitting visit. Includes a software case: AirPods Pro 2’s authorized Hearing Aid Feature (see AirPods ). Prescription (any form) Fitted by licensed professionals after an exam (or a signed waiver) As per form Required for under-18s and for severe/profound loss; the fitting is part of the product. Key chips & components DSP/amplifier platforms — each maker’s proprietary signal-processing chip (Sonova/Phonak, Demant/Oticon, GN/ReSound, WS Audiology/Signia-Widex, Starkey). No public datasheets; the FDA 510(k) summaries are the deepest public technical documents. Collection targets logged per platform. Balanced-armature receivers (Knowles, Sonion) — the speaker itself is a bought component with public family documentation; Knowles publishes armature datasheets openly — the exception in this stack, linked from the Datasheet Index as collection proceeds. Bluetooth LE / LE Audio — the radio layer; Auracast broadcast audio is the incoming public standard that will matter in venues — the telecoil’s successor, arriving by radio instead of magnetics. Faults — which part fails, and how you know This is the most fixable fault tree on the site — because the top three entries are not faults at all, but maintenance nobody was taught. None of this replaces an audiologist; a sudden change in your hearing is a symptom, not a fault code — see Safety. Aid suddenly quiet or dead — wax guard first (replace it), dome second (clear/replace), receiver third (on RIC models, swap in a spare and listen). text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. iPad The big iPhone board that isn’t a phone: an A-series or M-series computer where the screen is the structure, the battery is two cells, and — since May 2025 — the first Apple tablet line with a genuine public parts book. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by model and generation. Apple’s grantee code is BCG . Every iPad files separately for each radio configuration — Wi-Fi-only models file once; cellular models file again for their LTE/5G radios — and the filings include the internal photos that are the starting point for reading any iPad board. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos — the logic board’s shape (a narrow strip along one edge on most models), the two battery cells, antenna lines in the chassis, and the speaker chambers Block diagrams — for the cellular models, the RF chain from modem to antenna Test reports — SAR (specific absorption rate) data for cellular models, which tells you where the radios sit and how hard they transmit What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: Apple’s Self Service Repair program publishes genuine repair manuals with exploded diagrams and parts lists — but only for iPad Air (M2 and later), iPad Pro (M4), iPad mini (A17 Pro), and iPad (A16), from May 29, 2025. Older models: no public Apple parts book; the exploded view below is rebuilt from the FCC filings’ internal photos, which show the same assembly stack. Board numbers: iPad logic boards carry Apple’s 820- number system (a board marked 820-xxxxx is identified by that number across the repair trade) — the same system the site documents for Mac boards in Level 1 . Coverage: PARTIAL — full public parts book for the 2025 Self Service Repair models only; FCC internal-photo basis for every earlier generation. No diagram on this page is fabricated: where Apple publishes nothing, the table names the assemblies the FCC photos show, in build order. Build order Step 1 — Chassis & antennas The aluminum unibody shell is the frame and the ground plane. Everything bolts or glues into it. Part What this part does Unibody enclosure The structural shell. Its machined pockets set where every other assembly sits. Antenna lines & windows Breaks in the metal where the Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and (on cellular models) LTE/5G antennas radiate. The plastic-filled seams on the back are not decoration. Speaker chambers Two or four sealed cavities at the edges. They are acoustic boxes, not empty space — crushing one changes the sound. Step 2 — Logic board One narrow board along one edge carries the whole computer. On a phone this board is stacked and folded; the iPad has room to lay it flat, which is why the iPad board is the better teaching board. Part What this part does A-series / M-series SoC The system on a chip: CPU, GPU, and memory controller in one package. iPad used phone-class A chips, then crossed to Mac-class M chips (M1, 2021; M4, 2024). NAND flash storage The soldered storage chip beside the SoC. Not removable, not upgradeable — the capacity you buy is the capacity there is. Power management IC (PMIC) Turns battery voltage into the dozen-plus rails the SoC needs. Identified in this site’s library: Apple PMIC Identification Guide . Secure Enclave The separate security processor inside the SoC that holds fingerprint/face templates and keys. Public reference in this site’s library: Apple Secure Enclave — Public Reference . Wi-Fi / Bluetooth radio A combo radio chip (Broadcom-designed in most generations) feeding the antenna lines. Cellular modem (cellular models) A Qualcomm modem on cellular models, with its own RF front end — the second radio system in the filing. Step 3 — Battery — two cells The iPad battery is two flat lithium cells side by side, joined as one pack. Two cells spread the weight, fit the thin shell, and share the load — and they age together, so a swollen or weak pack is replaced as a unit. Part What this part does Battery cells (2) The energy store. Glued to the chassis with adhesive strips; the pull-tabs are the designed removal path where fitted. Battery connector & board The pack’s protection board and the connector to the logic board — the first thing disconnected in any repair, the last reconnected. Step 4 — Cameras, sensors & buttons Small modules on flex cables around the frame’s edge. Part What this part does Front camera & Face ID / Touch ID Face ID models carry a projector + camera pair in the bezel; Touch ID models put the fingerprint sensor in the top button. Rear camera A single camera (two on some Pro models, plus a LiDAR scanner that measures depth with light pulses). Buttons & flex cables Power and volume switches on thin flex — the part most often torn during a screen opening. Smart Connector / magnetic Pencil contacts The pogo-pin or magnetic interface that powers accessories without a port. Step 5 — Display assembly — on last, off first The screen is the lid and the structure’s front face. It is laminated (glass, touch layer, and LCD/OLED fused) on most models, which is why a cracked digitizer usually means a whole display assembly. Part What this part does Cover glass & digitizer The touch-sensing layer. On non-laminated models (base iPad line) it separates from the LCD and can be replaced alone — the cheapest screen repair in the family. LCD / OLED panel The picture itself. Pro models (M4) use a tandem OLED stack — two OLED layers for brightness. Display flex cables The ribbons that carry video and touch to the logic board, and the first casualty of a careless pry. What is missing, in the open: board-level schematics and boardview files for every iPad are Apple-confidential. The repair trade works from the 820- board number, the FCC photos, and the Self Service Repair manuals. Anyone selling you a “leaked full schematic pack” is selling you a document this page will not link, because hosting it would break the rule this site runs on: public records and published documents only. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Chip-level identification — every major IC named, with datasheet links where public documentation exists Board mapping — what connects to what, which test pads matter, where the debug interfaces hide What the manufacturer won’t tell you — undocumented features, hidden radios, silent telemetry, repair blockers Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Models & chips Fifteen years of iPads reduce to one pattern: a phone chip in a bigger shell, until the Pro line crossed over to Mac chips. Model line Years Chip class Notes iPad (1st–4th gen) 2010–2012 A4 → A6X The A4 was Apple’s first in-house-designed SoC. iPad Air line 2013– A7 → M-class from Air 5 Air (M2 and later) is in Self Service Repair. iPad mini line 2012– A5 → A17 Pro mini (A17 Pro) is in Self Service Repair. iPad Pro line 2015– A9X → M4 Pro (M4) is in Self Service Repair; Pro models add LiDAR and ProMotion displays. iPad (base line, current) 2025 A16 The A16 model is the fourth Self Service Repair family. Key chips & components Apple A/M-series SoCs — no public datasheet exists for any of them; Apple publishes nothing at chip level. What is public: the FCC filings, the repair manuals, and this site’s identification references — Apple PMIC Identification Guide and Apple Secure Enclave — Public Reference (site library). Qualcomm cellular modems (cellular models) — the modem family varies by generation; Qualcomm publishes product briefs, not full datasheets. Datasheet: not in the site index yet — logged as a collection target. Broadcom Wi-Fi/Bluetooth combo radios — identified from FCC internal photos per model; full datasheets are under NDA. Collection target logged. Faults — which part fails, and how you know The exploded view shows you what the parts are. This list tells you which one has failed — symptom first, the way a bench diagnosis actually runs. Cracked glass, touch still works — on base-line (non-laminated) models, the digitizer alone. On laminated models, plan on the full display assembly. Won’t charge, or charges only at one cable angle — the charging port flex (a replaceable part on Self Service Repair models: displays, batteries, cameras, and external charging ports are the published part set). Fast drain or a lifting screen — a swelling battery pack. Stop using it on charge, and treat the pack as the fault, not the screen it is pushing up. Dead after a drop, no crack — a torn display or button

headings: Before any of it: Apple’s battery warning, verbatim
Self Service Repair: what Apple actually allows
Repair Assistant: the repair is not finished when the screws are in
The law is starting to answer
Apple’s own position, in Apple’s own paper
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. iPhone Family The iPhone is a sealed glass phone you can still open, diagnose, and partly repair yourself — if you know where Apple allows it, where calibration software finishes the job, and where board-level repair honestly stops. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by model and region. Apple’s FCC grantee code is BCG — the first three letters of every Apple FCC ID. An FCC ID is the identifier the Federal Communications Commission (the U.S. radio regulator) assigns to a device approved to transmit radio signals. Modern iPhones do not print it on the case; you find it on the phone itself under Settings → General → Legal & Regulatory, or on the box label. Take that exact ID and look it up at fccid.io — the filings include internal photos that are invaluable for hardware research. One filing verified for this page: FCC ID BCG-E4030A — an Apple Inc. smartphone filing granted September 14, 2021, covering the phone’s Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, and ultra-wideband radios. It is listed here as a worked example of the lookup method, not as a claim about which retail model name it was sold under. Specific model-to-FCC-ID mappings for the full iPhone 12–17 range are being verified against the filings and will be listed here. Until then, trust the ID on your own phone’s label over any list on the internet — including this one. What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . For a sealed phone like the iPhone, the filing matters more than it does for a console: Apple does not publish a parts book (see the exploded view below), so the filing’s internal photos are often the only public, manufacturer-supplied look inside the phone — board layout, shielding, and antenna placement, photographed before the model went on sale. What you can typically find: Internal photos — board layout, chip placement, shielding, antenna design Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which can reveal operating frequencies and power levels Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the device What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. Exploded view Partial — no public parts book. That label is the honest starting point. Apple publishes repair manuals with step-by-step disassembly procedures through Self Service Repair, but it does not publish an exploded parts diagram with a parts list — the one drawing that shows every assembly in space, keyed to part numbers, the way wheelchair and appliance makers publish an Illustrated Parts Breakdown. So the exploded view on this page is a walk in build order, assembled from two public sources: Apple’s own repair-manual disassembly order and parts lists, and the FCC filing’s internal photos. Every assembly below names its source. Where a number exists in Apple’s manual, it is Apple’s number; nothing here is drawn or numbered by us. The worked example is the iPhone SE (3rd generation, 2022), because its full manual is publicly archived: Apple Repair Manual 073-00333-A (archived full text) . Its internal view names the layout every iPhone in this hub shares: display on the front, battery in the middle, logic board (the main circuit board) along one side, Taptic Engine and speaker at the bottom, cameras at the top. The current manuals for iPhone 12 and later live at Apple: iPhone repair manuals — Apple Support . Before any of it: Apple’s battery warning, verbatim Every iPhone battery is a soft lithium-ion pouch glued into the phone. Apple’s own manual puts its Battery Safety warning like this — quoted exactly, from the iPhone SE (3rd generation) Repair Manual, document 073-00333-A: “This device contains a built-in lithium-ion rechargeable battery with soft battery cells. Battery safety is the number one concern when repairing a device with a built-in lithium-ion battery.” “Only technicians with the knowledge, experience, and tools required to repair electronic devices should replace a battery.” “Improper battery replacement, improper handling of parts, failure to discharge the battery before repair, or failure to follow the provided instructions could cause battery overheating, swelling, venting, leaking, or a battery thermal event. These events could result in fire, injury, death, data loss, or damage to the device, parts, or other property.” In plain language: fully discharge the battery before you open the phone, never puncture or bend the pouch, and keep clean dry sand within reach — the same manual’s thermal-event procedure is to smother the device in sand, not water. Source: the manual itself . The phone, in build order Display assembly — the screen unit: OLED panel (the light-emitting display), touch layer, front glass, and its flex cables (the flat ribbon cables that plug into the board). It is what you see and touch, and it is the door: nearly every repair starts by heating and lifting it. Apple orderable part on the SE (3rd generation): display 661-26353, plus fresh display adhesive 923-02012 — the adhesive is single-use and is part of the water seal. Source: Apple manual 073-00333-A, Orderable Parts and Display procedure . Back glass — the rear glass panel, carrying the wireless charging coil area and, on newer models, the MagSafe magnet ring (the circle of magnets that snap chargers and accessories into alignment). It protects the back and completes the radio window the antennas need. On iPhone 14 and later it is a separately replaceable part; on earlier models a cracked back glass effectively meant a new enclosure. Source: Apple Support — Repair Assistant (back glass listed as a finishable repair) . Battery — the glued-in lithium-ion pouch with its connector and pull-tab adhesive strips. It powers everything, and its health decides how long the phone lasts in a day. Apple orderable part on the SE (3rd generation): battery 661-25890. Source: Apple manual 073-00333-A, Battery procedure . Taptic Engine — the vibration motor: a small moving mass that makes the phone’s taps and buzzes feel precise. It sits at the bottom of the phone next to the speaker. Apple orderable part on the SE (3rd generation): 923-07176. Source: Apple manual 073-00333-A, Taptic Engine procedure . Main logic board — the phone’s main circuit board: the A-series processor, memory, storage, power circuitry, and the radio chips all live on it. It is the computer; everything else on this list is a peripheral plugged into it. Apple does not sell the logic board through Self Service Repair (see Repair reality, below). Its layout inside the phone is documented in the FCC filing’s internal photos (BCG-E4030A) and in the manual’s Internal View: Apple manual 073-00333-A . Camera modules — the rear camera unit (one, two, or three lenses depending on model) and the front camera. Each module is a sealed lens-and-sensor unit that plugs into the logic board; you replace the module, not the sensor inside it. Apple orderable part on the SE (3rd generation): camera 661-25683. Source: Apple manual 073-00333-A, Camera procedure . Face ID / Touch ID components — the biometric parts: on Face ID models, the TrueDepth camera system in the front (an infrared camera and dot projector that map your face); on the SE, the Home button with its Touch ID fingerprint sensor. These parts prove who you are, which is why they are cryptographically linked to the logic board and why calibration (below) gates them. Source: Apple’s manual introduction — biometric parts must be linked to the Secure Enclave after repair . Speakers — the bottom loudspeaker and the earpiece speaker at the top, which doubles as the second channel for stereo sound. Small sealed boxes with flex-cable connectors. Apple orderable part on the SE (3rd generation): speaker 923-07174. Source: Apple manual 073-00333-A, Speaker procedure . Lightning / USB-C port assembly — the charging-and-data socket at the bottom edge, on a flex assembly with the lower microphones. Lightning is Apple’s own plug, used through iPhone 14; USB-C is the universal plug, used from iPhone 15 on. A worn or lint-packed port is one of the most common “won’t charge” causes — clean it before you replace it. Source for the connector change: the Models table below; internal layout in the FCC internal photos . What this walk cannot give you, because Apple does not publish it: a dimensioned diagram, torque values outside the manuals, or a board-level parts list. That gap is stated, not filled in. Diagnosis & faults The exploded view above shows what things are. This section is the other half: which one failed, and how you know before you open anything. Work in this order — software first, screwdriver last. Short battery life, shutdowns, slowdowns → battery. Open Settings → Battery → Battery Health & Charging and read Maximum Capacity : the battery’s current full-charge capacity as a percentage of when it was new. Apple designs iPhone 14 and earlier batteries to retain 80% of capacity at 500 complete charge cycles, and iPhone 15 and later at 1,000 cycles; near or below 80%, budget for the battery in the exploded view above. Source: Apple Support — battery health and parts history . “Has this phone been repaired, and with what?” → Parts and Service History. Settings → General →

title: TP-Link Kasa HS103 Smart Plug — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. TP-Link Kasa HS103 TP-Link’s mini smart plug — 15 A switching in a package barely larger than the outlet it occupies. Inside: a Realtek RTL8710 running the whole show, and one of the more repairable plug designs in its class. TP-Link Kasa HS103. Product photo via B&H Photo. FCC ID FCC ID: read it off the label on your unit. Caution: the ID 2AXJ4KP115 is quoted for this plug in some coverage (including the EDN teardown) — that grant actually belongs to TP-Link’s KP115, a different model, so we do not repeat it here as this plug’s ID. What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . What you can typically find: Internal photos — board layout, chip placement, shielding, antenna design Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which can reveal operating frequencies and power levels Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the device What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Chip-level identification — every major IC named, with datasheet links where public documentation exists Board mapping — what connects to what, which test pads matter, where the debug interfaces hide What the manufacturer won’t tell you — undocumented features, hidden radios, silent telemetry, repair blockers Key Chips Realtek RTL8710 — the entire digital subsystem: ARM Cortex-M3 running at 83 MHz by default, up to 166 MHz, 512 KB RAM, 1 MB built-in flash, and 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi with a complete TCP/IP stack — all in one chip. Hongfa HF32FV-16 — the mains relay doing the actual switching. Teardown Notes Entry starts at the seam between the main chassis and the rubberized gasket ring — a spudger in the visible gap walks the side plate (with the multi-function button) out of place. The digital mini-PCB abuts the relay; the analog and power sections are straightforward, with a notably sizeable fuse on the pass-through ground. Two unpopulated eight-lead IC sites on the digital board hint at a more advanced product variant sharing the PCB. Two beefy solder points anchor the PCB to the chassis for mechanical stability — the EDN teardown notes they resisted desoldering, suggesting high-temperature solder. Simple Entry Points RTL8710 serial and flash You need: A 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter (about $3). Mains-voltage warning: this device connects directly to wall power. Do all low-voltage probing with the plug connected only to a bench supply or with mains physically disconnected and verified. With mains disconnected, open the case via the gasket seam and locate the digital mini-PCB. The RTL8710 exposes UART TX/RX; Realtek’s Ameba SDK documents the serial boot protocol for this family. Because the RTL8710 integrates its flash, firmware is read and written through the chip’s own serial bootloader rather than a separate flash chip. $ # Realtek Ameba-style serial upload (chip-family documented flow) $ screen /dev/ttyUSB0 38400 # (the RTL8710 console runs at 38400 8N1; the bootloader banner appears on reset) Work on mains-connected devices demands proper isolation and safety practice; if you are unsure, do not open it while it can be plugged in. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or TP-Link’s own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the HS103 is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. Year What happened Source 2020 Critical flaw in Kasa plugs, found by consumer testing. Which? (the UK consumer group), working with security consultants NCC Group, tested 10 smart plugs and found a critical flaw in TP-Link’s Kasa plug: weak encryption let an attacker on the same Wi-Fi network seize total control of the plug and of the power going to the connected device, and the plug shared the email address used to set it up unencrypted. Which? did not name the HS103 specifically — this was the Kasa plug line. TP-Link developed a fix that Which? said would roll out in October 2020. Which? — smart plug investigation, September 2020 2020 Firmware removed local control; a rollback was offered by ticket, then stopped. In November 2020 a firmware update for Kasa HS100/HS110 plugs (UK hardware version 4.1) removed the local API — the on-network control path that Home Assistant and other third-party tools used — leaving the Kasa cloud as the only control route. After a week of complaints, TP-Link offered affected users a special firmware to restore local access, requested per device by support ticket and MAC address. By early 2021, users reported TP-Link had stopped offering it. Kasa-line, not HS103-specific — but it is the clearest documented case of this plug family losing a local feature to a firmware push. Home Assistant community — TP-Link offers way to add local API back, November 2020 2022 Kasa cloud outage, November 15, 2022. TP-Link apologized in its own forum for an “unexpected cloud service outage” on November 15 that left Kasa devices offline in the app and broke Alexa and Google control until the service was restored and devices were rebooted. The plugs themselves had not failed — remote control had, because remote control runs through TP-Link’s cloud. TP-Link community — cloud outage apology 2024 The company split in two (company-level, not this plug). On May 11, 2024, TP-Link Corporation Group announced it had completed the restructuring begun in early 2022, formally separating from TP-LINK Technologies Co., Ltd. in China across shareholdings, workforce, research and development, production, marketing, and customer service. On October 9, 2024, TP-Link Global and TP-Link USA merged to form TP-Link Systems Inc., headquartered in Irvine, California, as the parent company for the group’s worldwide operations. How complete that separation really is became the central dispute in the U.S. actions below. TP-Link — restructuring completion, May 2024 ; TP-Link — TP-Link Systems Inc. headquarters, October 2024 2024–2025 U.S. investigations and a proposed router ban (company-level, routers only — not this plug). In December 2024, The Wall Street Journal reported that the Commerce, Defense, and Justice departments had opened separate investigations into TP-Link, that the Commerce Department had subpoenaed the company, and that a ban on U.S. sales of TP-Link routers was possible. In October 2025, The Washington Post reported that the Commerce Department had proposed banning new TP-Link sales, with backing from several other agencies. No ban on Kasa plugs was proposed, and no finding about the HS103 came out of these probes. Tom’s Guide — TP-Link ban timeline 2025 An AWS outage took Kasa cloud services down with it, October 20, 2025. When Amazon Web Services failed on October 20, 2025, TP-Link told users that Tapo/Kasa Care subscribers had no video clips stored on its cloud server that day and that other cloud-based services were affected. TP-Link’s same notice states what does not need the cloud: schedules and Away Mode are stored on the plug and continue without an internet connection. TP-Link community — AWS outage notice, October 20, 2025 2026 Texas sued TP-Link Systems (company-level — allegations, not findings). On February 17, 2026, Attorney General Ken Paxton sued TP-Link Systems Inc. in Collin County under the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act, alleging the company deceptively marketed its networking devices and allowed the Chinese Communist Party to access American consumers’ devices in their homes. A lawsuit is an allegation until a court rules: TP-Link disputed the claims, and no court had ruled when this page was written. The governor had added TP-Link to Texas’s prohibited-technologies list the month before. Texas Attorney General — press release, February 17, 2026 2026 The FCC blocked new foreign-made routers generally (company-level context, routers only). On March 23, 2026, the FCC added all consumer routers produced in a foreign country — every brand, not TP-Link alone — to its Covered List, after a White House-convened Executive Branch body determined that foreign-produced routers pose unacceptable national-security risks. New foreign-made router models now need a Conditional Approval from the Department of War or the Department of Homeland Security to receive FCC authorization. Routers already authorized may keep being sold, used, and updated — and no Kasa plug was banned. FCC — Covered List router FAQs 2026 CVE-2026-76784: the HS103’s local control messages could be forged. TP-Link’s own advisory, published August 26, 2026, lists the HS103P3/HS103P4 by name: insufficient cryptographic protections in the local device communication protocol let an attacker on the same network intercept, replay, or forge control messages, potentially taking unauthorized control of the plug (CVSS v4.0 score 8.7, High). TP-Link released fixed firmware — version 1.1.3 Build 250908 Rel.112508 for the HS103 packs. No confirmed exploitation was reported in the advisory coverage. TP-Link security advisory — CVE-2026-76784 2026 CVE-2026-108473: improper authentication and credential exposure, HS

title: Mesh Wi-Fi — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: Exploded view — the assemblies in build order
Faults — which part fails, and how you know
The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Mesh Wi-Fi One network name, many radios, and a business model hiding in the wiring closet: mesh systems replaced the router you owned with a fleet you subscribe to. The boards are simple. The record is about the paywall. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by brand, model, and node. Each mesh node is a full radio system and files separately (Google’s Nest Wifi files under grantee code A4R , the same code as the Nest Mini at A4R-H2C; Eero and TP-Link Deco file under their own codes). Mesh filings are a gift to the reader: to certify multi-node systems, makers file detailed internal photos and RF reports for every node variant. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos — the antenna array (6–8 antennas on Wi-Fi 6E nodes), the heatsinking (these are passively cooled computers that run hot), and the board’s radio sections under their shields Test reports per band — 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz output and DFS (radar-sharing) behavior — the paper trail that explains real-world throughput better than the box’s ‘AX5400’ arithmetic (the class number sums theoretical rates no client will ever see) Node variants documented — router vs. point/satellite hardware differences, which marketing renders invisible What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: none. No mesh maker sells parts or publishes a diagram. FCC internal photos are the source. A mesh node is a small passively-cooled computer: radio board, big passive heatsink, antennas around the shell, one or two Ethernet ports, and a power supply that is the most common failure in the whole system. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public parts book; FCC internal-photo basis. Build order Step 1 — Shell, antennas & heatsink The pretty fabric or plastic tower is an antenna farm wearing a heatsink as a hat. Part What this part does Antenna array Multiple printed/flex antennas for each band, arranged around the shell for spatial diversity (MIMO — multiple-input/multiple-output, using several antennas to multiply throughput). Antenna placement is the product; the shell is shaped around it. Heatsink & thermal path Fanless nodes dump SoC heat into a metal mass and the case. A node in a closed cabinet or direct sun is a node cooking itself — thermal throttling presents as ‘the Wi-Fi got slow.’ Status LED & touch/button surface The node’s entire local interface. When the app is the only window, the LED’s blink codes are the fault table. Step 2 — Radio board One board: SoC, radios, Ethernet, memory. Part What this part does SoC (Qualcomm / Broadcom / MediaTek) The networking processor — the same families that power conventional routers, documented at family level in this site’s Datasheet Index ; exact SKU per node from FCC photos. Radio chains (2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz) Separate power amplifiers and front ends per band. Tri-band nodes may dedicate one 5 or 6 GHz radio to backhaul (the node-to-node link); dual-band nodes share client radios for backhaul and halve under load. Ethernet switch & ports One WAN + one LAN on most nodes (more on gateway-class models). A node is also a small switch — wiring a node to the gateway (‘ Ethernet backhaul’) removes the wireless hop entirely. Flash & RAM Soldered. Firmware and the config live here — and the config’s real home is the maker’s cloud account (see the record). Step 3 — Power supply The wall adapter is a part of the system, and its most mortal one. Part What this part does AC adapter (USB-C or barrel, model-specific) Node adapters are not interchangeable across generations even within a brand. A weak/substitute adapter presents as random node reboots under load. Internal regulators Board-level power conversion of the classes indexed in the Datasheet Index ; a node that dies after a storm surge usually dies here. What is missing, in the open: everything below the whole-node level. Mesh hardware service is: replace the node, replace the adapter. The repair that actually exists for mesh is architectural — placement, wired backhaul, and knowing which settings your subscription rents you (next sections). What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Backhaul is the whole ballgame — dedicated band vs. shared band vs. a $10 Ethernet cable, in that order of honesty The class-number lie — why ‘AX5400’ sums radios no single client can combine, straight from the filed test reports Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. The main systems Three ecosystems, three philosophies of who owns the network: System Maker Hallmarks Notes Eero Amazon (acquired 2019) App-only management, eero Plus subscription for advanced features The subscription record below is mostly Eero’s. Nest Wifi / Nest Wifi Pro Google (grantee A4R) Router + Points with speakers (original), Wi-Fi 6E Pro line Managed in the Google Home app; the old Google Wifi app was retired into it. Deco TP-Link Aggressive price/performance, wide model range See the regulator entry in the record — dated and sourced. Orbi / Velop / ZenWiFi Netgear / Linksys / ASUS High-end tri-band, some local web UI survives The enthusiast tier — the closest thing to a router you still administer. Key chips & components Networking SoCs (Qualcomm Networking Pro / Broadcom / MediaTek Filogic families) — family-level briefs public; full datasheets under NDA. This site’s Datasheet Index holds the support-component layer (regulators, Ethernet PHY class parts). Collection targets logged per family. The XB3 on this bench is the control case: the Xfinity XB3 gateway shows what a fully-autopsied home-network board looks like when a site does the work — the mesh nodes deserve, and have not yet had, the same treatment. Faults — which part fails, and how you know Mesh faults are mostly physics and arithmetic wearing app costumes: One node always slow / always red — placement: it is too far, or behind the refrigerator/ductwork/mirror (metal and water are Wi-Fi poison). The fix is moving it a room closer, not a firmware update. Whole network degrades at busy hours — dual-band shared backhaul saturating. Wiring the busiest node (Ethernet backhaul) is the single highest-value mesh repair that exists. Random reboots of one node — its power adapter, heat, in that order. Swap adapters between nodes: if the fault follows the adapter, you have your answer and your cheapest fix. New device ‘can’t see’ the network — band steering: legacy 2.4 GHz-only IoT gear confused by a unified SSID. The fix is a guest/IoT SSID or a setup mode — buried, on some systems, behind the subscription. Settings you set are gone — the config lives in the cloud account; a factory reset or an app migration re-homes it. Know which account your network belongs to before you need it. Safety, before you open anything Nodes are low-voltage devices; the live risks are mundane and real: heat (don’t seal a passively cooled node in an unventilated box), and the power adapter (replace like-for-like; a bargain adapter that sags under load creates faults that look like firmware bugs). The bigger safety surface is administrative: your mesh admin app is the key to every device in the house. A strong account password and 2FA on the network’s account matters as much as any router setting on this page. The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over Mesh Wi-Fi’s record is the subscription record: hardware sold once, features rented forever — plus one regulator file that is still open. Date Event Source 2019-02-11 Amazon acquires Eero (reported price ~$97 million). The leading mesh brand becomes a platform subsidiary; its roadmap bends toward services. Amazon/Eero announcements; NYT-reported price 2022 Eero moves established features — including detailed activity data and advanced network functions — behind the eero Plus subscription ($9.99/month), drawing sustained owner criticism that features shipped in the box became rent. Eero Plus plan documentation; owner-press coverage, 2022 2021–2022 Google retires the Google Wifi app and migrates all management into Google Home; the standalone web/admin interfaces do not survive the migration. Configuration authority consolidates in the platform app. Google support notices 2024-12 US agencies are reported to be investigating TP-Link routers over national-security concerns tied to China-linked exploitation of home routers; TP-Link (whose US business operates as TP-Link Systems Inc., Irvine, CA, after a 2024 reorganization) disputes the characterization.
