title: Google Nest Mini (2nd Gen) — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: Ports: there are none to use
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Your device, your rules. You bought it — you have the right to update its firmware, patch its security issues, and remove software you don’t want on it. Every method on this page is non-destructive: it uses the device’s existing ports, buttons, or software features. Nothing here requires breaking the enclosure. Google Nest Mini (2nd Gen) Google’s puck-shaped smart speaker — nearly identical outside to the 2017 Home Mini, but with a machine-learning engine integrated into its main processor, so speech recognition can run locally. Google Nest Mini (2nd gen). Photo: 9to5Google. FCC ID FCC ID: A4R-H2C (Grantee: A4R = Google LLC) for model H2C, filed September 2019. The filing sketch confirmed the wall-mount hole and 3.5 mm jack before launch. What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . What you can typically find: Internal photos — board layout, chip placement, shielding, antenna design Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which can reveal operating frequencies and power levels Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the device What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Chip-level identification — every major IC named, with datasheet links where public documentation exists Board mapping — what connects to what, which test pads matter, where the debug interfaces hide What the manufacturer won’t tell you — undocumented features, hidden radios, silent telemetry, repair blockers Key Chips Synaptics AS370 A1 — the main application CPU. ML engine integrated in the AS370 SoC — not a separate chip; it runs on-device speech recognition and natural-language understanding so common commands don’t need a round trip to Google’s servers. Toshiba TC58NVG2S0H — NAND flash. Nanya NT5CC128M16JR-EK — DRAM. Teardown Notes The fabric top lifts away to reveal a compact circular PCB. Google added a wall-mount screw hole on the bottom — the headline hardware change over the Home Mini. There is no 3.5 mm jack and no USB port on this device; the only connector is the proprietary DC power barrel. A third microphone was added (the Home Mini had two) to improve far-field voice pickup. The enclosure is fabric-over-plastic with adhesive; opening it is non-destructive if you work slowly with a thin spudger, but the fabric can stretch if forced. Simple Entry Points Ports: there are none to use What do I need? Nothing — there is no port to plug into. The Nest Mini has no 3.5 mm jack and no USB port. Its only connector is the proprietary DC power barrel, which carries power and nothing else. Any guide claiming a wired audio output or a USB data connection on this device is wrong. The device runs a locked bootloader; community research focuses on the documented Cast and Assistant APIs rather than hardware debug. For local control without Google’s cloud, the documented path is the open-source Home Assistant integration, which uses the official local APIs. $ # Check what the device exposes on your local network $ nmap -p 8008,8009 192.168.1.50 PORT STATE SERVICE 8008/tcp open http 8009/tcp open ajp13 The Nest Mini’s bootloader is locked and there is no documented hardware debug header; this page records what is verifiable rather than speculating. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or Google’s own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the Nest Mini is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. Scope note: the 2017 entry is the Nest Mini’s direct predecessor, the Google Home Mini, and is labeled as such. The other entries are the record of the Google Assistant platform this speaker runs on. No recalls, lawsuits, or regulator actions against the Nest Mini model itself were found in the public record as of November 2026 — the entries below are its platform’s record, plus its predecessor’s defining defect. Year What happened Source 2017 Predecessor model: the Home Mini that recorded on its own. Android Police’s Artem Russakovskii found that his Google Home Mini review unit had been recording and uploading audio from his home almost constantly. The cause was hardware: the touch sensor on top of the device registered “phantom” presses, repeatedly firing the long-press that was supposed to summon the Assistant only when a person held the top. Google first pushed an update on October 7, 2017 to stop the touch mechanism misbehaving, deleted the top-touch events from October 4–7 from users’ activity pages, and then made the stronger call: it permanently removed all top touch functionality from the Home Mini by software update, saying that although it had received only a few reports, it wanted people to have complete peace of mind. Some single-tap functions later returned as a long-press on the side of the device; the top long-press never did. TechCrunch — Google removes Home Mini top touch function 2019 Contractors listened to Assistant recordings; Google confirmed the program (platform-level). Belgian broadcaster VRT NWS obtained more than 1,000 Google Assistant recordings from a whistleblowing contractor and reported that 153 of them should never have been recorded because the wake phrase was not clearly said, and that some clips contained addresses and personal details enough to identify the speakers. Google answered in its own blog post: it partners with language experts who review and transcribe a small set of queries, only about 0.2 percent of all audio snippets, with snippets not associated with user accounts and reviewers directed not to transcribe background conversations. Google said the contractor who leaked the Dutch audio had violated its data security policies and that it was conducting a full review of its safeguards. Google — more information about our processes to safeguard speech data (Google blog, July 11, 2019) 2019–2026 $68 million Google Assistant privacy settlement (platform-level). A class action filed in July 2019 — Kumandan v. Google LLC, consolidated as In re Google Assistant Privacy Litigation, No. 5:19-cv-04286-BLF in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California — alleged that Google Assistant recorded and transmitted people’s communications without intentional activation, in what the settlement calls “false accepts” (a hot word detected when none was spoken), and disclosed recordings to third-party review vendors. Google denied the allegations and admitted no wrongdoing. The settlement created a $68 million non-reversionary fund for two classes covering May 18, 2016 to March 19, 2026: purchasers of Google-made devices, and Assistant users and household members whose communications were recorded through a false accept or shared with a review vendor. The court’s order names Google Home, Home Mini, Home Max, Nest Hub, Nest Hub Max, and Pixel phones as Google-made devices; the Nest Mini runs the same Assistant and was on sale throughout the class period, but is not named device by device. Judge Beth Labson Freeman granted final approval on October 13, 2026 (ECF No. 584), overruling all seven objections. The agreement provides no injunctive relief — Google’s sole obligation under it is payment. Recording Law — final approval of the $68M Google Assistant settlement (order ECF No. 584) Unverified: “Google used those accidental recordings to target ads.” The claim comes from the class action itself: the court’s class certification order records the plaintiffs’ allegation that Google did not destroy false-accept recordings but kept using them to improve Assistant and to target advertising , and routed some to human reviewers ( the allegation as recorded in the court record ). Evidence for the allegation: it was pleaded in a case that produced a $68 million settlement, and human review of a small sample of recordings is independently documented (2019, above). Evidence against: no court ever found the advertising claim true — the only class the court certified for litigation was a purchaser class on contract and unfair-competition claims, Google denied all allegations throughout the case, and the settlement contains no admission and no finding about advertising. Human review is fact; ad targeting from these recordings is not proven. Did you know One drinking bottle dresses more than two Nest Minis. The Nest Mini’s fabric top is made from 100% recycled plastic bottles, and Google’s product manager put the ratio plainly at launch: a single half-liter plastic bottle makes enough fabric to cover more than two Nest Mini devices. The enclosure underneath is 35% recycled plastic. Source: BetaNews — Nest Mini comes with an upgraded Google Assistant (Google launch statements) . It carries a machine-learning chip rated at up to one TeraOPS. That dedicated chip — a teraOPS is a trillion operations per second — lets the Nest Mini learn your most common commands and process them on the device instead of in Google’s data centers, for a faster response. At launch this local processing applied in the US. Source: BetaNews — Nest Mini co

text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Nintendo Switch Family Nintendo’s hybrid handheld that sold 155+ million units — and shipped with controllers that drift. FCC ID FCC ID: BKEHAC001 (Grantee: BKE = Nintendo Co., Ltd.) for the original HAC-001 model. Revealed before launch: 2.4/5 GHz Wi-Fi (802.11ac), Bluetooth, non-removable battery Model numbers decoded: HAC-001 (console), HAC-002 (AC adapter), HAC-015/016 (Joy-Cons) Available: Internal photos, test reports, RF exposure docs What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . What you can typically find: Internal photos — board layout, chip placement, shielding, antenna design Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which can reveal operating frequencies and power levels Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the device What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Chip-level identification — every major IC named, with datasheet links where public documentation exists Board mapping — what connects to what, which test pads matter, where the debug interfaces hide What the manufacturer won’t tell you — undocumented features, hidden radios, silent telemetry, repair blockers Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Variants Model Released Model No. SoC Display Switch (original) 2017 HAC-001 NVIDIA Tegra X1 6.2″ LCD Switch (2019 refresh) 2019 HAC-001(-01) Tegra X1 (Mariko) 6.2″ LCD Switch Lite 2019 HDH-001 Tegra X1 (Mariko) 5.5″ LCD Switch OLED 2021 HEG-001 Tegra X1 (Mariko) 7″ OLED Key Chips NVIDIA Tegra X1 — quad-core ARM Cortex-A57 + quad-core Cortex-A53, Maxwell GPU. The same chip family as the NVIDIA Shield TV. Mariko revision (2019+) — die-shrunk Tegra X1 on 16nm, fixing the unpatchable boot ROM exploit (fusée gelée) of the original. Controversies & Legal Joy-Con drift The defining hardware defect of the Switch era. Joy-Con analog sticks develop “drift” — registering input without being touched — caused by wear on internal components and dust ingress. UK consumer group Which? found that 40% of surveyed owners (919 respondents) reported drift on their original Joy-Cons. US class actions (2019–2024): Filed in 2019, alleging Nintendo knowingly sold defective controllers. After five years, the cases were dismissed — not on the merits, but because Nintendo’s EULA contains a binding arbitration clause that plaintiffs had not opted out of. French settlement (2026): France’s DGCCRF found Nintendo of Europe committed “misleading commercial practices” from 2018–2023 by failing to inform consumers of the defect. Nintendo agreed to pay €35 million (~$40M) — the first major financial penalty over Joy-Con drift. Nintendo denied intentional wrongdoing. Nintendo has offered free Joy-Con repairs since 2019, including out-of-warranty units. Sources: ReadWrite , Tech Xplore (AFP) , Nintendo Everything Right to repair Nintendo has historically opposed independent repair — lobbying against right-to-repair legislation, using proprietary screws, and restricting parts. Joy-Con drift made this a mainstream issue: a widespread defect on a $80 controller pair that users were told to send to Nintendo rather than fix themselves. Aggressive anti-piracy legal action Nintendo is the most litigious company in gaming regarding piracy and emulation. Notable actions include the 2024 lawsuit against the Yuzu Switch emulator developers (which ended in a settlement and Yuzu shutting down) and ongoing actions against ROM sites. Critics argue this chills legitimate homebrew and preservation work. Specific settlement terms were not independently verified for this page; Nintendo’s pattern of emulator litigation is well documented in gaming press. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or Nintendo’s own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the Switch is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. Year What happened Source 2018 Fusée Gelée — CVE-2018-6242. Researchers publicly disclosed a buffer overflow in the NVIDIA Tegra X1’s BootROM recovery mode (RCM) in April 2018. Anyone with physical access and a USB connection could bypass secure boot and run unverified code. Because the flaw sits in read-only mask ROM, it cannot be patched by software on units already shipped; Nintendo answered with revised hardware (the Mariko revision in the Key Chips section above). The same CVE also affected other Tegra X1 products, including Cisco conferencing hardware. Cisco advisory — CVE-2018-6242 2019–2024 Joy-Con drift: the U.S. class actions end in dismissal. Suits filed in 2019 and 2020 (Diaz and Carbajal) alleged Nintendo knowingly sold defective controllers. In May 2024 both sides jointly called for dismissal: Nintendo’s EULA binds buyers to arbitration and waives class actions, and the plaintiffs had not opted out. A third case had already been dismissed on the same grounds. Nintendo had offered free drift repairs, including out-of-warranty controllers, since 2019, and its president apologized for the trouble in 2020. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Nintendo Life — dismissal 2022 Which? takes drifting Joy-Cons into the lab. The UK consumer group sent five sets of drifting Joy-Cons to a specialist lab. Every set showed wear on the joystick slider contact points of its plastic circuit boards after only months of use, plus dust and contamination inside despite dust-proofing cowls; the lab concluded a mechanical fault was likely. Which?’s earlier survey found two in five UK owners of the original Switch reported drift. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Which? — lab tests 2020–2022 United States v. Bowser (Team Xecuter). Gary Bowser, the public face of Team Xecuter — a group that sold modchips and software for playing pirated games on the Switch and other consoles — was arrested in the Dominican Republic in September 2020 and deported to the U.S. He pleaded guilty in October 2021 to two federal circumvention felonies, and in February 2022 was sentenced to 40 months in prison. The money: $4.5 million in restitution under the plea, plus a separate $10 million judgment for Nintendo — $14.5 million in total. Prosecutors estimated the scheme caused more than $65 million in losses to game companies. GeekWire — sentencing 2024 Nintendo v. Tropic Haze (Yuzu). Nintendo sued the company behind the Yuzu Switch emulator on February 26, 2024, alleging it facilitated piracy at scale. The case settled in about a week: on March 4, 2024, Tropic Haze agreed to pay $2.4 million, accept a permanent injunction, hand over the yuzu-emu.org domain, and shut down both Yuzu and its sister 3DS emulator, Citra. Because it settled, the case set no court precedent on emulation. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Wikipedia — case record 2026 France fines Nintendo €35 million over drift disclosure. On June 8, 2026, France’s DGCCRF announced that Nintendo of Europe had accepted a €35 million transactional fine for misleading commercial practices from 2018 to 2023: investigators found Nintendo knew of the drift defect as early as 2018 but only began informing consumers in 2020, after a complaint from consumer group UFC-Que Choisir, and that its messaging steered some owners into buying replacements instead of seeking repair. Nintendo must also publish a notice on its French homepage; it denied intentional wrongdoing and said the payment is not an admission of guilt. At European level, Nintendo had already committed in 2023 to free repairs for affected controllers even beyond the legal warranty. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Engadget — DGCCRF fine Unverified: “Nintendo quietly fixed Joy-Con drift in later Joy-Cons.” Evidence for: Nintendo has said it made continuous improvements to the Joy-Con and that only a small percentage were reported faulty, and consumer groups have noted quiet revisions to later models. Evidence against: Nintendo has never announced a fix, named a revised part, or documented a change to the basic stick design; the Which? lab was still finding the same wear fault in 2022, drift was reported on Switch Lite and OLED controllers built years after launch, and the French case treated the defect as live through 2023. Until Nintendo documents a design change, “fixed” is a claim, not a fact. Did you know The Switch is Nintendo’s best-selling console ever. By December 31, 2025, it had sold 155.37 million units, passing the Nintendo DS at 154.02 million — the hybrid handheld outsold every Nintendo box before it. Source: Thurrott — Nintendo earnings report . More games have been sold for Switch than for any other Nintendo platform. Nintendo reported cumulative Switch software sales of 1.3061 billion units by late 2024, a company record. Source: Nintendo — financial briefing (PDF) . The Switch’s unpatchable flaw also lived in office conferencing gear. CVE-2018-6242 came from the shared Tegra X1 chip; Cisco listed its Webex Room 55 among the products built on the same process

Raspberry Pi Pico W Raspberry Pi’s $6 microcontroller board: a dual-core Cortex-M0+ RP2040 with Infineon Wi-Fi, castellated edges for soldering, and the friendliest firmware workflow in the industry — hold a button, plug in USB, drag a file. Raspberry Pi Pico W. Photo: Components101. FCC ID FCC ID: 2ABCB-PICOW (Grantee: 2ABCB = Raspberry Pi). Covers the Pico W wireless variant. What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . What you can typically find: Internal photos — board layout, chip placement, shielding, antenna design Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which can reveal operating frequencies and power levels Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the device What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Chip-level identification — every major IC named, with datasheet links where public documentation exists Board mapping — what connects to what, which test pads matter, where the debug interfaces hide What the manufacturer won’t tell you — undocumented features, hidden radios, silent telemetry, repair blockers Key Chips Raspberry Pi RP2040 — dual ARM Cortex-M0+ at 133 MHz, 264 KB SRAM, 2 MB external QSPI flash — Raspberry Pi’s first in-house silicon. Infineon CYW43439 — 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi 4 + Bluetooth 5.2 combo, connected over SPI. Teardown Notes There is barely anything to tear down — and that’s the point. The Pico W is a single small PCB with castellated edges, a micro-USB port, the RP2040, the wireless chip under a shield can, and 2 MB of flash. The debug interface is fully documented: three pins on the board edge carry SWD (serial wire debug) for the RP2040, and Raspberry Pi publishes the Picoprobe firmware that turns a second $4 Pico into a debug probe. This is the reference example of how open hardware documentation should work: full datasheet, hardware design files, and open-source SDK with no NDA. Simple Entry Points BOOTSEL: firmware in ten seconds You need: A micro-USB cable. That’s it. Hold the BOOTSEL button, plug the Pico W into your computer, release the button. It appears as a USB mass-storage drive. Drag a .uf2 firmware file onto the drive. The board reboots running your code. For debugging, flash Picoprobe onto a second Pico and connect its GP2/GP3 to the target’s SWD pins — a complete debug probe for $4. $ ls /media/$USER/ RPI-RP2 $ cp firmware.uf2 /media/$USER/RPI-RP2/ $ # board reboots and runs firmware.uf2 The Pico W is also the cheapest practical debug probe in existence: one Pico programs and debugs another. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or Raspberry Pi’s own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the Pico W is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. No recalls, lawsuits, or regulator actions against the Pico W appear in the public record as of November 2026. What is documented is quieter: the silicon errata Raspberry Pi publishes in its own datasheet, and — for the Pico line’s successor chip — a public hacking challenge Raspberry Pi ran on purpose. Both are recorded below, because the full record includes the boring parts. Year What happened Source 2021 RP2040-E11: the ADC is less accurate than designed. Raspberry Pi’s own datasheet errata record that the RP2040’s analogue-to-digital converter (ADC — the part that turns voltages into numbers) has differential non-linearity (DNL) error peaks at four values — 512, 1,536, 2,560, and 3,584 — caused by an error in the scaling of its internal capacitors. Measured effective resolution (ENOB) is 8.7 bits, not the 9 bits simulated. The erratum affects every RP2040 revision, has no workaround, and is marked “Not fixed.” RP2040 datasheet, Appendix B: Errata RP2040-E11 (PDF) 2021 RP2040-E9: the boot ROM cannot boot straight into cache-as-SRAM. The datasheet’s bootrom erratum records that a RAM-only UF2 program cannot boot directly into the XIP cache used as extra SRAM: the watchdog reboot that enters it re-enables the cache and causes an immediate bus fault. The documented workaround is code in main SRAM that re-disables caching first. Affects RP2040 B0, B1, and B2; resolution is documentation, not new silicon. RP2040 datasheet, Appendix B: Errata RP2040-E9 (PDF) 2024 RP2350-E9: the successor chip’s pins can latch (Pico 2, not Pico W). The RP2350 in the Pico 2 — the Pico W’s successor line, not this board — shipped with erratum E9: a GPIO input can latch at about 2.15V instead of falling back to 0V, an effect first tied to the internal pull-down resistors and later confirmed to occur even without them. Raspberry Pi blamed third-party IP in the chip and documented workarounds, including external pull-down resistors of 8.2kΩ or less. It is recorded here because Pico W buyers are routinely offered the Pico 2 W as the upgrade. Hackster — RP2350 erratum E9 2024–2025 Raspberry Pi paid hackers to break its next chip — and they did. At DEF CON 32 (August 2024) Raspberry Pi launched the RP2350 Hacking Challenge: retrieve a 128-bit secret from one-time-programmable memory protected by secure boot, win $10,000. Nobody claimed it in a month, so the prize doubled to $20,000. In January 2025 Raspberry Pi confirmed four winning attacks (plus a fifth independent one) — most by voltage glitching — and published the results itself, saying hiding vulnerabilities would be “grossly irresponsible.” The RP2040 in the Pico W has no secure boot to break; this is the record of how its successor’s security was tested in public. Hackster — RP2350 challenge winners Did you know RP2040 is a formula, not a model number. Raspberry Pi’s own datasheet decodes it digit by digit: 2 processor cores, 0 for the Cortex-M0+ core type, 4 for the RAM size (floor(log2(256kB / 16kB))), and 0 because the chip carries no non-volatile storage of its own. Source: RP2040 datasheet, §1.1 (PDF) . The chip at the heart of the Pico W holds no program at all. That final 0 is literal: the RP2040 has zero on-chip flash. The Pico W’s 2 MB of program storage is a separate external QSPI flash chip on the board, which the RP2040 executes from through its cache. Source: Raspberry Pi Magazine — behind the name 2040 . Its “12-bit” ADC honestly measures about 8.7 bits. The datasheet publishes the measurement against its own part: DNL error peaks at four codes cut the effective number of bits from a simulated 9 to a measured 8.7 (erratum RP2040-E11, in The Full Record above). Few vendors print that in the datasheet; Raspberry Pi does. Source: RP2040 datasheet, §4.9 and Appendix B (PDF) . The E9 pin-latching bug has since been fixed in silicon. Raspberry Pi’s RP2350 A4 stepping fixes erratum E9 and the glitching attacks found by its own hacking challenge, and adds 5V tolerance on all GPIO pins while powered — though the company cautioned it may be a while before A4 chips appear on Pico 2 boards. Source: Hackster — RP2350 A4 stepping . Further Reading Raspberry Pi microcontroller documentation — official docs RP2040 datasheet — Raspberry Pi “UNIX was not designed to stop its users from doing stupid things, as that would also stop them from doing clever things.” — Doug Gwyn

Exotic, powerful, notoriously hard to program. Emotion Engine (PS2) — MIPS-based, 294 MHz. Sony’s custom silicon peak. AMD APUs (PS4/PS5) — semi-custom x86-64. The industry converged on PC architecture. FCC IDs vary by model and revision. Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io — Sony’s grantee code is AK8. Controversies & Legal The 2011 PlayStation Network hack Between April 17–19, 2011, attackers breached Sony’s PlayStation Network and Qriocity services, compromising personal data from approximately 77 million accounts — names, addresses, emails, birth dates, passwords, and payment details. Sony shut down PSN on April 20; the outage lasted 24 days. Government officials worldwide criticized Sony’s week-long delay in notifying users. The UK Information Commissioner’s Office fined Sony £250,000 for breaching the Data Protection Act. Sony estimated the breach cost $171 million. A US class action settled with Sony offering up to $15M in compensation (free games, PS Plus time, and up to $2,500 for proven identity theft). At the time, it was one of the largest data breaches in history. Sources: Wikipedia , Silicon UK OtherOS removal (2010–2017) The original “fat” PS3 shipped with OtherOS — the ability to install Linux alongside the PlayStation OS. The US Air Force famously built the Condor Cluster, a 1,760-console supercomputer, from PS3s. On April 1, 2010, firmware update 3.21 removed the feature, citing security concerns (a hacker had demonstrated a fundamental exploit). A class action ( In re Sony PS3 “Other OS” Litigation ) was filed in 2010, dismissed in 2011, revived on appeal in 2014, and settled in 2016: $55 for users who proved they ran Linux, $9 for those who bought the PS3 valuing the feature. The initial settlement was rejected by the judge over attorney fees; a revised settlement followed in 2017, paying claimants up to $65. Sources: Wikipedia , GamesIndustry.biz PS5 repair restrictions The PS5 uses software pairing for certain components — notably the optical drive, which is married to the motherboard. Replacing a failed drive requires Sony’s proprietary calibration, limiting independent repair. This is part of a broader industry trend of parts pairing that right-to-repair advocates oppose. Specific pairing mechanisms vary by revision; this reflects widely reported teardown findings. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or Sony’s own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about PlayStation is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. Year What happened Source 2010–2018 OtherOS removal and the class action. Firmware 3.21 removed the PS3’s OtherOS (install-another-OS) feature on April 1, 2010. The class action that followed, In re Sony PS3 “Other OS” Litigation (N.D. Cal., No. 4:10-cv-01811), first produced a 2016 settlement paying $55 or $9 per claimant, which the judge rejected over attorney fees. A revised settlement in 2017 created a $3.75 million fund paying up to $65 per valid claimant; the court granted it final approval on June 8, 2018. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Court order — final approval (PDF) 2011 Sony v. Hotz. On January 11, 2011, Sony sued George Hotz (“GeoHot”) and others over the PS3 jailbreak and the publication of the console’s root signing key, alleging DMCA and computer-fraud violations. The parties agreed in principle on March 31, 2011, and announced the settlement on April 11: Hotz consented to a permanent injunction barring him from hacking any Sony product again, and denied wrongdoing. In their joint statement, Sony also confirmed Hotz was not involved in the attacks then hitting Sony’s websites and network. PlayStation Blog — joint statement 2011 The PlayStation Network breach. Attackers who entered Sony’s network between April 17–19, 2011, compromised personal data from approximately 77 million PSN and Qriocity accounts. Sony shut PSN down on April 20 and kept it down for 24 days, waited a week to notify users, and later estimated the breach cost $171 million. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Wikipedia — 2011 PSN outage 2013 UK regulator fines Sony £250,000. On January 24, 2013, the UK Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) fined Sony Computer Entertainment Europe £250,000 for a serious breach of the Data Protection Act over the 2011 hack, finding the attack could have been prevented if the software had been kept up to date and passwords properly secured. Sony said it strongly disagreed and planned to appeal; it later withdrew the appeal. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Computerworld — ICO fine 2014 The breach class action settles for $15 million. In July 2014 Sony agreed to a preliminary $15 million settlement of the U.S. class actions over the 2011 breach — free games, themes, and PlayStation Plus time for affected users, plus identity-theft reimbursement — while continuing to deny the allegations; Sony said it settled to avoid the cost of lengthy litigation. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Polygon — $15M settlement 2021 “CBOMB”: the PS4’s clock-battery time bomb, documented and defused. Preservation testers documented in 2021 that if a PS4’s internal CMOS battery (the small cell that keeps its clock) dies or is removed and the console cannot reach PSN to re-sync its clock, the console refuses to launch games — disc and digital alike — because the clock check guards the trophy system. That made every PS4 dependent on Sony’s servers staying up forever. Sony never announced a fix, but testers found that firmware 9.00 (September 2021) had quietly removed the block: games now launch with a dead battery, with trophy dates left blank. GameSpot — firmware 9.00 fix 2021–2023 DualSense drift lawsuit, filed and then dropped. Turner v. Sony Interactive Entertainment , filed in February 2021, alleged the PS5’s DualSense controller has a drift defect Sony knew about and did not disclose. The plaintiffs used Sony’s own paper opt-out — a letter sent within 30 days of first using the console — to escape its arbitration clause and demand a jury trial. In October 2023 all of the plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed their claims. No court ever ruled on whether the DualSense is defective. Top Class Actions — dismissal 2025 PSN goes dark for about a day. On February 7–8, 2025, PlayStation Network failed worldwide for roughly 24 hours — the longest PSN outage since 2011 — blocking sign-in, online play, and the PlayStation Store. Sony attributed it only to “an operational issue,” apologized, and automatically gave every PlayStation Plus member five extra days of service. It never published a cause. Tom’s Guide — outage coverage Unverified: “Iraq stockpiled 4,000 PlayStation 2s to build a military supercomputer.” Evidence for: in December 2000 a widely repeated report, citing unnamed intelligence sources, claimed as many as 4,000 PS2s had been bought in the U.S. and shipped to Iraq, and said U.S. Customs and the FBI were investigating; the PS2 was briefly subject to Japanese export controls because of its graphics performance. Evidence against: UK intelligence sources dismissed the claim as “nonsense” at the time, ordinary PCs of the era were more capable and easier to network, and no Iraqi PS2 weapons program has ever been confirmed in the

Raspberry Pi Family The single-board computer that put a Linux box in every hacker’s drawer. Over 77 million units sold — and a supply chain saga that tested the community’s loyalty. FCC ID FCC IDs by model (grantee code 2ABCB = Raspberry Pi). Check the label on your board and look it up at fccid.io : FCC ID: 2ABCB-RPI5 — Raspberry Pi 5 FCC ID: 2ABCB-RPI4B — Raspberry Pi 4 Model B FCC ID: 2ABCB-RPI3BP — Raspberry Pi 3 Model B / B+ FCC ID: 2ABCB-RPI0W — Raspberry Pi Zero W only (the plain Zero has no radio, so it has no FCC ID) FCC ID: 2ABCB-RPI0W2 — Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W FCC ID: 2ABCB-RPI400 — Raspberry Pi 400 FCC ID: 2ABCB-PICOW — Raspberry Pi Pico W What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. Key Chips Broadcom BCM2835/2837/2711/2712 — the application processors. Broadcom does not publish full public datasheets; documentation comes via Raspberry Pi’s own releases. RP2040 / RP2350 — Raspberry Pi’s in-house microcontrollers. Fully documented — RP2040 datasheet (PDF) is a model of open hardware documentation. Wireless: Cypress/Infineon CYW43455 (Pi 3B+, 4), CYW43439 (Pi Zero 2W) for Wi-Fi/Bluetooth. FCC IDs vary by model — see the list above. Check the label on your board and fccid.io for your specific revision. Controversies & Legal The 2021 price increase In October 2021, Raspberry Pi announced its first-ever price increase: the 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 went from $35 to $45, citing semiconductor supply chain costs. CEO Eben Upton stressed the change was temporary and that “in the entire history of Raspberry Pi, we have never increased the price of a product.” The 1GB variant was reintroduced at $35 as an alternative. Sources: TechSpot , Engadget Supply chain shortages (2021–2023) Global chip shortages hit Raspberry Pi hard. Production was capped at ~7 million units in 2021 (flat vs. 2020), with severe shortages of the Pi Zero and 2GB Pi 4. By 2022, scalpers were selling Pi 4 boards at 3× retail on Amazon. Approved resellers imposed quantity limits and anti-scalping measures. Supply did not meaningfully recover until 2023. Broadcom dependency Every full-size Raspberry Pi depends on a Broadcom SoC — a company famous for NDA-gated documentation and limited public datasheets. The community has long noted the tension between Raspberry Pi’s open-source ethos and its reliance on closed Broadcom silicon. The in-house RP2040/RP2350 microcontrollers, with fully public datasheets, represent Raspberry Pi moving toward greater openness. Commercial prioritization During shortages, Raspberry Pi prioritized industrial/commercial customers (Compute Module) over hobbyist retail, drawing criticism from the maker community that had built the brand. The company argued that commercial contracts kept the lights on during the crisis. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or Raspberry Pi’s own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the Raspberry Pi is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. Year What happened Source 2015 The Xenon Death Flash: the Pi 2 was camera-shy. Days after launch, forum user Peter Onion found that photographing his Pi 2 with a xenon camera flash powered it down, every time. Raspberry Pi traced it to the U16 core-power regulator chip, whose bare-die WL-CSP package lets intense light trigger the photoelectric effect inside the silicon and drop the core voltage. LED flashes and sunlight do not trigger it, it causes no permanent damage, and the published fix was gloriously low-tech: cover U16 with Blu-Tack, Sugru, or an opaque case. Raspberry Pi — Xenon Death Flash 2015 A Raspberry Pi went to orbit — and stayed. Two space-hardened Raspberry Pi computers, the Astro Pis, were waiting in the Columbus module of the International Space Station when ESA astronaut Tim Peake arrived on December 15, 2015. Students’ programs have run on them every year since through the European Astro Pi Challenge; upgraded Mark II units arrived in December 2021. Over 160,000 young people have taken part. ESA Education — Astro Pi is ten 2021 The first price increase in Raspberry Pi history. On October 20, 2021, Raspberry Pi moved the 2GB Pi 4 from $35 back to $45 and reintroduced the 1GB model at $35, citing shortage-driven cost increases, and stressed the change was temporary. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Raspberry Pi — supply chain announcement 2021–2023 Shortages, caps, and commercial prioritisation. Raspberry Pi made about 7 million units in 2021 — flat against 2020 despite much higher demand — and its own allocation guidance prioritised Compute Module and industrial lines while hobbyist boards stayed scarce and reseller prices spiked. Supply recovered through 2023. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Raspberry Pi — supply chain announcement 2024 Raspberry Pi goes public. Raspberry Pi Holdings plc listed on the London Stock Exchange on June 11, 2024, priced at £2.80 per share — a market capitalisation of about £541.6 million (about $690 million) and an offer size of £166 million. Shares surged to about £3.90 in early conditional trading; the Raspberry Pi Foundation remained the majority shareholder. The Register — IPO pricing and debut Did you know The name is two jokes layered together. “Raspberry” follows the fruit-named computer companies of the micro era — Apple, Apricot, Tangerine, Acorn — with a deliberate nod to blowing a raspberry; “Pi” is Python, because the early prototype booted straight into Python. Source: How-To Geek — Eben Upton on the name . The first field fix for a Pi was a pellet of bread. Raspberry Pi’s own Xenon Death Flash post records that one forum user shielded the light-sensitive U16 chip with bread — “the first yeasted bug fix we have encountered.” Source: Raspberry Pi — Xenon Death Flash . Students named the space Pis. The two Astro Pi Mark II computers on the ISS were named Nikola Tesla and Marie Skłodowska-Curie by Mission Zero participants in 2022. Source: Astro Pi — about the computers . Over 77 million Raspberry Pis have now been sold. Raspberry Pi Holdings’ H1 2026 interim results (September 2026) state cumulative sales of over 77 million units to date; the October 29, 2026 PDMR filing states the same figure. (A November 2, 2026 TVR filing still carries the older 73-million boilerplate figure.) Source: Raspberry Pi Holdings plc — H1 2026 interim results (RNS) . It is the third best-selling general-purpose computer platform in history. Behind only the PC and the Mac — a ranking reached before the 2024 IPO, on the strength of 60 million-plus units. Source: Colossus — A Foundation Model in Your Pocket . Faults — which part fails, and how you know
The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Robot Vacuums A floor computer that maps your home to clean it. Two sensor religions (camera and laser), one brush-and-fan drivetrain, and a record that runs from leaked living-room photos to the bankruptcy of the company that invented the category. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by brand and model — iRobot, Roborock, Ecovacs, and Shark file under their own grantee codes for Wi-Fi/Bluetooth (and, on dock-equipped models, sometimes a second radio in the dock). The internal photos show what the marketing hides: the navigation sensor stack and how much of the robot is dustbin. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos — the main board, the fan motor, the sensor turret (LiDAR models) or camera window (vSLAM models), and the battery pack’s true size Test reports — radio duty cycles that explain why a vacuum is a polite network citizen and a mapping dock is not The manual — filed publicly, including the maintenance schedule the makers themselves print (brushes, filters, wheels) — the closest thing to a service document the category publishes What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: none published — but this category is a partial exception on parts: iRobot and Roborock both sell owner-replaceable modules (wheel modules, brush cages, batteries, even main boards on some Roomba generations slide out as units). No exploded diagram is published; the stack below is rebuilt from FCC internal photos and the makers’ own module-replacement guides, which are public. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public parts book or exploded diagram; FCC internal-photo basis + manufacturers’ published module-replacement guides. Uniquely for this wave: several assemblies below are genuinely sold as owner-swappable modules, and the table says which. Build order Step 1 — Chassis, bumper & cliff sensors The robot’s body is a sensor platform that happens to hold a vacuum. Part What this part does Bumper + infrared window The front bumper is a switch (bump sensing) behind an IR-transparent strip (wall-following and dock homing receivers). A scratched IR window presents as navigation failure. Cliff sensors (4–6, downward IR pairs) Infrared emitter/detector pairs that see the floor’s reflection vanish at a stair edge. Dust on these is the #1 cause of a robot that refuses to run ‘in the dark’ it imagines. Top deck: LiDAR turret or camera window LiDAR models spin a laser rangefinder in a turret (a small motor + the LDS unit); camera (vSLAM) models look forward/up through a window. This part decides the robot’s whole navigation character. Step 2 — Drive & cleaning train Two drive wheels, a caster, brushes, and a fan. Every part here is a wear item and most are owner-replaceable modules on the major brands. Part What this part does Drive wheel modules (L/R) Spring-loaded motor + gearbox + treaded wheel, sold as slide-in modules on Roomba. A robot driving in circles has usually lost one. Main brush(es) Bristle or rubber extractors. Hair wrap is the design condition, not abuse; the rubber dual-roller designs exist to shed it. Side brush The spinning whisk that sweeps edges into the main brush’s path. A consumable. Suction fan (vacuum motor) A high-speed blower. It is why the dustbin’s seal matters: leaks upstream of the fan are suction lost forever. Dustbin + filter The bin and its HEPA-style filter. A clogged filter is the most common ‘weak suction’ fault and the cheapest fix in the category. Mop module (combo models) A pad + water tank that clips under or behind the bin; on dock models the dock washes it. Step 3 — Electronics & battery One main board, one battery, and the radios that make the map leave the robot. Part What this part does Main board + SoC Navigation compute (camera models run real vision pipelines), motor drivers, and the radio. Board-level parts are not sold; boards sometimes are, as modules, on older Roombas. Battery pack Li-ion, typically 1800–5200 mAh, screwed under a bottom plate — owner-replaceable on most major brands with a screwdriver, a fact worth naming because phones forgot it. Charging contacts & dock (base) Two metal pads mate with the dock. Auto-empty docks add a vacuum motor and a bag — a second appliance with its own consumables and its own failure modes. What is missing, in the open: schematics and any published exploded diagram. What exists — module sales and replacement guides — makes this category the least sealed in the smart home, and it still isn’t documented to the standard this site holds for a wheelchair. Both facts belong on the page. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. The map is the product — what vSLAM and LiDAR actually record, what leaves the house, and what the 2022 photo leak proved about test fleets Module economics — why this category sells wheels and brushes while phone makers glue batteries Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Navigation religions Pick a robot by how it sees; everything else follows. System Used by How it navigates Failure character LiDAR (LDS turret) Roborock, Ecovacs, Dreame Spinning laser builds a floor plan in minutes; methodical rows Turret motor/belt wear; map is precise, including in the dark vSLAM (camera) iRobot Roomba (j/i/s series) Ceiling-facing camera tracks visual landmarks; learns over runs Needs light; confused by dark rooms and changed furniture Camera + structured light / 3D avoidance Roomba j-series, Roborock flagships Adds obstacle recognition (cords, pet waste) to either base system The pet-waste avoidance guarantee exists because the failure mode is legendary Random / gyro (budget) Eufy and entry models Bump-and-turn with inertial dead reckoning No map to leak — and no map to use Key chips & components Navigation SoCs — camera models run ARM application processors doing visual SLAM; specific parts are identified per model in FCC internal photos. Public datasheets for the exact SKUs are uncommon — collection targets logged per family. Motor drivers & fan controllers — commodity power parts of the classes indexed in this site’s Datasheet Index (the same driver families that move the site’s stepper and DC projects). Faults — which part fails, and how you know Symptom first — this category’s faults are dominated by dirt, hair, and one famous wheel. Refuses to start, flashes a cliff/dark error in daylight — dust film on the cliff sensors. Wipe the sensor windows before anything else; this is the category’s most misdiagnosed fault. Drives in circles / one wheel’s tread gone — a drive wheel module: hair in the axle, a worn tread, or a dead gearmotor. On Roomba these are owner-swappable modules by design. Weak suction, loud fan — clogged filter or a dustbin seal leak. The fan is fine; its air is escaping. Filter first, always. Won’t dock / won’t charge — oxidized charging contacts (robot and dock), or the dock’s IR homing window blocked. Clean contacts with a melamine pad per the maker’s own guide. Map wrong, rooms merged, robot ‘lost’ — a dirty LiDAR window or camera lens, or a moved charging dock (the map’s origin). Software resets fix maps; they do not fix dirty optics. Error tones after a brush change — the brush cage isn’t latched or the end caps weren’t swapped onto the new brush. The robot is reporting a mechanical truth. Safety, before you open anything The battery lives under a screwed plate and is owner-replaceable on most major brands — replace it with the maker’s pack or a reputable equivalent, and recycle the old one. A swollen pack in a device that drives itself around your house is not a ‘monitor it’ situation. Auto-empty docks are mains appliances with their own motors and bags; unplug before clearing a dock clog. And a robot vacuum’s map of your home is sensitive data — know which account it lives in and what the maker’s retention policy says before you sell or scrap the robot (factory-reset it, like a phone). The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over The category’s record is a privacy record and a business record: what the mapping saw, and what happened to the company that mapped first. The images flow to data-labeling contractors for machine-learning training. MIT Technology Review investigation, Dec. 19, 2022 2022-

Step 1 — Bolt & cylinder — the part that is still just a lock
Step 2 — Motor & gear train — the ‘smart’ muscle
Step 3 — Electronics housing — batteries, board, radios
Faults — which part fails, and how you know
The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Smart Locks A motor, a radio, and the deadbolt you already own. A smart lock is the rare smart-home device whose failure mode is your front door — which is why its public record runs from FCC photos to DEF CON stage talks to fire codes. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by brand and model — August/Yale, Schlage, Kwikset, and Ultraloq each file under their own grantee codes, per radio configuration (Bluetooth-only locks file once; Wi-Fi and Z-Wave/Zigbee variants file for each radio). The internal photos are unusually informative here: they show the gear train and motor that are the whole product. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos — the gear motor, the tailpiece coupling, the battery pack (almost always 4×AA), and the radio board’s antenna placement against a metal door’s worst enemy: the metal door Test reports — Bluetooth/Z-Wave/Zigbee output power; explains why a lock on a steel door in a steel frame has the range it has The manual — filed publicly, and where the ANSI/BHMA grade claims and the handing (left/right door) setup are printed What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: none published by any major lock maker. FCC internal photos are the source. Two architectures exist and the split matters more than brand: retrofit locks (August-style) clamp over your existing deadbolt’s thumb turn and keep your key; full-replacement locks (Schlage Encode, Yale Assure) replace the bolt and cylinder entirely. The stack below is the full-replacement form; the retrofit form deletes Step 1 and keeps Steps 2–3 in a single housing. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public parts book; FCC internal-photo basis. Build order Step 1 — Bolt & cylinder — the part that is still just a lock Under the electronics sits a completely standard deadbolt. This is the page’s most important fact: the security of a smart lock is the security of this hardware, and it is graded on the same ANSI/BHMA scale as a $20 lock. Part What this part does Deadbolt (1-inch throw) The bolt itself. A 1-inch throw into a reinforced strike is what resists force; no radio feature changes this. Strike plate & door frame The part everyone skips. A long-screw reinforced strike does more against kick-in than any feature in the app. Key cylinder & tailpiece The mechanical key path. The motor turns the tailpiece; so does your key; so does the thumb turn. Three inputs, one bolt. ANSI/BHMA grade Grade 1 (heaviest duty) to Grade 3, tested under ANSI/BHMA A156.36 for deadbolts — cycle counts, torque, and force. The grade is printed on the box; believe it over the marketing. Step 2 — Motor & gear train — the ‘smart’ muscle A small DC gear motor drives the tailpiece. It is deliberately weak: it must stall safely against a misaligned door rather than force the bolt. Part What this part does DC gear motor Turns the tailpiece through a reduction gear train. Its current draw is the lock’s health signal — a straining motor means a binding door, and the lock’s ‘jammed’ alert is a current measurement. Position sensing A magnet + Hall sensor (a magnetic-field switch) or an encoder tells the board whether the bolt is thrown. Door-position sensing (open vs. closed) is a second magnet in the frame on equipped models. Clutch / manual override The thumb turn must always work with dead batteries. Any lock whose inside turn doesn’t mechanically drive the bolt is a lock to remove. Step 3 — Electronics housing — batteries, board, radios The inside escutcheon (the plate on the room side) holds everything electronic, because the outside of a door is weather and attack surface. Part What this part does Battery pack (typically 4×AA) Months of life because the motor sleeps between throws and the radio sips. Low-battery warnings start weeks early; a lock that dies silently has usually been warning an app nobody opened. Main board & radio(s) Bluetooth for phone-range control; Wi-Fi (power-hungry, often via a plug-in bridge instead) or Z-Wave/Zigbee for hub-based control. The radio choice is the battery-life choice. Keypad / fingerprint reader (outside unit) The exterior half: PIN pad and, on newer models, a capacitive fingerprint sensor. It is a data entry terminal only — the bolt authority lives inside. Speaker / status LED The beeps are diagnostics: distinct chirps for jam, low battery, and tamper. The manual’s chirp table is a fault-code table by another name. What is missing, in the open: replacement gear trains, motors, and boards are not sold. When the motor dies, the maker’s answer is a whole lock. The mechanical half, though, is standard hardware-store stock — bolts, strikes, and cylinders interchange across brands in a way the electronics never will. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. The bolt is the security — why the ANSI/BHMA grade on the dumb half of the product outranks every smart feature Jam alerts are current meters — the lock knows your door is sagging before you do, and the app buries the signal Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Architectures Brand matters less than form. Know which of these is on your door: Architecture Examples Keeps your key? Notes Retrofit (interior-only) August Wi-Fi Smart Lock Yes Clamps over the existing deadbolt’s thumb turn; outside of the door is unchanged. Renters’ form factor. Full replacement, keypad Schlage Encode, Yale Assure New key Replaces bolt + cylinder; keypad outside, electronics inside. Full replacement, fingerprint Ultraloq U-Bolt Pro, Lockly New key Adds a biometric reader to the exterior unit. Lever / commercial Yale nexTouch, Schlage FE/FE-series Varies BHMA commercial grades; different code and durability world. Key chips & components Bluetooth / Z-Wave / Zigbee radio SoCs — the locks are built on the same low-power radio families as the rest of the smart home (Nordic nRF52-class Bluetooth parts are common across the industry; this site’s Datasheet Index holds the ESP32 -family and nRF52840 documentation the category’s Wi-Fi bridges use). Model-specific radio identification comes from each lock’s FCC internal photos. Hall-effect position sensors — commodity magnetic switches; the datasheet class is in the site’s index under common ICs. Faults — which part fails, and how you know A lock’s faults announce themselves in sound and current before they strand you. In rough order of how often each is the real problem: ‘Jammed’ alerts, motor straining — the door, not the lock: seasonal swelling, a sagging hinge, a strike a millimeter off. Realign the strike before replacing anything electronic. Dead with no warning — batteries, almost always — and the warning usually existed in an app. The mechanical key (or the inside thumb turn) is the designed fallback; if you never tested your key, test it today. Keypad accepts the code, nothing turns — the motor or gear train (board alive, muscle dead) or a stripped tailpiece coupling. Listen: silence = motor/coupling; grinding = gears. Random relocking / phantom events — a failing door-position magnet alignment, or a hub automation doing exactly what it was told. Read the event log before suspecting the lock. Radio drops off the network — the metal door problem: range through a steel door and frame is a fraction of the open-air number in the test report. A hub or bridge on the room side fixes what a firmware update won’t. Safety, before you open anything Free egress is not optional. Fire and building codes (NFPA 101 and the IBC family) require that an occupant can always exit without a key, a code, or power. The inside thumb turn must mechanically open the lock with dead batteries, a dead board, and a fire on the other side of the door. If any lock you install fails that test, it is not a smart lock; it is a trap with an app. A smart lock is also an access log with a battery . Know who holds the codes, delete old ones, and understand that the lock’s event history (who came home, when) is exactly the data police and litigants ask platforms for. Your deadbolt now has a memory; treat it that way. The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over The smart lock’s record is a security-research record: the category’s weaknesses were demonstrated on conference stages, in public, years before most buyers heard of them.
