text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Smart Thermostats A wall computer whose entire job is closing the same 24-volt relays a 1950s mercury switch closed — plus a radio that lets your utility reach into the loop. The hardware is simple; the record is about who else holds the switch. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by model. Google’s Nest thermostats file under Google’s grantee code A4R (the Nest Mini on this bench is A4R-H2C; the thermostat models file under the same code), and Ecobee files under its own. The filings document the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth radios and, in the internal photos, the relay board and the wire terminals that are the actual product. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Internal photos — the two-board split: a display/compute board and a base plate carrying the wire terminals and relays — the thermostat’s real architecture in one picture The filed manual — wiring diagrams for the terminal letters (R, C, W, Y, G, O/B) that are the industry’s shared language Test reports — radio output; the thermostat is a low-duty-cycle radio and the reports show it What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: none published. FCC internal photos plus the makers’ own installation guides (which are genuinely public and genuinely good — HVAC is a trade that documents wiring) are the sources. A thermostat is two assemblies: the base on the wall (terminals + relays) and the head (display + computer) that clicks onto it. Coverage: PARTIAL — no public parts book; FCC internal-photo basis, with manufacturer installation guides (public) for the wiring layer. Build order Step 1 — The base plate — terminals and relays The base stays with the house. It is a terminal strip and a set of small relays (or solid-state switches) that connect the furnace’s 24 VAC control lines. Part What this part does Terminal block (R, C, W, Y, G, O/B, ...) Screw or spring terminals labeled with the trade’s letters: R = 24 VAC power, C = common, W = heat call, Y = cooling call, G = fan, O/B = heat-pump reversing valve. Every thermostat and every furnace board in North America speaks these letters. Relays / switching stage The actual product. A ‘call for heat’ is the thermostat connecting R to W. Everything smart is decoration on this switch. C-wire power path Smart thermostats power themselves from R and C. Homes wired without a C wire are the category’s defining problem: older stats ran on batteries or stole power in trickles (see Faults). Fuses & protection The furnace’s control board carries a 3–5 A automotive-style fuse that blows when thermostat wires short — the cheapest part in the system and the cause of many ‘dead thermostat’ calls. Step 2 — The head — display, sensors, radio The part you look at. It draws its power from the base and thinks about schedules; it contains no part of the heating circuit’s authority beyond asking the base to switch. Part What this part does Display & input ring/dial Nest’s rotating ring or Ecobee’s touchscreen — input devices over a small Linux-class computer. Temperature / humidity / occupancy sensors The thermostat knows the temperature at the thermostat — a hallway number the whole house is judged by. Remote room sensors exist because this is a real limitation, sold back to you as an accessory. Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / Thread radio The remote-control path — and the demand-response path (see the record). Backup battery (some models) A small cell that rides through power blips and, on C-wire-less installs, shares the load with power-stealing. What is missing, in the open: boards and relays are not sold as parts; a dead head is a whole-thermostat replacement. But the layer that actually fails in homes — wiring, fuses, C-wire power — is fully documented by the makers’ public installation guides, because HVAC contractors demanded paper. This is what a trade-documented category looks like. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. The thermostat is a switch, not a computer, at the wire — R-to-W is heat; everything else is commentary Power stealing, explained — how C-wire-less thermostats sip current through the furnace’s own relays, and the chattering/short-cycling faults it causes Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. The main lines Three design philosophies on the same 24 volts: Line Maker Hallmarks Notes Nest Learning Thermostat Google (grantee A4R) Rotating ring, learning schedule, no C-wire in many installs via power stealing The category’s reference design; see the Revolv entry in the record for its family history. Ecobee Smart Thermostat Ecobee (Generac-owned) Touchscreen, room sensors in the box, C-wire adapter (PEK) included Ships the fix for the C-wire problem instead of pretending it away. Honeywell T-series / T9 Resideo Trade-channel heritage, conventional setup The incumbent HVAC brand’s answer; strong contractor documentation. Amazon Smart Thermostat Amazon (built with Resideo) Budget price, Alexa-native The platform play: the thermostat as an Alexa endpoint. Key chips & components Main SoC & radio — thermostat heads run phone-class or MCU-class silicon with Wi-Fi/Bluetooth combos of the same families documented in this site’s Datasheet Index ; model specifics come from each unit’s FCC internal photos. The relay stage — small signal relays / triacs switching 24 VAC; commodity parts, indexed under common components in the Datasheet Index . Faults — which part fails, and how you know Symptom first. Most ‘smart thermostat failures’ are power or wiring wearing a smart costume: Screen blank, furnace silent — check the furnace control board’s 3–5 A fuse and the C-wire path before the thermostat. A tripped float switch (clogged condensate line) cuts R power on many air handlers and presents identically. Thermostat reboots when the furnace fires — power stealing starving: the voltage dips when the load it sips through energizes. The real fix is a C wire or the maker’s adapter kit, not a new thermostat. Short cycling / relay chatter — the same power-stealing pathology, or a heat anticipator setting fighting a high-efficiency furnace. Documented in every maker’s install guide because it is that common. House temperature wrong by degrees — the sensor is in a hallway with sun on it, or wall heat from the hole behind the base (seal the wire hole — draft air from inside the wall is a classic). ‘It changed my setpoint by itself’ — it did: learning schedules, utility demand-response enrollment, or a household member’s app. The thermostat’s event history (and your utility program enrollment) is the diagnosis. See the record. Safety, before you open anything Thermostat wiring is 24 VAC — low voltage that will not shock you, connected to a furnace that contains 120/240 VAC, gas, and a control board that costs real money. Kill power at the breaker before pulling the thermostat off its base : shorting R to C with the power on is how the little board fuse (and occasionally the board) dies. Never jumper terminals experimentally on a live system to ‘see what happens.’ R-to-W is a heat call; R-to-the-wrong-terminal on a heat pump can run heat and cooling against each other. The makers’ wiring guides are public — use them, photograph your old wiring before touching a wire, and label every wire by terminal letter, not by color (colors lie; letters are the contract). The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over No consumer device better documents the bargain of the smart home: convenience now, someone else’s hand on the dial later — all of it on the public record. Date Event Source 2014-01-13 Google acquires Nest Labs for $3.2 billion — the thermostat becomes a platform beachhead, and its founder-era promises about data begin their long renegotiation. Google/Nest acquisition announcements 2016-05-15 Nest shuts down the servers for the Revolv hub (a company Nest acquired in 2014): every Revolv hub in every home stops working, permanently, on schedule. The canonical cloud-bricking case, cited in every shutdown since. Revolv/Nest shutdown notice; coverage in Ars Technica, April 2016 2019-08-31 “Works with Nest” is terminated as Nest folds into Google Home; third-party integrations built on it break. Owners learn their thermostat’s ecosystem is a policy, not a property. Google Nest transition notices 2021-06 During a Texas heat wave, customers enrolled in utility ‘smart thermostat’ demand-response programs (via Smart Meter Texas and thermostat makers) find their setpoints

title: Smart TVs & Streaming — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: Sound but no picture — do the flashlight test first
No standby light, nothing at all
The TV that watches back: viewing-data collection
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Smart TVs & Streaming A modern TV is three circuit boards behind a sheet of glass — a power supply, a mainboard, and a small timing board — and most “dead” TVs have exactly one of the three at fault. Learn the three-board method and the flashlight test and you can name the bad board in minutes, with no parts cannon. Then look at the other end of the HDMI cable: the streaming stick, a complete computer that costs about $30 and hides a board smaller than its own remote’s. This page covers both — what is inside, how each one fails, what the public record shows, and what the manufacturers do not publish. FCC ID Every TV, stick, and box with a radio in it carries an FCC ID — the code the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC, the federal radio regulator) assigns when a device passes its radio tests. The ID is printed on the label on the back of the TV, or on the body of the stick. It has two parts: a grantee code (who filed) and a product code (which model). Read yours off the label and look it up at fccid.io — the filings include internal photos that are invaluable for hardware research. Verified examples from the filings themselves: Roku, Inc. — grantee code TC2. Roku’s full filing list is public under that code, from a 2005 SoundBridge music system to current streaming players. One streaming player, FCC ID TC2-R1042 , was granted in September 2021; an earlier IP set-top box, FCC ID TC2-R1019 , was granted on October 2, 2017. The label method is the same for all of them: the ID is on the unit, and the grant names the grantee, the equipment class, and the radio bands it was approved for. Samsung Electronics — grantee code A3L. A Samsung LED TV filing, FCC ID A3LHG40ND478 (model HG40ND478, application dated March 10, 2015), includes an Internal Photos exhibit — the exhibit this page’s exploded view is built from. Amazon files Fire TV under other company names. The Fire TV Stick 2nd generation (model LY73PR) carries FCC ID 2AE6S-0948 , approved September 14, 2017 — the grantee code 2AE6S belongs not to Amazon but to a filing company, Vlado L.L.C. The 3rd-generation Fire TV Stick and the Fire TV Stick Lite share one filing, FCC ID 2AUQI-7436 , because they are the same hardware (see Did you know). So for Amazon devices the label still works — but expect the name on the grant to be a stranger’s. FCC IDs vary by model and revision. Check the label on your specific unit. What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for a device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . What you can typically find: Internal photos — board layout, chip placement, shielding, antenna design. For a TV, this is the three-board layout — power, main, and timing — photographed before the set ever went on sale, so you can see what is inside your model before you ever take the back off yours. Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which can reveal operating frequencies and power levels Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the device What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. For TVs it also does not include the service manual — see the exploded view below for what that means. Exploded view Coverage: Partial — no public parts book. For most devices on this site the exploded view is keyed to the manufacturer’s own parts catalog. TVs are the exception, and this page labels it honestly: full TV service manuals and illustrated parts breakdowns are not published for owners. Makers route them through authorized service, so there is no public parts book to key this view to. What exists in public is the FCC internal-photo exhibits. The walkthrough below is built from those exhibits — the Samsung LED TV internal-photos exhibit ( FCC ID A3LHG40ND478 , 3 pages) for the set, and the Roku streaming player exhibits for the stick — with every part named in plain language and its job in one line. Nothing here is a fabricated diagram: it is the order the parts sit in the set, front to back, which is also the order they come apart and go back together. The television, front to back Panel (the screen itself) — the glass sandwich that makes the picture, pixel by pixel. Everything behind it exists to feed and light this one part. Backlight LED strips — rows of light-emitting diodes (LEDs) on thin strips behind the panel. The backlight is the lamp of the TV: the panel only shutters light, it makes none of its own. (OLED sets are the exception — each pixel lights itself, and there are no strips.) One failed LED in a series string can darken the whole set, which is why backlight failure tops the fault list below. T-Con board (timing controller) — the small board, usually at the top or bottom center, that takes the finished picture from the mainboard and times it out to the panel row by row and column by column, at the panel’s own speed. No T-Con signal, no coherent picture — even with a perfect mainboard and a perfect backlight. Mainboard — the computer: the TV’s processor, tuner, HDMI and USB ports, Wi-Fi, sound, and the smart-TV operating system all live here. It decides what the picture is; the T-Con and panel only display it. PSU board (power supply unit) — the board the mains cord plugs into. It converts wall power into the several voltages the other boards and the backlight need, and it holds a standby voltage alive at all times so the set can hear its remote. This is the board that makes a set fully dead when it fails — and the dangerous one. Read the safety box before you touch it. Speakers — usually two small drivers at the bottom corners, wired to the mainboard’s amplifier. Last in the stack, first to be blamed unfairly: most “no sound” faults are settings, sources, or the mainboard, not the speakers. Safety — the maker’s own words first. Samsung’s TV user manual (TU7000–8500 series, 2020) prints this panel verbatim: “CAUTION: RISK OF ELECTRIC SHOCK. DO NOT OPEN. CAUTION: TO REDUCE THE RISK OF ELECTRIC SHOCK, DO NOT REMOVE COVER (OR BACK). THERE ARE NO USER SERVICEABLE PARTS INSIDE. REFER ALL SERVICING TO QUALIFIED PERSONNEL.” Source: Samsung user manual BN68-11284A-01 (PDF) . The same manual adds that to avoid electric shock you should never touch the inside of the set. Our plain rule, which the manual’s warning is really about: unplugging the TV does not make the PSU board safe. The PSU’s large capacitors hold a charge after the cord comes out — that stored charge is the shock the warning means. Do not touch the hot side of the PSU board (the half around the mains inlet, fuse, and big capacitor). The diagnosis steps below are written so you can name the bad board without handling a live or charged PSU. The stick, in miniature The streaming stick is the same lesson at pocket scale. Its FCC exhibits show the whole computer on one small board: the Roku player’s internal-photo exhibits list top and bottom views of the stick’s board ( exhibit index for FCC ID TC2-R1042 ), and a teardown of the earlier Roku Streaming Stick (model 3500) shows what those photos contain: one board carrying the system processor under a metal shield/frame, a Wi-Fi chip (a Broadcom BCM43236 in that model), memory, and flash storage — with the antenna as traces and small structures at the board’s edge, and no fan, no heatsink tower, nothing else ( EDN teardown ). Amazon’s sticks are built the same way: one board, the SoC (system on a chip — the whole computer on one chip) under a shield, antenna at the end away from the HDMI plug. That is the whole exploded view of a stick, because a stick is one board. When one dies, there is no board to swap inside it — the diagnosis below is about proving the stick, not the TV, is at fault, and about the two fixable causes: power and heat. Diagnosis & faults Work a TV as three boards plus a lamp. Each symptom below points at one of them; change one board at a time, and only the one the symptom names. Sound but no picture — do the flashlight test first The flashlight test : with the set on and playing something with sound, hold a flashlight flat against the screen and look closely at an angle. If you can faintly see the picture moving under the light, the mainboard and the T-Con board are alive and doing their jobs — the image exists, it is just unlit. That is backlight failure: a dead LED strip, or the backlight driver section of the PSU board that feeds the strips. It is the single most common “dead TV” that is not dead at all. If the flashlight shows nothing at all, the fault is upstream: mainboard, T-Con, or panel. Picture but no sound Rule out the free causes first: mute, volume, the TV’s audio output setting (TV speakers vs. external), and a second source. Sound missing on every source with the settings right points at the mainboard, which holds the audio amplifier. A speaker itself failing is rare and usually announces itself with distortion first. No standby light, nothing at all The red standby light is fed by the PSU’s always-on standby output. No light with a known-good outlet and cord points at the PSU board. A standby light that blinks in a repeating pattern is the set reporting a fault code — blink counts are model-specific and are listed in the (unpublished) service manual, so count the blinks and search the exact model number plus the count before

title: Solar Basics — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: Exploded view — the assemblies in build order
Step 1 — The module (panel) — where light becomes voltage
Step 2 — Strings, combiners & rapid shutdown — the DC middle
Step 3 — The inverter — DC in, grid-grade AC out
Step 4 — Storage, loads & the meter — where the energy goes
Faults — which part fails, and how you know
Safety — the array has no off switch
The full record — dated, sourced, nothing smoothed over
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Solar panels are always on. There is no off switch for sunlight: a panel produces voltage whenever light hits it, and a string of panels produces up to 600 V DC in a home system. DC arcs don’t self-extinguish the way AC does. Roof work, string wiring, and anything inside an inverter belong to licensed electricians under NEC Article 690. This page teaches the system — how the pieces fit, what the terms mean, what the record shows — so an owner can talk to that electrician as an informed customer and read their own system’s data like an owner. Solar Basics A panel is a diode run backwards by the sun. Everything else — the inverter, the rapid-shutdown boxes, the monitoring app — exists to make that simple fact safe, useful, and legible to a grid built for one-way power. This is the whole system, in build order, with the vocabulary defined as it appears. FCC ID FCC IDs apply to the monitoring radios, not the power path. Inverters and gateways with Wi-Fi/cellular file under their makers’ grantee codes (Enphase, SolarEdge, Tesla, FranklinWH and others). Panels, racking, combiners, and batteries have no radios and no filings; their public record is their UL listing (UL 1741 for inverters, UL 61730 for modules), their datasheets — which in this industry are genuinely public — and NEC Article 690, the code that governs every installation. Every radio a device carries — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, ultra-wideband, NFC — needs an FCC equipment authorization before the device can be sold in the United States. To get one, the manufacturer files photographs and test reports with the FCC, and those filings are public record . Check the label on your specific unit and look it up at fccid.io . What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . Module datasheets (genuinely public) — solar is the one category on this site where the maker publishes the part’s full electrical character (Voc, Isc, Vmp, Imp, efficiency, temperature coefficients) as a sales document. Learn to read one and you can read every panel Inverter listings & manuals (UL 1741, IEEE 1547) — grid-interaction behavior is standards-defined and the manuals are public: anti-islanding, grid profiles, and rapid-shutdown behavior are documented, not secret The monitoring layer — what the apps show vs. what the hardware meters (see the record: monitoring is where owners get orphaned) What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (withheld under confidentiality requests where the maker files them), firmware, and the full bill of materials. Exploded view — the assemblies in build order This is the centerpiece of the page: the device taken apart into its assemblies, in the order they go together, every part named in plain language with what it does. An exploded view is the drawing a manufacturer makes showing every part separated along the path it assembles — the single most useful document in repair, and the one most often kept behind a dealer login. The source Parts book: not applicable in the usual sense — a solar system is an assembly of documented components , each with a public datasheet, assembled under a public code (NEC 690). The exploded view of a solar system is therefore architectural: the stack below is the system in energy order, each layer named with the terms its datasheet uses. Sources: module and inverter manufacturers’ published datasheets and manuals, UL 1741 / IEEE 1547 grid standards, NEC Article 690. Coverage: FULL as a system view — built from public datasheets and the governing code; there is no single maker’s parts book because there is no single maker. Component-level repair (inside an inverter) is a different, thinner record, labeled where it appears. Build order Step 1 — The module (panel) — where light becomes voltage A panel is 60–72 (residential) silicon cells in series under glass. Its datasheet’s five numbers are the whole language of this page: Part What this part does Voc — open-circuit voltage The voltage with nothing connected (e.g., ~41 V for a modern residential module). This is the number that adds up in a string toward the 600 V residential limit — and it rises in the cold, which is why string sizing is a winter calculation. Isc — short-circuit current The maximum current the module can produce (~11–14 A). Fuses and wire are sized from it, with the code’s safety factors. Vmp / Imp / Pmax Voltage and current at maximum power, and their product — the wattage on the label (e.g., ~400 W). Real output is this number minus heat, dirt, angle, and age (panels degrade ~0.5%/year, in the warranty’s fine print). Bypass diodes Diodes across cell groups that let current route around a shaded section. Without them, one shaded cell throttles — and cooks in — the whole string. Shading behavior (Faults) is these diodes’ biography. Step 2 — Strings, combiners & rapid shutdown — the DC middle Modules wire in series into strings; strings land in the inverter (or a combiner). The safety layer lives here. Part What this part does String wiring (series) Modules in series add voltage (10 modules ≈ 410 V on a bright cold morning). Series is why rooftop DC is lethal and why connectors (MC4) are locking, touch-safe, and not to be mixed across brands. Rapid-shutdown equipment (NEC 690.12) Since the 2017 NEC, module-level electronics must bring conductors within/about the array down to safe voltages (80 V inside the array boundary, 30 V outside it) within 30 seconds of initiation. Firefighters wrote this rule with their roofs in mind. Microinverters and DC optimizers satisfy it inherently; string systems add per-module shutdown boxes. Combiner / disconnects Where strings merge (with fuses per string in larger systems) and the labeled DC disconnect — the switch that does NOT make the array safe, since the modules themselves are still live (see the warning at the top of this page). Step 3 — The inverter — DC in, grid-grade AC out The system’s brain and its shortest-lived major part. Three architectures divide the market: Part What this part does String inverter One wall-mounted inverter for all strings. Cheapest per watt, one point of failure, needs add-on rapid-shutdown boxes. Its fans and capacitors set its lifespan (10–15 years is the planning number, against the panels’ 25+). Microinverters (e.g., Enphase IQ series) A small inverter under each module: no high-voltage DC on the roof, per-panel data, shade independence — at per-panel cost and per-panel roof electronics. The monitoring data owners love comes free with this architecture. DC optimizers + inverter (e.g., SolarEdge) A middle path: per-module DC-DC converters doing panel-level shutdown and optimization, feeding a simplified central inverter. Panel-level data, one proprietary ecosystem. Grid duties (UL 1741 / IEEE 1547) Whichever box: it must anti-island (stop energizing a dead grid instantly, for line workers’ lives), follow grid voltage/frequency profiles, and increasingly provide grid-support functions on the utility’s command. The inverter is a grid citizen by standard, not by courtesy. Step 4 — Storage, loads & the meter — where the energy goes Generation is half the system; the house and the grid negotiate the rest. Part What this part does Battery (LFP is the residential standard chemistry now) Stores the noon surplus for the evening. Hybrid inverters or AC-coupled units manage charge/discharge; the battery’s own BMS is its conscience, as on the e-bike page — at 100× the scale. Critical-loads panel / gateway The sub-panel of circuits that stay alive in an outage, and the transfer equipment that islands the home legally and safely. The bidirectional meter & net metering The utility meter spins both ways; the tariff decides what an exported kWh is worth. That tariff (see NEM 3.0 in the record) shapes system economics more than any hardware choice — the policy layer is part of the machine. What is missing, in the open: board-level documentation for inverters. Teardowns exist in the community record, but no maker publishes inverter schematics or sells boards; a dead inverter is a swapped inverter, warranty or not. The honest summary for this category: the system is the best-documented technology on this entire site (public datasheets, public code, public standards), while the boxes are as closed as anything Apple makes. Both facts matter. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. The datasheet is the lesson — five numbers (Voc, Isc, Vmp, Imp, Pmax) that fully describe any panel ever made: solar’s makers publish what phone makers classify MPPT, defined — Maximum Power Point Tracking: the inverter constantly hunts the voltage where V×I peaks as light and temperature shift. It is a control loop, not a feature badge — PWM charge controllers (the cheap alternative in small off-grid systems) simply don’t do it, and the harvest difference is the price gap Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. System shapes The architectures an owner will meet: Shape Inversion Data granularity Notes String One central inverter System/string level Lowest cost; shading on one panel drags its string. Microinverter Per module Per panel No rooftop HV DC; panel-level monitoring native. Optimized string Per-module DC + central inverter Per panel Middle cost; single-vendor ecosystem. title: Sonoff Basic R3 — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: Flash mode with one button and one cable
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Sonoff Basic R3 ITEAD’s in-line Wi-Fi switch — the device that taught a generation about ESP8266-family hardware. The R3 revision uses the ESP8285 (flash built into the chip), keeps the famous flash-mode button, and even ships a documented DIY mode. Sonoff Basic R3. Product photo via retailer. FCC ID FCC ID: 2APN5BASICR3 (Grantee: 2APN5 = ITEAD / Sonoff). The finished device is certified under its own grant. What the FCC filing revealed The filing exists: FCC ID 2APN5BASICR3, granted to ITEAD, holds the usual public record for this device — external and internal photos, RF test reports, and the filed user manual. Why the device needed its own grant: the Basic R3 does not contain a pre-certified radio module. Its ESP8285 is a bare SoC soldered directly to the board, so there was no module certification for ITEAD to inherit — the finished product was certified as a whole, under ITEAD’s own grantee code. (Contrast devices built around Espressif’s WROOM modules, which do carry Espressif’s own grants, 2AC7Z.) What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Chip-level identification — every major IC named, with datasheet links where public documentation exists Board mapping — what connects to what, which test pads matter, where the debug interfaces hide What the manufacturer won’t tell you — undocumented features, hidden radios, silent telemetry, repair blockers Key Chips Espressif ESP8285 — the Wi-Fi SoC with 1 MB of flash integrated into the package — no external flash chip needed, unlike the original ESP8266. Relay + power supply — mains switching and AC-to-DC conversion on the same compact PCB. Teardown Notes The R3 opens with screws — no glue — revealing a single PCB with clearly separated mains and low-voltage sections. A four-pin serial header footprint is on the board (3.3 V, TX, RX, GND); the case button is wired to GPIO0, which doubles as the flash-mode select. GPIO assignments are community-documented: GPIO0 = button, GPIO12 = relay, GPIO13 = LED. Simple Entry Points Flash mode with one button and one cable You need: A 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter (about $3) and four Dupont wires. Mains-voltage warning: disconnect from wall power; power the board only from the 3.3 V adapter during this procedure. Wire the adapter to the serial header: 3.3 V to 3.3 V, GND to GND, TX to RX, RX to TX. The 3.3 V wire is what powers the board during flashing — without it the chip never comes up. Do not connect the adapter’s 5 V line anywhere. Press and hold the case button (GPIO0 low), then apply 3.3 V power. Release the button — the ESP8285 is now in UART download mode. Back up the original firmware first, then write your replacement firmware with esptool. $ esptool.py --port /dev/ttyUSB0 read_flash 0x00000 0x100000 backup.bin esptool.py v4.0 Detected ESP8285 — 1 MB flash 1048576 bytes read successfully $ esptool.py --port /dev/ttyUSB0 write_flash 0x00000 tasmota.bin Writing at 0x00000000... 100% Leaving... Hard resetting via RTS pin... The R3 also offers a manufacturer-documented DIY mode (local REST API over Wi-Fi) for users who prefer not to open the case at all. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or ITEAD’s own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the Basic R3 is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. Year What happened Source 2021 Pairing sent the home Wi-Fi password in plain text (Sonoff S26 tested; the Basic line shared the app and the guide). In May 2021, A&O IT Group published its test of the Sonoff S26, a sibling plug on the same eWeLink system: during pairing, the app sent the home Wi-Fi network name and password to the device over unencrypted HTTP, where an attacker in radio range could capture them, along with the device’s ID and API key. The researchers also quoted the Sonoff Basic/RF user guide for the pairing access point’s default password — 12345678, printed in the manual and not changeable by the user — and said ITEAD had not responded to their disclosure by the time they published. The Basic R3 was not the unit on their bench; it pairs through the same eWeLink flow. A&O IT Group — smart plug security research, May 2021 2022 eWeLink cloud downtime, January 2022. For about two days in mid-January 2022, Sonoff users reported the eWeLink cloud unreachable — devices patchy or offline in the app and in cloud-linked integrations — while local-network control kept working for those who had it set up. There was no public status page to check; users traded reports in the Home Assistant forum and pointed to eWeLink’s Twitter account for news. That is this device’s cloud dependency in one episode: the switch on the wall still worked, the remote control did not. Home Assistant community — eWeLink cloud downtime reports, January 2022 2023 eWeLink retired the v1 cloud interface that community tools relied on (platform-level). In September 2023, after waves of “all disconnected” failures in the popular SonoffLAN Home Assistant integration, eWeLink support told a user that the project’s traffic had been observed, that it still used the v1 interface, that v1 was no longer under maintenance, and that eWeLink was gradually discontinuing it until it would be entirely inaccessible. Nothing about the Basic R3 hardware had changed — the cloud contract underneath community integrations had. Home Assistant community — Sonoff all disconnected, September 2023 2024 CVE-2024-7205: a person you shared a device with could take it over (eWeLink cloud, platform-level — not Basic R3 firmware). eWeLink’s own security advisory list records the flaw in the eWeLink Cloud Service homepage module before version 2.19.0, published July 30, 2024: when a device was shared, sharing exposed unnecessary device-sensitive information that let a secondary user take over the device as if they were the primary user. A stock Basic R3 lives on eWeLink’s cloud, so a cloud account flaw is part of this device’s real record even though the bug was not in the switch itself. eWeLink — security advisories & notices The empty part of the record, stated plainly: No CPSC recall, no lawsuit, and no CVE naming the Sonoff Basic R3 itself was found in the public record as of November 2026. ITEAD’s documented record for this device is the pairing and cloud record above — thin, and stated as thin, rather than padded. No Unverified aside is included on this page, because no widely believed claim about the Basic R3 itself met the bar of a documented allegation with evidence on both sides. Did you know DIY mode speaks plain HTTP on purpose. ITEAD’s DIY protocol document says the Basic R3 announces itself on your network using mDNS and takes control commands as HTTP POST requests — and recommends HTTP instead of HTTPS because of the LAN’s security and the device’s limited computing power. Local control and weak local encryption are the same design choice, seen from two sides. Source: SONOFF DIY Mode API Protocol v2.0 (PDF, ITEAD, March 2020) . The whole R3 family shares one 10 A relay board. A teardown of the R3 range found the same relay board — built around a GI-1A-5DH relay rated at 10 A — under the Wi-Fi, RF, and Zigbee variants, with components simply left off the versions that do not need them. One mains board, several radios. Source: NotEnoughTech — Sonoff Basic R3 teardown . DIY mode 2.0 deleted the jumper. The first DIY mode made you open the case and bridge a jumper to reconfigure the switch. DIY mode 2.0, on firmware 3.5.0 and later, needs only a long press of the pairing button to enter Compatible Pairing Mode — no disassembly at all. Source: SONOFF — DIY mode 2.0 announcement . You can flash Tasmota through DIY mode itself, with no cable. DIY mode’s over-the-air update function accepts a firmware file you point it at, and community guides use exactly that door to install Tasmota on a Basic R3 — the manufacturer’s own escape hatch from the cloud doubles as the community firmware’s front door. The guides warn the trip is one-way: there is no documented path back to stock ITEAD firmware. Source: Flashing Tasmota onto Sonoff devices over-the-air — guide . The manual covers a radio this model does not have. The combined BASICR3/BASICRFR3 manual lists a 433.92 MHz RF receiver in its specifications — then notes that the BASICR3 does not support the 433.92 MHz remote controller. That feature belongs to the RFR3 sibling; the plain R3’s only radio is 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. Source: Sonoff BASICR3/BASICRFR3 user manual . Further Reading Sonoff Basic Wi-Fi Smart Switch — Untangling the Ropes — EDN Sonoff Basic — Tasmota device documentation “The only sin is to make a choice without knowing you are making one.” — Jonathan Shewchuk

title: TI-84 Plus Family — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. TI-84 Plus Family The graphing calculator that ate American education. Powered by a Zilog Z80 — a CPU from 1976 — and protected by one of the most aggressive legal strategies in consumer electronics. FCC ID FCC ID: Not verified. Graphing calculators without wireless radios are not intentional radiators and typically do not carry FCC IDs. If you find an FCC ID printed on a TI-84 variant, let us know . What the FCC filing revealed There is no FCC filing for the TI-84 Plus family to reveal. These calculators carry no wireless radio, so they are not intentional radiators and never went through the FCC’s equipment authorization program: no FCC ID, no internal photos, no RF test reports, no filed manual. Compliance for a device like this runs under FCC Part 15 Subpart B — unintentional radiators, placed on the market under the manufacturer’s own declaration rather than an FCC grant. The public record for the TI-84 is Texas Instruments’ own documentation, not a regulator’s file. Everything under “What we reveal” comes from the physical device and TI’s published material. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Chip-level identification — every major IC named, with datasheet links where public documentation exists Board mapping — what connects to what, which test pads matter, where the debug interfaces hide What the manufacturer won’t tell you — undocumented features, hidden radios, silent telemetry, repair blockers Check our teardowns for full board-level analysis. Variants Model Released CPU Display Notes TI-84 Plus 2004 Z80 @ 15 MHz 96×64 mono The standard. Still sold today. TI-84 Plus Silver Edition 2004 Z80 @ 15 MHz 96×64 mono More flash/RAM. Discontinued. TI-84 Plus C Silver Edition 2013 Z80 @ 15 MHz 320×240 color First color screen. Short-lived. TI-84 Plus CE 2015 eZ80 @ 48 MHz 320×240 color Thinner, rechargeable. Current flagship. TI-84 Plus CE Python 2021 eZ80 @ 48 MHz 320×240 color Adds Python programming support. Key Chips Zilog Z80 (original Plus) — 8-bit CPU from 1976, clocked at 15 MHz. The same architecture as the Sinclair ZX Spectrum. Zilog eZ80 (CE models) — 24-bit enhanced Z80, clocked at 48 MHz. TI proprietary ASIC — integrates memory controller, display driver, and USB. TI does not publish datasheets for these. Controversies & Legal The 2009 signing key DMCA battle In 2009, hobbyists factored the 512-bit RSA keys TI used to sign calculator firmware, allowing custom operating systems on TI calculators. TI responded with DMCA takedown notices against bloggers and websites — including United-TI, Reddit, and Wikipedia — claiming the keys were circumvention devices. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) intervened pro bono , representing three bloggers. On October 13, 2009, the EFF sent TI a letter warning that publishing the keys did not violate the DMCA and that TI could face liability for misrepresentation. TI continued sending notices briefly but stopped after late 2009 and never pursued legal action. The incident became a textbook example of the Streisand Effect — TI’s attempts to suppress the keys ensured their widespread distribution, including on WikiLeaks. Sources: Wikipedia , EFF , The Register The calculator monopoly TI dominates the US graphing calculator market, with the TI-84 series effectively mandatory in many American classrooms. Critics note that the hardware has barely changed in two decades — the original TI-84 Plus used a CPU architecture from 1976 — while prices remained above $100. The College Board and ACT’s approved-calculator lists have been cited as entrenching TI’s position, as schools standardize on TI models to ensure test compliance. Exam mode and lockdown Newer TI calculators include “exam mode” features and increasingly locked-down firmware, limiting what users can do with hardware they own. This runs directly counter to the right-to-repair and device-ownership principles BareBoard stands for. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or Texas Instruments’ own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the TI-84 Plus is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. Year What happened Source 2009 The signing-key DMCA fight. In July 2009 hobbyist Benjamin Moody published the factors of the 512-bit RSA key TI used to sign calculator operating systems, and a volunteer distributed-computing project (the RSA Lattice Siever) factored the remaining keys, including the TI-84 Plus’s — making custom operating systems possible on calculators people owned. TI answered with DMCA takedown notices against sites including United-TI, Reddit, and Wikipedia, and against individual bloggers. The Electronic Frontier Foundation took three bloggers’ cases pro bono and wrote to TI on October 13, 2009, warning that posting the keys did not violate the DMCA and that TI risked liability for misrepresentation. TI sent a few more notices, stopped after late 2009, and never sued anyone; the bloggers reposted their material. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) Wikipedia — signing key controversy 2014 93 percent of the market, at a 2004 spec. The Washington Post, drawing on NPD Group figures, reported that TI took 93 percent of U.S. graphing-calculator sales in the year to June 2014 — about 1.6 million calculators — while the TI-84 Plus, launched in 2004 with a 96×64 screen and 24 KB of RAM, still sold for roughly $90–$120. Barclays analyst Blayne Curtis estimated the calculator cost $15–20 to manufacture, implying a profit margin above 50 percent. That cost figure is an analyst’s estimate; TI has never confirmed it. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) TechSpot — Washington Post analysis 2020 TI removes native programming from the CE. In May 2020, TI’s OS 5.5.x for the TI-84 Plus CE (OS 5.5.5 in the U.S., 5.5.1 in Europe; the same machine is sold in France as the TI-83 Premium CE) removed the ability to run programs written in assembly language or C — the languages of decades of community software — and blocked downgrading to an older OS that still could. TI said the change was made to “prioritize learning for students” and reduce the risk of exam cheating, after a video showed how to bypass test mode on an old OS version (5.2.2). TI-BASIC programs still ran; native code did not. Wikipedia — TI-84 Plus CE series 2020 arTIfiCE: the community restores what TI removed — unofficially. About four months after the OS 5.5 removal, the calculator community released arTIfiCE, an exploit that uses a flaw in one of TI’s own pre-installed apps to run assembly and C programs again on the new OS versions. TI never restored native support itself; it later patched the arTIfiCE flaw in OS 5.8.3; the exploit returned as arTIfiCE v2.0 and was patched again in OS 5.8.5, continuing the cat-and-mouse pattern. TI’s official answer to demand for a modern language was a separate model, the TI-84 Plus CE Python (2021), which adds Python while native code stays locked out. Wikipedia — TI-84 Plus CE series Unverified: “The TI-84 costs over $100 because exam boards require TI by name.” Evidence for: the College Board and ACT publish approved-calculator lists on which the TI-84 appears, schools standardize lessons and textbooks on TI models, and TI held about 93 percent of U.S. graphing-calculator sales in 2013–14, so families often have no practical alternative. Evidence against: the approved lists also name Casio, HP, and other brands — no board mandates TI — and no court or regulator has found that TI fixed prices or colluded with exam boards. The $15–20 manufacturing-cost figure behind the “price gouging” version of this claim is one analyst’s 2014 estimate, never confirmed by TI or by any audit. The dominance is documented; the mechanism commonly blamed for it is not proven. Did you know The original TI-84 Plus’s CPU outlived almost everything. Its Zilog Z80 was launched in July 1976 — it was already 28 years old when the TI-84 Plus shipped in 2004 — and Zilog kept the standalone chip in production until June 2024, a 48-year run. Source: All About Circuits — Z80 discontinued . In France, the TI-84 Plus CE is a TI-83. The same color CE hardware is sold to French students as the TI-83 Premium CE, with a French exam mode — which is why the 2020 programming removal landed first and hardest in France. Source: Wikipedia — TI-84 Plus CE series . The jailbreak that restored assembly hid in a geometry app. arTIfiCE works by exploiting a bug in Cabri Jr, the geometry application TI itself pre-installs on the CE — the locked door was opened with a key TI shipped in the box. Source: Cemetech — arTIfiCE discussion . Volunteers factored TI’s lock with spare computer time. After the first 512-bit signing key fell in 2009, the community set up the RSA Lattice Siever, a BOINC distributed-computing project, and factored the rest of TI’s calculator signing keys on donated home computers. Source: Wikipedia — signing key controversy . text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Windows Laptops, Desktops & Surface Windows PCs are the anti-Apple lesson and the anti-lesson in one family. Business laptops from Lenovo, Dell, and HP ship with full public service manuals — exploded diagrams, part numbers, and screw-by-screw removal steps, free for anyone to download. Desktops are the one platform that was designed from the start to be opened, built to a shared standard anyone can buy parts for. And then there is Microsoft’s Surface: a Windows PC glued shut like a phone. This page teaches all three worlds — how to read them, how to diagnose them, and what the documented record actually says about each. FCC ID A laptop rarely has one FCC ID of its own — it carries the FCC IDs of its radio modules. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC — the U.S. radio regulator) certifies things that transmit: the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth card, and the mobile-broadband card if one is fitted. The processor, the board, and the rest of the machine do not transmit, so they are not what the filing is about. The label method. Look on the bottom cover, under the battery on older machines, or under a service door. You will find either the module’s own FCC ID printed there, or a “Contains FCC ID: …” line naming the transmitter module inside. Lenovo states the method plainly in its ThinkPad Regulatory Notice: “The FCC ID for the wireless LAN and Bluetooth module is shown on the enclosure of your computer” — and the same notice lists each preinstalled module separately, for example FCC ID: PD97265NGU for the Intel 7265NGW wireless LAN/Bluetooth module and FCC ID: TX2RTL8192EEBT for the Realtek RTL8192EEBT module ( ThinkPad Regulatory Notice, Lenovo ). The first three characters are the grantee code — the company that holds the certification: PD9 is Intel, TX2 is Realtek. A current example, verified. The Intel Wi-Fi 6E AX211 module (model AX211NGW) fitted to many current laptops carries FCC ID: PD9AX211NG . Its filing on fccid.io is a radio test report — it describes the “Wireless Module installed in Convertible PC,” lists 802.11ax dual-band Wi-Fi 6E plus Bluetooth 5.2, and nothing about the laptop’s main board ( AX211 test report, fccid.io ; a second AX211 grant, fccid.io ). That is the point to remember: the filing covers the radio module, not the whole computer. Swap the Wi-Fi card and you have swapped the FCC ID that matters. Desktops usually have no FCC ID label at all unless a Wi-Fi card was installed — the same module rule applies. Surface devices carry their radio certifications the same way, module by module. What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for a radio module includes the documents the manufacturer is required to submit: external photos, internal photos of the module, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual for the module. These are public record at fccid.io . What you can typically find: Internal photos — of the radio card itself: its chips, shielding can, and antenna connectors Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which reveal operating bands, channels, and power levels Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the host machine What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. The twist for Windows PCs: on most platforms this site covers, the FCC filing is the deepest public document you will ever get. For business Windows laptops it is not. The FCC filing tells you about a radio card the size of a postage stamp. The manufacturer’s service manual — the subject of the next section — documents the entire machine, part by part. Read the filing to identify the radios; read the service manual to learn the computer. Exploded view On most device pages here, this section has to say “partial.” Here it can be real. Lenovo publishes its ThinkPad Hardware Maintenance Manuals (HMMs) as free PDFs, and they contain exploded parts illustrations keyed to numbered part lists. The current manual used for this walk is the ThinkPad L14 Gen 7 and ThinkPad L16 Gen 3 Hardware Maintenance Manual (Lenovo). Lenovo’s own description of the section, verbatim: “By the exploded view and the part list, you can find the images, names, and types of all the CRU/FRUs of your computer.” Two terms first. A FRU (Field Replaceable Unit) is a part the manufacturer defines as a replaceable whole — you do not repair the fan’s motor, you replace the fan assembly, and the FRU list gives that assembly its own number in the diagram. A CRU (Customer Replaceable Unit) is the subset Lenovo designates for the customer to swap, split in the manual into self-service and optional-service CRUs. Every callout number below is the manual’s own number for the ThinkPad L14 Gen 7. One machine, in build order Read the exploded view the way the machine comes apart — outside in. This is also the order of the manual’s own replacement chapter. Base cover assembly (callout 19) — the bottom panel. On the L14 Gen 7 the manual’s first hardware step is: “Loosen the 10 captive screws and pry at the right hinge area.” Captive means the screws stay in the cover — they cannot fall into the machine or get lost on the bench. Everything else is behind this one panel. Built-in battery (callout 24) — the flat battery pack across the front of the chassis, held by screws (the manual’s battery step lists three M2 screws), not glued. It comes out second because every later step is safer with it disconnected and removed. The coin-cell battery (callout 25) — the small round cell that keeps the clock and settings — sits nearby. Storage — M.2 solid-state drive (callout 16, with bracket 15) — the gum-stick drive in its slot. One screw and it slides out. A second, shorter M.2 2242 slot (callouts 13–14, on selected models) can hold a smaller drive or the wireless WAN module (callouts 21–22). Memory module (callout 20) — the RAM (random-access memory — the machine’s short-term workspace) stick in its socket. It unclips and lifts out at an angle. A socketed stick you can upgrade in minutes: hold this picture in mind when the Surface section below talks about soldered memory. Thermal fan (callout 8) and heat sink (callout 7) — the fan that moves the air, and the metal heat sink, listed by the manual as “Heat sink with thermal grease,” that carries heat off the processor. Cooling is two numbered parts, each replaceable on its own. System board (callout 10) — the main board, listed as “System board with solid-state-drive thermal pad.” Everything above plugs into it. Around it in the same drawing: the USB I/O board (callout 11) and its cable (callout 9), the speaker assembly (callout 23), the trackpad (callout 30) and its cable (callout 29), and the smart card reader (callout 17, selected models). Keyboard (callout 2) — a self-service CRU: the owner-tier part, removable from the top after loosening its screws, sitting in the keyboard bezel assembly (callout 3) with the power button (callouts 5a/5b, with or without fingerprint reader). Display assembly / display unit (callout 1) — the whole lid, one FRU. The manual gives the lid its own second exploded view (LCD FRUs): LCD bezel (1), LCD panel (2), camera and microphone module (3), EDP cable (5) — the cable that carries the picture — wireless LAN antenna assembly (7), hinges (8), and LCD cover assembly (9). The antennas for your Wi-Fi live in the lid, which is why the radio cables run up through the hinges. That is what a real parts book looks like: one drawing, every assembly numbered, every number named, and a parts-lookup page behind it for the orderable part numbers. Lenovo keeps the same series of manuals for older machines in its Hardware Maintenance Manuals library , and the current ThinkPad T14 Gen 7 Hardware Maintenance Manual follows the same structure — safety chapter, diagnostics chapter, exploded view and part list, then removal steps. The manual’s own safety warnings, verbatim From the L14 Gen 7 / L16 Gen 3 HMM, quoted exactly, before any part is removed: “DANGER: Before removing any CRU/FRU, turn off the computer, unplug all power cords from electrical outlets, disable the built-in battery, and then disconnect any interconnecting cables.” “CAUTION: Use only the Lenovo-authorized battery specified for the computer. Any other battery could ignite or explode.” “If the battery is incorrectly replaced, there is danger of an explosion. The battery contains a small amount of harmful substances.” — ThinkPad L14 Gen 7 and ThinkPad L16 Gen 3 Hardware Maintenance Manual , Lenovo (linked above). Follow them literally: disable the built-in battery in the BIOS setup before the base cover comes off, exactly as the manual’s “Disable Fast Startup and the built-in battery” step instructs. Surface: partial — no public parts book Surface: partial — no public parts book. For the Surface line there is no equivalent of the HMM above for the classic models: no manufacturer exploded view with a numbered FRU list that an owner can download and work from. What exists publicly for those machines is the FCC module filings (photos of the radios), teardown photography by repair shops, and — for newer models only — the service guides and replacement components Microsoft began publishing years later (see Repair reality, below). The exploded-view standard this site holds every device to cannot be met for Surface from the manufacturer’s own public documents, so this section does not pretend otherwise and does not fab

title: Wyze Cam v3 — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Wyze Cam v3 The $30 camera that proved good hardware doesn’t need a luxury price. An Ingenic T31 video SoC, color night vision, and — unusually for a budget camera — serial pads the community has already mapped. Wyze Cam v3. Product photo via retailer. FCC ID FCC ID: 2AUIUWYZEC3 (Grantee: 2AUIU = Wyze Labs). Internal photos in the filing show the board layout, including test pads near the main SoC. What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . What you can typically find: Internal photos — board layout, chip placement, shielding, antenna design Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which can reveal operating frequencies and power levels Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the device What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. What we reveal The FCC tells you what a device emits. We tell you what’s inside and how it works. Chip-level identification — every major IC named, with datasheet links where public documentation exists Board mapping — what connects to what, which test pads matter, where the debug interfaces hide What the manufacturer won’t tell you — undocumented features, hidden radios, silent telemetry, repair blockers Key Chips Ingenic T31 — video SoC with H.265 encoding and on-chip AI acceleration — the same family used across Wyze’s camera line. SPI NOR flash — holds the bootloader and firmware; readable in-circuit with a clip programmer. Wi-Fi module — 2.4 GHz 802.11 b/g/n. Teardown Notes The v3 splits into front and rear housings with screws under the base — no glue on the main seam, a pleasant surprise at this price. The lens assembly, IR filter, and image sensor sit on a small sensor board connected by ribbon cable to the main board. Community members examining the FCC internal photos identified three pads adjacent to the largest IC that appear to be a serial port — documented in a community firmware project’s issue tracker. Simple Entry Points Serial pads beside the SoC You need: A 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter (about $3) and fine probe wires or pogo pins. Open the housing and locate the three pads adjacent to the largest IC (the Ingenic SoC), as identified in community analysis of the FCC internal photos. Identify GND with a multimeter (continuity to the USB shield), then probe the remaining pads at 115200 baud for boot output to find TX. A serial console typically drops into the bootloader, where you can inspect the firmware layout and boot parameters. Illustrative example only — the log below shows the shape of the U-Boot output to expect on these pads; it is a reconstruction from the documented bootloader version, not a captured transcript from a specific unit. $ screen /dev/ttyUSB0 115200 U-Boot 2013.07 (Nov 04 2020 - 14:22:10) DRAM: 128 MiB SF: Detected MX25L12805D with page size 256 Bytes # (bootloader prompt — firmware layout visible here) Pad functions are community-identified, not manufacturer-documented; verify with a multimeter before connecting anything. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or Wyze’s own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the Wyze Cam v3 is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. Scope note: the Cam v3 went on sale in October 2020. The 2019 database exposure below is company-level and predates the v3; the 2023 and 2024 mix-ups happened in Wyze’s cloud services and affected the camera line as a whole. Entries are labeled accordingly. Year What happened Source 2019 Database of about 2.4 million users left open to the internet (company-level; predates the v3). Security firm Twelve Security found a Wyze database copy exposed online, and Wyze confirmed that user data “was not properly secured and left exposed from December 4th to December 26th” after an employee removed the database’s security protocols while working with it. Wyze confirmed the exposed data included customer emails, camera nicknames, Wi-Fi network names (SSIDs), device information, about 24,000 tokens for Alexa integrations, and body metrics (height, weight, gender) for 140 external beta testers of a new scale. Wyze said the database held no user passwords and no financial or government-regulated personal information. While investigating, Wyze logged all users out and unlinked third-party integrations to refresh tokens. BleepingComputer — Wyze exposes user data via unsecured database (Wyze confirmation) 2019–2022 Serious camera flaws reported in 2019, publicly disclosed in 2022 (v3 affected). Bitdefender told Wyze in March 2019 about three flaws across the Cam line: an authentication bypass (CVE-2019-9564) that could give an attacker control of the camera, a stack-based buffer overflow allowing remote code execution (CVE-2019-12266) that, chained with the bypass, exposed the live feed, and unauthenticated access to the contents of the camera’s SD card through a web server on port 80. Wyze patched the first two in September 2019 and November 2020 and the SD-card flaw on January 29, 2022; the Cam v3 was affected before firmware 4.36.8.32. Bitdefender published the full research only on March 29, 2022 — three years after its first report. The discontinued Cam v1 never received the SD-card fix; Wyze told v1 owners that continued use after February 1, 2022 was at their own risk, and later said the v1’s limited memory prevented patching. Bitdefender — vulnerabilities identified in Wyze Cam 2023 Web viewer showed some users other customers’ cameras (platform-level). On September 8, 2023, a Wyze engineer fixing a bug on the web viewing portal view.wyze.com deployed the wrong CloudFront caching setting. In Wyze’s own words, for about 40 minutes up to 2,300 users who logged in to the portal may have seen cameras from one of the 10 affected users who had also logged in during that time. Wyze took the portal down to investigate, brought it back hours later, and stated the incident did not affect the Wyze app or customers who only use the app. Wyze — Web View Service Advisory, 9/8/2023 (Wyze forum) 2024 Outage recovery mixed up about 13,000 users’ camera images (platform-level). After an AWS outage on the morning of February 16, 2024 took Wyze devices offline for hours, cameras reconnecting all at once overloaded a recently integrated third-party caching client library, which crossed device and user ID mappings. Wyze’s own final update confirms about 13,000 users received thumbnails from cameras that were not their own and 1,504 tapped on them; most taps only enlarged the thumbnail, but in a few cases an event video from another user’s camera was viewed. Live streams were not affected, and Wyze put the total impact at a little less than 0.25% of its users. Wyze said it removed the caching library, stopped using caching for user-device checks, and added a new layer of verification before users are connected to event videos. Wyze — outage and investigation of security issue, update 2/19/24 (Wyze forum) Unverified: “Wyze sends user data back to Alibaba Cloud in China.” Twelve Security, the firm that found the 2019 exposure, said there were “clear indications” that data was being sent back to the Alibaba Cloud in China, and gave that as one reason it published without notifying Wyze first ( Twelve Security’s claims, via Android Police ). Evidence for the claim: Twelve Security’s assertion alone; it published no proof that other researchers could check, and no regulator or second research team has corroborated transfers to Alibaba Cloud. Evidence against: Wyze co-founder Dongsheng Song denied it directly — “We do not send data to Alibaba Cloud” — and said Wyze does not share user data with any government; Wyze also showed that other Twelve Security claims in the same report were wrong, including that Wyze collected bone-density and daily protein-intake data ( Wyze’s response, via BleepingComputer ). The 2019 exposure itself is documented; the China-transfer claim is one firm’s unverified assertion against the company’s denial. Did you know Its night vision is in color, down to near-darkness. The v3’s Starlight Sensor and wide f/1.6 aperture record full-color video at night in environments up to 25 times darker than traditional cameras can manage, gathering twice the light. Source: Wyze Cam v3 user manual — Color Night Vision . Waterproofing arrived with the v3. The v3 carries an IP65 weather-resistance rating — sealed against dust and water jets — which made outdoor installation a headline feature of this generation; earlier Wyze Cams were indoor cameras. Source: Wyze Cam v3 user manual — specifications . It records around the clock with no subscription. With a microSD card (up to 256 GB), the v3 records continuously to local storage; the subscription Wyze sells is for cloud features, not for the camera to keep its own recordings. Source: HomeCamCafe — Wyze Cam v3 review . Wyze was founded by former Amazon employees. The Seattle startup behind this $30-class camera was started by people who came from Amazon — the same company whose cloud (AWS) outage set up the February 2024 mix-up above. Source: TechSpot — Wy

title: Xbox Family — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: What Microsoft sells you: controller parts (2023)
The storage question: socketed, but paired
The repair turn: As You Sow (2021)
text: Educational purpose. Everything on this page is published for education and research. Teardowns document hardware the author legally owns. Datasheets link to public sources. FCC filings are public record. Lawsuits and controversies cite public reporting. Nothing here is stolen, leaked, or confidential. If you use this information, you’re responsible for complying with the laws where you live. This isn’t legal advice — it’s a workbench. Xbox Family Four generations of Microsoft consoles — from a PC in a black box in 2001 to the Series X|S — and the most expensive hardware failure in gaming history. FCC ID FCC IDs vary by model and revision. Microsoft’s grantee code — the first three characters of every FCC ID it files, identifying the company the grant was issued to — is C3K . Check the label on your specific console and look it up at fccid.io — the filings include internal photos that are invaluable for hardware research. Verified on fccid.io from the grants themselves (grantee: Microsoft Corporation, One Microsoft Way, Redmond, WA): FCC ID: C3K1525 — the WLAN module (the Wi-Fi radio board) fitted in the original Xbox One. Grants dated June 19, 2013 and September 18, 2013 list the equipment notes as “WLAN MODULE” and the modular type as “Limited Single Modular” — in plain terms, this filing covers the radio board inside the console, not the whole console. FCC ID: C3K1914 — a Microsoft filing granted June 20, 2020, listed in the grant as a “Wireless Computer Device” covering 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands. It is one of the filings from the Series X|S launch generation; the grant text itself does not name a retail product, so we do not either. Other model-to-FCC-ID mappings are being verified and will be listed here. The label on your unit is the authority for your unit. What the FCC filing revealed The FCC filing for this device includes the documents manufacturers are required to submit: external photos, internal photos, test setup photos, RF test reports, and the user manual. These are public record at fccid.io . What you can typically find: Internal photos — board layout, chip placement, shielding, antenna design Block diagrams — sometimes included, showing the RF chain architecture Test reports — conducted and radiated emissions data, which can reveal operating frequencies and power levels Label placement — where the FCC ID lives on the device What the FCC filing does not include: schematics (usually withheld under confidentiality requests), firmware, bill of materials, or debug interface documentation. Exploded view Coverage: Partial — no public parts book. Microsoft publishes no console service manual and no illustrated parts book (a manufacturer document that draws every assembly apart and numbers every part) for Xbox consoles. There is no official exploded diagram to reproduce, and we do not invent one. What follows is a text exploded view — the assemblies in build order, outside in — built from the public record that does exist: the FCC filings above (whose exhibits include internal photos) and independent teardown documentation of the Series X, principally iFixit’s Xbox Series X teardown . Where a fact comes from a teardown rather than a Microsoft document, it is a teardown finding. Safety first. Microsoft’s own Xbox Series X|S product guide warns, verbatim: “Always select and use an appropriate AC power supply and/or power cord for your device. Failure to take the following precautions can result in serious personal injury or death from electric shock or fire or in damage to your device.” ( Microsoft Xbox Series X|S Product and Regulatory Guide .) In plain language: the power supply is inside these consoles, and a power supply can hold a stored electric charge in its capacitors (parts that store electricity) even after you unplug the console. Unplug the console and leave it unplugged before opening it, and treat the power supply unit itself as a sealed box to swap whole, not a board to probe. Shell (outer case and base). The plastic and metal skin of the tower. It protects the inside and shapes the airflow. On the Series X, teardown finding: the first screws are bright green T8 Torx screws, hidden under stickers and a trap door in the base. Fan and heatsink. The fan is the part that moves air; the heatsink is the metal block that soaks heat away from the hot chips. Series X teardown findings: one large 130 mm fan at the top, exhausting upward, and a copper vapor-chamber heatsink (a flat sealed chamber that spreads heat evenly) bolted over the main processor, with an aluminium centre chassis between the boards that also carries heat away. Together they are most of the volume inside the case — this console is mostly a cooling system with a computer inside it. Power supply unit (PSU). The box that turns wall power into the low-voltage power the boards run on. Series X teardown findings: an internal unit whose main rail supplies up to 21.25 amps at 12 volts (255 watts), plus a 60-watt peripheral output — 315 watts in total — and which uses polymer capacitors, a longer-lived type, to filter its 12-volt output. Optical drive (Series X only). The disc drive that reads game discs and 4K Blu-ray discs. The Series S has no disc drive. Series X teardown finding: the drive is the same model used in the Xbox One S and Xbox One X — and its circuit board is paired to the mainboard (see Repair reality ). Mainboard with APU. The main circuit board, and on it the APU (accelerated processing unit — the single chip that combines the CPU, which runs the game code, and the GPU, which draws the picture). Almost everything else plugs into or solders onto this board, including the HDMI port (the socket your TV cable plugs into) at its edge. Storage. The drive that holds the operating system and your games. On Series X|S this is an NVMe SSD (a small, very fast solid-state drive with no moving parts) in a standard M.2 2230 socket — a short card held by one screw, sitting under thermal compound (heat-transfer paste) on the board sandwich, per the teardown. It is mechanically removable. Whether a replacement will actually work is a separate question, answered in Repair reality . Read this view next to Diagnosis & faults : the view shows you what each part is, not which part has failed. Diagnosis & faults Xbox consoles diagnose themselves first in software. Microsoft’s own recovery environment is the Xbox Startup Troubleshooter — a recovery menu built into the console that loads before the main system software, so it works even when the console will not boot to its home screen. Getting to it (from Microsoft’s startup-error guidance): power the console off and unplug the power cord; wait 30 seconds and plug it back in; press and hold the Pair button and the Eject button, then press the Xbox button on the console; keep holding Pair and Eject for 10–15 seconds, through two power-up tones. On the Series S, which has no Eject button, hold Pair alone. The console powers up straight into the Startup Troubleshooter. Microsoft’s pages: Xbox startup error support and Perform an offline system update . Error-code driven diagnosis. When startup fails, the console shows an error code (a short code such as E101 or E102). The code is the diagnosis: Microsoft’s startup-error guidance routes each code to a fix order — restart, then reset from the Startup Troubleshooter choosing “Keep games and apps” (which resets the operating system and deletes possibly corrupted data without deleting your games or apps), then an offline system update, then a full factory restore, then service. Codes in the E100–E102 family are, in Microsoft’s framing, problems installing the latest console operating-system update. The Offline System Update (OSU). If the console cannot download or install its update normally, Microsoft publishes an offline route: on a Windows PC, download the Offline System Update file — OSU1 for Series X|S and most Xbox One models — from the Xbox Support page above, put the extracted $SystemUpdate folder on a USB flash drive of at least 6 GB formatted as NTFS (a Windows file-system format), plug the drive into the console, and choose “Offline system update” in the Startup Troubleshooter. The original 2013 Xbox One is the exception: depending on the system version it is stuck on, it may need an older file (OSU2 or OSU3) first. Take OSU files only from Microsoft’s support page — the file changes with each system release. The hardware failures independents actually see (repair-community documented — these are the fault patterns independent repair shops report on their benches, not a Microsoft list): HDMI port damage — the console powers on but the TV shows no signal, or the picture only works with the cable held at an angle. The port is soldered to the mainboard and its pins bend when a console is moved with the cable plugged in. Shops also report failure of the small HDMI retimer chip (the chip that cleans up the video signal on its way to the port) when the port itself looks undamaged. Sources: iAssist Series X|S repair page , iFixForU Series X repair cost guide . Fan and cooling failure — a normally quiet console turns loud, or shuts down mid-game: dust packed into the top exhaust and heatsink, dried-out thermal compound, or a failing fan bearing. Fixed by a full clean and thermal service, per the same repair-community sources. Power supply failure — a completely dead console, or one that dies after a power surge. Because the PSU is internal on Series X|S, One S and One X, there is no external brick to swap-test; the unit inside has to be tested or replaced.
