Specifications SoC: Intel DHCE2652 (Puma 6) — Atom 652 (1 core / 2 threads) 1.2 GHz x86 + ARM1176-class ARMv6 (~450 MHz, DOCSIS side) RAM: 512 MB (2× Samsung K4B2G1646B DDR3) MoCA: 2.0 Flash: 128 MB (Spansion S34ML01G200TFI00) DOCSIS: 3.0, 24 downstream × 8 upstream channels Wi-Fi: 2.4 GHz ( Qualcomm Atheros AR9381 ) + 5 GHz ( Qualcomm Atheros QCA9880 ), 802.11ac Ethernet: 4× Gigabit ( Broadcom BCM53124S switch) Voice: 2× telephone ports ( DSP Group DCX81 DECT/VoIP SoC) USB: 2× USB 2.0 ports Power: TI TPS54328 buck regulator Controversies & Legal The Puma 6 latency defect The Intel Puma 6 chipset at the heart of the XB3 has a documented hardware flaw: under certain traffic patterns (bursts of small TCP/UDP packets), an internal lookup table fills up, causing severe latency spikes and jitter. This ruins online gaming, VoIP calls, and other real-time applications. In 2017, a class action lawsuit ( Reyna v. ARRIS International plc , Case No. 3:17-cv-01834, N.D. Cal.) was filed over the Arris SURFboard SB6190 — a retail modem using the same Puma 6 chip. The suit alleged Arris knew about the defect but sold the modem as “the fastest and most reliable” anyway. Intel released firmware mitigations, but the underlying hardware limitation remained. Note: The class action specifically concerned the SB6190 retail modem, not the TG1682G gateway. However, the Puma 6 latency flaw is a property of the chipset itself and affects all devices built on it, including the XB3. Sources: The Register , Class action complaint (PDF) Comcast rental fees The XB3 is a rented gateway — Comcast charges subscribers a monthly fee (historically around $14–15/month) for the device. Critics have long argued that the cumulative rental cost far exceeds the retail price of an equivalent modem, and that Comcast has made it difficult for customers to use their own equipment for voice service (which requires the telephony features of gateways like the XB3). Specific fee amounts and policies change over time; check Comcast’s current terms. Default credentials The TG1682G shipped with well-known default admin credentials (admin/password), documented in the FCC filing and widely published. While standard for ISP equipment of this era, default credentials on millions of deployed gateways represent a significant attack surface. The Full Record Everything in this timeline is documented — a court outcome, a regulator’s action, a published security analysis, or Comcast’s and Arris’s own statements — and each entry links its source. Where a popular claim about the XB3 is not proven, it is labeled Unverified at the end, with the evidence on both sides. Year What happened Source 2014 Default admin credentials. The TG1682G shipped with the well-known default admin login admin/password, documented in the filed manual and widely published. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) FCC filing UIDTG1682 2014–2015 The home-hotspot lawsuit: Grear v. Comcast. In December 2014, San Francisco customers Toyer Grear and Jocelyn Harris sued Comcast (Case No. 4:14-cv-05333-JSW, N.D. Cal.), alleging Comcast turned the second radio in rented home gateways into the public “xfinitywifi” hotspot network without their authorization — shifting electricity and network costs onto subscribers and adding security risk. Comcast said it disagreed and that the program benefits customers. The case never reached the merits: on March 3, 2015, Judge Jeffrey White stayed the lawsuit and compelled arbitration, holding that the arbitration clause in the plaintiffs’ service agreement covered the claims. Top Class Actions — judge stays hotspot case, compels arbitration ; Fast Company — the original suit, December 2014 2016 The Puma 6 latency defect is documented in public. Users on the DSLReports forums measured the spikes first; in December 2016 The Register reported the mechanism — the Puma 6’s x86 processor stalls on a high-priority maintenance task every couple of seconds, adding at least 200 ms of latency and dropping about six per cent of packets over time — and Intel acknowledged a software issue affecting latency and said a fix was being prepared. Community testers later built a dedicated DSLReports Puma 6 test and maintained do-not-buy lists of Puma 6 models, this gateway’s TG1682 family among them (community testing, not a regulator finding). (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) The Register — Puma 6 latency, December 2016 2017 Reyna v. ARRIS filed over the SB6190. On March 31, 2017, Carlos Reyna’s class action was filed in the Northern District of California over the retail Arris SURFboard SB6190 — a different box from the XB3, built on the same Intel Puma 6 chip — alleging Arris sold the modem as fast and reliable without disclosing the latency defect. (Details in Controversies & Legal above.) The Register — the lawsuit, April 2017 2018 Intel gives the flaw a CVE: CVE-2017-5693. In advisory INTEL-SA-00097, published with the CVE on July 31, 2018 — more than eighteen months after the latency reporting — Intel stated that firmware in the Puma 5, 6, and 7 series “might experience resource depletion or timeout, which allows a network attacker to create a denial of service via crafted network traffic.” In plain language: the same weakness that made these gateways lag under ordinary small-packet bursts could be triggered deliberately, with a relatively small packet payload, to knock a targeted modem offline or degrade it. Intel said it was working with ISPs and manufacturers to deliver mitigating firmware, which could only reach rented gateways like the XB3 through the ISP. Intel advisory INTEL-SA-00097 2018–2021 How Reyna actually ended: Arris won. The case was not settled for a payout. On August 10, 2018, the district court certified a class of California SB6190 purchasers (buyers on or after October 1, 2015). On August 20, 2019, Judge Lucy Koh granted Arris summary judgment on the California class claims. The plaintiffs (by then led by Greg Knowles and Brian Alexander) appealed, and on May 14, 2021 the Ninth Circuit affirmed (Knowles v. ARRIS International plc, No. 19-17468): the panel held, among other things, that the plaintiffs had failed to raise a material issue of fact that the SB6190 failed to meet a minimum level of quality for the implied-warranty claim, and that summary judgment on the false-advertising and failure-to-disclose claims was also proper. The defect’s existence and the lawsuit’s failure are both part of the record. Order granting summary judgment, August 20, 2019 (Justia) ; Knowles v. ARRIS, Ninth Circuit, May 14, 2021 2020 Intel sold the Puma business. On July 31, 2020, MaxLinear completed its acquisition of Intel’s Home Gateway Platform Division — the DOCSIS silicon line that includes Puma — for $150 million in cash, under an agreement dated April 5, 2020. The chip in this gateway has not been an Intel product since; its later descendants (Puma 8, and the ARM-based Puma 9 announced in 2026) are MaxLinear designs. title: The DMCA Medical-Device Repair Exemption Is Under Threat — BareBoard
headings: The DMCA medical-device repair exemption is under threat — comments due December 7
What the exemption does — and does not — cover
text: The DMCA medical-device repair exemption is under threat — comments due December 7 There is a federal rule that says you may pick the software lock on your own medical device to repair it. That rule is an exemption, renewed every three years, and this cycle the Copyright Office has singled it out: it is the only existing exemption the Register intends not to renew automatically. If you own a powered wheelchair — or you repair one — this is the legal hinge under much of the work this site teaches. The first round of public comments is due December 7, 2026 . This page explains what the exemption does, what losing it would mean, and where to comment. What Section 1201 is Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) makes it illegal to circumvent a technological protection measure — a software lock, encryption, or access control — that guards a copyrighted work. The law was written for piracy, but it reaches much further: the firmware inside your wheelchair, your tractor, or your car is copyrighted software, and the lock that stops you reading its fault codes is a technological protection measure. Every three years, the Copyright Office runs a triennial rulemaking in which the public can ask for exemptions — specific, lawful uses that the ban should not cover. One long-standing exemption covers diagnosis, maintenance, and repair of medical devices : circumventing a lock to diagnose or repair a device you lawfully own. Without it, reading a wheelchair’s fault codes through a locked interface, or using an owner tool to back up its settings, could be a federal copyright violation even though the chair is yours. What is happening now In the tenth triennial proceeding, the notice of proposed rulemaking issued on October 28, 2026, the Register of Copyrights intends to recommend renewal of all existing exemptions — except one. The medical-device repair exemption drew meaningful opposition, and it will be treated as a new petition, meaning its supporters must make the case for it from scratch. It is the only exemption singled out this way. The timetable: December 7, 2026 — first-round comments from supporters are due. February 22, 2027 — opposition comments are due. March 22, 2027 — replies are due. The proceeding is at the Copyright Office: copyright.gov/1201/2027 . What the exemption does — and does not — cover It covers: circumventing a software lock on a medical device you lawfully own, to diagnose, maintain, or repair it. That is the legal basis for an owner reading their own chair’s fault codes, backing up its settings before a module swap, or using an owner-built tool such as our Chair Control to read what the dealer’s programmer reads. It does not cover: making or distributing the tools that do the circumventing. Section 1201’s anti-trafficking ban has no exemption, and the Librarian of Congress has no authority to exempt it. Owners may legally pick the lock; selling them the pick is still banned. Our PMD law section states this half-gap plainly. It does not cover: piracy, or copying the manufacturer’s firmware. The exemption is for repair of your own device, nothing else. What losing it would mean If the exemption lapses, the legal ground under owner repair of medical devices narrows sharply. Repairing your own chair would still be protected in some ways — the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act still limits warranty voiding, and state wheelchair repair laws in eight states still require manufacturers to provide firmware and tools — but the federal permission to get past a software lock to diagnose your own device would be gone. The practical effect is to hand the manufacturer a copyright argument against any owner or independent shop that works around a lock, even when the work is ordinary repair. The permanent fix, stalled A permanent statutory exception would end the three-year cycle: the federal Wheelchair Right to Repair Act (H.R. 5039), introduced August 26, 2025, would write a repair exception into law. It has not advanced — no movement was found in the last two weeks of November 2026. Until it does, the exemption — and the comment deadline — is the fight that matters. What to do before December 7 Comments go to the Copyright Office through its proceeding page at copyright.gov/1201/2027 . What helps most is concrete, first-hand evidence: that you own a device, that a software lock blocked a repair, what the lock cost you in time or money, and what happened when the repair was delayed. A short, specific, true account from an owner or a repair shop is worth more than a long general argument. Say plainly that you support renewal of the medical-device repair exemption. Sources Tenth triennial Section 1201 proceeding — U.S. Copyright Office: copyright.gov/1201/2027 . NewsNet 1097, notice of proposed rulemaking, October 28, 2026 — U.S. Copyright Office: copyright.gov . October 2026 summary — Copyright Alliance: copyrightalliance.org . On this site: The Shield: right-to-repair law ; the PMD law section ; Chair Control . BareBoard — free hardware education. The exemption is the permission slip for fixing your own chair. It expires unless someone defends it. December 7 is the date.

title: DMCA Policy — BareBoard
text: DMCA Policy How we handle copyright complaints. Last updated: October 7, 2026. Our approach BareBoard respects the intellectual property rights of others and complies with the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. § 512). We will respond to legitimate takedown notices and have a designated agent for receiving them. We believe our content — educational teardown documentation, commentary, and reference archival of manufacturer-published technical documents — is consistent with fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107. However, we take all good-faith complaints seriously and will review each one individually. Designated DMCA agent Under 17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(2) and 37 CFR § 201.38, a service provider’s designated agent must be identified by name, physical address, telephone number, and email address, and that designation must be filed with the U.S. Copyright Office. BareBoard’s formal designation has not yet been filed, so the complete agent listing the regulation requires is not published here yet — we will not invent one. Until the filing is in place, notifications of claimed infringement should be sent to: Email: contact@bareboard.org Subject line: DMCA Takedown Notice Filing a takedown notice To be effective under 17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(3), your notice must include: Identification of the copyrighted work claimed to have been infringed (or a representative list if multiple works). Identification of the material claimed to be infringing, with enough detail for us to locate it (specific URLs). Your contact information: name, address, telephone number, and email address. A statement that you have a good-faith belief that the disputed use is not authorized by the copyright owner, its agent, or the law. A statement that the information in the notification is accurate and, under penalty of perjury, that you are authorized to act on behalf of the copyright owner. Your physical or electronic signature. What happens next Upon receiving a valid notice, we will: Review the complaint promptly. Remove or disable access to the identified material if the complaint appears valid. Notify the affected party where applicable. Please note: filing a false takedown notice may expose you to liability under 17 U.S.C. § 512(f). Counter-notice procedure If you believe your material was removed in error, you may file a counter-notice to contact@bareboard.org including: Identification of the removed material and its prior location (URL). Your contact information: name, address, telephone number, and email address. A statement under penalty of perjury that you have a good-faith belief the material was removed by mistake or misidentification. A statement consenting to the jurisdiction of the federal district court for your judicial district (or any U.S. district if outside the United States). Your physical or electronic signature. Upon receiving a valid counter-notice, we may restore the material within 10–14 business days unless the original complainant notifies us that they have filed a court action. Datasheet archive Our datasheet archive hosts manufacturer-published technical documents for educational and reference purposes. Each document includes original source attribution. If you are a rights holder and believe a specific document should not be hosted here, contact us at contact@bareboard.org and we will review the request promptly. See our Copyright Policy for more detail. For the repair exemptions that keep independent service lawful — and the defense framework built on them — see The Shield: Right-to-Repair Law . Not legal advice This page is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Consult a licensed attorney for guidance on your specific situation.

title: The Five Eras — BareBoard
headings: The 2000s — The Hyper-Integration & Mobile Dawn Era (2000–2009)
The 2020s — The Multi-Die & Security Mesh Era (2020–today)
text: The Five Eras How hardware went from open to sealed — and what we do about it. Hardware history moves in decades: each one redraws what a repairer can see, probe, and document. Eras are a lens, not a cage. Every entry on BareBoard carries three facets — Era (this page), Domain (medical, civic, infrastructure, transport, financial, consumer, industrial), and Status (public / public-research / sealed / excluded — the Registry ). And one rule stands above all of them: an era never makes a sealed document fair game. The 1980s — The Open-Silicon & Blueprint Era (1980–1989) What changed: chips shipped with full public datasheets; the IBM PC Technical Reference — sold separately, not in the box — included complete circuit diagrams; repair manuals were public; parts were through-hole and probe-able. What it means for repair: repair was normal, expected, documented. The golden age. What BareBoard does: preserves this documentation before it vanishes. The Library's first shelf exists because of this era. The 1990s — The Obfuscation & Encapsulation Era (1990–1999) What changed: surface-mount components, multi-layer boards, PCI configuration spaces; game consoles add security chips; baseband processors reach phones (2G GSM); firmware becomes a replaceable blob; service manuals stop shipping with the product and go internal. What it means for repair: the schematic stops coming in the box. Repair becomes a specialty instead of a given. What BareBoard does: autopsies the transition — the last devices you could fully understand, and the first you couldn't. The 2000s — The Hyper-Integration & Mobile Dawn Era (2000–2009) What changed: whole boards collapse into system-on-chips; baseband and application processors merge into single-chip smartphone SoCs; SSD controllers seal their flash translation layers; probing live signals needs real (and expensive) gear. What it means for repair: the "chip" you could read a datasheet for is now a city you can't map. What BareBoard does: the Watchmen W³ R2 board — audit the tools that can still see inside, and trust only the open ones. The 2010s — The Multi-Ring & SoC Era (2010–2019) What changed: hidden management cores run beneath the OS ( Intel CSME , AMD PSP , Apple's Secure Enclave ); hardware parts-pairing locks components to boards; the sealed register map becomes a business model. What it means for repair: documentation isn't just missing — it's deliberately withheld. The Registry's sealed column is mostly this decade. What BareBoard does: compiles original references from public research (the SEP, PSP, and CSME manuals in the Library ). We document the phenomenon honestly. We never chase the sealed documents. The 2020s — The Multi-Die & Security Mesh Era (2020–today) What changed: chiplets and interposers, security modules welded to boards, real-time sensor silicon (e.g. the Apple Vision Pro's R1), anti-circumvention design as a default. What it means for repair: the bench needs better tools — and audited ones. What BareBoard does: the Most Wanted board lives here. Nominate a device, autopsy a retired unit, publish verified findings. Where an entry lives is decided by what it is (section), who it matters to (domain), and what state it's in (status). The decade tells you when. Start browsing: Top 100 · Most Wanted · Registry . “Nobody who uses XML knows what they are doing.” — Chris Wenham

title: Foundry — BareBoard
text: Foundry A layered reference for understanding hardware from the transistor up. Four levels, from silicon to complete systems — each one built on the last. Level 0 — Silicon The transistor layer: foundries, lithography nodes, process technology, and the secure elements baked into silicon. Fabs & lithography nodes Secure elements & roots of trust Level 1 — Interconnect Board-level documentation: publicly released schematics, board identifiers, bus standards, and repair references. Bus standards & protocols Level 2 — Controllers Peripheral and interface controllers: the chips that move data between silicon and systems, and the firmware that runs below the OS. Firmware & flash Level 3 — Systems Complete systems where hardware failure has human consequences: medical devices, industrial controllers, avionics. Listed for awareness and lawful research on retired units only. title: Glossary — BareBoard
text: Glossary Every technical term we use, in plain language. If a term is missing, that's a bug — tell us on Contribute . Term Plain meaning Datasheet The manufacturer's public document describing a chip: what it does, its pins, its limits. The most valuable public document in repair. Schematic A map of how components are wired together on a board. Tells you what connects to what. PCB Printed circuit board — the physical board components are soldered onto. Register A chip's internal control slot. Writing a value to a register changes what the chip does. MMIO Memory-mapped I/O — a way chips expose their registers as if they were memory addresses the CPU can read and write. Firmware The software running inside a chip or device, below the operating system. JTAG A hardware debug interface on chips, used by factories and repair benches. Often locked after manufacturing. e-fuse / OTP One-time-programmable hardware fuses inside a chip. Once "burned," they can't be undone — they set permanent security states. PMIC Power management IC — the chip that decides which parts of a board get which voltage, and when. SoC System on a chip — CPU, GPU, memory controller, and more on one piece of silicon. SEP / Secure Enclave Apple's isolated security coprocessor. Holds keys and biometric data so the main processor can't read them. PLC Programmable logic controller — the industrial computer that runs pumps, motors, and whole plants. FTL Flash translation layer — the controller layer in an SSD or flash device that maps logical addresses to physical flash locations, and handles wear leveling, garbage collection, and retiring bad blocks. VSC Vendor-specific command — a hidden command a manufacturer adds to a standard interface, outside the public specification. NDA Non-disclosure agreement — a contract that keeps a document secret. Sealed documents are not public documents. I²C / SPI / UART Three common low-speed ways chips talk to each other over short wires. DFU Device firmware update — a mode that lets you reflash a chip. Its presence is a good openness sign. Autopsy report BareBoard's core document: what's actually inside a device, verified and dated. “Never attribute to funny hardware that which can be adequately explained by broken locking.” — Erik Quanstrom

title: The 16-Pin Connector That Keeps Melting — BareBoard
headings: When a card or power supply is salvageable
text: The 16-pin connector that keeps melting Four years after RTX 4090 owners first reported melted power plugs, the same failure is back — and it is no longer only a flagship problem. In November 2026 alone, more than ten melted GeForce 16-pin connectors were reported, spanning the RTX 5090 down to the RTX 5070, and even an RTX 4090. This page is the failure analysis: what melts, why it melts, how to inspect your own connector in thirty seconds, and when a melted card or power supply can still be saved. It complements our GPU Repair hub, which carries the full documented record back to 2022 and the CPSC recall — this page is the November 2026 evidence and the inspection procedure. What the connector is High-end NVIDIA cards since the RTX 40 series take power through one 16-pin plug. The original version is called 12VHPWR : twelve power pins carrying 12 volts, plus four small sense pins that tell the card what the cable can deliver. It is rated for up to 600 watts through a plug smaller than the 6- and 8-pin plugs it replaced. The revised version, 12V-2x6 , arrived with the ATX 3.1 power supply standard in September 2023. The revision shortened the sense pins, so a plug that is not fully seated should receive no power at all — a fail-safe against the exact failure that melted the first plugs. The November 2026 cases show the failure mode is not gone. What melts, and why What melts is the plastic housing of the plug and socket, and sometimes the metal pins inside it. The cause is heat from electrical resistance at a bad contact. The chain works like this: A pin does not make full contact. The plug is not fully seated, a retaining clip is broken, debris is in the socket, or the cable pulls sideways on the plug. Less contact means more resistance. The same current forced through a smaller contact area heats that spot. Heat softens the plastic. The housing deforms, the contact gets worse, the heat rises further. The loop feeds itself until the plastic melts and, in the worst cases, chars. The key point is that this is a contact failure, not a wattage failure. A 5070-class card draws far less power than a 5090, but if only one or two pins are carrying the load, those pins overheat anyway. That is why the November cases include lower-power cards, and why “only 5090s at 600 watts” was never the full story. The November 7, 2026 case makes the mechanism concrete. A Galax RTX 4080 SG owner found melted plastic and carbon deposits on the 12VHPWR housing after freezes and black screens in Cyberpunk 2077. The retaining clips were broken on both the cable plug and a Cooler Master MWE Gold V2 1050W ATX 3.1 power supply. With nothing holding the plug firmly home, vibration shifted it, the contact area shrank, and the connector heated locally until it melted. The card had been warning the owner first — freezes and black screens under load are the symptoms of a connector going bad, and they should be treated as a stop-and-inspect signal, not a driver problem. The November 2026 case list VideoCardz documented more than ten melted GeForce power connector and cable cases shared in November 2026 alone, drawn from Reddit, Weibo, Taiwanese forums, Facebook, and the Thermal Grizzly community. The spread: RTX 5090 and 5090 D — melted GPU sockets and melted adapters. RTX 5080, 5070 Ti, and 5070 — melted connectors on cards well below flagship power draw. RTX 4090 — the original melting card, still appearing in the case list four years on. Damage on both ends — cases include melted GPU sockets, melted adapters, and damaged power-supply-side connectors. A melted PSU-side connector means the power supply itself is part of the failure, not just the cable. No manufacturer and no regulator has published an overall failure rate for the connector, so anyone who quotes you one is inventing it. What the case list does prove is that the failure is ongoing, that it spans the whole RTX 50 stack, and that the 12V-2x6 revision did not end it. The thirty-second inspection Do this with the PC switched off and unplugged. Do it when you first install a card, after moving the PC, and any time the card crashes or black-screens under load. Look for a gap. The plug must sit fully home in the socket, with no visible gap between the plug body and the socket. A gap means it is not seated — push it in firmly and evenly until it is flush. Listen for the latch click. The plug has a retaining latch (a small clip that snaps over a tab on the socket). When the plug seats, the latch clicks. No click, no seat. If the clip is broken — on the plug or on the socket — the plug can walk out with vibration, exactly as in the November 7 case. A broken clip is a failed connector: replace the cable, and if the socket’s clip is broken, have the socket replaced. Check the bend. Do not bend the cable sharply right at the plug. Give it a gentle run of cable first; cable makers commonly specify about 35 mm before any bend. A sharp bend at the plug pulls the pins sideways and unseats them. Look and smell. Brown discoloration, softened or shiny plastic, a burnt smell, or black carbon deposits mean the connector has already overheated. Stop using the card. This is a fire hazard, not a quirk. Seat the cable before the card. NVIDIA’s own guidance, from its November 2022 statement, is to plug the power cable into the card first, firmly and evenly, before installing the card into the machine. It is easier to seat the plug properly when the card is in your hands than when it is wedged in a case. Use the right cable. Use the cable that came with your power supply, or the card’s own adapter. Do not use third-party angled adapters: the CableMod angled 12VHPWR adapters were recalled by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission on February 8, 2024 (recall 24-112, about 25,300 units, 272 reports of loosening, overheating, and melting). If you own one, the CPSC instruction still stands: stop using it. When a card or power supply is salvageable A melted connector is a repair, not an obituary — but only if the damage stopped at the connector. Card socket melted, board otherwise fine: the 16-pin socket is a soldered part, and replacing it is routine work for a board-level repair shop. One U.S. repair shop reported fixing on the order of a hundred melted-connector RTX 4090s a month. Do not power the card again until the socket is replaced and the board is checked for heat damage to nearby parts. Only the cable plug melted: replace the cable with the power supply maker’s own cable for that exact model. Then inspect the card’s socket closely — a melted plug usually leaves heat damage in the socket too. PSU-side connector damaged: replace the power supply, not just the cable. A damaged PSU-side connector means the power supply’s own socket has been overheated, and it cannot be trusted to hold contact again. Never open the power supply itself — it stores lethal charge even unplugged. Not salvageable: if the heat spread into the board — charred circuit board, melted solder on nearby components, or a burnt smell from the board itself rather than just the connector — the repair gets expensive fast, and a shop should quote it before you commit. A card that still black-screens after a socket replacement has damage beyond the connector. Sources “Here are all the melted GeForce power connector and cable cases reported in November alone” — VideoCardz, November 2026: videocardz.com . “Damaged 12VHPWR connector triggers RTX 4080 PC crashes” — Nerds Magazine, November 7, 2026: nerdsmagazine.com . 12V-2x6 connector explainer — OMC Network forum, November 18, 2026: forum.omc.network . On this site: GPU Repair — the full 16-pin connector record from 2022, the CPSC recall 24-112, and the board-level repair levels. BareBoard — free hardware education. If the plug does not click, it is not seated. If it smells burnt, stop using it.

title: Spot a Fake or Stripped GPU Before You Pay — BareBoard
headings: Spot a fake or stripped GPU before you pay
What about the rest of the market?
text: Spot a fake or stripped GPU before you pay Graphics cards cost more than ever — an RTX 5090 sells on the street for around $4,900 against a $1,999 manufacturer’s price — and where the price goes, the fakes follow. In November 2026, buyers reported receiving empty shells, cards with their chips harvested out, and a “broken RTX 3090” that turned out to contain a decade-old Radeon board sawed in half. This page is the inspection guide: the tells that give a fake away, and the in-person test that catches what your eyes cannot. It builds on the counterfeit record in our GPU Repair hub; everything here is new evidence from the November 2026 wave. Why now Three things collided. First, the memory shortage (see our repair-economics page ) pushed street prices to 1.6 to 2.5 times the manufacturer’s price, so a single card is worth thousands. Second, AI-server operators have been harvesting GPU chips and memory off boards, leaving “corpse cards” — boards with the valuable silicon removed — that get sold on as faulty or for repair. Third, the secondhand market runs on trust and photos, and a photo cannot show you what is inside the shroud. Engadget published a full “how to spot a fake GPU” guide on November 10, 2026, after buyers reported receiving pasta and rice, photos of GPUs, and empty shells instead of cards. The sawed Radeon inside a 3090 The clearest case of the month came from repair creator Blighted Agent, who bought a “$50 broken RTX 3090 Founders Edition” on Facebook Marketplace and opened it to find a decade-old Gigabyte Radeon R9 280 circuit board, physically sawed in half, wedged inside the NVIDIA frame. The tells, in order of how easy they are to spot: The NVLink cover was glued shut. NVLink is the bridge connector on top of high-end NVIDIA cards. On a real 3090 Founders Edition it is a proper fitted cover. On this fake it had been glued shut — because there was nothing underneath it to show. Hollow display and power bays. The display output sockets and the power connector area were empty shells: no circuit board behind them, nothing to plug into. The solder mask gave it away. Solder mask is the colored coating on a circuit board, usually printed with the maker’s name and model. The board inside read “GIGABYTE GV-R928XOC-3GD REV: 2.0” in glossy print — a Radeon R9 280, a card from 2013, not a GeForce RTX 3090 from 2020. Any board whose printed model does not match the card being sold is a fake, full stop. The weight was wrong. A real 3090 Founders Edition is a heavy card — a large heatsink, a full board, memory chips all around the die. A hollow shell with half a donor board inside weighs noticeably less. If a card feels light for its size, open it or walk away. The stripped “corpse cards” A second pattern is harder to spot and more expensive. Russian repair specialist Vik-On reports counterfeit RTX 4090 “corpse cards” sold as faulty or for repair, with fake GPU cores and fake memory chips soldered on — convincing enough that even a professional inspecting the die by eye may not spot it. In September 2026, Tom’s Hardware reported two German buyers who lost about $5,000 on RTX 5090s whose GPU cores and memory had been physically removed. An Instagram reel of an empty INNO3D RTX 5090 shell drew 15,000 likes on November 3, 2026. The story sellers use is always the same: “sold as faulty, for repair.” That listing type is the cover. A genuine faulty card still has its chips on it; a harvested card never works again, and no repair can fix a missing die. Treat every “for repair” listing of a high-end card as a harvested card until proven otherwise. The tells, before you pay Read the board, not the shroud. The plastic cover and the backplate are the easiest parts to fake or swap. Ask for a photo of the bare board, or open the card yourself before paying. Check the printed model number on the solder mask against the card being sold, and check that the GPU die markings match the model. Check the NVLink cover and the ports. A glued NVLink cover, ports with nothing behind them, or a power socket with no board under it are immediate walk-away signs. Weigh it in your hand. Compare against the manufacturer’s stated weight for the model. A card that is much lighter than it should be is hollow or harvested. Look for the older tells too. From the earlier counterfeit record: screws showing tool wear on a “new” card, broken or missing seals, and memory chips whose printing looks oddly uniform or wrong for the model — the painted GDDR memory scam of 2023, where ex-mining cards were sold as new after their memory chips were painted to hide heat yellowing. Relabeled cards — RTX 3080 and 3090 boards re-marked and sold as RTX 4090s — were documented in 2025. Price is a tell. A 5090 at a fraction of the $4,900 street price is not a bargain; it is a warning. Scammers price just low enough to make you hurry. The in-person test procedure Never buy a used high-end card sight unseen if you can avoid it. If you can test in person, do this, in order, before money changes hands: Buy through a channel with returns, and test immediately, inside the return window. This is the single most important rule. A seller who refuses a return window is telling you something. Run GPU-Z (free, from TechPowerUp). Since version 2.12 it flags a known class of counterfeits — old chips whose BIOS lies about what they are — with a [FAKE] tag. It does not catch everything: it will not catch a harvested board or every re-marked die. So also compare the die name, memory type, and memory size it reports against the specification for your exact model. Run a sustained load test. A benchmark or game at full load for at least 15 minutes, watching for visual artifacts (wrong pixels, repeating patterns, garbage textures), crashes, and abnormal temperatures. A harvested or re-marked card fails here if it produces a picture at all. If the card produces no picture at all, stop and return it. “It just needs a driver” is not an explanation for a card with no output. Harvested boards exist, and the return window is shorter than the argument. Check the 16-pin connector while you are there. A melted or discolored power socket is a separate failure — see our 16-pin failure analysis — and a card sold “for repair” with a burnt connector may be a melted card being passed on. What about the rest of the market? The scam wave is not only GPUs. How-To Geek’s November 20, 2026 Black Friday scam roundup lists RTX 5090 bricks, fake Ryzen CPUs (an AMD heatspreader fitted to an old Intel CPU), DDR2 memory sold in DDR5 kits, and counterfeit Samsung 990 Pro SSDs. The defense is the same in every case: buy through a channel with returns, verify the part against its specification, and test it before the return window closes. A deal that cannot survive a test is not a deal. Sources “Used RTX 3090 scam: sawed Radeon R9 280 PCB” — Pro Gamer, November 2026: pro-gamer.gg . “Fake GPU scam: what to look for” — Engadget, November 10, 2026: engadget.com . “Counterfeit GeForce RTX 4090 corpse cards with fake GPU cores and VRAM sold as faulty units” — Guru3D, November 2026: guru3d.com . “Black Friday scams you need to watch out for when buying PC hardware this year” — How-To Geek, November 20, 2026: howtogeek.com . On this site: GPU Repair (the counterfeit record: painted memory, relabeled cards, harvested boards); the 16-pin connector failure analysis ; why repair now makes economic sense . BareBoard — free hardware education. Read the board, not the shroud. Test it before you pay for it.

title: GPU Repair — BareBoard
headings: Step one: prove it is the card
Level 2: board-level repair — what it actually involves
The locked drawer: what NVIDIA does not publish
The supply-chain record: variants and smuggling cases
The backdoor question: what is and is not on the record
text: Repairing a graphics card (GPU) A graphics card — the board that draws everything on your screen, built around a GPU (graphics processing unit) chip — is two different repair problems in one box. At the service level it is one of the most repairable parts in a PC: fans, paste, pads, and connectors are all owner-serviceable with screwdrivers. At the board level it is repairable too, but the manufacturer keeps the circuit diagrams and the factory test software locked away, so the work is slower than it should be. This page covers both levels, the documented failure record of the current power connector, how to spot a counterfeit used card, and — stated plainly, with the record — exactly what is and is not published. Safety first Read this before you open anything. The power supply can kill you; the card cannot. A PSU (power supply unit — the box that converts wall power for the PC) stores electrical charge in its capacitors even after it is unplugged, and that charge can be lethal. Work on the graphics card only, with the PC switched off and unplugged. Never open the PSU itself — no repair on this page needs it. Mind static. ESD (electrostatic discharge — a static spark, often too small to feel) can kill a memory chip silently. Wear a grounding wrist strap, or touch a grounded metal object often, and work on a plain hard surface rather than carpet. Burnt plastic means stop. If a power connector smells burnt or shows brown, softened, or melted plastic, stop using the card. That failure mode has a government recall attached to it (see the connector record below); it is a fire hazard, not a quirk. The oven trick is a myth, and it is harmful. Baking a dead card in a kitchen oven does not repair it. A home oven cannot run the controlled temperature profile that solder needs, the heat warps the board and cooks plastic connectors and fan bearings, and flux fumes contaminate an oven that later cooks food. When a baked card “revives,” what usually happened is that heat temporarily closed a cracked solder joint — the crack is still there, and it fails again. Professionals rework boards with hot-air stations and controlled profiles. Skip the oven. Step one: prove it is the card Most “dead GPU” reports turn out to be something else. Work this order before you blame the card — each step rules out a whole family of causes, cheapest first. Reseat everything. Power off, unplug. Pull the card and push it back into its PCIe slot (the long connector slot on the motherboard) until the latch clicks. Reconnect every power cable until each plug is fully home. On the 16-pin connector this matters most: NVIDIA’s own guidance is to plug the power cable into the card first , firmly and evenly, before installing the card into the machine. A visible gap between plug and socket means it is not seated. Swap the display path. Try a different cable, a different port on the card, and a different monitor or TV input. If one port is dead and the others work, you have a port problem (Level 1), not a dead card. Rule out the slot and the motherboard. Try the card in a second PCIe slot or in another PC. Or put a known-good card in this PC. Whichever way the fault moves tells you which part owns it. Rule out the power supply. A failing PSU imitates a failing GPU almost perfectly: black screens and crashes under load. Test with a known-good PSU of at least the wattage the card maker specifies. Test by swapping, never by opening the PSU (see the safety box). Rule out software. Boot into safe mode, or boot the PC from a live USB operating system. If the picture is clean there, the card is fine and the driver is not: remove the graphics driver completely with a driver-cleaning tool in safe mode, then install a fresh copy from NVIDIA or AMD. Watch heat and fans. Free monitoring tools — GPU-Z (from TechPowerUp) is the standard one — show the card’s temperatures and fan speeds. Fans that never spin, or temperatures climbing steeply at light load, point at the cooling hardware (Level 1 fixes), not at dead silicon. If the card still fails after all six, the fault is on the card itself. Start at Level 1 anyway — it is cheap — and treat Level 2 as the step after. Level 1: service anyone can do Tools for everything in this section: small Phillips screwdrivers, a soft brush, compressed air, isopropyl alcohol at 90% or stronger, lint-free wipes, new thermal paste, replacement thermal pads, and a cheap digital caliper (a measuring tool with a sliding jaw and a digital readout) for the pads. Work powered off, keep every screw with the part it came from, and take a photo before each step — the photo is your reassembly manual. Cleaning Dust mats itself into the heatsink fins (the stack of thin metal plates that carry heat away) and chokes the airflow; overheating that cures with a cleaning is common. Remove the card, hold each fan still with a finger — never let compressed air spin a fan freely, which can overspeed it — and blow the dust out from the back of the heatsink toward the front. Brush what stays. The gold contacts on the PCIe edge connector can be wiped gently with a lint-free cloth dampened with isopropyl alcohol. Fan replacement The fans are wear items and they are replaceable — as assemblies matched to your exact card model, not as universal parts. Remove the fan shroud (the plastic cover) screws, unplug the small fan connector (2 to 4 pins) from the board, and read the part number printed on the sticker in the center of the fan hub. Order that part number, refit, and route the cable so it cannot touch the blades. A fan that grinds, wobbles, clicks, or refuses to start is a fan to replace, not a card to bury. Thermal paste replacement Thermal paste is the heat-conducting compound between the GPU die (the silicon chip itself) and the cooler. Over years it dries out and pumps out from between the surfaces, and the die temperature climbs while everything else looks normal. The repair, in order: Remove the cooler: undo the screws around the die first — they are usually spring-loaded and arranged in a square — then the remaining shroud and backplate screws, keeping each set separate. Separate the cooler from the board with a gentle twist. Old thermal pads (next section) will resist; never pry against the die. Clean the die and the cooler’s contact plate with isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free wipe until both are mirror-clean. Keep every thermal pad in place and note where each one sat — you need them for the pad step below. Apply a pea-sized dot of new paste in the center of the die (or a thin, even spread; either is fine — coverage is what matters). Refit the cooler, tightening the die screws a little at a time in an X pattern so pressure stays even, then the rest of the screws. Test under load and compare temperatures with before. Do not substitute liquid-metal compounds unless you fully understand them: they conduct electricity, they can short the small components around the die, and they corrode aluminum coolers. Thermal pads: measure, then replace Thermal pads are the soft, squishy squares that carry heat from the memory chips and the power circuitry into the cooler. The memory chips — VRAM (video RAM; on modern cards these are GDDR chips, arranged around the die) — have no other cooling path, so the pads are not optional. The classic self-inflicted injury in GPU service is fitting pads of the wrong thickness : too thick, and the cooler cannot sit flat on the die, so the core overheats and the board flexes; too thin, and the pad never touches, so the memory overheats. Measure first: As you lift the cooler, keep each pad with its location. Thickness often differs from spot to spot on the same card. Measure each removed pad with the caliper at an edge that sat outside the contact patch. Pads compress in service, so the squashed middle reads thinner than the pad really was. Replace like-for-like. Pads are sold in 0.5 mm steps, commonly 0.5 to 3.0 mm. When you must choose between two sizes, a softer pad in the thicker size conforms better than a hard pad. If a pad crumbled and cannot be measured, measure the gap instead: with the cooler resting in place, use the caliper’s depth rod or a feeler gauge (a set of thin metal blades of known thickness) to find the distance between the component’s top and the cooler’s raised landing above it. That distance is the pad thickness the card was built with. Output ports Work every port before condemning one: swap cables, swap the monitor input, and look into the port with a light. Pocket lint and dust pack into HDMI and DisplayPort sockets and can be teased out with a wooden toothpick and isopropyl alcohol, powered off. A port with bent pins or a cracked housing is a soldered component: replacing it is hot-air soldering work (Level 2 territory), and many repair shops will replace a single port for far less than a card costs. The 16-pin connector: the documented record The RTX 40-series and later high-end cards take power through one 16-pin plug — 12VHPWR: twelve power pins and four sense pins, rated for up to 600 watts through a connector smaller than the plugs it replaced. Its failure record is not folklore; it is documented, and you should know it before you trust or blame one. What NVIDIA said. After owners reported melted plugs on RTX 4090 cards in the autumn of 2022, NVIDIA published its findings on November 18, 2022: it was aware of “about 50 cases globally,” and “a common issue is that connectors are not fully plugged into the graphics card.” It recommended plugging the power cable into the card before installing the card, and promised an expedited replacement process regardless of which cable or card was used. That is the manufacturer’s own statement, and the prevention advice in it is worth following — it is step 1 of the diagnosis order above. What independent testing found. headings: Level 0 — Silicon: Secure Elements & Root of Trust
text: Level 0 — Silicon: Secure Elements & Root of Trust The secure enclaves and trust anchors baked into silicon. Public knowledge only — no register maps, no internal documentation. Element Vendor Public interface What's public Secure Enclave (SEP) Apple No public interface Research talks (BH2016, MOSEC2020) Platform Security Proc. AMD No public interface coreboot docs, BH2020 research CSME / Management Eng. Intel No public interface REcon2014 research, coreboot tools Titan M2 Google No public interface Public security whitepapers Pluton Microsoft No public interface Public architecture overviews Secure Element SE050 NXP I2C, public datasheet Full public datasheet OPTIGA Trust M Infineon I2C, public datasheet Full public datasheet ATECC608 Microchip I2C, public datasheet Full public datasheet + app notes The pattern Consumer secure elements fall into two camps: documented (NXP, Infineon, Microchip publish full datasheets) and sealed (Apple, AMD, Intel, Google, Microsoft publish security-architecture documentation — the Secure Enclave chapter of the Apple Platform Security guide, Google’s Titan M2 material, Intel and AMD’s CSME/PSP documents — but no public interface or datasheet for the parts themselves). The sealed ones are where public research — conference talks, open-source firmware projects — becomes the documentation of last resort. Scope: public product briefs, research talks, and open-source project documentation only.

title: Level 3 — Systems: Critical Infrastructure, Medical & Avionics — BareBoard
headings: Level 3 — Systems: Critical Infrastructure, Medical & Avionics
text: Level 3 — Systems: Critical Infrastructure, Medical & Avionics Complete systems where hardware failure has human consequences. Listed for awareness and lawful research on retired/surplus units only — never in-service equipment. Medical devices Device Examples Why it matters Research rule Infusion pump Baxter Plum 360, B. Braun Infusomat Drug dosing is life-critical Retired units only; air-gap networked Pacemaker / ICD Medtronic, Abbott, Boston Scientific Implanted; wireless telemetry Explanted/retired only; no RF attacks Insulin pump / CGM Medtronic MiniMed, Dexcom G6/G7 Closed-loop dosing Retired units only Patient monitor Philips IntelliVue , GE CARESCAPE Vital-signs aggregation Decommissioned units only Industrial / infrastructure PLCs Device Examples Why it matters Research rule Water-treatment PLC Allen-Bradley ControlLogix , Siemens S7 Public water supply Lab/test rigs only; coordinated disclosure Power-grid RTU / relay SEL, ABB, Schneider Electric Grid stability Never touch live grid assets Traffic-signal controller Econolite, Siemens M50 Road safety Decommissioned cabinets only Smart meter Itron, Landis+Gyr Billing + grid telemetry Own meter / lab units only Avionics Device Examples Why it matters Research rule GPS / FMS unit Garmin G1000, Honeywell Primus Navigation integrity Bench units only; no RF spoofing Transponder / ADS-B Garmin GTX, uAvionix Air-traffic visibility Receive-only research Engine controller (FADEC) Woodward, BAE Systems Engine control authority Surplus/bench units only Responsible-research rules Retired/surplus units only. Never probe in-service life-critical or infrastructure equipment. Air-gap networked gear. Anything with a network interface gets isolated before power-on. Coordinated disclosure. Findings affecting safety go to the vendor and ICS-CERT/CISA before any publication. No weaponization. Research is defensive: understanding failure modes, not creating them. Scope: public device identification and research safety rules. No firmware internals, no bypass techniques.

text: Autopsy Report #001 — Siemens SIMATIC S7-300 PLC Family Target class: Level-3 Systems (Industrial control) Status: PUBLIC (vendor-published documentation) / retired hardware Date: 2026-10-08 Standard: Verified findings only. Uncertainty dated and marked. --- 1. Target identification Field Value Family Siemens SIMATIC S7-300 Launch 1994 Status Discontinued — Siemens announced phase-out Oct 1, 2023 (PM400); type discontinuation Oct 1, 2025 (PM410); S7-1500 successor Form factor Modular rack PLC (DIN-rail mounting rail) CPU range CPU 312 → 319 (increasing memory, speed, interfaces) 2. Public architecture (from Siemens-published manuals) Subsystem Public detail Processor Siemens-proprietary ASIC per CPU variant; specs in public system manual Memory Load memory via SIMATIC Micro Memory Card (MMC); work memory on-CPU Backplane bus Proprietary S7-300 backplane; modules daisy-chain via bus connectors Fieldbus MPI (Multi-Point Interface), PROFIBUS-DP, PROFINET (later CPUs) Programming STEP 7 (TIA Portal for later); STL/LAD/FBD languages Power 24 V DC via PS 305/307 power supply modules 3. Module anatomy (retired unit) Slot position Typical module Function 1 PS 307 24 V DC power supply 2 CPU 314 Central processor 3 Interface/dummy Reserved slot 4+ SM 321 / SM 322 Digital input / digital output 4+ SM 331 / SM 332 Analog input / analog output 4+ CP 342-5 PROFIBUS communication processor 4+ FM 350-1 Counter / function module 4. What the documentation tells us (and doesn't) Publicly documented (Siemens manuals): Full module catalog with ordering numbers, pin assignments, wiring diagrams Backplane addressing rules and slot constraints MMC memory-card file system behavior PROFIBUS-DP slave configuration via public GSD files Diagnostic buffer structure and error codes Not public (correctly excluded from this report): CPU ASIC internals and firmware structure Proprietary backplane protocol timing Any technique for bypassing access protection on live systems 5. PERFORMING THE CORRECTION You will be notified when repair kits are available and the process to follow to obtain the proper kit for the serial number you are correcting. The web portal will include a template letter to send to end users explaining the hazard and the need to cooperate with this correction effort. Correction instructions and related supporting materials will also be available. We are also providing the end user with a certificate for a free light kit towards the purchase of a new Permobil power chair. Please contact your Permobil sales representative if you have any questions regarding this correction. Product Code ITI Product Invacare TDX SP2 with LiNX Gyro Power Wheelchair (with LiNX Gyro Module Model Numbers DLX-GRY100-A and DLX-GRY101-A) Models: TDX SP2: TDXSP2, TDXSP2-CG, TDXSP2X-CG, TDXSP2-MCG, TDXSP2X-MCG, TDXSP2V, TDXSP2V-HD, TDXSP2HD, TDXSP2HD-CG, TDXSP2HD-MCG Code Information LiNX Gyro firmware version 6.1.2 UDI-DI Numbers: TDXSP2 00841447100911 TDXSP2-CG 00841447100942 TDXSP2-MCG 00841447100966 TDXSP2HD 00841447108641 TDXSP2HD-CG 00841447111207 TDXSP2HD-MCG 00841447111214 TDXSP2V 00841447101512 TDXSP2V-HD 00841447102052 TDXSP2X-CG 00841447101000 TDXSP2X-MCG 00841447101017 FEI Number 1525712 Recalling Firm/ Manufacturer Invacare Corporation 1200 Taylor St Elyria OH 44035-6248 For Additional Information Contact Invacare Corporation 877-413-6008 Manufacturer Reason for Recall Power Wheelchairs with a LiNX Gyro component running firmware version 6.1.2 can experience a more aggressive deceleration rate than the programmed rate due to the system following the incorrect deceleration profile, resulting in potential injury FDA Determined Cause 2 Software design Action Invacare issued Urgent Medical Device Letter issued on 11/12/21 to consignees who received devices with LiNX Gyro modules containing firmware version 6.1.2. This letter also contains instructions for consignees who upgraded devices in the field to version 6.1.2. A Consumer Letter will be provided on the recall website for Providers to send to end users who are impacted. Letter states reason for recall, health risk and action to take: Visit www. Invacare.com/RC916 within five (5) business days of receiving this notice. Enter the requested identification information to access the list of power wheelchair serial numbers and/or LiNX Gyro Modules sold to you and instructions to conduct this field correction. You will be prompted to provide responses to information requested regarding this field correction and affected units. " The account number required to access your list of impacted devices appears directly at the end of your company name in the mailing address. For example, ABC COMPANY-XXXXX. " The mailing postal code will also be required to log into your account. 2. Stop using LiNX Gyro Module firmware version 6.1.2 on all power wheelchair programming tools and stored electronic media. 3. Immediately update any LiNX Access iOS and LiNX Access PC tools containing LiNX Gyro Module firmware version 6.1.2 to the latest LiNX Access iOS or LiNX Access PC tool version. 4. Locate the power wheelchairs with affected LiNX Gyro Modules per the date ranges above. 5. For power wheelchairs built prior to the date ranges above, review your customer records to identify whether you have installed LiNX firmware version 6.1.2 on any LiNX Gyro-equipped power wheelchairs since the January 14, 2021 release date of firmware version 6.1.2. Note: If you do not have record of the firmware version installed on the LiNX Gyro Modules you have purchased from Invacare, you must connect to the LiNX system on the wheelchair using the LiNX Access tool to determine the firmware version of the Gyro Quantity in Commerce 1477 units US; 1226 units OUS Distribution Worldwide distribution - US Nationwide and the countries of Canada, Australia, Thailand, New Zealand. The record is updated if the FDA identifies a violation and classifies the action as a recall, and it is updated for a final time when the recall is terminated. Learn more about medical device recalls . 2 Per FDA policy, recall cause determinations are subject to modification up to the point of termination of the recall. 3 The manufacturer has initiated the recall and not all products have been corrected or removed. Stop using LiNX Gyro Module firmware version 6.1.2 on all power wheelchair programming tools and stored electronic media. 3. Immediately update any LiNX Access iOS and LiNX Access PC tools containing LiNX Gyro Module firmware version 6.1.2 to the latest LiNX Access iOS or LiNX Access PC tool version. 4. Locate the power wheelchairs with affected LiNX Gyro Modules per the date ranges above. 5. For power wheelchairs built prior to the date ranges above, review your customer records to identify whether you have installed LiNX firmware version 6.1.2 on any LiNX Gyro-equipped power wheelchairs since the January 14, 2021 release date of firmware version 6.1.2. Note: If you do not have record of the firmware version installed on the LiNX Gyro Modules you have purchased from Invacare, you must connect to the LiNX system on the wheelchair using the LiNX Access tool to determine the firmware version of the Gyro Quantity in Commerce 1 unit US Distribution Worldwide distribution - US Nationwide and the countries of Canada, Australia, Thailand, New Zealand. Serial Numbers: 08BE000082; 08BE000088; 08BE000089; 08BE000090; 08BE000323; 08BE001102; 08BE001105; 08BE002283; 08BE002803; 08BE003025; 08BE003250; 08BE003251; 08BE003472; 08BE003473; 08BE003632; 08BE004402; 08BE004414; 08BE004415; 08BE004835; 08BE005297; 08DE002040; 08EE000277; 08EE001539; 08EE001540; 08EE001775; 08FE003254; 08FE003257; 08FE003668; 08FE004681; 08GE003570; 08GE003936; 08HE001169; 08HE005013; 08IE001081; 08IE001316 & 08IE002729. FEI Number 1525712 Recalling Firm/ Manufacturer Invacare Corporation 1200 Taylor St Elyria OH 44035-4190 For Additional Information Contact Carroll L. Martin 440-329-6356 Manufacturer Reason for Recall For some Invacare chairs, the stability lock feature may not be engaging properly or consistently. If the stability lock feature does not engage properly, the wheelchair may do one or more of the following: (1) veer to one side; (2) rock forward onto its front riggings; (3) drive in an unintended circular motion; and/or (4) fall forward or to one side. In these cases there is a risk to injury for FDA Determined Cause 2 Device Design Action On 9/15/2009 the firm sent recall notification letter to their customers instructing them to immediately contact the dealer to have the stability lock inspected and/or adjusted. If the dealer is unavailable or the repair will take longer than 60 days, they are to contact the firm and arrange for an inspection and/or adjustment. Invacare requested contact names to whom it can send additional information. Invacare plans to mail, via FEDEX, information regarding the recall to each consignee. Initial consignees received a response card and instructions to forward cards to any customer to whom they have distributed the product. The products are to be inspected at the cylinder label and if the label does not have a long alpha-numeric string demonstrated in the label, the cylinders on the chair have to be replaced. Questions are directed to Recalls@Invacare.com or to 800-333-6900. Quantity in Commerce 36 Distribution Product was distributed to the following states: AZ, CA, CO, CT, DC, FL, GA, IA, IL, IN, KS, MA, ME, MI, MN, MO, MS, NC, ND, NM, NY, OH, SC & TX. text: Quick Links: Skip to main page content Skip to Search Skip to Topics Menu Skip to Common Links U.S. Food & Drug Administration Follow FDA En Español Search FDA Home Food Drugs Medical Devices Radiation-Emitting Products Vaccines, Blood & Biologics Animal & Veterinary Cosmetics Tobacco Products Class 2 Device Recall TRUBalance3 Power Positioning System FDA Home Medical Devices Databases - 510(k) | DeNovo | Registration & Listing | Adverse Events | Recalls | PMA | HDE | Classification | Standards CFR Title 21 | Radiation-Emitting Products | X-Ray Assembler | Medsun Reports | CLIA | TPLC New Search Back to Search Results Class 2 Device Recall TRUBalance3 Power Positioning System Date Initiated by Firm December 01, 2016 Date Posted January 03, 2017 Recall Status 1 Terminated 3 on March 19, 2020 Recall Number Z-0942-2017 Recall Event ID 75881 510(K)Number K041346 Product Classification Wheelchair, powered - Product Code ITI Product TRU-Balance 3 Power Positioning Systems, TB3 Lift/Tilt/Recline (Gen 1). Mobility Medical Device Code Information Numerous serial numbers affected (12,343 units) FEI Number 3005068474 Recalling Firm/ Manufacturer Pride Mobility Products Corp 182 Susquehanna Ave Exeter PA 18643-2653 For Additional Information Contact 800-800-8586 Ext. 1381 Manufacturer Reason for Recall The interface between the TB3 back and tilt base can separate when tilted beyond the specified angle. FDA Determined Cause 2 Use error Action Pride Mobility Products Corp. mailed a letter to affected customers to inform them of the issue. Systems were not required to be returned. Customers were informed that a TB3 Seat Depth Adjustment Reinformcement Kit which contains (2) reinforcement plates and associated hardware to strengthen the interface will be installed to address the issue. Direct accounts were asked to contact patients to inform them of the product correction. Customers were also requested to complete and return Pride's completion card once the correction has been made. Pride will issue a $65.00 credit once the completion card is received. Customers with questions were instructed to call Pride's Upgrade Department at 866-222-6212. For questions regarding this recall call 800-800-8586. Code Information All serial numbers manufactured between August 17,2023 through November 21, 2024 FEI Number 3008370857 Recalling Firm/ Manufacturer Max Mobility LLC 300 Duke Dr Lebanon TN 37090-8115 For Additional Information Contact Audra Watt 800-736-0925 Manufacturer Reason for Recall Due to faulty circuit board in speed control remote use in conjunction with a wheelchair power assist, their is a potential for lost of control of device potentially resulting in minor and major injuries. FDA Determined Cause 2 Component change control Action Initially Max Mobility notified consignees of their Urgent Medical Correction between the dates of 12/20/24 - 01/17/2025. Since this time, Max Mobility has expanded the recall due to recalled product that may have been inadvertently comingled with redesigned product and shipped after December 20, 2024. Starting 3/25/25, Max Mobility began reaching out to customer via phone, email and mail about the expansion. In addition, Max Mobility updated their press release on 4/7/2025 1. Click on the link or scan QR code to enter the portal within the letter 2. Complete requested portal information. 3. If you are a dealer and have distributed the affected product to someone else, you will be asked to select a transmission method. You may either (a) notify your end users directly and include a copy of this notice with your communication or (b) provide end user contact information to Max Mobility through the online portal and we will contact them for you. 4. After acknowledgement, instructions for obtaining replacement SpeedControl Dial units will be provided. You will need the associated client ID provided in ATTACHMENT 1 of this letter when requesting SpeedControl Dial replacement(s). 5. Once the replacement SpeedControl Dial has been issued to the end user, you will be asked to verify that the correction was completed via the field action portal and destroy or return the effected SpeedControl Dial to Max Mobility. AProvider Response Form was enclosed for customers to complete and return via fax to 888-345-0289. Contact the firm at 888-641-9738 for assistance with this recall. Quantity in Commerce 665 affected power wheel chairs and 15 post-fuse assembly service parts have been identified. If this happens, the motor on the power assist device continues to run and the user may not be able to stop the device using tap gestures. FDA Determined Cause 2 Software design Action Permobil began notifying customers via in-person and through letters on 05/10/2023. Customers were instructed to examine their device and update their software to SmartDrive MX2+ Version 1.1.00, to acknowledge the update was conducted and the notification letter was understood through the field action portal, notify customers if the affected devices were further distributed. They were also instructed to discontinue using the affected device while waiting for the correction. Quantity in Commerce 18,905 units Distribution Worldwide distribution. Code Information All Serial Numbers distributed between the dates of April 25, 2022 - July 8, 2025 FEI Number 3008370857 Recalling Firm/ Manufacturer Max Mobility LLC 300 Duke Dr Lebanon TN 37090-8115 For Additional Information Contact Audra Watt 800-637-2980 Manufacturer Reason for Recall Due to a faulty electrical connection between the speed control Dial and the wheelchair motor, their is a potential for lost of control of the device potentially resulting in minor or major injuries. FDA Determined Cause 2 Component design/selection Action On August 12, 2025, Permobil issued a "Urgent Medical Device Recall Expansion/Update" via email. This expansion supersedes the Class I recall ((Z-1116-2025, Z-1117-2025), initiated on December 20, 2024. Permobil asked consignees to take the following actions: 1. Immediately discontinue use of the SpeedControl dial to reduce the likelihood of a potentially hazardous or harmful situation. 1. Since all SpeedControl Dials are impacted by this recall, remove SpeedControl Dials from your sellable / distribution inventory 2. Use an alternate method to control the SmartDrive MX2+ Power Assist Device. Alternate controls include: " A wired SwitchControl, which can be ordered with a mono jack port to connect with an optional Buddy Button " Wirelessly through the SmartDrive MX2+ App utilizing a Apple iWatch or Samsung Galaxy watch. 3.Immediately contact any customers you have distributed the device to and provide a copy of this notice. It is also recommended that this notice be posted in your clinic/facility 4. You are required to acknowledge that you received this Urgent Medical Device Recall letter. Please complete within 10 days of receipt of the letter. Please use the QR code below to access the field action portal to record your acknowledgement Quantity in Commerce 15,834 units Distribution US: AK AL AR AZ CA CO CT DC DE FL GA HI IA ID IL IN KS KY LA MA MD ME MI MN MO MS MT NC ND NE NH NJ NM NV NY OH OK OR PA PR RI SC SD TN TX UT VA VT WA WI WV WY OUS: CAN, NZL, KOR, BMU, GBR, JPN, TWN, AUS, BRA, COL, MEX, ABW, SWE, CHL, ARG, HKG Total Product Life Cycle TPLC Device Report 1 A record in this database is created when a firm initiates a correction or removal action. The record is updated if the FDA identifies a violation and classifies the action as a recall, and it is updated for a final time when the recall is terminated. Learn more about medical device recalls . 2 Per FDA policy, recall cause determinations are subject to modification up to the point of termination of the recall. 3 The manufacturer has initiated the recall and not all products have been corrected or removed. title: Class 2 Device Recall Jazzy Select with XLR Port Harness
headings: Class 2 Device Recall Jazzy Select with XLR Port Harness
text: Quick Links: Skip to main page content Skip to Search Skip to Topics Menu Skip to Common Links U.S. Food & Drug Administration Follow FDA En Español Search FDA Home Food Drugs Medical Devices Radiation-Emitting Products Vaccines, Blood & Biologics Animal & Veterinary Cosmetics Tobacco Products Class 2 Device Recall Jazzy Select with XLR Port Harness FDA Home Medical Devices Databases - 510(k) | DeNovo | Registration & Listing | Adverse Events | Recalls | PMA | HDE | Classification | Standards CFR Title 21 | Radiation-Emitting Products | X-Ray Assembler | Medsun Reports | CLIA | TPLC New Search Back to Search Results Class 2 Device Recall Jazzy Select with XLR Port Harness Date Initiated by Firm February 01, 2010 Date Posted September 29, 2010 Recall Status 1 Terminated 3 on November 20, 2014 Recall Number Z-2618-2010 Recall Event ID 54617 510(K)Number K001970 Product Classification Wheelchair, Powered - Product Code ITI Product Jazzy Select with XLR Port Harness Code Information all serial numbers FEI Number 3005068474 Recalling Firm/ Manufacturer Pride Mobility Products Corp 182 Susquehanna Ave Exeter PA 18643 For Additional Information Contact Customer Support 866-222-6212 Manufacturer Reason for Recall Improper set-up of the wire harness can allow wires to be pulled from their intended position and become caught under the motor mounting bracket located under the powered wheelchair. This can cause the wire connector and/or the wire itself to be pulled or pinched which can lead to a short or open circuit. FDA Determined Cause 2 Other Action The recalling firm issued recall notifications with response cards to their dealers. Included with the notification was fasteners and an example letter for customer notification of the problem. Dealers were instructed to contact the end users to make arrangements with the customer/end user to verify that the devices were properly set up. If the dealers' inspection revealed that additional fasteners were required they dealer would install them. The recalling firm also issued a recall letter to consumers. The consumer recall letter included instructions that if the correction was completed by anyone other than the wheelchair provider, then the consumer should schedule an appointment with the wheelchair provider to ensure the correction was completed properly. Distribution The product was shipped to dealers nationwide who further shipped the product to end users. The product was also shipped to distributors in Canada, Australia and United Kingdom Total Product Life Cycle TPLC Device Report 1 A record in this database is created when a firm initiates a correction or removal action. headings: Class 2 Device Recall MS Corpus Power Wheelchair
text: Quick Links: Skip to main page content Skip to Search Skip to Topics Menu Skip to Common Links U.S. Food & Drug Administration Follow FDA En Español Search FDA Home Food Drugs Medical Devices Radiation-Emitting Products Vaccines, Blood & Biologics Animal & Veterinary Cosmetics Tobacco Products Class 2 Device Recall MS Corpus Power Wheelchair FDA Home Medical Devices Databases - 510(k) | DeNovo | Registration & Listing | Adverse Events | Recalls | PMA | HDE | Classification | Standards CFR Title 21 | Radiation-Emitting Products | X-Ray Assembler | Medsun Reports | CLIA | TPLC New Search Back to Search Results Class 2 Device Recall MS Corpus Power Wheelchair Date Initiated by Firm June 19, 2025 Date Posted July 24, 2026 Recall Status 1 Open 3 , Classified Recall Number Z-2805-2026 Recall Event ID 99267 510(K)Number K123290 Product Classification Wheelchair, powered - Product Code ITI Product M5 Corpus Power Wheelchair REF,120032 Code Information Power Platform firmware versions 1.27 through 1.57 UDI-DI 17330818334562 FEI Number 1221084 Recalling Firm/ Manufacturer Permobil Inc 300 Duke Dr Lebanon TN 37090-8115 For Additional Information Contact david Rider 615-547-1890 Manufacturer Reason for Recall This recall is being reported retroactively. Power Platform firmware is missing specific drive inhibit logic. This issue may allow the chair to drive under restricted conditions, and may create an unstable condition in certain circumstances. FDA Determined Cause 2 Process design Action On June 10, 2025 Permobil issued a technical bulletin (recall notice) via Email to affected consignees. Permobil informed consignees of the following: 1. Cellular connection is required to receive and install the firmware update. 2. It is important to not use the wheelchair when the firmware update is in process (as indicated on the display of the input device). 3. Specific Remote Update Instructions are available if needed in addition to the on-screen information. 4. A confirmation of the completed update will be shown on the joystick display when the update successfully completes. 5. If you have any questions or concerns, please contact the Permobil Customer Experience team at (800) 736-0925. 1. title: Class 2 Device Recall Quantum Rehab
text: Quick Links: Skip to main page content Skip to Search Skip to Topics Menu Skip to Common Links U.S. Food & Drug Administration Follow FDA En Español Search FDA Home Food Drugs Medical Devices Radiation-Emitting Products Vaccines, Blood & Biologics Animal & Veterinary Cosmetics Tobacco Products Class 2 Device Recall Quantum Rehab FDA Home Medical Devices Databases - 510(k) | DeNovo | Registration & Listing | Adverse Events | Recalls | PMA | HDE | Classification | Standards CFR Title 21 | Radiation-Emitting Products | X-Ray Assembler | Medsun Reports | CLIA | TPLC New Search Back to Search Results Class 2 Device Recall Quantum Rehab Date Initiated by Firm June 25, 2026 Date Posted July 31, 2026 Recall Status 1 Open 3 , Classified Recall Number Z-2842-2026 Recall Event ID 99286 510(K)Number K112815 Product Classification Wheelchair, powered - Product Code ITI Product Brand Name: Quantum Rehab Product Name: Quantum Outback Model/Catalog Number: Quantum Outback Software Version: 2.0.11, new version: 2.0.13 Product Description: Wheelchair, Powered (ITI), 890.3860 Component: Controller Code Information Lot Code: Quantum Outback 0060650920024*0 K112815 D143578 41875 ITI FEI Number 3005068474 Recalling Firm/ Manufacturer Pride Mobility Products Corp. 401 York Ave Duryea PA 18642-2025 For Additional Information Contact Kelly Livingston 1-800-8008586 Ext. 1381 Manufacturer Reason for Recall If the "Remind Me Later" option is selected for user reminders, reminder pop-up messages may appear while the wheelchair is in use. If this occurs while driving the wheelchair, the wheelchair may perform an unexpected park brake stop, which may result in fall or injury. If this occurs while not driving the wheelchair, the control system may crash and remain in pre-operational mode. FDA Determined Cause 2 Under Investigation by firm Action Firm notified dealers and consumers via mailed letters on June 25, 2026. Dealers were instructed to locate affected units and inform consumers of the required software update. Dealers should schedule service appointments with affected consumers. Systems should be updated to Q-Logic software version 2.0.13 or later. The update must be completed following a system power cycle. Consumers were instructed to disable the "Remind Me Later" feature immediately. Consumers should contact their dealer to schedule an appointment for software update. Quantity in Commerce 1102 Distribution Worldwide - US Nationwide distribution including in the states of AZ, NJ, PA, OK, CO, IN, AR, KS, CT, MD, WI, TX, FL, WA, NY, MO, LA, UT, OR, VA, RI, CA, TN, MN, KY, NV, GA, WV, IL, OH, SC, WY, AL, MI, ME, NC, SD, DE, MA, NE, ND, IA, NH, NM, MT, ID, MS, DC, AK and the countries of Canada and Australia.
