title: Why the Military Cannot Fix Its Own Gear — BareBoard
headings: Why the military cannot fix its own gear
What “right to repair” means for the military
Why it is likely to be dropped
The “zero examples” claim, against the record
FY26 versus FY27: do not mix them up
Why this is on a repair-education site
text: Why the military cannot fix its own gear The United States military buys some of the most expensive machines on Earth — fighter jets, ships, trucks, generators — and then, in many cases, is not allowed to fix them. The repair manuals, the diagnostic software, and the right to make a spare part often stay with the company that sold the machine. In 2026, both houses of Congress voted to change that. As of late November 2026, the change looks likely to be stripped out of the final defense bill — for the second year in a row. What “right to repair” means for the military A right to repair is the right of the owner of a machine to fix it: to have the manual, the parts, the tools, and the software access needed to diagnose and repair it, instead of being forced to go back to the seller. For a phone or a tractor, that is a consumer question. For the military, it is a readiness question: a jet that waits months for a contractor to fly in is a jet that does not fly. The specific right at stake in this fight is technical data rights — the government’s legal right to use the drawings, manuals, and software that describe a weapons system. When the Pentagon buys a system without those rights, the contractor keeps them, and every repair that needs that information has to go through the contractor, on the contractor’s schedule, at the contractor’s price. The Project On Government Oversight (POGO), a nonpartisan watchdog, notes that maintenance and repair can make up as much as 70% of a weapons program’s total lifetime cost. What Congress voted for The annual defense policy bill is the National Defense Authorization Act , usually shortened to NDAA . It is the law that sets defense policy and spending for the fiscal year. Fiscal year 2027 (FY27) runs from October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2027. Both chambers of Congress put military right-to-repair provisions into their versions of the FY27 NDAA: House, Section 861 — an amendment by Representatives Maggie Goodlander and Pat Harrigan giving the Department of Defense default government-purpose rights to the technical data and software it needs to maintain its own equipment. Government-purpose rights mean the government may use the data for its own purposes, including repair, without paying again for each use. Senate, Section 804 — language by Senators Elizabeth Warren and Tim Sheehy, approved by the Senate Armed Services Committee 27–0. The same idea: the Pentagon gets the data rights it needs to repair what it owns. Both provisions passed with bipartisan support. Neither is law yet: the House and Senate versions have to be reconciled into one final bill in a conference committee, and then passed and signed. Why it is likely to be dropped On November 18, 2026, House Armed Services Committee Chair Mike Rogers (Republican, Alabama) said at a Hudson Institute event that the provision will not survive the final bill. Reporting by Military.com on November 24, 2026 put it plainly: “The top Republican on the House Armed Services Committee has alluded to the ‘right to repair’ provision likely being left out of the final version of the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), even as it garnered support from both congressional chambers.” Rogers gave two reasons. First, he said repairs can be dealt with contractually — that is, the Pentagon can negotiate repair rights into individual contracts instead of having them by law. Second, he said the Department of Defense gave him zero examples over a year of being unable to get what it needed. He also said, “I’m not going to start telling people I’m going to take your [intellectual property].” Critics of the decision, including POGO, blame the power of defense contractors: the companies that profit from repair and sustainment contracts have lobbied hard against the provisions. A POGO-led letter urging Congress to keep the provisions was published on November 19, 2026. The “zero examples” claim, against the record The claim that there are no examples of the military being unable to repair its own equipment does not match the public record. Examples reported by POGO, by the Government Accountability Office (GAO — Congress’s own audit agency), and in a letter from a Marine Corps logistics officer to the Federal Trade Commission include: The F-35 fighter. POGO reports the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter program — expected to cost about $1.6 trillion in sustainment alone — faces delays, inadequate repair equipment, and costly maintenance problems, in part because the Department of Defense does not have the access to repair information and materials it needs. Maintainers have needed contractor help for corrosion repairs because they lack certain technical data, with too few contractor personnel to respond promptly. Marine Corps engines in Japan. Marines stationed in Japan waited months for repairs on engines that had to be shipped back to the United States, because repair by Marines would have violated the repair-support contracts. The same pattern applied to other costly repairable parts shipped from Okinawa. $900 a page for manuals. The Air Force paid $900 per page for upgrades to contractor-owned maintenance manuals. A contractor flown in for a simple repair. The Navy once had to spend thousands of dollars to fly in a contractor to make simple repairs. A generator in Korea. A mechanic on exercise in Korea was prohibited from maintaining a generator because the warranty would be voided — the unit had to choose between voiding a warranty and losing the equipment. Marines who did fix warrantied equipment were reprimanded. A ship’s crane motor. The GAO documented a Navy littoral combat ship with a broken crane motor: a qualified repair contractor would not finish the job without the original manufacturer present. The Navy waited two and a half weeks, and shipyard officials considered that quick. Congressional reporting has also named the T-38 trainer fleet among the programs affected. And a Department of Defense survey of more than 200 sustainment programs found half of the respondents reporting data-rights deficiencies that obstructed competition or in-house support. None of this proves that every repair problem is a data-rights problem. But it does show that the “zero examples” claim is not the whole record — the examples are public, documented, and specific. FY26 versus FY27: do not mix them up This is the second year of the same fight, and much of the search traffic mixes the two years up. Here is the distinction: FY26 NDAA: similar right-to-repair provisions appeared in both chambers’ proposals for the fiscal 2026 defense law, and were stripped from the final version in December 2025 after industry pushback. What survived was a requirement for improved tracking of technical-data problems — a system to catalog the reasons repairs stall, not the means to fix them. FY27 NDAA: the provisions came back — House Section 861 and Senate Section 804, described above — and as of November 24, 2026 they look likely to be stripped again in conference. The final bill had not yet passed at the time of writing. If you read a story about right-to-repair provisions being “stripped from the NDAA,” check the date: a December 2025 story is FY26; a November 2026 story is FY27. What happens next The final FY27 NDAA has to pass before the lame-duck session of Congress ends, with government funding running to a December 11, 2026 deadline. Three outcomes are possible: the provisions survive in some form; they are dropped again; or they are replaced with a weaker compromise, such as better tracking or a study. Senators Warren and Sheehy have also pushed a standalone bill, the Warrior Right to Repair Act, which would require contractors to provide the technical data and materials the military needs — that route does not depend on the NDAA conference. Why this is on a repair-education site This is the same pattern this site documents everywhere else, at the largest possible scale: the owner of a machine — here, the taxpayer, through the military — is told it may not fix what it owns, because the instructions are someone else’s property. A wheelchair owner waiting on a dealer’s programmer and a maintainer waiting on a contractor’s manual are waiting on the same idea. The difference is only the stakes: when a chair waits, a person is stranded; when a jet waits, a squadron is grounded. Sources “Top Republican Opposes Right to Repair in FY27 NDAA; Critics Blame Defense Contractors’ Power” — Military.com, November 24, 2026: military.com . “Congress Must Keep Right to Repair in the NDAA” — Project On Government Oversight, November 19, 2026: pogo.org . “Fact Sheet: The Right-to-Repair for the United States Military” — Project On Government Oversight: pogo.org . NDAA Section 804/861 background — ndaa.ai, November 9, 2026: ndaa.ai . “Pentagon Reconciliation Dead: Coons, Rogers, NDAA Right to Repair” — GovConFeed, November 24–25, 2026: govconfeed.com . “U.S. Military Contracts Are Restricting Repair” — iFixit News, November 2026 (Marine Corps logistics officer letter to the FTC): ifixit.com . On this site: The Shield: right-to-repair law ; the PMD law section . BareBoard — free hardware education. The military owns the machines. The question is whether it is allowed to fix them.

title: The BBO Top 10 Most Wanted — BareBoard
text: The BBO Top 10 Most Wanted The bounty board. These are the devices we most want on the teardown bench — ranked not by fame, but by how badly they need examining and how hard they are to find. When a device is acquired, it graduates off the board and the next one moves up. The ranking 50% Rarity. How hard is it to find? Used-market scarcity, active listing counts, discontinued with no new stock. The harder to source, the higher the bounty. 30% Darkness. How little public research exists? No teardown, no FCC internal photos, no public documentation. Zero prior examination outranks everything except rarity itself. 20% Reach. Installed base × still in use. A rare device nobody owned matters less than a rare device millions once owned. Score = 0.5 × Rarity + 0.3 × Darkness + 0.2 × Reach, each scored 0–10. Recomputed whenever the device universe updates or a bounty is claimed. The board Humane AI Pin Sought for: Wearable from a startup founded in 2018. HP bought most of Humane’s assets — its CosmOS software, 300+ patents, and staff — for $116M in February 2025, and Humane shut the AI Pin servers down on February 28, 2025, killing cloud functions (offline functions such as the battery check still worked). Snapdragon-based wearable with almost no public board-level documentation. Why it matters: documents an entire product category's rise and fall at the silicon level. Priority: HIGH PRIORITY Rabbit R1 Sought for: MediaTek-powered AI handheld. iFixit’s Chip ID teardown has identified the main silicon; board-level detail on its power design and component choices is still thin. Why it matters: independent examination of heavily marketed AI hardware. Priority: HIGH PRIORITY Apple Vision Pro Sought for: Dual-chip (M2 + R1) spatial computer. Apple publishes nothing about the board; iFixit’s Chip ID guide (February 2024) identified the main silicon, but board-level documentation is still thin and the display stack is unique. Why it matters: the most complex consumer board of its generation, still barely documented beyond chip identification. Priority: HIGH PRIORITY Nintendo Switch 2 Sought for: New generation hardware; its Tegra T239 silicon was identified in April 2025, but board layout and repairability characteristics are still undocumented. Why it matters: baseline documentation before revisions and cost-downs change the design. Priority: HIGH PRIORITY Meta Quest Pro Sought for: Discontinued headset with pancake-lens optics and Snapdragon XR2+ board. Units are vanishing; the display assembly deserves recording. Why it matters: preservation of a short-lived premium design. Priority: ELEVATED DJI Avata 2 Sought for: FPV drone with OcuSync video pipeline and tight firmware lockdown. Why it matters: independent examination of video transmission hardware the manufacturer keeps closed. Priority: ELEVATED Amazon Astro Sought for: Home robot, rare in the wild, with an unknown sensor and compute stack. Why it matters: almost no public hardware analysis of a shipping home robot. Priority: ELEVATED Oura Ring 4 Sought for: Extremely compact wearable; TechInsights has published a teardown of this generation, but no open board-level documentation exists. Why it matters: miniaturization techniques worth studying and recording. Priority: ELEVATED Peloton Bike+ Sought for: Subscription-linked exercise hardware. Why it matters: documents the “connected hardware” category where software decisions can limit hardware you own. Priority: STANDARD Steam Deck OLED Sought for: Valve handheld with some existing coverage. Why it matters: the HDR OLED panel supply chain and revised board layout deserve a complete record. Priority: STANDARD Have one of these on a shelf? Contact BareBoard to suggest a device or offer hardware — every bounty claimed is documented and the board updates. “The computing scientist’s main challenge is not to get confused by the complexities of his own making.” — E. W. Dijkstra

title: Access & Control: Nintendo — Switch RCM, Maintenance Mode and the Storage Board — BareBoard
headings: Door one: Maintenance Mode — Nintendo’s, on every Switch
Door two: RCM — NVIDIA’s, in the chip
The storage board: the part Nintendo got right
The Joy-Con rail, and what is not documented
text: Access and Control: Nintendo The Nintendo Switch has two recovery modes, and they share a name in most people’s heads. One is Nintendo’s — a menu for fixing a console that will not start. The other is NVIDIA’s — a factory mode built into the processor itself, which on launch-era hardware hands the owner the deepest access any modern console has ever given up: a complete backup and restore of the machine. This page keeps them separate, and maps the rest of Nintendo’s doors besides. This is access documentation: what the doors are, which consoles have them, and what an owner can do with them — above all, make the backup that turns a dead console from a total loss into a repair. There are no keys here and no software downloads. The Switch hub page covers the hardware and the drift lawsuits; this page covers the doors. Provenance: Nintendo’s support pages document Maintenance Mode and nothing deeper — Nintendo has never published a word about recovery mode, the rail pinout, or test points. Everything beyond Maintenance Mode is attributed to the community documentation it comes from (the NH Switch Guide, the ConsoleMods wiki, repair and preservation communities) and labelled as community knowledge, never as Nintendo fact. The map Hardware The doors an owner has What it unlocks, in one line The catch Switch, launch era (2017 – mid-2018) Maintenance Mode, plus RCM (recovery mode in the processor) A complete backup and restore of the console’s entire internal storage — the fullest owner access on any modern console Only launch-era chips have the flaw that makes RCM useful; it cannot be added to later units Switch, patched / 2019 refresh / Lite / OLED Maintenance Mode only Recover a console that will not boot, update it, or reset it without deleting save data RCM still exists in the chip, but patched units refuse owner payloads — the door opens onto a wall Switch 2 (2025) Settings-level recovery, plus a tethered software jailbreak (ns2jb, October 2026) Userland code execution via the SmileBASIC 4 app on firmware 23.0.1 — homebrew, game mods, save backups Tethered (re-run each reboot), no kernel access, no persistent custom firmware; Nintendo pulled SmileBASIC 4 from the eShop within hours Wii U / Wii / 3DS / DS / GameCube Summary in the last section Older, simpler machines with deep community documentation Nintendo documented almost none of it; backups made by owners are the recovery path Door one: Maintenance Mode — Nintendo’s, on every Switch Maintenance Mode is Nintendo’s built-in recovery menu. It exists on every Switch — original, Lite, OLED, patched or not — and Nintendo’s own support pages walk owners through it when a console freezes, will not start properly, or is stuck after an update. What it unlocks, in one line: update the system, or reset the console to factory condition without deleting save data — the official way to un-brick a sick Switch while keeping what matters. Nintendo’s steps: Turn the console completely off. If it will not respond, hold the POWER button for about twelve seconds to force it off. Hold both volume buttons — Volume Up and Volume Down — and press POWER once. Keep holding both volume buttons until the Maintenance Mode screen appears, then let go. The menu offers a system update, Initialize Console Without Deleting Save Data , and a full initialize that erases everything. The middle option is the one to know: it resets the system software while keeping save data, screenshots and user information. It is the last official step in Nintendo’s own troubleshooting for a console that keeps crashing — everything before it is updates and restarts. Know this menu exists before you need it, because the day the console will not boot is the wrong day to learn it exists. Door two: RCM — NVIDIA’s, in the chip The Switch’s processor is NVIDIA’s Tegra X1 . Like every Tegra, it contains a recovery mode — shortened to RCM — built into its bootROM . The bootROM is the very first program the processor runs, stored in read-only memory inside the chip itself (ROM = memory whose contents are fixed forever). Recovery mode is a factory and repair feature: instead of starting the console’s system, the chip stops, and waits for a computer to send it a small program — a payload — over the USB-C cable. Nintendo did not add this mode and cannot remove it; it is part of the silicon it bought. On its own, RCM accepts only NVIDIA-authorised payloads. What changed everything is a flaw in that check, disclosed in April 2018 by the fail0verflow team and researcher Kate Temkin and catalogued as CVE-2018-6242 — the community calls it fusée gelée . On chips made before Nintendo and NVIDIA corrected it, the flaw lets an owner’s payload run. Because the flaw lives in read-only silicon, no system update can close it on those units — and no update can open it on units made after the correction. How an owner enters RCM The trigger is electrical, and it runs through the right Joy-Con rail. One contact in that rail is a signal line the processor samples as it starts: connect it to ground at power-on, and the chip enters recovery mode instead of booting. Turn the console fully off. Slide a jig — a small moulded tool that bridges the correct rail contacts, and nothing else — into the right Joy-Con rail. The contact that must be grounded is pin 10. Hold Volume Up and press POWER. If it worked, the screen stays completely black: no logo, no backlight glow of a normal boot. That black screen is RCM — the console is now waiting for a payload over USB-C. Connect the console to a computer or phone and send a payload with one of the community launcher tools (on Windows, the community tool is called TegraRcmGUI ). Remove the jig; it is only needed for the moment of power-on. The community guide’s warning, verbatim, because people keep learning it the expensive way: “USING A PAPERCLIP OR TIN FOIL CAN/WILL DAMAGE YOUR CONSOLE, DO NOT DO THIS!” — and on making a jig: “Make sure your jig NEVER touches pin 4. Pin 4 provides 5 volts of power to the Joy-Con, and can permanently damage the rail or console if shorted.” (NH Switch Guide, a community source.) A proper jig costs a few dollars. A rail costs a board repair. Two confusions to avoid. RCM is not Maintenance Mode — different mode, different entry, different maker; the volume-buttons-both menu above is Nintendo’s, and RCM needs the rail signal as well as Volume Up. And a console can also fall into RCM on its own if its internal storage is missing or too corrupted to boot — which is why a completely black, unresponsive Switch is not always a dead one. Which Switches have the door Launch-era units (model HAC-001, made from March 2017 until Nintendo’s production change around mid-2018): open. These carry the uncorrected Tegra chip. The community maintains serial-number checkers that sort units into unpatched, possibly patched, and patched — the serial is on the sticker on the bottom of the console. If you are buying a used Switch for repair research, this is the number that matters. Later HAC-001 units (“patched”): the wall. Nintendo quietly shipped chips with the flaw corrected during 2018. These consoles still enter RCM — the mode is in every Tegra — but they refuse owner payloads. Entering RCM on one proves nothing except that the mode exists. The 2019 refresh (HAC-001(-01)), Switch Lite (HDH-001) and Switch OLED (HEG-001): closed. All use the revised chip (the community and Nintendo’s filings call it by its codename, Mariko) with the corrected bootROM. Every one of them, always. There is no setting, update or accessory that moves a console between these groups. The group was decided on the production line, in the silicon. Community projects have since built soldered-in hardware for the closed models; that is a different trade — board surgery, not a door — and it is outside what this page documents. What RCM unlocks Send the community bootloader Hekate as the payload and the black screen becomes a workbench. Each capability, in one plain line: Full storage backup. Hekate copies the console’s entire internal storage to the microSD card — the two small boot partitions (called BOOT0 and BOOT1) and the full raw image of everything else. This is a bit-for-bit snapshot of the machine’s memory. Full storage restore. The same tool writes a backup back. A console whose storage failed, corrupted, or was wiped can be returned to the exact state of its backup — system, games and save data together. Storage inspection from a PC. Hekate can present the internal storage to a connected computer as a USB drive, so its contents can be examined and copied with ordinary tools. Running owner software. From the bootloader, the console can start community system software and homebrew — programs written by owners, running on their own hardware — or other operating systems entirely, such as Linux. Diagnostics. The bootloader reports on the storage chip’s health and identity before any system software is involved — the first thing to check on a console that will not boot. The backup is the one that matters for this site’s mission, so be blunt about the discipline: take the backup before anything goes wrong. The Switch’s storage contents are encrypted with keys unique to each individual console. A backup from another Switch is useless to yours, and a console whose storage dies with no backup of its own generally cannot be brought back — the keys died with it. Owners of launch-era units hold the only complete insurance policy Nintendo never sold. The honest risks, stated with the capabilities and not after them. A payload runs with total control of the machine, so a careless restore can leave a console worse off — the backup is also the protection against that, which is why it comes first. System updates permanently burn microscopic eFuses inside the chip (one-way fuses that record the newest system version, to prevent downgrades), so restoring an old backup needs the bootloader’s help to boot at all. title: Bench Notes — BareBoard — Free Hardware Education
headings: Don’t connect VCC on your serial adapter
The FCC ID is a cheat code
Your boards are tougher than you think (but ground yourself anyway)
Read the datasheet before you probe
text: Bench Notes Short observations from the workbench. No fluff, no filler — just things worth knowing. 115200 is almost always the answer If you’re hunting for a serial console and getting garbage, try 115200 first. It’s the default baud rate on the overwhelming majority of embedded Linux devices, routers, and IoT gadgets. The runner-ups are 57600 and 9600, but in my own bench notes 115200 hits more often than everything else combined — that is one tinkerer’s observation, not a measured statistic. TX idles high — use it Not sure which pad is TX? Power the board and probe with a multimeter. UART TX idles at logic HIGH (3.3V or 1.8V). The pin sitting at a steady rail voltage while the board boots is almost certainly TX. RX idles high too but won’t show boot chatter on a scope. Don’t connect VCC on your serial adapter The board powers itself. Your USB-to-serial adapter powers itself. Connecting VCC between them joins two power supplies that were never meant to meet. You only need three wires: TX, RX, GND. Leave VCC unconnected. The FCC ID is a cheat code Every wireless device sold in the US has an FCC ID printed on it. Look it up at fccid.io and you’ll find internal photos, test reports, block diagrams, and sometimes full schematics — all legally public. It’s the single best free intelligence source in hardware hacking. Your boards are tougher than you think (but ground yourself anyway) Modern chips have decent ESD protection. You’re unlikely to kill a board by touching it. But “unlikely” isn’t “never” — a $5 grounding strap is cheaper than a dead SoC. Ground yourself, especially in dry environments. Read the datasheet before you probe Five minutes with the pinout diagram saves an hour of guessing. The datasheet tells you which pins are power, which are ground, and which ones will release magic smoke if you short them. Our datasheet index is a good place to start. “I had a nightmare once in which I a had convinced a friend how wonderful C++ is. A while later he came back., and he was mad.[sic]” — Robin Rosenberg [ groups.google.com ]

title: Planned Obsolescence Archive — BareBoard
headings: Spot it on your own shelf
text: Evidence archive Planned Obsolescence Archive Documented cases of software updates, firmware locks, and corporate policy bricking or degrading hardware people already owned. Every case carries its sources — court filings, regulator rulings, or the company’s own admission. Evidence labels: confirmed = court filing, regulator ruling, or company admission. likely = reputable reporting with a documented mechanism, but no ruling on record. Where “obsolete” devices end up. Every case below is hardware that was pushed into this pile early — on purpose. Photo: Wikimedia Commons. Loading… Spot it on your own shelf You don’t need a lab to catch this happening. Warning signs: Your phone gets slower right after an update — then speeds up again with a fresh battery. That’s throttling, and it’s exactly what Apple was fined for. Your printer rejects third-party ink — a firmware “security” update that only blocks competitors’ cartridges isn’t security. It’s a subscription you never signed up for. A trade-in program destroys your old device — if “recycling” requires bricking a working product, the program serves the manufacturer, not the planet. Features disappear from something you own — check the changelog. If an update removed something you paid for, take screenshots and note the dates. That’s evidence. On a Linux laptop, you can check whether your battery is genuinely worn out or just being managed aggressively: $ upower -i /org/freedesktop/UPower/devices/battery_BAT0 | grep -E 'percentage|capacity' percentage: 82% capacity: 91% capacity is the battery’s health compared to new — 91% here is fine. If your system claims the battery is dead while capacity reads high, something else is going on. “The X server has to be the biggest program I’ve ever seen that doesn’t do anything for you.” — Ken Thompson

title: Access & Control: PlayStation — PS1 to PS5 — BareBoard
headings: The map: five generations, five sets of doors
The door three generations share: Safe Mode
PS3 — the recovery menu arrives, and so does pairing
PS5 — one open slot, and the rest soldered or paired
text: Access and Control: PlayStation Every PlayStation has doors. Some Sony built and documented for you. Some it built for its own service benches and never mentioned. Some it welded shut. This page maps them, generation by generation — what each door is, how an owner opens it, and what it unlocks. This is access documentation, not a jailbreak guide. It tells you what access exists on hardware you own, what an owner can legitimately do with it — back up, diagnose, repair, replace worn parts — and where the wall genuinely is. There are no keys here, no exploit code, no firmware files. The PlayStation hub page covers the chips and the history; this page covers the doors. Provenance: Sony’s own support pages and manuals are the source for everything labelled “official”. Board-level material is attributed to the community documentation it comes from (iFixit repair guides, the PSDevWiki, the fail0verflow team’s published research) and is never dressed up as Sony fact. Where nobody outside Sony knows, this page says so. The map: five generations, five sets of doors Console The doors an owner has What it unlocks, in one line The hard limit PS1 (1994) Parallel and serial ports on early models; Sony’s own Net Yaroze hobbyist kit Run your own code on your own console, with Sony’s permission and Sony’s tools Nothing to unlock below that: the system software is a fixed ROM chip — no updates, no pairing, no locks PS2 (2000) Sony’s Linux kit; expansion-bay hard drive; Yabasic interpreter on PAL demo discs Turn the console into a small Linux computer No recovery menu on this generation — that starts with the PS3 PS3 (2006) Safe Mode recovery menu; owner-swappable hard drive; OtherOS (Linux install) on early firmware Repair the file system, rebuild the database, reinstall the system from a USB stick The Blu-ray drive’s circuit board is paired to the motherboard PS4 (2013) Safe Mode; owner-swappable hard drive; the deepest board-level documentation of the whole line Full system reinstall from USB, plus community-documented debug output for dead consoles The optical drive’s daughterboard is paired; below Safe Mode, the firmware stays closed PS5 (2020) Safe Mode; an official M.2 slot for adding storage Recover, rebuild, reinstall, and expand — without opening more than the side cover The built-in SSD is soldered down; the disc drive electronics are paired; board-level access is not publicly documented The pattern runs downhill: the older the console, the more of it an owner was allowed to touch. The PS1’s maker sold hobbyists a development kit. The PS5’s maker solders its storage to the board. Everything below fills in the middle of that slope. The door three generations share: Safe Mode Safe Mode is a recovery menu built into the PS3, PS4 and PS5. It starts the console with only the most basic functions running, so a console that cannot boot normally can still be repaired. It is official — Sony documents it on its support pages — and it is the single most useful owner door on any modern PlayStation. What it unlocks, in one line: repair a corrupted file system, rebuild the console’s content database, reinstall the system software from a USB stick, and reset a console that will not start — all without opening the case. On the PS4 and PS5, Sony’s steps are: Turn the console fully off (hold the power button for three seconds). Press and hold the power button again. Let go after the second beep — one beep when you press, another about seven seconds later. Connect the controller with a USB cable and press the PS button. A wireless controller does not work in Safe Mode; the cable is required. The PS3’s sequence is one step longer: from standby, hold the power button until the console turns on and then off again; then hold it again until you hear two quick beeps, and connect the controller by USB. Sony’s own warning, carried verbatim because it is the manufacturer’s: “Some Safe Mode options will result in the loss of data. Be sure to back up data to a USB drive or Cloud Storage before selecting these options.” The menu mixes safe repairs (rebuild the database) with full wipes (reset / initialize). Read the label before you press it. What is in the menu PS3 (called the recovery menu): Restart System; Restore Default Settings; Restore File System (repairs corrupted system areas on the drive); Rebuild Database; Restore PS3 System (the full wipe); System Update (installs the system file from a USB stick — on the PS3, Safe Mode updates come from storage media only, not the network). PS4: Restart PS4; Change Resolution; Update System Software (by internet, USB stick, or disc); Restore Default Settings; Rebuild Database; Initialize PS4 (the wipe); Initialize PS4 (Reinstall System Software) — the full reinstall, which needs the complete system file on a USB stick and is the recovery path after fitting a new hard drive. (PS4 Pro only: an eighth option, Set HDCP Mode.) PS5: Restart PS5; Change Video Output; Repair Console Storage (on current system software — for consoles that do not start properly, and it does not erase data); Update System Software; Restore Default Settings; Clear Cache and Rebuild Database; Reset PS5 (the wipe); Reset PS5 (Reinstall System Software). Note what Safe Mode is not : it is a repair menu, not a control panel. It exposes no settings an owner can tune, no logs an owner can read, and no way to run your own software. Sony built it so a broken console can be made whole again — by the book, to Sony’s specification. PS1 — the open era The original PlayStation (1994) has no recovery menu, no firmware updates, and nothing to unlock: its system software is a ROM — a chip whose contents were fixed at the factory (“read-only memory”). It cannot be updated, locked down later, or paired to anything. Access on a PS1 is physical: ports, boards, and drives, all of which simply work when replaced. Early models (the SCPH-100x through 750x series) carry two expansion connectors on the back: a parallel port (a wide connector for exchanging data with external devices) and a serial port (a slower connector for sending data one stream at a time). Sony removed the parallel port on the final 900x revision. Those ports are how the era’s accessories — cheat cartridges, link cables, development hardware — talked to the console. Then there is the door Sony sold. Net Yaroze (1996 in Japan, 1997 elsewhere, about $750 by mail order) was an official hobbyist development kit: a matte-black PlayStation, a boot disc and access card, a serial cable to your PC, and a C compiler toolchain with Sony’s documentation. You wrote a program on your computer, sent it down the cable, and ran it on the console. By design it could not boot a burned disc — your program had to fit in the console’s memory and live there. What it unlocked, in one line: official permission to run your own code on a PlayStation, in 1996, from the manufacturer itself. PS2 — the Linux kit Sony did it once more. Linux for PlayStation 2 (2002) was an official kit for owners: Linux discs, a 40 GB hard drive, a network adaptor, a keyboard and mouse, and a monitor adaptor. Fitted to a console, it turned the PS2 into a small Linux computer you could program. The kit’s hard drive is itself an owner door: the original “fat” PS2 has an expansion bay (an empty drive slot at the back) that takes a standard 3.5-inch desktop hard drive together with Sony’s Network Adaptor. The slim PS2 removed the bay. PAL-region consoles also shipped with a demo disc carrying Yabasic , a BASIC programming interpreter — a simple built-in language for writing small programs — that could save your work to a memory card. Small, but official, and on every PAL machine. There is no Safe Mode on the PS2, and no pairing anywhere: the optical drive is a plain replaceable part, and fitting a different one needs no permission from the motherboard. What the generation unlocks, in one line: with Sony’s own kit, the console becomes a computer; without it, it is still a machine any repairer can service part for part. PS3 — the recovery menu arrives, and so does pairing The PS3 (2006) is the hinge. It introduced Safe Mode (above) and a genuinely owner-serviceable drive: the internal 2.5-inch SATA hard drive (SATA is the standard connector used by ordinary laptop drives) sits behind a cover on the side, and Sony’s manual documents replacing it. The console formats a fresh drive itself; the full system file goes back on from a USB stick through Safe Mode. A built-in backup utility copies your data to a USB drive first. Early “fat” PS3s also shipped with OtherOS — an official menu option to install Linux on the console alongside the PlayStation system. Sony removed it in the 3.21 firmware update in 2010; the hub page tells that story, including the Air Force supercomputer built from PS3s and the class action that followed. The door existed, was advertised, and was taken back. That sequence is the whole modern argument in one console. Two honest limits. First, the PS3’s Blu-ray drive carries a small circuit board whose identity is paired to the motherboard — parts pairing means the console checks that a part is the exact one it shipped with, and rejects strangers. Repair documentation is consistent on the fix: when you replace the drive mechanism, you move your original drive board onto the replacement, or the console will not play discs. Lose that board and no owner procedure re-pairs a new one. Second, the PS3’s system firmware also lives on a flash chip on the motherboard (a chip that holds data without power and can be rewritten) — NOR or NAND type depending on the model — and the community has documented reading and writing it with external programmers to revive consoles with corrupted firmware. Sony documents none of that; it is community work, named as such. PS4 — the best-documented PlayStation The PS4 (2013) kept the owner’s storage door: Sony publishes the procedure for replacing the 2.5-inch internal drive yourself, and Safe Mode

title: Driving Without a Standard Joystick — PMD — BareBoard
headings: The input modules — the boxes that translate
What you can check, no programmer needed
Head arrays — driving with head movement
Chin controls and small joysticks — proportional, just not by hand
Switches — one button, several buttons, no buttons to push
Scanning — driving with a single switch
The stop switch — the most important switch on the chair
When it stops working — the ordered checklist
text: Driving Without a Standard Joystick A standard joystick needs a hand that can push it in every direction and hold it there. Plenty of riders do not have that hand — and they drive anyway. They breathe through a tube, press pads with their head, nudge a tiny stick with their chin, or tap one switch and let the chair offer the choices. This page explains each of those controls in plain language: how it works, what it plugs into, how it fails, and what you can check yourself before anyone quotes you a replacement. Provenance: this page is compiled from the manufacturers’ own published documents — Curtiss-Wright / PG Drives Technology’s R-net programming manual and R-net PC Programmer manual , Invacare’s LiNX service manual , Permobil’s M3 Corpus and F5 Corpus VS owner manuals , and Quantum Rehab’s Q6 Edge 2.0 owner manual and public order-form documents — and checked against them. Where a manual could not confirm a claim, the claim is not on this page. Documentation, not bench measurement: if your chair disagrees with this page, the chair wins. Before any check on this page that touches a plug, cable, tube, switch, or battery terminal: put the chair on level ground, switch it OFF, and disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker. Do not do the check while seated in the chair. The Invacare LiNX service manual warns, word for word: “Connector pins on cables connected to the power module can still be live even when the system is off.” Keep a disconnected cable from touching skin, jewelry, tools, or metal, and cover or restrain it so the pins cannot short. If you cannot disconnect power, inspect visually only and stop. The same manual limits who does the deeper work, word for word: “The procedures in this service manual, must be performed by a specialized dealer or qualified service technician.” And: “Do not handle this product or any available optional equipment without first completely reading and understanding these instructions and any additional instructional material such as user manuals, installation manuals or instruction sheets supplied with this product or optional equipment.” True — for work inside the modules and for programming. Looking at a tube, a plug, or a switch pad, reading what the screen says, and reporting it exactly needs no one’s permission. That is the part this page teaches. The chain, once, plainly Every alternative control on every system is the same five links in a row. Learn the chain once and you can locate any failure on any chair: You. A movement you can make reliably — a breath, a head turn, a chin nudge, one finger tap, a tongue or foot press. The whole system is fitted to that one movement. The sensor or switch. The part that feels the movement: a pressure sensor in a breath tube, a pad in a headrest, a tiny joystick, a button. The manuals call the whole device at this link a Specialty Input Device , or SID — any control that is not the standard joystick. The input module. A small electronic box that translates the SID’s signals into the language the rest of the chair speaks. This is the link that makes alternative controls possible at all: the chair’s other parts never see breath or head movement, only ordinary drive commands that happen to have come from breath or head movement. Each system has its own input module — they are named in the next section. The bus. The cable network the chair’s parts talk on. The input module puts the translated commands on the bus, the same way a standard joystick does. The power module. The heavy box in the base that takes commands off the bus and sends battery power to the motors, brakes, and seat actuators (the motors that move the seat). It does not know or care whether a command came from a hand, a chin, or a breath. Two kinds of signal travel that chain, and the difference matters everywhere below: Proportional input — how far is how fast. Push a little, go slowly; push further, go faster, in any direction, like a standard joystick. Chin joysticks and some head controls are proportional. Switched input — on or off, nothing between. A switch is either pressed or not, so speed is not in the signal at all; the chair applies the programmed speed when it sees the press. Breath commands, head-array pads, and buttons are switched inputs. A switched chair is not broken when it feels step-like — that is what switched means. One more word used everywhere below: a quadrant is one drive direction treated as a slot — forward, reverse, left, right. A control that can offer all four at once runs in 4-quadrant (4Q) mode. A control that can only offer three — a head array is the classic case, explained below — runs in a 3-quadrant (3Q) mode, and the missing direction is reached by a toggle (a flip between two states, here forward and reverse) instead. The input modules — the boxes that translate These are the named boxes at link three of the chain. If your chair has an alternative control, one of these is fitted, and knowing which one is the first thing to write down. System Input module What plugs into it What the maker’s documents say R-net (Curtiss-Wright / PG Drives Technology) Omni and Omni2 SIDs plug into 9-way D-type connectors (a 9-pin plug, Port 1 and Port 2 ); a separate user switch (your personal switch for menus and, on switched systems, stopping — see The stop switch ) plugs into a 3.5 mm jack socket; a sip-and-puff tube plugs into a dedicated air (pneumatic) input Permobil’s M3 Corpus owner manual describes a fitted Omni2 in one sentence: “An Omni2 is a device that makes it possible to operate the wheelchair with something other than a standard joystick.” The Omni2 user manual (SK82613-01) describes the same ports and the SID types each port accepts. The R-net programming manual lists the input-device types a profile can be set to, including Omni, and a separate Input/Output Module (IOM). LiNX (Dynamic Controls, fitted by Invacare) DLX-IN500 — the manual shortens it to IN5xx — and the TPI route named in the service manual’s connection table IN500: a DB9 connector (the same 9-pin family as R-net’s D-type) for proportional and switched inputs, a stereo jack input, and a built-in sip-and-puff nozzle — the breath sensor itself is inside this module. TPI: the route the manual’s table assigns to head arrays, chin controls, and switch arrays The LiNX service manual lists the IN500’s parts directly: DB9 connector for proportional and switched inputs, 12 V (200 mA) power supply for sensors, sip-and-puff nozzle, jack input, two LiNX bus connectors. Dynamic Controls’ public LiNX 500 Series page confirms the same module supports proportional and switch inputs, including sip-and-puff, through the DLX-IN500-A. Q-Logic 3 (Quantum Rehab / Pride Mobility) SCIM module , a dedicated Sip and Puff Module , and the Q-Logic 3 controller module with expandable harness Specialty devices connect through the SCIM or the dedicated module; a standard Q-Logic joystick or an enhanced display provides the screen Quantum’s public Alternative Controls and Electronics Order Form states the SCIM “allows use of joystick display for specialty devices” with up to 5 profiles for drive, seat, and auxiliary functions, excluding sip-and-puff and single switch functions — those need their own path: the order form lists a separate Sip and Puff Module for Q-Logic 3, and Quantum’s Q-Logic 2 electronics brochure states an enhanced display is still required for sip-and-puff and single-switch driving on that generation. Do not assume a SCIM alone covers breath or one-switch driving; on paper, it does not. Third-party SIDs — head arrays, chin sticks, and switch sets made by companies such as Stealth Products, Switch-It, and ASL (Adaptive Switch Laboratories), all named as SID makers in the Omni2 user manual — are built to plug into these modules. That is the design: the module is the standard socket, and the SID makers build to the socket. It is also why a fault can live in three different companies’ parts on one chair, and why naming the exact module and the exact SID when you call is not pedantry — it is the diagnosis. Sip-and-puff — driving on breath Sip-and-puff means exactly what it sounds like: you sip (draw air in) or puff (blow air out) through a tube held at your mouth, the way you would through a straw. A pressure sensor turns each breath into a command. It is a switched input: the chair reads which breath, not a continuous push. The sensor sorts every breath two ways at once — direction (sip or puff) and strength (soft or hard). That gives four commands, and four commands are exactly the four quadrants. On an R-net Omni2, the user manual’s own table maps them like this: Breath command Drive direction (Omni2 default mapping) Hard puff Forward Hard sip Reverse Soft sip Left Soft puff Right LiNX describes the same sorting as three pressure zones for each direction, in its service manual : a neutral zone (too weak to count — ignored, so ordinary breathing does not drive the chair), a soft zone , and a hard zone . The manual’s sentence, word for word: “A Sip and Puff module provides the user with the ability to activate four digital inputs with their breath via a tube depending on pressure level, hard or soft, and direction, sip or puff. These inputs can be used to control driving or seating actions.” On LiNX the module is inside the IN500 input module, and the tube connects to its nozzle. On R-net the tube connects to the Omni’s or Omni2’s dedicated pneumatic input. A combined sip-and-puff head array also exists on LiNX — breath for forward and reverse, head pads for turning — and it also routes through the IN500, per the same service manual’s connection table. How it fails Tube off, kinked, or pinched — commands go weak or vanish. A tube trapped under a mount or a cushion is the breath version of a loose plug. Moisture in the tube — breath is wet. Condensation collects in a low-hanging loop of tube, and water in the line dulls or blocks the pressure signal: soft c

title: The Attendant Control — PMD — BareBoard
headings: What it is, and where it mounts
Who has control — and how it changes hands
Speed in attendant mode — the attendant is deliberately slowed down
Faults the attendant control itself causes
The manufacturers’ own warnings — word for word
text: The Attendant Control Some power chairs carry two driving controls. The main one sits in front of the person in the chair (the occupant ). The second one — the attendant control — mounts at the back, on a push handle, so a carer (the attendant ) walking behind can drive the chair for them. A chair wired so either control can drive, with a way of passing control between them, is a dual-control chair. This page explains how the two controls share one chair: who is in charge at any moment, how control changes hands, how fast the attendant is allowed to go, and the faults a second live control creates all by itself. Two people, two joysticks, one chair is a safety question before it is a convenience. Every system below answers it the same basic way — only one control drives at a time — but each maker decides which one, and how the other one takes over , differently. Some of those decisions are switches you can touch. Some are set in programming, where you cannot. This page names which is which. Provenance: this page is compiled from the manufacturers’ own published documents — Invacare’s LiNX service manual and TDX SP2 owner’s manual , Dynamic Controls’ DX2-REM42x and DX2-REMB-ACS2 technical manuals , PG Drives Technology’s mobility diagnostics guide and R-net programming manual , the R-net operation text carried in Sunrise Medical’s Quickie S-636 / S-646 owner’s manual , and Quantum Rehab’s Q6 Edge 2.0 owner’s manual — and checked against them. Behaviour that could not be confirmed in a manufacturer’s document is not stated as fact. Documentation, not bench measurement: if your chair disagrees with this page, the chair wins — write down what yours actually does. Before any check on this page that touches a plug or cable: put the chair on level ground, switch it OFF, and disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker. Do not do the check while anyone is seated in the chair. Connector pins can remain live after switch-off. Keep a disconnected cable from touching skin, jewelry, tools, or metal, and cover or restrain it so the pins cannot short. If you cannot disconnect power, inspect visually only and stop. A second control is a second way for the chair to move. Treat it as live whenever the chair is powered, even when it is not the control in charge: on several systems its power button still works, and on one system below its power button is an emergency stop for the whole chair. What it is, and where it mounts An attendant control is a small hand control — a joystick (the stick you push to steer; further means faster), an on/off (power) button, and usually a speed dial or speed buttons that cap the top speed — fitted at the rear of the chair, where a person walking behind can reach it while holding the push handles. It is not a separate machine: it plugs into the same bus (the cable network the chair’s electronic modules talk to each other on) as the occupant’s control, and it talks to the same power module (the box in the base that feeds the motors). Driving from it feels like driving from the front, except that forward is away from you and the chair’s weight is in front of your hands. Makers sell it under different names. These are the ones this page covers, with the document that describes each: System The attendant hardware Where it mounts Invacare LiNX (Dynamic Controls electronics) DLX-REM050 , a drive-only attendant remote, and DLX-ACU200 , an attendant control unit with a display, seating control and a “who’s in charge” indication. Both are documented in Invacare’s LiNX service manual . On a bracket on the push handle or the push bar, per the same manual’s mounting sections. Dynamic Controls DX / DX2 DX-ACU Attendant Control module, with a physical User/Attendant switch on it. Operation is described in the DX2-REM42x technical manual and the DX2-REMB-ACS2 technical manual . At the rear, as part of the DX system; the switch that hands over control is on the ACU itself. PG Drives R-net (Curtiss-Wright) Two different things: an Attendant Control Module (attendant only) and a Dual Attendant Module (user or attendant, switchable). The R-net user manual, carried in Sunrise Medical’s Quickie S-636 / S-646 owner’s manual , states the difference in its intended-use text: with an Attendant Control Module fitted the chair “may be operated by an assistant on behalf of the user”; with a Dual Control Module fitted it “may be operated by the user, or control may be switched to an assistant.” The attendant module connects at any point on the R-net bus and is used from the rear of the chair. Invacare MK6i (TDX line) An attendant remote in the G90A family. Invacare’s TDX SP2 parts catalog lists the hardware plainly: “Remote Support attendant control G90A” and left- and right-hand “Bracket for attendant control” parts. On a rear bracket, left or right side. Quantum Q-Logic (Q6 Edge and others) A dedicated Attendant Control unit: joystick, on/off button, mode button and LED, actuator (powered seating) indicators and a battery meter, per Quantum’s Q-Logic 3 Basic Operation Instructions . Quantum’s Q6 Edge 2.0 owner’s manual notes one visible side effect: “If your power chair is equipped with an attendant control, the fender lights will activate using the single switch when the controller is turned on.” At the rear of the chair, up by the push handles. Permobil Corpus chairs Permobil’s own M3 Corpus owner’s manual and F5 Corpus VS owner’s manual describe no Permobil attendant drive control at all — “attendant” appears in them only for freewheel pushing and general assistance. On Permobil chairs the driving electronics underneath are commonly R-net, so an attendant setup follows the R-net rules above; do not expect the Permobil owner’s manual to explain it. — One naming trap: an attendant control is not the same as freewheel mode (the motors disengaged so the chair can be pushed by hand, covered on Start Here ). Freewheel is muscle power with the brakes off. The attendant control is full powered driving, from behind. Who has control — and how it changes hands This is the heart of dual control. No system on this page mixes the two joysticks together, and none lets both drive at once. Each one picks a single control to be in charge (the makers’ own words: in charge , in control , in focus ) and ignores the other one’s joystick. What differs is how the chair decides, and how the two people swap. Per system, as documented: System Who is in charge How control changes hands What the other control can still do Invacare LiNX (two remotes, e.g. occupant remote + DLX-REM050) Whichever remote powered the system up . Invacare’s LiNX remote user manual, word for word: “Either remote can power up the system. The remote that powers up has control (remote-in-charge).” There is no mid-drive grab on the standard setup: “To change control, power down the system with either remote, then power up again with the remote that requires control.” One exception: if the system is locked and you unlock it from the DLX-REM050, the REM050 is in charge automatically. Nothing except its power button — and that button still matters: either remote can power the whole system down , and pressing the power button while driving is an emergency stop. You can tell who is in charge from the battery gauge: on the remote that is not in charge, the battery gauge is switched off. PG Drives R-net (Dual Attendant Module) Whichever side the module’s Control Switch selects. The module’s Control Indicator shows it: “If the red wheelchair light is on, the user’s input device has control. If the green attendant light is on, the Attendant Module has control.” On screen-based R-net systems the module in control displays the In Focus symbol. The Control Switch “transfers drive control of the wheelchair between the User Input Device and the Attendant Module” — a deliberate switch flip at the back of the chair, not a power cycle. The side not in control does not drive. Whether the occupant can take control back from the attendant is not a switch at all: it is a programmed setting (R-net calls the idea allow grab , set under Input Device Type in programming). Traditional attendant setups are configured so the user can never gain control from the attendant; R-net can be programmed to allow it. Which way your chair is set is invisible from the joystick — ask, and see The Keys . Dynamic DX / DX2 (DX-ACU) The attendant, whenever the User/Attendant switch on the DX-ACU is set to “Attendant”. The occupant remote shows it: the Attendant Profile LED lights, and the chair locks into the Attendant Drive Profile (Drive Profile 6) . The attendant releases control back by switching the User/Attendant switch back. Until that happens, the profile cannot be changed: the Attendant Drive Profile “will stay active until the attendant releases control back to the user.” The occupant’s joystick does nothing . The occupant remote’s buttons still work as normal — but pressing its Drive Profile button cannot take the drive profile away from the attendant; at most it returns the remote to Drive Mode. Quantum Q-Logic 2 The input device that powered the chair up . The Q-Logic 2 Basic Operation Instructions state it in one sentence: “When multiple input devices are used, the device that powered up the chair is in control.” Power the chair up from the control that should drive. The newer Q-Logic 3 instructions describe the attendant unit’s layout but defer its use to the provider — “For more information on these applications, contact your Quantum Rehab Provider” — so on a Q-Logic 3 chair, get the handover rule for your chair in writing from the provider. Not stated for the attendant pairing in the public Q-Logic documents this page could check — treat the other joystick as live until you have tested otherwise, with the chair unoccupied. Invacare MK6i The attendant, when the attendant control is switched in. The chair announces it rather than hiding it: code W05, “attendant control active” — w

title: Batteries & Chargers — PMD — BareBoard
headings: Three chemistries — and one that does not belong
Charging: the habit that decides the lifespan
Gel and AGM need different chargers — or the right profile
Voltage: reading the pair’s state of charge
Storage: park it full, keep it cool, top it up
Replacement: both, same size, and recycle the old pair
text: Batteries & Chargers A power wheelchair does not run on a battery. It runs on a pair — two batteries, wired together, charged together, and replaced together. Treat them as one system and a pair can last for years. Treat them as two separate boxes and the weaker one will take the other down with it. This page is that system, in plain language: what the pair is, what the chemistry words mean, what the numbers on the side really promise, and how charging decides whether a pair lives two years or five. Words in bold are defined where they first appear. Where a maker’s own safety warning matters, it is quoted word for word, with the maker and the document named. Provenance: capacities, break-in, charging and storage guidance on this page come from the makers’ own publications — above all MK Battery’s HME Battery Care Guide (LIT-HME1017) and MK’s gel specification sheets, Invacare’s TDX SP2 owner’s manual , and Lester Electrical’s charger manuals. Air-travel limits are the Federal Aviation Administration’s; funding limits are the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’. If a fact could not be checked in a primary source like those, it is not on this page. Safety first — the makers’ words Before any work at a battery terminal: put the chair on level ground, switch it OFF, and disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker. Work on one terminal at a time with an insulated tool, and remove rings, watches and other metal jewellery. A dropped tool across both terminals is a short circuit. Invacare, in the TDX SP2 owner’s manual (document 1578997-P), section 6.3.3: “DO NOT attempt to recharge the batteries and operate the power wheelchair at the same time.” “DO NOT sit in the power wheelchair while charging the batteries.” “NEVER attempt to recharge the batteries by attaching cables directly to the battery terminals.” On the charger itself, same manual, same section: “Only ever use the battery charger supplied with your power wheelchair, or a charger that has been approved by Invacare.” And on running a pair flat, section 6.3.6 of that manual: “Avoid ultra-deep discharges and never drain your batteries completely.” MK Battery, on the battery label reproduced in its HME Battery Care Guide : “WARNING: RISK OF FIRE, EXPLOSION OR BURNS. DO NOT DISASSEMBLE OR INCINERATE.” “NOT RECOMMENDED FOR INVERTED USE. FOLLOW PROPER CHARGING INSTRUCTIONS.” The pair is a system Almost every power chair runs on two 12-volt batteries wired in series . Series means one after the other in a chain, so their voltages add: 12V + 12V = 24V , which is what the chair’s motors and controller are built for. MK Battery’s HME Battery Care Guide puts it plainly: wheelchairs and scooters typically require two batteries with a 24-volt series connection. Because they are chained, the pair is only as strong as its weaker half. If one battery ages faster, it drags the other down on every ride and every charge. That is why every rule on this page is about the pair, not the single battery: Buy them as a matched pair — same maker, same model, same size, similar date codes. MK’s guide says never to mix and match different manufacturers, sizes or technologies, and never to mix gel with AGM. Charge them together, every time, with the chair’s charger. Test them separately when there is trouble (see Cheap Fixes, Procedure 3 ), but replace them together. Capacity is how much charge a battery holds, measured in amp-hours (Ah) — roughly, how many amps it can give, for how many hours, before it is empty. A 50 Ah battery and a 75 Ah battery can both be 12V; the bigger number is a bigger fuel tank, not more power at the plug. Deep-cycle means a battery built to be used and recharged every day, giving up a large share of its charge each time. A chair battery is a deep-cycle battery. That one fact explains most of this page. Three chemistries — and one that does not belong All chair batteries in this section are lead-acid underneath: lead plates in sulphuric acid. What differs is what holds the acid. Chemistry What it is, in plain words What it means for you Flooded (wet) The acid is liquid, sloshing free inside. The caps open so water can be topped up. Needs watering, can spill, and vents gas. Not sealed — and Medicare’s wheelchair policy denies a non-sealed battery as not reasonable and necessary (see Sources). Chairs do not ship with these. AGM — Absorbed Glass Mat The acid is soaked into fibreglass mats squeezed between the plates. Sealed. No watering, no spills. A common chair fitment, often a little cheaper than gel, with a higher charging voltage than gel (see Charging). Gel The acid is set into a jelly (a gelled electrolyte) so it cannot move. Sealed. No watering, no spills. MK Battery built its name on genuine gel for power mobility. Gel is sensitive to charging voltage: too high damages it, which is why charger profile matters. AGM and gel are both VRLA — valve-regulated lead-acid , meaning sealed batteries with a safety valve that lets out gas only if pressure builds too far. MK’s guide calls them “Sealed VRLA Gel and AGM batteries” and notes they require no watering. Sealed is why chairs ship with gel or AGM: the chair can tilt, travel and sit in a living room without acid on the floor, and the user never has to open a battery. Never fit car starting batteries. A car battery is built for one job: a huge burst for a few seconds to start an engine, then an immediate refill from the alternator. Its plates are thin, to give that burst. Used as a chair battery — drained deeply every day — those thin plates wear out fast, range falls, and the pair dies early. A chair needs the opposite design: thicker plates, built for slow, deep, daily use. That is what “deep-cycle” on the label is promising, and a starting battery does not have it. Group sizes and real capacities Group size is a standard box size — length, width and height — set by the Battery Council International (BCI). It says whether the battery fits your chair’s tray. It does not fix the capacity: two batteries in the same group size, from different makers or chemistries, can hold different amounts. The table below is one maker’s own numbers, stated exactly: MK Battery’s gel batteries , capacity at the 20-hour rate (written C/20 — the capacity measured when the battery is drained steadily over 20 hours; drain it faster and you get less, which is why the rate must always be named). Group size MK gel model Capacity at C/20 U1 MU-1 SLD G 31.6 Ah 22NF M22NF SLD G 51.0 Ah Group 34 M34 SLD G specification sheet 60.0 Ah Group 24 M24 SLD G specification sheet 73.6 Ah Source: MK Battery’s published gel specifications — the general specifications in MK’s HME literature and the individual M34 SLD G and M24 SLD G specification sheets linked in the table. MK notes on those sheets that amp-hour capacity is a nominal rating and that all ratings are after 15 cycles — which is the break-in point in the next section. Why these numbers look lower than the ones in Cheap Fixes, Procedure 3 . Procedure 3 quotes generic ranges across makers and chemistries — U1 34–35 Ah, 22NF 55 Ah, Group 34 60–65 Ah, Group 24 75–85 Ah. There is no contradiction. Those ranges are dominated by AGM batteries and by makers who rate generously; gel of the same box size commonly rates a few amp-hours lower, and MK rates its gel honestly at the same 20-hour rate. Same tray, different chemistry, different maker, different number. When you are comparing a quote, compare like with like: chemistry, maker, and the C/20 rate, all three. One more honest point: the pair’s capacity is the capacity of one battery in the chain, not double. Two 51.0 Ah batteries in series give you 24V at 51.0 Ah — the voltage added, the amp-hours did not. Break-in: the first 15 to 20 cycles A new gel or AGM pair does not give its full capacity on day one. MK Battery’s HME Battery Care Guide explains that the design trades some initial capacity for longer life, and states that gel battery performance improves once the battery has been cycled (discharged and recharged) 15–20 times — a break-in period MK calls necessary to fully activate the battery for maximum performance and longevity. Invacare’s TDX SP2 owner’s manual says the same thing in its own range: new batteries reach full capacity after about 10–20 charging cycles. At one charge a night, that is roughly two to three weeks of normal use. Two practical consequences: Do not judge a new pair by its first week’s range, and do not let a supplier judge it either. Short range in week one is the design, not a defect. Charge fully before first use, and charge daily and fully through the break-in. MK also notes there is no “memory” effect to train away — gel and AGM do not need to be run flat to stay healthy, and running them flat harms them. Charging: the habit that decides the lifespan MK’s guidance is blunt and simple: charge daily, and for as long as possible, even on days with low usage. Charge immediately after use; if you cannot, do not leave the pair in a discharged state for more than 24 hours. MK recommends a minimum charge of 8 hours to return about 80% of capacity, more time to return 100%, and a 12-hour charge at least once a week. Chronic undercharging — short, skipped charges — is, in MK’s words, a common cause of sulfation : hard crystals that form on the plates of a battery left partly empty, permanently blocking capacity. Depth of discharge — how much of the tank you use before recharging — sets cycle life. The harder a battery works, the shorter its life: Invacare’s manual gives the scale, about 500 cycles at 80% discharge against about 5,000 cycles at 10% discharge. You cannot avoid using your chair, but you can avoid the deep end: charge before the gauge is in the red, not after. Gel and AGM need different chargers — or the right profile A charge profile is the charger’s recipe: what voltage it holds at each stage of charging. Gel and AGM recipes are different, and the difference is voltage. F

text: Chair Control — the owner tool This is BareBoard’s own software, written here, for the person who rides the chair. Plug your phone into your chair, read what it is saying in plain English, see the settings the dealer menu hides, and — where the manufacturer’s own documents prove the path — change them yourself. New here? Start with the practice chair. It is a make-believe wheelchair inside this page. Every button works. Nothing real can break. Learn the whole tool on it first — that is what it is for. Version 1. Original software, built from this site’s own published research and the manufacturers’ public manuals. Not a copy of any dealer tool, and not affiliated with any manufacturer. Not connected Pick your chair below to begin. Step 1 — What chair are you connecting to? Practice chair (recommended first) A virtual R-net chair inside this page. No cables, no risk. Everything works. My real R-net chair Curtiss-Wright / PG Drives R-net (CJSM, CJSM2, Omni screens). Read-only in version 1 — see why below. VR2 or VSI chair Fault-code lookup in version 1: count the flashing bars, we translate them. LiNX chair Fault-code lookup in version 1: count the red flashes, we translate them. Curtis (enAble / P&W) chair Coming in a later version. The connection notes are written and waiting. How will your phone talk to the chair? USB cable + CAN adapter (Web Serial) Works in Chrome on Android phones and computers. The browser asks you to pick the adapter — nothing is installed. Bluetooth CAN bridge Wireless. Bridge protocols differ by maker — version 1 cannot pair yet. Listed honestly, not faked. USB CAN adapter (WebUSB / gs_usb) In development for version 2. The adapter family is documented; the browser driver is not finished. Connect Disconnect What the chair is saying Fault codes Settings How to connect What the chair is saying Every message your chair’s parts send each other, translated as it happens. The chair’s parts talk constantly — the joystick announcing itself, the power module reporting battery volts. Plain English first; the raw numbers are behind the details switch. Show the raw numbers (for the curious) Pause Clear Nothing yet. Connect to a chair (or the practice chair) and its messages will appear here. Fault codes, in plain English When a chair trips, it already tells you what is wrong — a code on the screen, or lights that flash a count. This reader uses the same tables published on Fault Codes, Translated , compiled from the manufacturers’ own manuals. The manuals behind them are in this site’s library: R-net trip codes (PG Drives) , VR2 / VSI flash codes , and LiNX flash codes (LiNX LE manual, section 10.3) . Read faults from the chair No connection? Read the code off your chair yourself If your chair shows a code or flashes a count, pick your system and enter what you see: System R-net — 4-digit screen code VR2 / VSI — flashing bars LiNX — red flashes Code or count Translate it Practice chair: make something go wrong On a real chair, faults happen to you. On the practice chair, you order them — so you can learn what each one looks like before it strands you. Motor unplugged (3B00) Low battery (2C00) Brake / freewheel lever (1505) Fix everything Your chair’s settings These numbers decide how your chair drives. They are shown, not changed , until you unlock them — and unlocking first saves a backup of every value, automatically. Full explanation of each setting: The Settings, in Plain Language . Unlock changing settings Connect to a chair first. Reading is always allowed — it is your chair and your data. No backup yet. Download my backup Put everything back (restore) How to connect — slowly, in order The idea Your chair’s parts talk to each other on a private little network inside the chair called its bus — one cable that runs from the joystick down to the power module in the base. This tool joins that conversation. Your phone cannot plug into the chair directly, so one small box sits in between: a CAN adapter . (CAN is the name of the network language cars and chairs both use.) Your phone → USB cable → CAN adapter → the chair’s bus cable → your chair The one safety fact that matters The chair’s bus cable carries 24-volt battery power on the same plug as the data wires . So the adapter must be galvanically isolated — built with an electrical barrier between the chair side and the phone side, rated 2500 volts or better. Isolation is what stops a wiring fault from travelling up the cable into your phone. Only ever connect through an isolated adapter. No exceptions, including “just for a second.” (This is the same rule as Reading the Chair .) What to buy (real products, named plainly) CANable (isolated model) — a small open-hardware USB-to-CAN adapter. Buy the isolated version specifically; not every CANable is isolated. It speaks a simple text protocol (called SLCAN) that this page can use directly through the browser — no software to install. Roughly the price of a pizza. PCAN-USB (PEAK) — the professional classic. Excellent hardware, but it uses its maker’s own computer driver, which a web page cannot use. Fine with desktop tools; not for this page in version 1. Bluetooth CAN bridges (various makers) — a wireless adapter that plugs into the chair and talks to the phone by Bluetooth. Each maker uses its own wireless language, so version 1 lists them honestly as not-yet-pairing instead of pretending. The chair end: the adapter’s chair-side wires land on the chair’s round 4-pin bus cable — the cable between the joystick and the power module. Adapter makers sell short pigtail cables for this; the bench method for identifying the connector is on Reading the Chair . The steps Park the chair on level ground. Switch it off . You do not need to be sitting in it — better if you are not. Plug the adapter into the chair’s bus cable first, while everything is off. Plug the USB cable from the adapter into your phone (Android) or computer. Chrome browser open on this page. Pick My real R-net chair above, pick the USB connection, and press Connect . The browser will show a list — choose your adapter. Switch the chair on. Its messages appear under “What the chair is saying.” You are listening to your own chair. What version 1 does on a real chair — honestly On a real chair, version 1 listens and reads only : messages, fault codes, and your settings, shown to you. It does not change settings on a real chair yet. Why: this site proved the reading path on captured dealer sessions, but the writing path has not yet been proven on a live power module on the bench — and this site does not guess at writes to a machine a person’s body depends on. The full changing flow — unlock, automatic backup, change, one-tap restore — works today on the practice chair, and moves to real chairs when the bench proof lands. The whole story is on Honest Limits . Phones Works in Chrome on Android and on computers (Chrome/Edge). An iPhone cannot do this in a browser — Apple does not let web pages use USB accessories or Bluetooth the way this needs. That is a limit of the phone’s system, not a missing feature here. Before you touch a real chair Before any step that touches a plug, cable, motor, brake, actuator, or battery terminal: put the chair on level ground, switch it OFF, and disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker. Do not work while seated in the chair. Connector pins can remain live after switch-off. At a battery terminal, work on one terminal at a time with an insulated tool. If you cannot disconnect power, inspect visually only and stop. (The same rule heads the fault-code tables .) ← Back to PMD · The Settings →
