text: Exploded View: Quantum 4Front 2 / 4Front 2 HD The whole 4Front 2, taken apart by the people who built it. Quantum’s Illustrated Parts Breakdown for this chair covers two models — the 4Front 2 and the heavier-duty 4Front 2 HD — in one book of 94 pages, exploding 42 assemblies into numbered parts. Every diagram below is Quantum’s own page, followed by the book’s parts table with a plain-language line added for every part. Where the two models differ, the book says so in the part name — the HD suspension packages, the HD drive motors, the HD drive programs, and the HD badge decal are all called out below. Coverage: full IPB. Every assembly in the book that carries a parts list is here: 42 assemblies, 460 parts. The book’s last pages are its two appendices — a pages index and a parts index — which carry no new parts and are used here to check the tables, not repeated as steps. The book’s cover plate is a caster-arm diagram with no parts list, so it is not a step either. The chair in numbers From the owner’s manual and the parts book — the numbers the maker itself prints: Drive: front-wheel drive — the big powered wheels sit at the front, swivelling caster wheels trail at the rear, and small anti-tip wheels sit ahead of the drive wheels. Two motor/brake assemblies, one per side. Motors: Linix motors, 5 mph — or 6.25 mph with the anti-tips drive program (the book’s Q-Logic 3 SD card listings name both speeds). Drive wheels: 14 in × 3 in, flat-free or pneumatic — or 14 in × 4 in with knobby tires. Rear casters: 9 in flat-free wheels, 215 mm tires. Anti-tip wheels: 100 mm, with bearings and spacer. Batteries: two 12 V batteries — Group 24 AGM, 69.2 Ah (C/5), handles removed (MK) — or a Group 24 gel option the book lists as a pair. Always replace both together. Charger: 8 amp offboard CTE charger, with US, UK, EU, and AU power cords listed. Controller: Q-Logic 3, with EX, 3e, and stand-alone joystick options. The full specification table — weight capacity, range, turning radius, seat sizes — lives in the product-insert specification sheets the book lists in the Owner’s Package (INFINFB4329 for the 4Front 2, INFINFB4335 for the 4Front 2 HD). Those sheets are not in the library yet, so those numbers are not stated here rather than guessed. If you hold a copy, the library would take it. The source Guide: Quantum Rehab Illustrated Parts Breakdown for the 4Front 2 and 4Front 2 HD power chairs. Document: INFMANU5204 Rev. D — 94 pages, US edition (the book’s own footer reads “4Front 2 / 4Front 2 HD IPB (S/N JF6,JF7), US”; Documoto export 2022-04-26). An Australian edition, INFMANU5263 Rev. A, also exists; this page follows the newer US Rev. D. Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): quantum_4front-2_ipb.pdf — also at the dealer repost it was collected from, alliedmedical.co.nz . Owner’s manual (PDF, in this site’s library): quantum_4front-2_owner.pdf — INFMANU4864 Rev. E, February 2020, 28 pages, from Quantum’s own site. The book is honest about its own scope, in its introduction: “An IPB is a graphically portrayed parts listing of product components which have been deemed to have serviceable, maintenance significance.” Items are also listed by parent assembly: “The parent assembly reference number is A1 — A5. That part contains all of the items listed as and contained within A1, A2, A3, A4, & A5. As long as these subcomponents have a callout associated with them, they can be selected for replacement or quote.” Parent rows below keep the book’s own callout ranges (A1 – A6 and the like). This US edition prints no price column — its tables are Item, Part No., Name, and Qty only. The book also prints 14 “web link” rows inside its tables — pointers to separate Quantum breakdowns for joystick shrouds, mounts, knobs, SD cards, and the backup camera. Those rows are cross-references, not parts, and are not counted in the 460. The book prints its Q-Logic 3 SD Cards plate twice, under Joysticks and under Electronics, with identical rows; both steps are reproduced as printed. One row’s part number is blank in the book’s table (Joystick Receiver Mounts, E1); the number ACC123525 is taken from the book’s own Appendix B parts index, which lists it on that plate’s page and nowhere else in the table — the index and the table agree everywhere else, checked row by row. Publishing basis: our own original writing, plus facts — part numbers, names, and quantities — from the manufacturer’s published guide (facts are free for all to use, Feist v. Rural Telephone ). The diagrams are the manufacturer’s, reproduced with attribution; nothing is redrawn or presented as ours. The maker’s own warnings, word for word The parts book prints no warning paragraphs. On Quantum’s chairs the safety warnings are decals, and the book lists them as parts in the Decal Package assembly. The warning and caution decals in this book include: DWR1234L957 · DECAL,WARNING,DEFLATE TIRE COMPLETELY,L-1234-957 DWR1235L515 · DECAL,WARNING,BATTERY WARNINGS,L-1235-515 DWR1235L516 · DECAL,WARNING,DEFLATE TIRE COMPLETELY,FRENCH,L-1235-516 DWR1235L520 · DECAL,CAUTION,EXTENSION CORD/GROUNDING PRONG,L-1235-520 DWR1235L521 · DECAL,WARNING,CONTROLLER CORD PLACEMENT,L-1235-521 LAB2005393 · DECAL,4FRONT REAR CASTER NUT WARNING LABEL If a warning decal on your chair is peeling or unreadable, it is a replaceable part — its number is in that table. A warning you cannot read cannot warn you. The owner’s manual (INFMANU4864 Rev. E) states the safety rules in its own words. These are quoted verbatim: “Do not operate your new power chair for the first time without completely reading and understanding this owner’s manual.” “Do not remove the anti-tip wheels.” “Place unit on level ground and stand to one side when changing from drive mode to freewheel mode or freewheel mode to drive mode.” “The spring tension on your power chair was factory set to meet the needs of the demographic majority of users. Do not adjust the tension of any spring on your power chair.” “Do not replace batteries when seat is occupied.” “Do not mix old and new batteries. Always replace both batteries at the same time.” “Keep tools and other metal objects away from the battery terminals. Contact with tools can cause electrical shock.” “Battery posts, terminals, and related accessories contain lead and lead compounds. Wear goggles and gloves when handling batteries and wash hands after handling.” “The batteries in your power chair should only be serviced or replaced by a Quantum Rehab Provider or a qualified technician.” “CAUTION! Federal law restricts this device to sale by or on the order of a physician or other certified personnel licensed by the law of the State (US only) or region in which this personnel practices to use or order the use of the device.” The manual also says there are more warnings in the Consumer Safety Guide (INFMANU5075) that ships with the chair. That guide is not in the library yet; its warnings are not paraphrased here. The full record: an open FDA recall This chair has an open Class 2 FDA recall, and it matters to every owner, because it is about the chair stopping without warning. The FDA record (recall event 99286, initiated June 25, 2026, posted July 31, 2026, status open and classified) covers the 4Front 2 (recall Z-2841-2026) and the 4Front 2 HD (recall Z-2851-2026); the FDA recall record lists 510(k) K143383 for the recall. The manufacturer’s reason, as the FDA records it: if the “Remind Me Later” option is selected for user reminders, reminder pop-up messages may appear while the wheelchair is in use; if this occurs while driving, the wheelchair may perform an unexpected park brake stop, which may result in fall or injury; if it occurs while not driving, the control system may crash and remain in pre-operational mode. The fix is a software update to Q-Logic version 2.0.13 or later, and owners were told to disable “Remind Me Later” immediately and contact their dealer to schedule the update. Quantity in commerce: 1,102 units for the 2 HD record. Sources: FDA recall record Z-2851-2026, preserved copy in this site’s library: recall_Z-2851-2026.html . FDA recall record Z-2841-2026 (4Front 2): FDA accessdata — no library copy held yet. Contents The assemblies are laid out in the book’s own order, under its 17 numbered sections. Every step is one exploded view from the maker’s guide, followed by its parts table. The Callout column is the label printed on the diagram. The Part number column is the maker’s own number — the number a parts desk cannot argue with. The IPB page for each step is printed with it. 1. text: Exploded View: Amylior Alltrack M3 The Alltrack M3 is Amylior’s mid-wheel-drive complex-rehab chair: a Canadian-built power base (Vaudreuil-Dorion, Quebec) with a patented six-wheel Dual Action Suspension, PG Drives VR2 or R-net electronics, and a 300 lb capacity. It is also the rare chair whose maker publishes the full parts book openly, on its own website — every suspension arm, motor, wheel, and battery-box part, numbered. The catch is that the book is in French only. This page reproduces Section 3.1.3 of Amylior’s Livre de pièces — the M3 powered base in all five of its drive configurations — with every part number, plus the labeled overview from the owner’s manual. Coverage: full IPB. The maker’s parts book for this base is complete and public: five exploded diagrams, 136 numbered parts. The maker’s descriptions are in French, as printed; the plain-English column next to them is ours. What the book does not cover — seating, electronics, the M3-HD — is named at the bottom of the page, not hidden. The sources Guide 1: Livre de pièces (Parts Book), Section 3 — Bases motorisées, document PM | P24026 | R09, section updated 2026/06/15, Amylior Inc. (71 pages, French). Section 3.1.3, “La série Alltrack M”, is the M3 base: five subsections, 3.1.3.1–3.1.3.5. Full record (PDF, in this site’s library): Parts Book, Section 3, Part 1 (pages 1–36) · Part 2 (pages 37–71) (split to fit the 25 MB file limit; complete original at Amylior: amylior.com — Livre de pièces R09, Section 3 ). Link-only: no copy of the summary is held in this site’s library — the summary PDF is not posted by the FDA at its standard paths (checked 2026-11-17: cdrh_docs/pdf09, pdf10, and pdf all return 404). (24 pages), and Alltrack M3 order form, document MKT.F113 | OF | PD-A20602 | R01, November 2025 (15 pages) — used to corroborate the specifications and the option list. The chair’s fault codes are translated on this site: VR2 fault codes, translated and R-net fault codes, translated . The battery lesson is on this site: Batteries & chargers . The maker’s own warnings Amylior prints these in the Alltrack M3 Owner’s Manual (OM | PD-A20601 | 1000896 | R03), Section VI, General Warnings. The wording below is the maker’s own, quoted word for word. Read the warnings. “Read all warnings in this section. If you do not comply with these warnings, a fall, tip-over or loss of control may occur and cause severe injury to you or others.” Get trained first. “Before using this power wheelchair, you should be trained in its safe use by your health care professional.” Wear the positioning strap. “ALWAYS wear a positioning strap.” Check the joystick every time. “DO NOT use your power wheelchair if the joystick does not spring back to the neutral position.” “DO NOT use your power wheelchair if the joystick rubber gaiter is ripped or damaged.” Stay under the weight limit. “The user and items carried should NEVER exceed the total weight capacity identified on your power wheelchair.” Going over the limit is likely to damage the seat, the power seating options, the frame, or the fasteners, and may cause severe injury. Do not modify the chair. “NEVER make any customizations, changes or modifications to any part of your Alltrack power wheelchair unless explicitly authorized by AMYLIOR. Doing so will void the warranty and may create a safety hazard.” Freewheel and brake release levers. “DO NOT engage or disengage freewheel/brake release levers unless power to the wheelchair is off.” “Make sure both levers are completely engaged before turning power on to ensure proper control of the wheelchair.” With the levers disengaged the chair has no braking ability. Turn it off when parked. “ALWAYS turn off all power to your wheelchair when you are parked, even for a moment.” That stops accidental movement from contact with the joystick and unintended movement from EMI sources. Keep it out of water. “Your power wheelchair is not designed for use in a heavy rain storm, or in snowy or icy conditions.” “NEVER take your power wheelchair into a shower, tub, pool or sauna.” Transport without the WC19 option. “NEVER allow anyone to sit in the wheelchair while it is secured in a moving vehicle” unless the chair has the WC19-ISO occupied-transport option. The built-in brackets are for securing an unoccupied chair only. Quoted from the Owner’s Manual, Section VI (pp. 10–16). How to read this page The parts book is French only. No English edition of Amylior’s parts book was found in public. The Maker’s description column reproduces the book’s French text exactly as printed — those short labels are the part names, and they are what you quote to a parts desk. The What this part does column is our plain-English explanation of each part. Colour codes. Parts whose number ends in -XXX* take a colour suffix: add the code for your chair’s colour to the part number (the book’s example: S-XXXX-BAO). The codes are PRISMA (noir Prismacolor, black), BAO (noir opale métallique, metallic opal black), BOR (orange brûlé métallique, metallic burnt orange), CBU (bleu bonbon, candy blue), CRE (rouge bonbon, candy red), GMC (gris charbon, charcoal grey), MLP (mauve minuit, midnight mauve), MWT (blanc mat, matte white), BLK (noir lustré, gloss black), MYG (vert militaire, military green), MYT (sable militaire, military sand), OPM (orange étincelant, sparkling orange), PKP (rose perlé, pearl pink), RZB (violine, violet), SBM (noir mat, matte black), SVM (argent métallisé, metallic silver). Effective dates. The Effective column is the date from which that part applies, as printed in the book. Where a part was superseded, the book lists the newer number with its later date. Which of the five sections is your chair? The book is organized by base generation and motor type. Generation 1 is the original M3 base; Generation 2 is the current base. The motor type is on the motor’s own label: SRG04 (gear release), SRG06 (brake release), SRG01 (brake release), or LiNX (brake release, with encoder). Gear-release motors have freewheel release levers; brake-release motors have brake release levers — the owner’s manual shows both (Section III, callouts 7 and 11). Not illustrated. Rows marked “not illustrated” are parts the book lists in its tables with no callout on the diagram — hardware kits and pivot kits that are ordered by number alone. Availability. Each page of the book carries a legend — COURANT (current), DISPONIBLE (available), DISCONTINUÉ (discontinued) — marking each part’s status. Those marks did not survive text extraction, so per-part status is not reproduced here; check the book itself before ordering. Build order The assemblies are laid out in the order you would build the chair: the whole chair first, then the powered base in its five drive configurations. Every step is one labeled figure from the maker’s guides, followed by its parts table. The Callout column is the number printed on the diagram. The owner’s manual labels the M3 once, with fifteen numbered parts, and that is the map for everything that follows: the seat and its frame sit on the powered base, the drive wheels sit in the middle, and the casters sit at the front and back. Step 1 — The Alltrack M3, labeled by Amylior Fig. 1. The Alltrack M3, labeled by Amylior — overview reproduced from the owner’s manual (Section III, p. 6). Callout Part (maker’s label) What this part does 1 Joystick The hand control you drive with: push it the way you want to go. On this chair it is a VR2 or R-net joystick — VR2 fault codes and R-net fault codes are translated on this site. 2 Backrest The padded back you lean against; part of the seating system. 3 Front Riggings The legrest assemblies at the front that support your legs and feet. 4 Foot Platform The one-piece foot platform your feet rest on. 5 Seat Pan The flat pan under the seat cushion; the cushion sits on it. 6 Base Frame The powered base — the frame that holds the motors, batteries, and suspension. Steps 2–6 take it apart. 7 Freewheel Release Levers (optional motors) The levers that disconnect the motor gears so the chair can be pushed by hand. Only on gear-release motors (Steps 2 and 3). 8 Caster Fork The fork that holds a caster wheel and lets it swivel. 9 Caster Tire The small unpowered wheel at the front or back. It is not powered — it follows where the chair turns. 10 Drive Wheel The big powered wheel, 12.5 or 14 inches. On the M3 it sits in the middle — that is what mid-wheel drive means. 11 Brake Release Levers (std motors) The levers that release the motor

text: Exploded View: Invacare AVIVA FX The AVIVA FX is Invacare’s front-wheel-drive complex-rehab chair: the front-wheel-drive version of the TDX SP2, running Dynamic’s LiNX electronics with the Ultra Low Maxx seating system, cleared by the FDA in January 2020. It is also a chair whose parts book does not exist in public. Invacare publishes no Illustrated Parts Breakdown and no spare parts catalogue for it — not for owners, not openly at all. Their service manual says it in one line: “You can find information about ordering spare parts in the spare parts catalogue.” No exploded views, no part numbers, no way to order a caster bearing without a dealer in the middle. Coverage: manual-only. What Invacare does publish is the labeled overview in the User Manual — Figs. 4-1 and 4-2, eleven lettered parts, showing the FX itself in its two seating configurations — and a full Service Manual written for technicians, whose drive and battery figures are lettered part by part. That is everything the maker gives the person who rides in it and the technician who services it. We reproduce those figures exactly, as callout tables, and we name the gap exactly: every assembly-level parts breakdown for this chair is a source gap until Invacare publishes one. The FX shares its LiNX electronics with the TDX SP2 — the chair it was derived from — and the TDX SP2’s full parts catalogue is on this site , but the FX base is a different base, and the SP2 catalogue does not cover it. The sources Guide 1: User Manual — Invacare AVIVA FX Power Wheelchair Base, document 60101916-A, Invacare Corporation, ©2020 (108 pages; models IFX-20R, IFX-20SP, IFX-20MP, IFX-20C). Link-only: no copy of this manual is held in this site’s library — no Invacare-published PDF of it was found, and the dealer-hosted copy is unreachable from here. The full text was verified from the public copy on the manual aggregator ManualsLib at manualslib.com — Invacare AVIVA FX User Manual ; the overview figures are on page 22 . A second public copy on ManualOwl was used to cross-check the callouts, and both copies agree. Guide 2: Service Manual — Invacare AVIVA FX Series, document 1675507-A, Invacare Corporation, ©2023. Link-only: no copy is held in this site’s library. The full text was verified from the public copy on the manual aggregator Manuals+ at manuals.plus — Invacare AVIVA FX Series Service Manual . iFixit hosts the same document behind a free account; that copy was not used. Guide 3: FDA 510(k) summary K192216 — Invacare AVIVA FX Power Wheelchair, Model IFX-20MP, cleared 2 January 2020 (Class II, product code ITI; predicate: Invacare TDX SP2, K170507). Full record (PDF, in this site’s library): K192216.pdf (also at FDA: accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf19/K192216.pdf ). Guide 4: FDA Class 2 recall Z-0446-2022 (event 89062, 12 November 2021) — AVIVA FX with LiNX Gyro, firmware 6.1.2. Full record (in this site’s library): recall_Z-0446-2022.html (also at FDA: accessdata.fda.gov — recall Z-0446-2022 ). The LiNX service manual the battery procedure points to is held in this site’s library: Invacare LiNX Service Manual . The chair’s fault codes are translated on this site: LiNX fault codes, translated . The maker’s own warnings Invacare prints these in the AVIVA FX User Manual (60101916-A) and the AVIVA FX Service Manual (1675507-A). The safety wording below is paraphrased into plain language, except the short lines in quotation marks, which are the maker’s exact words. Do not modify the chair. “DO NOT modify this mobility device or any of its components.” Changing the chair or any of its parts can make it fail, and a failure can kill or seriously injure you. The positioning strap is not a seat belt. “The seat positioning strap is NOT a seat belt. It is NOT designed to restrain the user in the event of a collision or tip over.” It only holds you in the right seated position. Never use it if it is damaged, frayed, or broken — get a replacement from your provider. Use only Invacare-approved parts. Wrong or improper replacement parts can make the chair fail. Tighten all hardware securely after any adjustment, and make sure every electrical connection is secure — a loose connection can cut power without warning. Keep lit cigarettes away from the seating. A lit cigarette dropped on the upholstery can start a fire that kills. Anyone using oxygen must take a lit cigarette out of their mouth before driving the chair, and keep ashtrays at a safe distance. Watch the batteries. Check the charge before you drive — a dead battery can leave you stranded, so do not drive on depleted batteries. “The POSITIVE (+) RED battery cable MUST connect to the POSITIVE (+) battery terminal(s)/post(s).” “NEVER allow any of your tools and/or battery cable(s) to contact BOTH battery post(s) at the same time.” Batteries are heavy — up to 52 lb each — always use the lifting strap, and keep battery acid off skin, eyes, and clothing. Do not use the Sip-n-Puff while the chair is moving. It can make the chair move unexpectedly. Keep it dry. Do not expose the chair to liquids or rain, and do not drive it outside the operating conditions in the manual. The USB charger is for mobile phones only — nothing else, never in wet conditions, never if it is damaged. Mind the pinch points when adjusting the chair, and keep your feet on the footplate at all times, never hanging over the edge. Do not store the chair near heat, open flames, or combustible products. Do not exceed the weight capacity. Going over the limit can make the chair unstable — 300 lb (136 kg) with the Captain’s seat or the non-elevating Ultra Low Maxx, 250 lb (113 kg) with the elevating seat. Paraphrased from the User Manual, sections 2, 6, 7.4, and 13.1, and the Service Manual, sections 6.7 and 6.10; the quoted lines are verbatim. Build order The assemblies are laid out in the order you would build the chair: seating and frame first, drive second, batteries last. Every step is one labeled figure — or a set of figures — from the maker’s guides, followed by its parts table. The Callout column is the letter printed on the diagram. There is no part-number column on this page — Invacare publishes no part numbers for this chair, and we do not invent them. Frame and seating: Step 1: The AVIVA FX, labeled by Invacare Drive: Step 2: The motor/gearbox unit Batteries: Step 3: The batteries and the battery door Stage 1 — Frame and seating Start with the chair itself. The maker’s overview shows the FX twice — once with the Ultra Low Maxx seating system (Fig. 4-1) and once with the Captain’s seat (Fig. 4-2) — and labels both with the same eleven letters. The front-wheel-drive layout is the thing to notice: the big powered wheels sit at the front, under the front of the seat, with small castors at the back and anti-tippers at the front. Step 1 — The AVIVA FX, labeled by Invacare The two overview diagrams (User Manual, §4.1, p. 22) are reproduced here as their callout table. No downloadable scan of the page could be hosted, so the diagrams themselves are linked: see Figs. 4-1 and 4-2 on page 22 of the public ManualsLib copy . Callout Part (maker’s label) What this part does A Back Cushion The padded back you lean against; part of the seating system. B Armrest Supports your arm, and helps you transfer in and out of the chair. C Remote (Joystick) The hand control you drive with: push it the way you want to go. It is the LiNX remote — what its fault codes mean is on this site . D Seat Cushion The cushion you sit on. E Drive Wheel The big powered wheel, 14 × 3 with rim inserts. On the FX it sits at the front — that is what front-wheel drive means. F Fork The single-sided fork that holds the caster wheel and lets it swivel. G Caster The small unpowered wheel at the back, 8 × 2 and puncture-proof. It is not powered — it follows where the chair turns. H Front Rigging The legrest and footplate assembly at the front that supports your legs and feet. I Back Cane The upright post of the seat back; the back cushion mounts to it. J Headrest Supports your head. K Anti-tipper The small wheel that stops the chair tipping over. Stage 2 — Drive One motor per side, each bolted to its own gearbox. The service manual treats the motor and gearbox as one unit that can be replaced together or split apart. Step 2 — The motor/gearbox unit Fig. 6-13 in the Service Manual (§6.7.1) labels the unit in two parts. The motors are DuraWatt 4-pole units, maintenance-free with lifetime brushes — there is no brush service in the manual. When a motor is fitted to a gearbox, the scale on the motor is lined up with the mark on the gearbox: 200° for the left motor, 350° for the right. The nut that holds the sealing ring is tightened to 8.5 Nm. Callout Part (maker’s label) What this part does A Gearbox The gear set between the motor and the drive wheel. It slows the motor down and multiplies its turning force. B Motor The DuraWatt electric motor that turns the drive wheel — one per side, 24 volts, 324 watts. The engaging lever — the freewheel lever that disengages the drive so the chair can be pushed by hand — has its own figures in the same section: its set screw is tightened to 6.2 Nm, and the cap screw to 1.7 Nm with thread-locking adhesive. The rubber bumper and the shock damper are separate service items in the same section (§6.7.6, §6.7.7). Stage 3 — Batteries The two batteries live in a box under the seat, behind a rear door that carries the electronics with it. That is the design detail that matters for service: the LiNX power module and the G-Trac sensor stay attached to the battery door assembly while you change the batteries — you lift the whole door, electronics and all, over the rear swing arm and set it on the ground. text: Permobil C300, Opened — Every Part, Named This page takes the Permobil C300 apart on paper — every assembly, every part, named. It is built from Permobil’s own parts catalog, callout by callout, with Permobil’s part numbers and a plain-language line for every part. The C300 is a front-wheel-drive complex-rehabilitation power base; this page covers the base and its seating — PS, Corpus II, and Corpus 3G — across all four electronics generations the chair was sold with: VSI, Pilot+, VR2, and R-net. How to use this page: open the catalog page linked under each table. The catalog’s diagram shows the assembly pulled apart, each part marked with a numbered callout. Find the callout in the table below it: that row gives you Permobil’s part number, the part’s number in Permobil’s current ordering system, the part’s name, and what it does, in one plain line. One warning before you start: four electronics generations fit this chair — VSI, Pilot+, VR2, and R-net — so find which one your chair has before ordering electronics. And the chassis covers changed in January 2012: the covers are split into two assemblies, before and after that date. The headrest assembly is the one exception on this page: its catalog table is a list of 6,615 image-only entries with no descriptions, and it is not reproduced as a table — see that assembly for why. About this chair The C300 is Permobil’s front-wheel-drive complex-rehabilitation power base — the chair underneath the seating that clinics fit to the rider. Permobil’s own words on the Corpus 3G sheet: the company calls itself the inventor of front-wheel-drive powerchair technology. The drive wheels sit at the front, with the casters behind — the layout that lets the chair turn in tight indoor spaces and climb obstacles with the big wheels first. Seating came three ways: the PS seat (adjustable, VR2 as standard), the Corpus II seat, and the Corpus 3G seat with its ergonomic backrest. Power functions run to 50° of tilt and 175° of recline on the Corpus 3G sheet; the PS seat’s elevator lifts 8 inches. The electronics changed across the chair’s production: VSI, Pilot+, VR2, and R-net with the ICS seating bus. The R-net configuration sheets in this catalog are dated by the chairs they shipped on: the PS sheet covers chairs shipped on or after 14 April 2008, the Corpus sheet chairs shipped on or after 19 August 2008. Both use an 80-amp PG R-net power module. It runs on two Group 34 batteries and carries up to 300 lb. Its funding codes are K0856 and K0861. The source for this page is Permobil’s own parts catalog at catpages.permobil.com , fetched 22 November 2026: 36 category pages for the C300, each with a diagram and a parts table. A parts catalog is the manufacturer’s own list of every serviceable part, with a drawing of each assembly pulled apart and a table of callouts, part numbers, and names. How to read this exploded view Pos — the catalog’s position code. The number before the dot is the callout on the diagram; the number after the dot separates rows at the same callout. The same callout can carry two rows when two versions fit there — callout 9 on the old chassis lists the brake-release arm for pre-2012 chairs and for chairs after 2013 — and the same part can appear at two callouts when the chair takes two of them. A callout with a list under it on the diagram (like “1: 2, 17–27”) is a parent assembly — the parts listed under it belong to it. Permobil part no. — the catalog number. D365 part no. — the part’s number in Permobil’s Dynamics 365 ordering system, as the catalog lists it. Where the catalog shows one, that is the current ordering number. Where it is blank, the catalog lists only the catalog number. What it is — the catalog’s own description, word for word. What it does — our plain-language line, written for this page. It says what the part type does, not which exact parts it joins to — the catalog does not say that, so neither do we. No quantities. The catalog lists parts per assembly without counts, so this page lists none. OBSOLETE — the maker no longer sells the part. Order the replacement the catalog names, if any. Left and right are from the rider’s point of view, sitting in the chair. The headrest assembly is the exception. Its catalog table lists 6,615 entries, every one marked “Image Only” with no position and no description — a list of headrest pad variants by part code. They are not reproduced as a table here; the assembly section below says so and links the catalog page. 1. text: Exploded View: Permobil F3 Corpus This page is different, and the difference is the story. text: Exploded View: Pride Jazzy 1107 This page is different, and the difference is the story. Pride Mobility does not publish an Illustrated Parts Breakdown for the Jazzy 1107 — not for owners, not openly at all. What Pride does publish is the labeled overview in the owner’s manual — the whole chair, the power base, the electrical parts, the seat adjustments, the drive wheel taken apart, and the batteries, each with its own diagram — plus a four-page troubleshooting sheet that names the fault codes for both controllers the chair was sold with. This page puts both together, and names the gap exactly: everything below the manual — motors, gearboxes, casters, shrouds, harnesses — has no public part number, because Pride sells those parts through its dealers. Coverage: manual-only. The Jazzy 1107 is a mid-wheel-drive power chair: two motors, Active-Trac suspension, and two 12-volt U-1 batteries. Mid-wheel drive means the powered wheels sit in the middle of the chair, with a small swivelling caster wheel at the back and an anti-tip wheel at the front — that is why it turns in a tight circle. The controller is the electronics that drive the chair: the joystick you hold and the power module inside the base that connects it to the motors and batteries. This chair was sold with one of two controllers: Pride’s own FLIGHT, shown in the manual’s electrical diagram, or a PG Drives VSI. U-1 is a battery size standard — the size, not a brand. Weight capacity is 300 lb (136 kg). The chair is 23.375 inches wide and, by the manual’s own drawing, turns in a 21.875-inch radius. Not the Quantum 1107. Pride also sold the same base as the Quantum 1107, with its own manual (INFMANU2980, 2008) under the Quantum Rehab brand. The chairs share the base and most of the diagrams; the branding and the manual are different. That chair is not covered here. The sources Guide: Owner’s Manual — Jazzy 1107, INFMANU2846 Rev. The maker’s own warnings, word for word Pride prints these in the 1107 owner’s manual. Word for word, UK spelling and all: An authorised Pride Dealer or a qualified technician must perform the initial setup of this power chair and must perform all of the procedures in this manual. Do not use the power chair while the drive motors are disengaged! Do not disengage the drive motors when the power chair is on an incline or decline, as the unit could roll on its own! Only engage the freewheel mode when on a level surface. It is important to remember that when your power chair is in freewheel mode, the braking system is disengaged. Do not use freewheel lever handles as tie-down points to secure this product. Explosive gases may be generated while charging the batteries. Keep the power chair and battery charger away from sources of ignition such as flames or sparks and provide adequate ventilation when charging the batteries. You must recharge your power chair’s batteries with the supplied off-board charger. Do not use an automotive-type battery charger. Battery posts, terminals and related accessories contain lead and lead compounds. Wear goggles and gloves when handling batteries and wash hands after handling. Always use two batteries of the exact same type, chemistry and amp-hour (Ah) capacity. Refer to specifications table in this manual and in the manual supplied with the battery charger for recommended type and capacities. Corrosive chemicals contained in batteries. Use only AGM or Gel-Cell batteries to reduce the risk of leakage or explosive conditions. Do not replace battery when seat is occupied. The batteries on your power chair should only be serviced or replaced by an authorised Pride Dealer or a qualified technician. Do not mix or match new and old batteries. If you encounter a situation where one battery needs to be replaced, then replace both batteries. Refer to the specifications table in this manual and the manual supplied with the battery charger for recommended type and capacities. Make sure your tyres are inflated to 2.4 bar (35 psi). Do not underinflate or overinflate your tyres. Low pressure may result in loss of control, and overinflated tyres may burst. Overinflating tyres can cause them to explode. When climbing an incline, do not zigzag or drive at an angle up the face of the incline. Drive your power chair straight up the incline. This greatly reduces the possibility of a tip or a fall. Always exercise extreme caution when negotiating an incline. Any attempt to climb or descend a slope steeper than 8.7% (5°) may put your power chair in an unstable position and cause it to tip. Never travel down an incline rearward. Doing so may cause the power chair to tip. Always exercise extreme caution when negotiating an incline. Do not pick up the seat frame by the armrests. They are free to pivot, and you may lose control of the seat if they do so. Make sure the seat latch safety is flipped down before using your power chair. Consult your authorised Pride Dealer before attempting to change the anti-tip wheel height! Changing the anti-tip wheel height affects handling under acceleration! Do not remove the anti-tip wheels. The wheels on your power chair should only be serviced or replaced by an authorised Pride Dealer or a qualified technician. When changing a tyre, remove only the centre lug nut and washer, then remove the wheel. If any further disassembly is required, deflate the tyre completely or it may explode. text: Exploded View: Pride Jazzy 1450 This page is the full breakdown. Pride Mobility publishes a complete Illustrated Parts Breakdown for the Jazzy 1450 — INFMANU5144 Rev. A, 113 pages — and this page works through it for the VR2 chair: the frame, the suspension, the motors, the wheels, the electronics, the joystick, the shrouds, the batteries, and the charger, each with the maker’s own part numbers. One thing to know up front: the breakdown Pride published is the Australian export, for chairs whose serial numbers start JC4. The part numbers are Pride’s own global system and the chair is the same chair — but the charger in the Australian book comes with an Australian plug. The US chair ships with the US cordset, and the same parts list names it. Coverage: full IPB — VR2 configuration. The Jazzy 1450 is a bariatric power chair — bariatric means built for a heavier user, 600 lb here — with front-wheel drive: the big powered wheels sit at the front of the chair, which is what lets it turn in tight indoor spaces. It runs on a 90-amp PG VR2 controller — PG is Penny & Giles, the company that makes the controller, and VR2 is the model — and two 12-volt Group 24 batteries. Group 24 is a battery size standard, the size, not a brand. Top speed is up to 4.9 mph and range up to 16.5 miles per charge, on Pride’s current specifications sheet. The same book also covers the Quantum 1450, the sister chair, which can be ordered with Q-Logic electronics instead of VR2. Q-Logic is Quantum Rehab’s own controller family. This page follows the Jazzy 1450 with VR2 — the standard Jazzy configuration, models 1450-2VHD and 1450-2SPVHD, Medicare codes K0826, K0827, and K0839. The Q-Logic assemblies are in the library copy of the book if you need them. One naming wrinkle, stated in the book itself: the motors listed for the VR2 chair are Hammer II motors, while the electronics assembly is labeled for Hammer XL motors. The Hammer II replaced the Hammer XL, from serial number JC528113047020 for the Jazzy 1450 (JC427313082020 for the Quantum 1450) onward. If your chair is older than that cutoff and a motor must be replaced, both motors must be replaced together. The sources Guide: Owner’s Manual — Quantum/Jazzy 1450 Series, INFMANU4342 Rev. text: Exploded View: Pride Jazzy 614 & 614 HD This page is different, and the difference is the story. Pride Mobility does not publish an Illustrated Parts Breakdown for the Jazzy 614 or the Jazzy 614 HD — not for owners, not openly at all. What Pride does publish is the labeled overview in the owner’s manual — the whole chair, the power base, the electrical parts, the seat adjustments, the drive wheel taken apart, and the batteries, each with its own diagram — plus a sell sheet that names the heavy-duty model’s controller. This page puts both together, and names the gap exactly: everything below the manual — motors, gearboxes, casters, shrouds, harnesses — has no public part number, because Pride sells those parts through its dealers. Coverage: manual-only. The Jazzy 614 is a mid-wheel-drive power chair: two in-line motors, Active-Trac suspension, and two 12-volt NF-22 batteries. Mid-wheel drive means the powered wheels sit in the middle of the chair, with a small swivelling caster wheel at each corner — that is why it turns in a tight circle. The Jazzy 614 HD is the same chair built heavier: 450 lb weight capacity instead of 300 lb, solid 14-inch drive wheels instead of pneumatic or solid, and a 50-amp Dynamic Shark controller. The controller is the electronics that drive the chair: the joystick you hold and the power module inside the base that connects it to the motors and batteries. NF-22 is a battery size standard — the size, not a brand. Weight capacity is 300 lb for the 614 and 450 lb for the 614 HD. The chair is 25.125 inches wide and, by the manual’s own drawing, turns in a 20-inch radius. Not the Jazzy EVO 614. Pride also sells a newer, different chair called the Jazzy EVO 614 (and EVO 614HD), with 13.75-inch perforated drive wheels, a 60-amp LiNX controller, and its own manual (INFMANU5238, 2022). That chair is not covered here. The sources Guide: Owner’s Manual — Jazzy 614 Series, INFMANU3823 Rev. B, September 2009, Pride Mobility Products Australia Pty. Ltd. — the Australian edition, covering the Jazzy 614 and the Jazzy 614HD. The US edition of the same manual is INFMANU3677 (Rev. C, November 2011), covering models 614 2S, 614 2SP, and 614 2HD. Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): pride_jazzy-614_owner.pdf (44 pages) Specifications (614 HD): Jazzy 614 HD sell sheet, CA053119, May 2019, Pride Mobility Products Corp. — the maker’s own specifications for the heavy-duty model, including the 50-amp Dynamic Shark controller and the seat sizes. Full sheet (PDF, in this site’s library): pride_jazzy-614-hd_specs.pdf (2 pages) FDA record: 510(k) premarket notification K042612, summary, U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Full summary (PDF, in this site’s library): K042612.pdf (5 pages, scanned) — see the note in the full record about what this number actually clears. No Illustrated Parts Breakdown, parts catalogue, order form, or service manual for the 614 or 614 HD is published openly by Pride — searched Pride Mobility’s own site, ManualsLib, ManualsBase, iFixit, retailer parts pages, and archive.org (23 November 2026). The Jazzy 600 IPB that circulates on iFixit (INFMANU2831, 2008) is for the older Jazzy 600 and 1100, not this chair. If Pride publishes a 614 breakdown, this page gets the full exploded treatment the same week. The maker’s own warnings, word for word Pride prints these in the 614 owner’s manual. Word for word, Australian spelling and all: An authorised Pride Provider or a qualified technician must perform the initial setup of this power chair and must perform all of the procedures in this manual. Do not use the power chair while the drive motors are disengaged! Do not disengage the drive motors when the power chair is on an incline or decline, as the unit could roll on its own! Only engage the freewheel mode when on a level surface. It is important to remember that when your power chair is in freewheel mode, the braking system is disengaged. Do not use the freewheel lever handles as tie-down points to secure this product. Explosive gases may be generated while charging the batteries. Keep the power chair and battery charger away from sources of ignition such as flames or sparks and provide adequate ventilation when charging the batteries. The batteries in your power chair should only be serviced or replaced by an authorised Pride Provider or a qualified technician. Do not mix old and new batteries. Always replace both batteries at the same time. Failure to ensure that the axle key is properly installed into the axle slot when mounting the wheel can result in electronic brake failure, personal injury, and/or product damage. Make sure pneumatic tyres are inflated to the psi/bar/kPa air pressure rating indicated on each tyre. Do not underinflate or overinflate your tyres. Low pressure may result in loss of control, and overinflated tyres may burst. Overinflating tyres can cause them to explode. Battery posts, terminals, and related accessories contain lead and lead compounds. Wear goggles and gloves when handling batteries and wash hands after handling. Verbatim from the Pride Jazzy 614 Series Owner’s Manual, INFMANU3823 Rev. B, sections II, III, VI, and VII. text: Exploded View: Pride Jazzy Air 2 The whole Jazzy Air 2, taken apart by the people who built it. Pride Mobility publishes an Illustrated Parts Breakdown (IPB) for this chair — the dealer document that shows every assembly exploded into its parts, each part numbered. This page reproduces all 18 assemblies in build order, with Pride’s own part numbers and a plain-language line for every part. Coverage: full IPB. Every assembly in the guide is here, down to the decal package. The prices printed in this export are Australian list prices, so they are not reproduced — the part numbers are the point. With a part number, you order the $6 part, not the $300 assembly. The source Guide: Illustrated Parts Breakdown (IPB) — Jazzy Air 2 Document: INFMANU4980, Rev. A / 100218 — Pride Mobility Products Corporation Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): pride_jazzy-air-2_ipb.pdf Pride posts its IPBs openly; this copy was retrieved from a dealer-posted public copy (Allied Medical, New Zealand). The owner’s manual quoted below is also in the library: pride_jazzy-air-2_owner.pdf (INFMANU4922, Rev. D). The maker’s own warnings, word for word Pride prints these in the owner’s manual. They are reproduced exactly — including the parts that tell you a technician must do the work. Read them, then decide for yourself: WARNING! An authorized Pride Provider or a qualified technician must perform the initial setup of this power chair and must perform all of the procedures in this manual. WARNING! Do not use the power chair while the drive motors are disengaged! Do not disengage the drive motors when the power chair is on an incline or decline, as the unit could roll on its own. Only engage the freewheel mode when on a level surface. WARNING! It is important to remember that when your power chair is in freewheel mode, the braking system is disengaged. WARNING! Avoid applying excessive force to the manual freewheel levers. WARNING! When faced with an emergency situation, the batteries can be quickly disconnected by pressing the manual shut-off button on the circuit breaker. See figure 2. Use caution. Be advised that turning off power to the power chair may cause the power chair to stop abruptly. To release the emergency stop and restore driving capability to the power chair, follow the circuit breaker reset instructions. Verbatim from the Jazzy Air 2 Owner’s Manual, INFMANU4922, Rev. D — also in the library below. Build order The assemblies are laid out in the order you would build the chair: frame first, batteries last. Every step is one exploded view from the maker’s guide, followed by its parts table. The Callout column is the label printed on the diagram. The Part number column is the maker’s own number — the number a parts desk cannot argue with. text: Exploded View: Pride Jazzy EVO 613 This page is different, and the difference is the story. Pride Mobility does not publish an Illustrated Parts Breakdown for the Jazzy EVO 613 — not for owners, not openly at all. What Pride does publish is the labeled overview in the owner’s manual — the whole chair, the power base, and the electrical parts, each with its own diagram — plus an order form that names real part numbers for the batteries, joysticks, seats, armrests, and leg rests. This page puts both together, and names the gap exactly: everything below the order form — motors, gearboxes, casters, shrouds, harnesses — has no public part number, because Pride sells those parts through its dealers. Coverage: manual-only, plus order-form part numbers. The Jazzy EVO 613 is a mid-wheel-drive power chair: two in-line motors, Active-Trac suspension, a 40-amp PG GC3 controller, and a choice of two batteries — two sealed lead-acid U-1 batteries, or, as the EVO 613 Li, one 25-volt lithium iron phosphate pack. The Li version is the same chair with a different battery and joystick: 160.5 lb instead of 189 lb, and up to 21 miles per charge instead of 17.1. Weight capacity is 300 lb. The chair is 22 inches wide and turns in a 22-inch radius, which is why it fits through tight indoor corners. The sources Guide: Owner’s Manual — Jazzy EVO 613, Jazzy EVO 613 with Power Elevating Seat, and Jazzy EVO 613 Li, INFMANU5239 Rev. B, April 2022, Pride Mobility Products Corp. Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): pride_jazzy-evo-613_owner.pdf (44 pages) Order form: Jazzy EVO 613 Quick Ship Order Form, INFINFB4362 Rev. A, 13 August 2021, Pride Mobility Products Corp. — the maker’s own list of orderable parts and part numbers. Full form (PDF, in this site’s library): pride_jazzy-evo-613_order-form.pdf (4 pages) Specifications: Jazzy EVO 613 / 613 Li Specifications, Pride Mobility Products Corp. Full sheet (PDF, in this site’s library): pride_jazzy-evo-613_specs.pdf (2 pages) FDA record: 510(k) premarket notification K042612, summary, U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Full summary (PDF, in this site’s library): K042612.pdf (5 pages, scanned) — see the note in the full record about what this number actually clears. No Illustrated Parts Breakdown, parts catalogue, or service manual for the EVO 613 is published openly by Pride — searched Pride Mobility’s own site, ManualsLib, iFixit, and retailer parts pages (19 November 2026). The Jazzy 600 IPB that circulates on iFixit (INFMANU2831, 2008) is for the older Jazzy 600 and 1100, not this chair. If Pride publishes an EVO 613 breakdown, this page gets the full exploded treatment the same week. The maker’s own warnings, word for word Pride prints these in the EVO 613 owner’s manual. Word for word: An authorized Pride Provider or a qualified technician must perform the initial setup of this power chair and must perform all of the procedures in this manual. Never operate your power chair if it is behaving abnormally or erratically. Do not use the power chair while the drive motors are disengaged! Do not disengage the drive motors when the power chair is on an incline or decline, as the unit could roll on its own. Only engage the freewheel mode when on a level surface. It is important to remember that when your power chair is in freewheel mode, the braking system is disengaged. The power elevating seat option is intended for use on a level surface only. Never raise the seat from its lowest position on an inclined surface. Failure to heed this warning can result in the power chair tipping over. The batteries in your power chair should only be serviced or replaced by an authorized Pride Provider or a qualified technician. Explosive gases may be generated while charging the battery. Keep the power chair and battery charger away from sources of ignition such as flames or sparks and provide adequate ventilation when charging the battery. Verbatim from the Pride Jazzy EVO 613 Owner’s Manual, INFMANU5239 Rev. B, sections II, III, VI, and VII. Build order The assemblies are laid out in the order you would build the chair: the whole chair first, then the base, then the electronics, then the seat, then the batteries. Every step is one labeled diagram from the maker’s manual, followed by its parts table. The Callout column is the number printed on the diagram. Part numbers appear only where Pride publishes them — in the order form — and those are in the parts table , not invented here. The chair has two main assemblies: the seat assembly (A) and the power base assembly (B). The seat assembly is the armrests, seatback, and seat base. The power base assembly is two motor/brake assemblies, two drive wheels, the batteries, and the wiring harnesses. Step 1 — The Jazzy EVO 613, labeled by Pride Fig. 1. The Jazzy EVO 613 Power Chair — diagram reproduced from the manufacturer’s owner’s manual (INFMANU5239 Rev. B), page 7. Callout Part (maker’s label) What this part does 1 Seatback The padded back you lean against; part of the seat. 2 Armrest Supports your arm and helps you transfer in and out of the chair; it flips up out of the way. 3 Seat Base The platform under the seat cushion; the seat bolts to it. 4 Controller The joystick hand control: the stick, the buttons, and the battery display you drive with. 5 Top Shroud The plastic cover over the top of the power base; it comes off to reach the batteries. 6 Main Circuit Breaker A safety switch on the front of the base. It cuts power if the motors and batteries are strained; push it back in to reset it. 7 Front Caster Wheel A small wheel at the front that is not powered; it swivels so the chair can turn. 8 Front Riggings (Foot Platform Shown) The mounts at the front that hold the foot platform or leg rests. 9 Drive Wheel The big powered wheel in the middle of the chair; the motor turns this one. 10 Seat Release Lever Pull it to release the seat so it can be lifted off the power base. 11 Rear Caster Wheels Small unpowered wheels at the back that keep the chair from tipping backwards. Step 2 — The power base Fig. 2. The Jazzy EVO 613 Power Base — diagram reproduced from the manufacturer’s owner’s manual (INFMANU5239 Rev. B), page 8. Callout Part (maker’s label) What this part does 1 Rear Shroud The plastic cover at the back of the power base. 2 Seat Post The post the seat sits on; it carries the seat’s weight down to the base. 3 Top Shroud The plastic cover over the top of the power base. 4 Main Circuit Breaker The safety switch; push it in to reset it after it trips. 5 Front Caster Wheels The small swivelling wheels at the front. 6 Controller Connector The plug where the controller’s cable joins the power base. 7 Rear Caster Wheel A small unpowered wheel at the back. Step 3 — The power-seat base On chairs ordered with the power elevating seat, the base looks different: the seat post is replaced by a power seat actuator, and the front cover changes shape. Everything else is the same chair. Fig. 3. The Jazzy EVO 613 with Power Seat Power Base — diagram reproduced from the manufacturer’s owner’s manual (INFMANU5239 Rev. B), page 9. Callout Part (maker’s label) What this part does 1 Rear Shroud The plastic cover at the back of the power base. 2 Power Seat Actuator The motor that raises and lowers the power elevating seat. 3 Front Cover The cover over the front of the power-seat base. 4 Main Circuit Breaker The safety switch; push it in to reset it after it trips. 5 Front Caster Wheels The small swivelling wheels at the front. 6 Controller Connector The plug where the controller’s cable joins the power base. 7 Rear Caster Wheel A small unpowered wheel at the back. One thing the power seat does that the manual is blunt about: once the seat is raised more than about 0.75 inches (19 mm), the chair cuts its own speed by two-thirds. Check that this speed cut works before you rely on it. Stage 2 — Electronics The electrical parts live on or inside the power base. The main circuit breaker is on the front of the base; the power module sits under the front cover. The power module is the box that connects the joystick to the motors, the batteries, and the off-board charger. If the circuit breaker trips — it trips when the batteries and motors are heavily strained — let the chair rest for about a minute, push the breaker button back in, turn the controller on, and carry on. If it keeps tripping, call your Pride Provider. Step 4 — Electrical parts, SLA batteries Fig. 4. Jazzy EVO 613 with SLA Batteries Electrical Components — diagram reproduced from the manufacturer’s owner’s manual (INFMANU5239 Rev. B), page 10. Callout Part (maker’s label) What this part does 1 Battery Connectors Where the battery cables plug into the power module. 2 Controller Power Module The box that connects the joystick to the motors, the batteries, and the off-board charger. 3 Controller Connector Where the controller plugs into the power module. 4 Motor Connectors Where the power module connects to the two motors. 5 Main Circuit Breaker The safety switch on the front of the base. Step 5 — Electrical parts, lithium battery The 613 Li has the same five connections in the same places; only the battery is different. Their user manual says it in one line: “Spare parts must be ordered through Permobil.” No exploded views, no part numbers, no way to order a caster bearing without a dealer in the middle. The serial number label (callout I) is the one key you hold: every part on this chair is orderable by a dealer using it. The full record FDA recall Z-2795-2026 (Class II, open). The M3 Corpus with Heavy Duty Shock (REF 120031, Model version 3) runs firmware that lacks a speed restriction to maintain stability when the seat lift exceeds 50 mm; without it, the user may fall from the chair or the chair may tip over. The recall covers 140 chairs running firmware version 1.26.2, was initiated by Permobil on February 29, 2024, and was posted by the FDA on July 24, 2026. No service manual for the M5 Corpus was found in public, and Permobil distributes service manuals through dealers and its documentation portal requires a login, so no openly published copy is hosted here. The serial number label — callout I — is the one key you hold: every part on this chair is orderable by a dealer using it. Until Permobil publishes the breakdown, a dealer’s parts screen is the only copy — and anything a dealer can see for your chair, you are entitled to ask them to show you. The full record FDA recall Z-2805-2026 (Class II, open). Permobil’s Power Platform firmware versions 1.27 through 1.57 are missing specific drive-inhibit logic; the chair may drive under restricted conditions and become unstable. The recall covers 715 M5 Corpus chairs (REF 120032), was initiated by Permobil on June 19, 2025, and was posted by the FDA on July 24, 2026. Permobil’s June 10, 2025 technical bulletin tells owners the fix is a firmware update delivered over a cellular connection, and not to use the chair while the update is in process. If your chair runs one of those firmware versions, the update — not a part swap — is the remedy. FDA recall record Z-2805-2026 . ← All exploded views · PMD section

text: Exploded View: Sunrise Quickie Q500 M This page is different, and the difference is the story. Sunrise Medical does not publish an Illustrated Parts Breakdown or a parts catalogue for the Quickie Q500 M — not for owners, not openly at all. Their service instructions say it in one line: “For spare parts please refer to separate manuals.” No exploded views, no part numbers, no way to order a caster bearing without a dealer in the middle. Coverage: manual-only. What Sunrise does publish is the labeled overview in the General Manual — Fig. 3.1, eleven numbered parts, showing the Q500 M itself: the mid-wheel-drive chair, the big drive wheels under the seat, a small castor at each corner, and the suspension system the manual calls the range’s distinctive feature. That is everything the maker gives the person who rides in it. We reproduce that diagram exactly, and we name the gap exactly: every assembly-level breakdown for this chair is a source gap until Sunrise publishes one. The Q500 M shares its manual with the smaller Q400 M; the European edition of the same manual covers the whole Q500 family — M, F, and R — and labels it in twelve parts, adding a Side Cushion as part 4. The sources Guide 1: General Manual — Quickie Q500 M / Q400 M, document P/N 248035, Revision H, Sunrise Medical (US) LLC Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): sunrise_quickie-q500m-q400m_general-manual_248035-rev-h.pdf Guide 2: Instructions for Use — Quickie Q500 M/F/R, Revision B, Sunrise Medical (European edition). Link-only: no downloadable PDF of this edition was found; the full text was verified from the public copy on the manual aggregator Libble at libble.eu/sunrise-medical-quickie-q500 (p. 8, the overview figure) . Its specification table (p. 35) is the source for the Q500 M numbers below, and its Fig. 3.1 labels the M, F, and R chairs in one figure, in twelve parts. Guide 3: Service Instructions — Quickie Q400 / Q500 / Q700 F/R, document 000690852.01, Revision B, Sunrise Medical (40 pages). Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): sunrise_quickie-q400-q500-q700-fr_service-instructions_000690852-rev-b.pdf (also posted on Sunrise Medical’s own document asset bank at sunrisedice.com/asset-bank/assetfile/52975.pdf ). It covers the F and R bases only — it says so on its own cover — not the M base. An older printing of the US manual, Revision G, is also in public circulation; this page is built from Revision H, the edition held in the library, with the numbers cross-checked against Revision B. The maker’s own warnings, word for word Sunrise prints these in the Q500 M / Q400 M General Manual (Rev. H) and in the Q400/Q500/Q700 F/R Service Instructions (Rev. B). Word for word — including the one that explains why this page cannot give you part numbers: For spare parts please refer to separate manuals. Please only use genuine spare parts supplied by Sunrise Medical, failure to do so may result in the invalidation of your warranty. The intended lifetime of the wheelchair is five (5) years. Please DO NOT use or fit any third party components to the wheelchair unless they are officially approved by Sunrise Medical. Follow the instructions carefully next to these warning symbols! Not paying careful attention to these instructions could result in physical injury or damage to the wheelchair or the environment. The signs, symbols, and instructions affixed to the wheelchair comprise part of the safety facilities. They must never be covered or removed. They must remain present and clearly legible throughout the entire lifespan of the wheelchair. Avoid physical contact with the wheelchair’s motors at all times. Motors are continuously in motion during use and can reach high temperatures. After use, the motors will cool down slowly. Physical contact could cause burns. Allow the motors after using at least 30 minutes to cool down. Do not fit car batteries to the wheelchair. Fit only deep cycle, maintenance free mobility batteries. Be extra cautious to reduce the risk of dropping a metal tool onto the battery. It could spark or short circuit the battery or other electrical parts that may cause an explosion. We recommend the use of Sunrise Medical authorized spare parts only. Verbatim from the General Manual, sections 1.0, 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, 6.1, and 8.3; the spare-parts rule from the Service Instructions, section 4.0. Build order The assemblies are laid out in the order you would build the chair: frame first, batteries last. Every step is one labeled diagram from the maker’s guide, followed by its parts table. The Callout column is the number printed on the diagram. There is no part-number column on this page — Sunrise publishes no part numbers for this chair, and we do not invent them. Frame: Step 1: The Q500 M, labeled by Sunrise Stage 1 — Frame Start with the skeleton. Every other system bolts to the frame, so it goes together first. The photograph is the Q500 M itself, mid-wheel drive: the drive wheels are the big wheels under the seat, and the small wheels at the front and back corners are castors. Step 1 — The Q500 M, labeled by Sunrise Fig. 1. The Q500 M, labeled by Sunrise — Fig. 3.1 reproduced from the manufacturer’s guide (source above). The same eleven callouts label the chair. Part (maker’s label) What this part does 1. Headrest Supports your head. It adjusts so your head rests in a comfortable position. 2. Joystick The hand control you drive with: push it the way you want to go. It is the joystick module of the chair’s R-net control system — what its fault codes mean is on this site . 3. Arm Rest Supports your arms, and helps you transfer in and out of the chair. 4. Seat Cushion The cushion you sit on, part of the Sedeo seating system. 5. Leg Rest Supports your legs. Powered versions tilt to change their angle. 6. Front Caster The small swivel wheel at the front corner. It is not powered — it follows where the chair turns. 7. Drive Wheel The big powered wheel. The motor turns this one. On the Q500 M it sits under the seat, in the middle — that is what mid-wheel drive means. 8. Rear Caster The small swivel wheel at the back corner. It is not powered — it follows where the chair turns and keeps the chair steady. 9. Motors Two electric motors, one for each drive wheel. They get hot in use — see the maker’s warning above, and give them 30 minutes to cool before you touch them. 10. Battery Box The box that holds the two 12-volt batteries. Together they make the 24 volts the chair runs on — the battery lesson is on this site . 11. Back Upholstery The fabric back of the seat. It supports your back. The chair in numbers, from the manuals’ own tables All of these come from the Q500 M specification table in the European edition (Rev. B, p. 35) and section 10.0 of the US edition (Rev. H): Maximum user weight: 136 kg (300 lbs) with Sedeo Lite seating; 160 kg (350 lbs) with Sedeo Pro seating. Maximum speed: 6–12.5 km/h (4–7.7 mph). Maximum safe slope: 8°. Standard: EN 12184, Class B. Batteries: two 12-volt deep-cycle gel batteries in series (24 V total). The manual lists three fitted sizes: 50 Ah AGM, 60 Ah GEL, or 80 Ah GEL (C20 rating), always as a matched pair. Size: total length 1,100–1,130 mm with Sedeo Lite and a central footplate, or 1,280 mm with Sedeo Pro and swingaway hangers; total width 610–620 mm with 13-inch drive wheels. Range (80 Ah batteries): 32.5–40 km at 6 km/h; 25–32.5 km at 12.5 km/h. Turning radius: 560–630 mm. Ground clearance: 90 mm. Obstacle climbing: 75–100 mm. Weight: 130–138 kg in basic configuration, without batteries. If the chair will not move , the manual’s own troubleshooting list (section 9.0) is six checks before you call anyone: are the batteries charged; switch the chair off and back on; are the battery plugs all securely in place; is the freewheel switch in the DRIVE position; where is the speed regulator set; is the controller locked. Anything beyond that, the manual sends you to the separate controller booklet — the R-net fault codes, translated, are on this site . What the service documents add, and where they stop The Service Instructions (000690852.01 Rev. B) are written for technicians, and they are honest about their own limits: “This manual contains the instructions for repairs and general maintenance of the Q400/Q500/Q700 F and R bases.” The M base is not in it. What it does cover, for the F and R bases — including the Q500 F and Q500 R, the Q500 M’s siblings — is real work: removing the castor wheel from its fork, the fork from the castor arm, the drive wheel from the base, the motor from the base, the battery cover, the brake lever, the brake, and the motor brush — and one procedure that is Q700-only, the removal of the castor damper. It also lists the tools the work needs (flathead and crosshead screwdrivers, ring spanners 13/16/17/19, open-ended spanners 13/22/24, sockets 16/22, hex keys 1.5/2.5/3/4/5/6, a gear puller, and pliers). No service document written for the M base was found in public in this run. The Q700 M has one — a swing-arm installation sheet, document 248013 — but no Q500 M equivalent surfaced. The one M-specific procedure in the owner manuals is in the European edition, section 6.6, for disconnecting the batteries for air transport: on mid-wheel drive, release the two handle screws under the front of the seat frame, flip the seat frame backwards, and disconnect the 2-pin Anderson connectors from each battery. What is missing, in the open Frame, drive, seating, and electronics breakdowns for this chair: not published by the maker . That is not a gap in our research — it is the gate, documented. No Illustrated Parts Breakdown or parts catalogue for the Q500 M is published openly by Sunrise; the service instructions that do exist cover the F and R bases and exclude the M; and the separate spare-parts manuals the service instructions point to are not published openly either. The serial number label — Fig. 2.1 in the manual, which says it is located on the right side of the base, on the bottom

text: Exploded View: Quantum Q6 Edge 4 The whole Q6 Edge 4, taken apart by the people who built it. Quantum’s Illustrated Parts Breakdown for this chair runs 258 pages and explodes 110 assemblies into numbered parts. Every diagram below is Quantum’s own page, followed by the book’s parts table with a plain-language line added for every part. Coverage: full IPB. Every assembly in the book that carries a parts list is here: 110 assemblies, 1,025 parts. Four pages of the book are wiring diagrams and a configuration chart — they carry no parts lists, so they live in the linked book only; they are named in the source note below. The source Guide: Quantum Rehab Illustrated Parts Breakdown for the Q6 Edge® 4 power chair. Document: INFMANU5556 Rev. B — 258 pages, Australian edition (the book’s own footer reads “Q6 Edge® 4 (S/N JH7) IPB, AU”; the chargers are listed per region, and the decal package is the AU set). Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): quantum_q6-edge-4_parts.pdf Two kinds of book pages are not steps here, because they carry no parts lists: the QLNES configuration chart (book page 87), the PTO QBC wiring configurations (book page 173), and the iLevel® suspension-lock “Y” harness wiring diagrams (book pages 231 and 237). The book also prints 46 “web link” rows inside its tables — pointers to separate Quantum breakdowns for joystick shrouds, mounts, and knobs. Those rows are cross-references, not parts, and are not counted in the 1,025. A few parts in the book have no part number yet — the book prints them as “(COMING SOON)” or “(NO LONGER AVAILABLE)”; their rows are here with an em dash where the number will go. The diagrams carry the book’s own rule, printed on the plates: “Only parts with callouts are available individually. For parts without callouts, the complete assembly must be selected.” The maker’s own warnings This breakdown prints no warning paragraphs. On Quantum’s chairs the safety warnings are decals, and the book lists them as parts in the Decal Package assembly. The warning decals in this book include: N/A · DWR1235L515 · DECAL,WARNING,BATTERY WARNINGS,L-1235-515 N/A · DWR1235L521 · DECAL,WARNING,CONTROLLER CORD PLACEMENT,L-1235-521 If a warning decal on your chair is peeling or unreadable, it is a replaceable part — its number is in that table. A warning you cannot read cannot warn you. Build order The assemblies are laid out in the order you would build the chair: frame first, batteries last. Every step is one exploded view from the maker’s guide, followed by its parts table. The Callout column is the label printed on the diagram. The Part number column is the maker’s own number — the number a parts desk cannot argue with. text: Quantum Q6 Edge, Opened — Every Part, Named This page takes the original Quantum Q6 Edge apart on paper — every assembly, every part, named. It is built from Quantum’s own Illustrated Parts Breakdown, callout by callout, with Quantum’s part numbers and a plain-language line for every part. If your chair is an original Q6 Edge — not an Edge 2.0, 3, or 4 — this is the map of it. How to use this page: open the Q6 Edge IPB to the page number given under each table. The IPB’s diagram shows the assembly pulled apart, each part marked with a callout letter and number. Find the callout in the table below it: that row gives you Quantum’s part number, the part’s name, how many the chair takes, and what it does, in one plain line. One warning before you start: the electronics changed at serial number JB616611306020: every electronics configuration in this book comes in two versions, and the part numbers differ. Find your serial number — on the chair’s label, usually on the base — before ordering electronics. And this book does not cover the batteries or the charger; those are in the owner’s manual, in the batteries section below. About this chair The Q6 Edge is Quantum Rehab’s complex-rehabilitation power base — the chair underneath the seating that clinics fit to the rider — sold from about 2007. Its funding codes are K0848, K0849, K0856, K0857, and K0861 (models 3S-SS, 3S-C, 3SP-SS, 3SP-C, and 3MP-SS on the maker’s sell sheet). It is a mid-wheel-drive chair: the big powered wheels sit in the middle, with small swivelling casters front and rear — six wheels on the ground, which is what lets it turn in tight indoor spaces. The motors are 4-pole, rated for 5 or 6 miles per hour, standard or Accu-Trac. It runs on two NF-22 batteries and carries up to 300 lb. TRU-Balance 3 power positioning was available. The source for this page is Quantum’s Illustrated Parts Breakdown for the chair, document INFMANU4040 Revision I, dated 27 June 2012, 106 pages. A parts breakdown — an IPB — is the manufacturer’s own list of every serviceable part, with a drawing of each assembly pulled apart and a table of callouts, part numbers, names, and quantities. How to read this exploded view Callout — the letter-and-number mark on the IPB’s drawing (A1, B1, J1). Find it on the drawing, find it in the table. Parent assembly — a callout range like A1–A3 means one part number buys the whole assembly: the part plus everything listed under it. The IPB says most parts live inside assemblies and may not be sold separately. No callout (—) — the IPB lists the part as “N/A”: paperwork and labels that have no place on a drawing. An asterisk (*) on a callout — the part is not shown in the diagram. The book says so in the notes under the table. Qty — how many of that part one chair takes. What it is — Quantum’s own name for the part, word for word from the IPB. What it does — our plain-language line, written for this page. It says what the part type does, not which exact parts it joins to — the IPB does not say that, so neither do we. Left and right are from the rider’s point of view, sitting in the chair. Only serviceable components are shown. The book’s own note, printed under most tables: parts Quantum does not sell on their own are not in the drawings. Serial numbers matter. The electronics split at JB616611306020; some front-suspension and freewheel parts split at JB621711001C30. Check your chair’s serial number before ordering. Colors are Quantum’s names (Candy Apple Red, Viper Blue, Sunburst Orange). Every color appears in the shroud table with its own part number. 1. Main frame The main frame is the chair’s steel skeleton, sold as complete assemblies: a standard articulating beam frame and a suspension articulating beam frame. The front stabilizer bridge ties the front of the frame together. The book shows only serviceable components — the frame itself is not broken down further.
