title: Exploded View: Sunrise Quickie Q700 M — PMD — BareBoard
headings: Exploded View: Sunrise Quickie Q700 M
The maker’s own warnings, word for word
Step 1 — The Q700 M, F, and R, labeled by Sunrise
The chair in numbers, from the manual’s own tables
What the service documents add, and where they stop
What is missing, in the open
text: Exploded View: Sunrise Quickie Q700 M This page is different, and the difference is the story. Sunrise Medical does not publish an Illustrated Parts Breakdown or a parts catalogue for the Quickie Q700 M — not for owners, not openly at all. Their service instructions say it in one line: “For spare parts please refer to separate manuals.” No exploded views, no part numbers, no way to order a caster bearing without a dealer in the middle. Coverage: manual-only. What Sunrise does publish is the labeled overview in the Instructions for Use — Fig. 3.1, eleven numbered parts, drawn once and used for all three drive layouts in the family: mid-wheel (Q700 M, top), front-wheel (Q700 F, middle), and rear-wheel (Q700 R, bottom). That is everything the maker gives the person who rides in it. We reproduce that diagram exactly, and we name the gap exactly: every assembly-level breakdown for this chair is a source gap until Sunrise publishes one. The Q700 M is the mid-wheel-drive member of the family — the big drive wheels sit under the seat, in the middle, with a small castor at each corner. The sources Guide 1: Instructions for Use — Quickie Q700 M/F/R, document 000690770.02, Revision E (2021), Sunrise Medical Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): sunrise_quickie-q700-mfr_instructions-rev-e.pdf Guide 2: Service Instructions — Quickie Q400 / Q500 / Q700 F/R, document 000690852.01, Revision B, Sunrise Medical (40 pages). Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): sunrise_quickie-q400-q500-q700-fr_service-instructions_000690852-rev-b.pdf (also posted on Sunrise Medical’s own document asset bank at sunrisedice.com/asset-bank/assetfile/52975.pdf ). It covers the F and R bases only — it says so on its own cover — not the M base. Guide 3: Q7ME Swing Arm Installation — document 248013, Revision A (May 2018), Sunrise Medical (US) LLC. The one service document found that is written for the Q700M base itself: removing and refitting the rear swing arm (the caster arm), with torque figures. Full sheet (PDF, in this site’s library): sunrise_quickie-q700m_swing-arm-installation_248013-rev-a.pdf A newer Revision G of the Instructions for Use exists (it adds the Q700 M HD and the standing Q700-UP M / Q700-UP F to the same manual). This page is built from Revision E, the edition held in the library. The maker’s own warnings, word for word Sunrise prints these in the Q700 M/F/R Instructions for Use (Rev. E) and in the Q400/Q500/Q700 F/R Service Instructions (Rev. B). Word for word — including the one that explains why this page cannot give you part numbers: For spare parts please refer to separate manuals. Please only use genuine spare parts supplied by Sunrise Medical, failure to do so may result in the invalidation of your warranty. The intended lifetime of the wheelchair is 5 years. Please DO NOT use or fit any 3rd party components to the wheelchair unless they are officially approved by Sunrise Medical. Follow the instructions carefully next to these warning symbols! Not paying careful attention to these instructions could result in physical injury or damage to the wheelchair or the environment. The signs, symbols and instructions affixed to the wheelchair comprise part of the safety facilities. They must never be covered or removed. They must remain present and clearly legible throughout the entire lifespan of the wheelchair. Avoid physical contact with the wheelchair’s motors at all times. Motors are continuously in motion during use and can reach high temperatures. After use, the motors will cool down slowly. Physical contact could cause burns. Allow the motors after using at least 30 min. to cool down. Do not fit car batteries to the wheelchair. Fit only deep cycle, maintenance free mobility batteries. Be extra cautious to reduce the risk of dropping a metal tool onto the battery. It could spark or short circuit the battery or other electrical parts that may cause an explosion. Verbatim from the Instructions for Use, sections 1.1, 2.0, 2.1, 2.2 and 6.1; the spare-parts rule from the Service Instructions, section 4.0. Build order The assemblies are laid out in the order you would build the chair: frame first, batteries last. Every step is one labeled diagram from the maker’s guide, followed by its parts table. The Callout column is the number printed on the diagram. There is no part-number column on this page — Sunrise publishes no part numbers for this chair, and we do not invent them. Frame: Step 1: The Q700 M, F, and R, labeled by Sunrise Stage 1 — Frame Start with the skeleton. Every other system bolts to the frame, so it goes together first. The three photographs are the same eleven parts on the three drive layouts: mid-wheel on top, front-wheel in the middle, rear-wheel at the bottom. On the Q700 M, the drive wheels are the big wheels under the seat; the small wheels at the front and back corners are castors. Step 1 — The Q700 M, F, and R, labeled by Sunrise Fig. 1. The Q700 M, F, and R, labeled by Sunrise — Fig. 3.1 reproduced from the manufacturer’s guide (source above). The same eleven callouts label all three chairs. Part (maker’s label) What this part does 1. Headrest Supports your head. It adjusts so your head rests in a comfortable position. 2. Joystick The hand control you drive with: push it the way you want to go. It is the joystick module of the chair’s R-net control system — what its fault codes mean is on this site . 3. Arm Rest Supports your arms, and helps you transfer in and out of the chair. 4. Seat Cushion The cushion you sit on, part of the Sedeo seating system. 5. Leg Rest Supports your legs. Powered versions tilt to change their angle. 6. Front Castor The small swivel wheel at the front corner. It is not powered — it follows where the chair turns. 7. Drive Wheel The big powered wheel. The motor turns this one. On the Q700 M it sits under the seat, in the middle — that is what mid-wheel drive means. 8. Rear Castor The small swivel wheel at the back corner. It is not powered — it follows where the chair turns and keeps the chair steady. 9. Motors Two electric motors, one for each drive wheel. They get hot in use — see the maker’s warning above, and give them 30 minutes to cool before you touch them. 10. Battery Box The box that holds the two 12-volt batteries. Together they make the 24 volts the chair runs on — the battery lesson is on this site . 11. Back Upholstery The fabric back of the seat. It supports your back. The chair in numbers, from the manual’s own tables All of these come from section 11.0 (Technical specifications) of the Instructions for Use, Rev. E: Maximum user weight: 160 kg. The manual’s weight warning decal says the same. Maximum speed: 10 km/h. Rated slope: 6°. Standard: EN 12184, Class B. Batteries: two 12-volt deep-cycle gel batteries in series (24 V total). The manual lists three fitted sizes: 50 Ah AGM, 60 Ah GEL, or 80 Ah GEL (C20 rating), always as a matched pair. Size: total length 1,070–1,190 mm including legrests, total width 622–660 mm, depending on seating and legrest configuration. Range: 25–40 km depending on battery size and drive-wheel size. If the chair will not move , the manual’s own troubleshooting list (section 10.0) is six checks before you call anyone: are the batteries charged; switch the chair off and back on; are the battery plugs all securely in place; is the freewheel lever in the DRIVE position; where is the speed regulator set; is the controller locked. Anything beyond that, the manual sends you to the separate controller booklet — the R-net fault codes, translated, are on this site . What the service documents add, and where they stop The Service Instructions (000690852.01 Rev. B) are written for technicians, and they are honest about their own limits: “This manual contains the instructions for repairs and general maintenance of the Q400/Q500/Q700 F and R bases.” The M base is not in it. What it does cover, for the F and R bases, is real work: removing the castor wheel from its fork, the fork from the castor arm, the drive wheel from the base, the motor from the base, the battery cover, the brake lever, the brake, and the motor brush — and one procedure that is Q700-only, the removal of the castor damper. It also lists the tools the work needs (flathead and crosshead screwdrivers, ring spanners 13/16/17/19, open-ended spanners 13/22/24, sockets 16/22, hex keys 1.5/2.5/3/4/5/6, a gear puller, and pliers). The one service document written for the M base itself is the swing-arm installation sheet (248013 Rev. A). It takes you through removing and refitting the rear swing arm — the caster arm — on one side of the Q700M base, and it prints the torque figures: the M10 pivot bolt to 45 ft-lbs (61 Nm), the transit tether to 2.3–2.7 ft-lbs (3.1–3.7 Nm), and the caster locknut to 37 ft-lbs (50 Nm). Its warning is aimed at the person doing the work: “Attention dealers and qualified technicians, do not operate or service this device without first reading the owners manual.” What is missing, in the open Frame, drive, seating, and electronics breakdowns for this chair: not published by the maker . That is not a gap in our research — it is the gate, documented. No Illustrated Parts Breakdown or parts catalogue for the Q700 M is published openly by Sunrise; the service instructions that do exist cover the F and R bases and exclude the M; and the separate spare-parts manuals the service instructions point to are not published openly either. The serial number label — Fig. 2.9 in the manual, which shows the label and its contents for each drive layout — is the one key you hold: every part on this chair is orderable by a dealer using it. Until Sunrise publishes the breakdown, a dealer’s parts screen is the only copy — and anything a dealer can see for your chair, you are entitled to ask them to show you. ← All exploded views · PMD section

text: Exploded View: Sunrise Quickie Pulse 6 Sunrise Medical publishes a Complete Parts Manual for the Quickie Pulse 6 — a real parts book, assembly by assembly. The one public copy we could find sits on a dead host that answers every request with 403 Forbidden. So this page is built from what is openly readable: the labeled diagram in the chair’s owner’s manual, “Your Chair and Its Parts,” with every numbered part explained in plain language. Coverage: manual-only. The diagram covers the Pulse 6 BC, SC, and CC. The parts book (serial prefix PLS) is listed below as a known source gap; when a readable copy is public, this page gets the full treatment. The source Guide: Owner’s Manual — Quickie Pulse (6BC, 6SC, 6CC, 5BC, 5CC, 6MPC) Document: Document 119832 — Sunrise Medical (US) LLC Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): sunrise_quickie-pulse-6_owner.pdf This copy was retrieved from a dealer-posted public copy (Open Box Medical, S3). The Pulse 6 Service Manual (111425, Rev. B, 2011) is a troubleshooting guide without parts breakdowns. The Complete Parts Manual for this chair exists — its only located public copy is unreachable, so it is named here as a source gap, not silently skipped. The maker’s own warnings, word for word Sunrise prints these on the first page of the Pulse owner’s manual. Word for word: WARNING — Attention wheelchair users, do not operate this wheelchair without first reading the owner’s manual. If you do not understand the instructions and warnings of this owner’s manual please contact your dealer or qualified technician before operating this Quickie wheelchair. Failure to do so may result in damage and/or injury. DEALER/TECHNICIAN WARNING — Attention dealers and qualified technicians, do not operate or service this wheelchair without first reading this owners manual. If you do not understand the instructions and warnings of this owners manual please contact the Quickie Technical Service Department before operating and/or servicing this Quickie wheelchair. Failure to do so may result in damage and/or injury. Verbatim from the Quickie Pulse Owner’s Manual, document 119832. Build order The assemblies are laid out in the order you would build the chair: frame first, batteries last. Every step is one exploded view from the maker’s guide, followed by its parts table. The Callout column is the label printed on the diagram. The Part number column is the maker’s own number — the number a parts desk cannot argue with. Step 1 — Your chair and its parts — Pulse 6 BC / SC / CC Fig. 1. Your chair and its parts — Pulse 6 BC / SC / CC — exploded view reproduced from the manufacturer’s guide (source below). Part (maker’s label) What this part does 1. Flip-back, height-adjustable armrest Supports your arm. It flips back and adjusts up or down so you can transfer in and out of the chair. 2. VR2 controller joystick (RNET optional) The hand control you drive with. VR2 is the standard control system on this chair; R-Net was the optional upgrade. 3. Captain’s Seat The padded seat the rider sits in. 4. Front caster 7" The small front swivel wheel, 7 inches across. Not powered — it follows where the chair turns. 5. Rear stabilizing caster 6" The small rear caster, 6 inches across, that keeps the chair stable. 6. Single plate foot platform (shown); swing-away (optional); 70° hangers; swing-away ELR hangers (optional) The plate your feet rest on. The optional hangers swing away so your feet can reach the floor for transfers; ELR hangers can also lift your legs. 7. Drive wheels The big powered wheels. The motors turn these. 8. Brake release Releases the brakes so the chair can be pushed by hand. 9. Caster fork (front) Holds the front caster wheel and lets it swivel. 10. Caster fork (rear) Holds the rear caster wheel and lets it swivel. 11. Shroud The plastic cover over the base. It protects the parts underneath. What is missing, in the open The full parts book for this chair: published by Sunrise, currently not openly downloadable from anywhere we can reach . Invacare’s Spare Parts Catalogue for this chair — one book covering the TDX-SP, the narrow-base TDX-SP nB, and the TDX Sprint — runs 228 pages. Every plate below is the catalogue’s own page, diagram and table together, followed by the same table with a plain-language line added for every part. Coverage: full parts catalog. 183 of the catalogue’s plates carry orderable parts — 1,356 rows — and all of them are here. The catalogue’s overview plates list options by name with no part numbers; those are pointers to the detail plates, which are all here. The source Guide: Invacare Spare Parts Catalogue for the TDX-SP, TDX-SP nB, and TDX Sprint power wheelchairs. Document: Version 2015/08/21c EN — 228 pages. Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): invacare_tdx-sp_parts.pdf The catalogue prints a “Valid from → until” date column beside many parts; those dates are not reproduced here — the part numbers are what a parts desk orders by. Rows the catalogue prints without a part number are cross-references to other plates, not parts, and are not counted in the 1,356. The maker’s own warnings, word for word A parts catalogue is a book of diagrams, not the chair’s user manual — Invacare’s safety warnings for the TDX SP live in that manual, and the catalogue’s first plates (Stage 7) list the manuals themselves as orderable parts. The one instruction the catalogue prints in its own voice is on the Batteries plate: “Change batterys only pairwise and from the same type!” — printed on the Batteries plate of the catalogue itself (position “i”), spelling as printed. Change the pair together, and match the type: the plate lists gel and AGM batteries side by side, and they are not interchangeable. Build order The assemblies are laid out in the order you would build the chair: frame first, batteries last. Every step is one exploded view from the maker’s guide, followed by its parts table. text: Exploded View: Invacare TDX SP2 The whole TDX SP2, taken apart by the people who built it. Invacare’s Spare Parts Catalogue for this chair runs 296 pages and explodes 210 assemblies into numbered parts. Every plate below is the catalogue’s own page — diagram and the maker’s table together — followed by the same table with a plain-language line added for every part. Coverage: full parts catalog. The catalogue’s group and index pages carry no parts, so they are not reproduced; every page that lists parts is here. The catalogue covers both the TDX-SP2 and the narrow-base TDX-SP2 NB. The source Guide: Spare Parts Catalogue — Invacare TDX-SP2 & TDX-SP2 NB Document: Version 2015/08/24e EN — Invacare (Parts-Publisher Workbench export), 296 pages Full guide (PDF, in this site’s library): invacare_tdx-sp2_parts-catalog.pdf This catalogue was retrieved from a dealer-posted public copy (Camp Mobility, Finland). The user manual quoted below is also in the library: invacare_tdx-sp2_owner.pdf . Position numbers in the “Callout” column are the catalogue’s own “Pos.” numbers printed beside each part on the plate. The maker’s own warnings, word for word Invacare prints these in the TDX SP2 user manual, section 2.1, “General Safety Notes”. Word for word: WARNING! Risk of serious injury or damage. Improper use of this product may cause injury or damage. — If you are unable to understand the warnings, cautions or instructions, contact a health care professional or provider before attempting to use this equipment. — Do not use this product or any available optional equipment without first completely reading and understanding these instructions and any additional instructional material such as user manual, service manual or instruction sheet supplied with this product or optional equipment. WARNING! Risk of damage or injury if power wheelchair is accidentally set into motion. — Switch the power wheelchair off before you get in, get out or handle unwieldy objects. — When the drive is disengaged, the brake inside the drive is deactivated. For this reason, pushing the power wheelchair by an attendant is only recommended on flat surfaces, never on gradients. Never leave your power wheelchair on a gradient with its motors disengaged. Verbatim from the Invacare TDX SP2 User Manual, section 2.1 — the manual is in the library. Build order The assemblies are laid out in the order you would build the chair: frame first, batteries last. Every step is one exploded view from the maker’s guide, followed by its parts table. The Callout column is the label printed on the diagram. The Part number column is the maker’s own number — the number a parts desk cannot argue with. text: Exploded Views A power wheelchair is not one expensive assembly. It is a frame, two motors, a handful of wheels, a seat, a controller, and two batteries — and every one of those parts has a number. These pages take each chair apart using the manufacturer’s own parts guide : the exploded diagram the dealer sees, the callout for every component, and the maker’s part number, with one plain line explaining what each part does. 883 manufacturer diagrams and 8225 component rows, across 24 chairs. Where a maker publishes the full breakdown, the page is complete. Where a maker publishes nothing, the page says so, in the open, with the maker’s own words quoted. Nobody should have to guess what their chair is made of. No diagram on this site is redrawn or invented: if it is not the manufacturer’s own picture, it is not here. How to use an exploded view Find your chair’s symptom first, then the assembly that contains it. On the diagram, each part carries a callout — a short label like A1 or a position number. The table under the diagram turns that callout into the maker’s part number and description. That part number is the whole game: it is how you order the $6 bearing instead of the $300 assembly, and it is the number a parts desk cannot argue with. Assemblies are laid out in build order — frame, drive, motors, wheels, seating, electronics, batteries — so a reader with zero experience can follow how the chair goes together, one step at a time. Dynamic Controls DX & DX2 — the status light codes
Invacare MK6i — read the E-code on the screen
text: Fault Codes, Translated: The Other Systems Part one translated the codes for VR2, VSI, R-net and LiNX. Three more systems cover most of the chairs that were left: Dynamic Controls Shark , Dynamic Controls DX and DX2 , and Invacare’s MK6i . Same deal as part one: what the code means, what you check first, in what order. Find your system, read the code the way the chair shows it, and write it down before you call anyone: a code you can name is a repair you can argue about. Provenance: these tables are compiled from the manufacturers’ own published documents — Dynamic Controls’ Diagnostic Flash Code Listings and SHARK manuals , and Invacare’s MK6i Field Reference Guide (part no. 1141471) and TDX service manuals — and checked against them. Codes that could not be confirmed in the manufacturers’ documents are not listed. Documentation, not bench measurement: if your chair disagrees with this page, the chair wins — write down what yours actually does. Before any check in these tables that touches a plug, cable, motor, brake, actuator, or battery terminal: put the chair on level ground, switch it OFF, and disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker. Do not do the check while seated in the chair. Connector pins can remain live after switch-off. Keep a disconnected cable from touching skin, jewelry, tools, or metal, and cover or restrain it so the pins cannot short. At a battery terminal, work on one terminal at a time with an insulated tool. If you cannot disconnect power, inspect visually only and stop. The manufacturers’ own warning, carried word for word from a Shark owner’s manual: “Note: SHARK is not user serviceable. Specialized tools are necessary for the repair of any SHARK component.” True — for repairs inside the components. Reading a flash code needs no tools at all: the chair displays it for free, on purpose, where you can see it. That is the part this page uses. Dynamic Controls Shark — count the flashes on the gauge Shark is the system on a large share of scooters and mid-range power chairs. Its joystick unit has a row of lights (the information gauge ). The lights speak before any code appears: Left red light flashing: battery charge is low. Charge as soon as you can. All lights flashing steadily: the joystick was out of neutral at power-up (Dynamic’s name for it: OONAPU — something was pushing the stick when you switched on). Let go of the stick; it clears itself. This is not a fault. All lights flashing in a counted, repeating pattern: the chair has detected a fault. Count the flashes in the repeating pattern — that count is the code. Two amber lights flashing: a communication fault between the joystick unit and the power module. Check the power module for a fault, check the cable between them for damage, and make sure the battery is charged. Lights chasing right-to-left just after switch-on: the chair is coming out of lock mode. Press the horn twice within 10 seconds of switching on to unlock it. Bottom-left green light flashing: the chair is in speed-limit mode (often because the seat is raised) — a mode, not a fault. Flashes What it means What you check first 1 flash User fault Dynamic lists this as a possible stall timeout or user error: the chair was driven against something it could not move, or held at stall. Reverse away, let the joystick return to center, and try again. 2 flashes Battery fault Check the batteries and their cabling: main plugs, terminal bolts, breaker. Load-test the pair if it keeps happening (see Cheap Fixes, Procedure 3 ). Dynamic’s note is blunt: the batteries may require replacing. 3 flashes Motor 1 fault (M1 is normally the left motor) Check the motor, its heavy plug at the power module, and the cable run for pinches or cuts. 4 flashes Motor 2 fault (M2 is normally the right motor) Same checks as 3 flashes, on the Motor 2 side. 5 flashes Left park brake fault The electric brake in the left motor. First: the left freewheel lever — flip it firmly to DRIVE. Then the small 2-pin brake plug behind the motor (Procedure 1). 6 flashes Right park brake fault Same checks as 5 flashes, on the right: freewheel lever to DRIVE, then the brake plug. 7 flashes Shark control unit (joystick unit) fault The fault is inside the joystick unit itself. Check its cable and plug first — a bad connection can condemn a good unit. If the code stays, the unit is the fault. 8 flashes Shark power module fault Check every connection and wire at the power module in the base. If all are sound and the code stays, the fault is inside the power module. 9 flashes Shark communications fault The joystick unit and power module have lost contact. Unplug the bus cable between them, check the pins, reconnect firmly (Procedure 4). 10 flashes Unknown fault The system knows something is wrong but cannot name it. Check all connections and wiring; photograph the gauge and note the code before calling — Dynamic’s own action for this code is “consult a service agent,” and the code is your evidence. 11 flashes Incompatible control unit A part that does not belong to this system has been fitted: Dynamic states the branding of the power module must match the control unit. This code appears after a wrong-part swap — ask what was changed. Dynamic Controls DX & DX2 — the status light codes DX is Dynamic’s older modular system: separate power, seating and lighting modules on one bus (the DX Bus — the cable network the modules talk on). Faults show as flash codes on the remote’s status light: count the flashes, pause, repeat. Dynamic names the drive channels M1 and M2 — M1 is normally the left motor, M2 normally the right; identify a motor by its plug, not only by side. Flashes What it means What you check first 1 flash DX module fault If the chair has just been reprogrammed this may not be a real fault: switch off and on to clear it. Otherwise check the DX Bus connectors and cables, look at the status lights on the other modules, and confirm every module that should be present is connected. 2 flashes DX accessory fault An accessory device (anything connected to the system other than the power module) is sending a slow/stop signal or has a fault. Unplug accessories one at a time to find it. 3 flashes Motor 1 fault (normally left) Check the motor, its connections and cabling. 4 flashes Motor 2 fault (normally right) Check the motor, its connections and cabling. 5 flashes Left park brake fault Freewheel lever firmly to DRIVE; then the brake’s connections and cabling (Procedure 1). 6 flashes Right park brake fault Same checks as 5 flashes, on the right brake. 7 flashes Low battery fault Check battery connections and terminals, then the batteries’ condition (Procedure 3). 8 flashes Over-voltage fault Dynamic’s check: battery voltage must be below 32V . Check the battery wiring and that every terminal is secure — and suspect the charger if this follows charging. 9 flashes CAN L fault A fault on one wire of the DX Bus. Check the condition of the bus cables and connectors along their whole run. 10 flashes CAN H fault The other bus wire. Same cable checks as 9 flashes; Dynamic also notes to check the hazard lights were not switched on at power-up. 11 flashes Stall timeout fault The motors were held stalled too long (a wheel against a wall or a high threshold). Make sure both motors can turn freely, then switch off and on. 12 flashes Module mismatch A module or its software does not belong with the rest of the system — Dynamic’s action is reprogramming, which is a programmer job (see The Keys ). This code after a part swap means the swap was never configured. Name the code when you call. Invacare MK6i — read the E-code on the screen MK6i is Invacare’s own electronics, fitted to the TDX line and other Invacare chairs. On chairs with the colour MPJ+ joystick, faults appear on the screen as E-codes , and the chair keeps a fault log — a dated, time-stamped history of every code, which is evidence: do not let anyone clear it before it has been read. On the simpler SPJ+ joystick (no screen), codes are shown on the joystick’s information gauge and read in full with the Remote Programmer. Code What it means What you check first E01 / E02 / E03 / E04 Joystick or input value out of range (one code per direction: forward, reverse, left, right) Something is holding the stick or input off centre, or it was deflected at switch-on. Clear the stick, let it centre, power-cycle. If one direction’s code returns, the input itself is suspect. E09 / E10 Left / right park brake fault Invacare’s guide: make sure the motor lock levers are engaged before switching on. Then check the motor plugs at the controller and the brake cabling; if the code stays, call Technical Services. E18 Joystick or input device failed Release the joystick and try to get it back to the centre-most position, then switch off and on. If the code returns with the stick centred, the input has failed its neutral test. E19 Joystick calibration values out of range The chair no longer trusts where the stick’s centre is. Recalibration is done through the programmer — name the code and ask for a calibration before anyone quotes a new joystick. E32 Joystick or input device disconnected The controller cannot see its input at all. Follow the cable from the joystick down: unplugged, pinched, or cut are the usual causes. E41 Communications fault latched at switch-off The controller recorded a fault during the previous shut-down. Power the chair off and back on; if E41 returns, write it down with the date — it points at an intermittent cable or module. E200 Controller not connected — the input device does not recognize the controller Switch off and back on. If it persists, replace the cable from the display or joystick to the controller; then the display or joystick; then the controller. W05 Attendant control active Not a fault. The attendant control (the second control some chairs carry for a carer) is switched in and is driving. The chair is doing what it was told. One lock r
