text: Q-Logic, Translated Thirty-nine Quantum Rehab chairs in this site’s census run Q-Logic electronics — and until now they had no fault lesson, because nobody had translated Q-Logic into plain language. This is that translation: what the screen shows, what it means, and what you check first. Q-Logic is not one box. It is a system: a hand control (the joystick unit in front of you, with the screen), a power module (the box in the base that drives the motors — Quantum’s manuals also call it the powerbase module), and bus cables (the cables the parts use to talk to each other). When something fails, the hand control is where the chair tells you. Provenance: compiled from the manufacturers’ own published documents — Quantum Rehab’s Q-Logic 3 Basic Operation Instructions (INFMANU4809) , its Q-Logic 2 Basic Operation Instructions (INFMANU4499) , the published Q-Logic 3 Fault List , and the Q6 Edge 2.0 owner’s manual held in this site’s library — and checked against them. Codes that could not be confirmed in published material are not listed. Documentation, not bench measurement: if your chair disagrees with this page, the chair wins — write down what yours actually does. Before any check in these tables that touches a plug, cable, motor, brake, actuator, or battery terminal: put the chair on level ground, switch it OFF, and disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker. Do not do the check while seated in the chair. Connector pins can remain live after switch-off. Keep a disconnected cable from touching skin, jewelry, tools, or metal, and cover or restrain it so the pins cannot short. At a battery terminal, work on one terminal at a time with an insulated tool. If you cannot disconnect power, inspect visually only and stop. The manufacturer’s own warning, carried word for word from the Q6 Edge 2.0 owner’s manual : “Do not use the power chair while the drive motors are disengaged! Do not disengage the drive motors when the power chair is on an incline, as the unit could roll on its own! Only engage the freewheel mode when on a level surface.” And its mandatory instruction on the same levers: “You must turn off the power before disengaging the drive motors; otherwise, you may get an error code on the controller. To clear this code, turn off the controller and place the power chair in drive mode. Then, turn on the controller. The error message should be cleared. If it is not, contact your Quantum Rehab Provider.” Keep that sequence. Half the “faults” on this page are that sequence done out of order. What Q-Logic is, and which chairs have it Quantum Rehab is the complex-rehab division of Pride Mobility Products. Its chairs are sold through providers, not off a shelf. Q-Logic is the electronics family Quantum fits to them: Quantum’s own parts books label the assemblies “Q-LOGIC, CURTIS” — the system is built by Curtis Instruments , the mobility-electronics maker whose own controller manuals carry its enAble name (see Curtis’s Model 1212 manual for the smaller enAble controllers). Quantum sells the chair and the support. Curtis built the brain. Quantum’s own “What Can I Do with Q-Logic 3?” page lists Q-Logic 3 on the Edge 3 Stretto, Edge 3, 4Front, Q6 Edge 2.0, Q6 Edge 2.0 X, Q6 Edge HD, Q6 Edge Z and Q1450. The library holds the paper trail for the Q6 line: the Q6 Edge 2.0 owner’s manual , the Q6 Edge 3 Stretto parts book , the Q6 Edge 3 Illustrated Parts Breakdown , and the earlier 2012 Q6 Edge parts book from the Q-Logic 2 era — its joystick pages list Q-Logic 2 and Q-Logic 3 hand controls side by side, which is why both generations live on the same chairs. Three words you need before the tables: Motor 1 and Motor 2 are the two drive motors. Q-Logic does not promise that Motor 1 is the left one on your chair — identify a motor by its plug at the power module, not only by side. Brake 1 and Brake 2 are the electric parking brakes, one inside each motor. A brake code is very often a freewheel lever (the lever on each motor that disconnects it so the chair can be pushed) left in the push position. An encoder is the sensor that reports how far a motor has turned. An actuator is a powered seat motor (tilt, recline, elevate, legrests). An inhibit is a deliberate “do not drive” signal — the charger being plugged in is the common one. Q-Logic 3 — read the words on the colour screen The Q-Logic 3 hand control has a colour LCD screen (LCD = the flat display). It shows three kinds of message, in Quantum’s own definitions: Information (does not affect how the chair runs), Warning (may affect it), and Error (does affect it). Error codes appear on the screen by number , with a short text. The chair also warns you before a fault: pop-up screens appear when the battery falls to 50%, 30% and 15%, and if the electronics get too hot the chair slows itself down first ( thermal rollback — a protective speed cut, not a breakdown). One honest wrinkle: Quantum’s guides do not all number two joystick codes the same way — the Basic Operation Instructions print them as 34 and 35, the Fault List and the Q-Logic 3 Programming Guide as 35 and 36. The words on the screen are the same. Trust the words first, the number second, and write down both. What the chair shows What it means What you check first #1 — Motor 1 not connected The power module cannot see Motor 1 Power off. Inspect the Motor 1 connections at the power module and along the cable. Power on. #2 — Motor 2 not connected Same fault, Motor 2 side Same checks as #1, on the Motor 2 side. #3 — Brake 1 not connected The brake in Motor 1 is not answering Power off. Move the freewheel lever: disengage, then firmly re-engage to DRIVE. Inspect the motor connections. Power on (see Cheap Fixes, Procedure 1 ). #4 — Brake 2 not connected Same fault, Brake 2 side Same checks as #3, on the other motor. #14 — Proportional input device not connected The drive input the chair was programmed to expect (usually the joystick) is missing at switch-on Power off. Disconnect and reconnect the 9-pin D-sub plug (the wide plug with nine pins) on the input device. Power on. If the wrong input is programmed, that fix needs a programming device — name the code and ask for the input selection to be corrected before anyone quotes a new joystick. Quantum Canada’s Interactive Assist page lists this exact code as one a provider can resolve remotely. #15 — Drive motor encoder not connected A motor’s turn sensor is not answering Power off. Disconnect both encoder cables, inspect them, reconnect both. Power on. #20 — Undervoltage Battery voltage too low Charge the battery pair. If it returns on a charged pair, load-test both batteries (Procedure 3) and check the main plugs and breaker. #21 — Overvoltage Battery voltage too high Check whether the batteries were overcharged. Quantum’s own help text adds: avoid driving downhill fast with fully charged batteries — the motors charge the batteries on a descent. #23 — Motor 1 output defect The power module’s output to Motor 1 has failed its check Power off. Inspect the motor connections. Power on. If it stays, the fault is in the output stage or the motor — say the code when you call; do not let the whole power module be condemned before the cable is checked. #24 — Motor 2 output defect Same fault, Motor 2 output Same checks as #23, on the Motor 2 side. #25 — Brake 1 error Brake 1 failed a check that is not simple disconnection Power off. Disengage then re-engage the freewheel lever. Inspect the motor connections. Power on. #26 — Brake 2 error Same fault, Brake 2 Same checks as #25, on the other motor. #28 — Main contactor (main relay) warning The main power relay in the base did not behave as expected; Quantum Canada links this code to under-voltage from undercharging Power off. Wait 5 seconds. Power on. Then look at your charging habit and the battery pair before anything else — this code is a battery story until proven otherwise. #31 — Motor stall detected A motor was held still under power — the chair was driven against something it could not move Back up and try the obstacle again with more speed, or go around it, or find where it is lower. This code is the chair protecting itself, not a broken motor. #32 / #33 — Overtemperature / speed reduction (overtemperature) The electronics are too hot. At #32 the chair stops to protect itself; at #33 it slows down first Power off and let the system cool down. Quantum’s help text is explicit: “This is the normal system behavior.” #34 / #35 — Joystick not centered (numbering varies by guide — see above) The joystick was pushed away from centre at power-up Power off. Release the joystick to its centre (neutral) position — take bags, sleeves and attendant hands off it. Power on. #42 — Incompatible secondary module A module on the system does not match the rest — it appears after a part is added, removed or updated Power off. Remove the incompatible device if one was just fitted. Power on. If this follows a firmware update or a part swap, say so when you call: the swap was never configured. #46 — Bluetooth not working The chair’s wireless link failed its check Power off. Wait 5 seconds. Power on. A reboot is Quantum’s whole published fix for this code. #47 — Suspension lock not engaged — seek level ground The suspension lock (the mechanism that steadies the chair) is not engaged Move to level ground. Check the suspension lock mechanism. #49 — DMS fault DMS is the dead-man’s switch line — the signal that proves an input is being held deliberately. The line was interrupted Power off. Wait 5 seconds. Power on. If it returns, check the switch and input cables along their run. #56 — Actuator overcurrent A powered seat function is drawing too much current Power off. Disconnect and reconnect the seat module cables one at a time. Power on. A pinched actuator cable is the usual cause (Procedure 4 checks the cable run). #75 — “Chair is not charging / Please check charger” The charger is plugged into the controller but not into the wa

title: Fault Codes, Translated — PMD — BareBoard
headings: Curtiss-Wright VR2 & VSI — count the flashing bars
Dynamic Controls LiNX — count the red flashes
text: Fault Codes, Translated Your chair already tells you what is wrong. It shows a flashing light or a code on the screen — and nobody ever gave you the list that explains it. This is the owner-actionable list for the systems covered here. Three control systems cover most power chairs. Find yours, read the code the way the chair shows it, and start with the owner checks. Write the code down before you call anyone: a code you can name is a repair you can argue about. Where the codes live: the circuit board inside a powered-wheelchair joystick — the board that drives the battery lights and the screen your codes appear on. Photo: ‘Joystick’s Powered Board 1.JPG’ by Mbroemme5783, Wikimedia Commons. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Joystick's_Powered_Board_1.JPG. Licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/. Provenance: these tables are compiled from the manufacturers’ own published manuals — the PG Drives VR2 and R-net technical manuals and the Dynamic Controls LiNX manuals — and checked line by line against them (R-net Technical Manual SK77981-14; PP1A Programmer Guide SK73747). Codes that could not be confirmed in the manuals are not listed. The PG Drives manuals in the library: the Mobility Diagnostic Guide (newVSI, VSI, VR2, Pilot+, S-Drive) , the VSI Technical Manual (SK80151-1) , and the R-net On-Board Programming Manual (SK78571) . Documentation, not bench measurement: if your chair disagrees with this page, the chair wins — write down what yours actually does. Before any check in these tables that touches a plug, cable, motor, brake, actuator, or battery terminal: put the chair on level ground, switch it OFF, and disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker. Do not do the check while seated in the chair. Connector pins can remain live after switch-off. Keep a disconnected cable from touching skin, jewelry, tools, or metal, and cover or restrain it so the pins cannot short. At a battery terminal, work on one terminal at a time with an insulated tool. If you cannot disconnect power, inspect visually only and stop. Curtiss-Wright VR2 & VSI — count the flashing bars When a VR2 or VSI chair trips, the battery gauge lights flash. Count how many bars are flashing. Flashing bars What it means What you check first 1 bar Low battery voltage Charge the batteries overnight. Check the main battery plugs and the circuit breaker/fuse. If it keeps happening, load-test each 12V battery for a dead cell (see Cheap Fixes, Procedure 3 ). 2 bars Left motor disconnected The controller cannot see the left drive motor. Check the heavy motor plug at the power module, look for a pinched or cut cable under the seat, and check the motor brushes. 3 bars Left motor wiring trip (short) A left motor wire is shorting to battery power. Inspect the cable where it passes frame hinges. Unplug the left motor: if the fault clears, the short is in the motor or its cable. 4 bars Right motor disconnected Same checks as 2 bars, on the right motor: plug, cable, brushes. 5 bars Right motor wiring trip (short) Same checks as 3 bars, on the right motor cable. 6 bars Inhibit active (charger connected) The chair thinks it must not drive — usually because the charger is plugged in. Unplug the charger. If it is already unplugged, check the charger socket for a bent pin or dirt (Procedure 2), and check for a stuck seating lockout switch. 7 bars Joystick fault at power-up Usually your own hand: something was resting on the joystick when you switched on. Switch off, take everything off the stick, let it center, switch on without touching it. 7 bars + S light Bus communication fault The joystick and the power module lost contact. Unplug the round bus cable between them, check the pins for corrosion or bends, and plug it firmly back in (Procedure 4). 8 bars Control system / power module trip The power module failed its own self-check. Check every heavy power and bus connection, switch off for 30 seconds, and try again. If it persists, the fault is inside the power module. 8 bars + A light Actuator / seating trip A fault in a power seating actuator (tilt, recline, elevate, legrest). Inspect the 2-pin actuator plugs; unplug actuators one at a time to find the bad one. 9 bars Parking brake fault The most owner-fixable code on this page. One or both freewheel levers are in the PUSH position, or a brake plug is loose. Flip both levers firmly to DRIVE and power-cycle (Procedure 1). 10 bars (all flashing) High battery voltage Too much voltage reached the controller — a faulty charger, or loose battery terminals spiking on a downhill. Tighten the terminal bolts and check battery health. Curtiss-Wright R-net — read the screen On R-net chairs with a color screen (CJSM, CJSM2, Omni), a trip shows three things: the module that complained (PM = power module, JSM = joystick module, ISM = seating module), a short text, and a 4-digit code. The code is the exact sub-circuit. Note that R-net names the two drive channels Motor 1 and Motor 2 — never “left” and “right”. Which side of the chair Motor 1 and Motor 2 are on depends on how the chair was set up, so identify the motor by its plug at the power module, not by side. Here are the ones an owner can act on. Code Module What it means What you check first 1505 / 1506 PM Parking brake error (Motor 1 / Motor 2 brake) Check both freewheel levers are in DRIVE; inspect the small 2-pin brake wires at the back of each motor (Procedure 1). 1D05 JSM Joystick stationary time exceeded The joystick was held in one position too long. Power-cycle the chair — this code clears on restart. If it returns at once, check that the stick springs back freely to center; a binding boot or gaiter can hold it off-center. 2C00 PM Low battery voltage Charge; check the main disconnect plug and terminal bolts for looseness or corrosion. 2F00 JSM Joystick deflected at power-up The stick was pushed during boot. Center it; if it will not clear, power off and on, hands free. 3B00 PM Motor 1 disconnected Check the Motor 1 plug and brushes. 3C00 PM Motor 2 disconnected Check the Motor 2 plug and brushes. 3D00 / 3D01 PM Motor 1 short circuit Short in the Motor 1 cable or winding. Inspect the cable run. 3E00 / 3E01 PM Motor 2 short circuit Short in the Motor 2 cable or winding. Inspect the cable run. 4401 PM Internal controller trip Power-cycle after 30 seconds off. If it persists, the power module needs replacement. Trip text: Over-current PM / ISM Actuator channel over-current Unplug seating actuators one by one to isolate the shorted cable. Dynamic Controls LiNX — count the red flashes On LiNX chairs, the light inside the round on/off button flashes red: a number of flashes, a pause, then it repeats. Count the flashes. Red flashes What it means What you check first Battery gauge LEDs flash continually Out of neutral at power-up The joystick was held off-center at switch-on. Return it to centre — the warning clears by itself. 1 flash Remote / joystick error Check the bus cable into the joystick: unplug, inspect the pins, reconnect. 2 flashes Network or configuration error Check every bus plug; charge the batteries (low voltage below cut-off triggers this too). A replacement module fitted without configuration also causes it. 3 flashes Left motor fault Open or short circuit on the left motor, its cable, or its connector. 4 flashes Right motor fault Open or short circuit on the right motor, its cable, or its connector. 5 flashes Left park brake fault Left brake open/short — or the left freewheel lever is in push mode . Flip it to DRIVE; check the 2-pin brake plug. 6 flashes Right park brake fault Right brake open/short — or the right freewheel lever is in push mode . Flip it to DRIVE; check the 2-pin brake plug. 7 flashes Module error Includes: chair stalled against an obstacle (reverse away, cycle power), or the chair was pushed while switched off (cycle power to clear), or a power module fault. Before you call anyone Read the code. Write it down with the date. Try the owner check in the table — the most common codes on this page (brake levers, charger inhibit, a loose bus plug, a dying battery) are fixed in minutes with no tools or a $10 meter. If the fault is inside a module, you now know which module, and you can say so. ← Back to PMD · The cheap fixes →

title: The Cheap Fixes — PMD — BareBoard
headings: Procedure 1 — Freewheel lever & brake switch reset
Procedure 2 — Charger socket & inhibit pin cleaning
Procedure 3 — Battery pair load test & matched replacement
Procedure 4 — Bus cable inspection & contact restoration
text: The Cheap Fixes Five repairs that strand more power chairs than any broken part — and every one of them is yours to do today, with no dealer tool and no computer. Chair off, wheels blocked, steps in order. Words in bold are defined where they first appear. Every procedure ends with how you know it worked. Provenance: these procedures are compiled from the manufacturers’ published service documentation. The project’s bench phase will run each one on real hardware and mark it here. Until a procedure carries that mark: if a step disagrees with your chair, your chair wins — stop, and write down what you found. Procedure 1 — Freewheel lever & brake switch reset Fixes: VR2 9 bars · R-net codes 1505/1506 · LiNX 5 or 6 flashes. You need: A small brush or rag. Nothing else. The freewheel lever is a small lever on each drive motor. In DRIVE, the chair drives normally. In PUSH (freewheel), the motor is released so someone can push the chair by hand. The solenoid brake is an electric brake inside each motor that holds the chair still when power is off, and a small switch in the lever reports which position it is in. Turn the chair OFF at the joystick, disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker, and block the drive wheels so the chair cannot roll. Find the freewheel lever on each drive motor — one per motor; check both. Brush or wipe the dirt, road salt, and grit away from the base of each lever, where it pivots. Packed dirt can stop the lever traveling all the way — and a lever that stops halfway causes this fault. Push each lever firmly all the way to DRIVE. You should feel or hear a small click as it seats. A lever left in PUSH — or stuck halfway — opens the brake switch on purpose, and the controller reads that as a brake fault and refuses to drive. Behind each motor is a small plug with two wires. Push it in with your fingers until it is fully seated. A loose plug causes the same fault as a lever left in freewheel. Prove the brakes hold before you ride. Reconnect the main battery harness or reset the breaker. Put the chair on level ground, unoccupied. Turn the chair ON, then OFF, and try to push it by hand — it must not roll. If you cannot safely move around the chair and stop it yourself, have another person beside it for this test. Then drive at low speed in an open area and confirm it stops and holds. You cleared a brake fault; do not trust it until the brakes have proven themselves. How you know it worked: Turn the chair back ON. The brake fault is gone and the chair drives when you push the joystick. Procedure 2 — Charger socket & inhibit pin cleaning Fixes: VR2 6 bars — the chair acts as if the charger is plugged in when it is not. You need: A flashlight, a can of electrical contact cleaner, and a small non-metal flat tool (a plastic spudger) for the last step. The charger socket is a round socket with three pins (a 3-pin XLR socket — the same connector family as a stage microphone). Pin 3 is the inhibit pin : while the charger is plugged in, it tells the chair “do not drive,” so you cannot drive off plugged into the wall. Dirt, moisture, or a bent contact can fake that signal permanently. Know the shape: a 3-pin XLR connector — round metal shell, three pins. This photo shows the audio version (microphone into a mixing desk); your chair’s charger socket is the same connector family and shape, on the chair. Photo: ‘XLR.jpg’ by Doktorcik, Wikimedia Commons. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:XLR.jpg. Licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/. Make it safe first. Turn the chair OFF and disconnect the battery — unplug the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker. The socket’s pins carry battery voltage (Pin 1 is +24V) even with the chair switched off, and they sit millimetres apart: a metal tool bridging them is a direct short. Nothing goes into the socket until the battery is disconnected. Then unplug the charger and find the 3-pin socket — usually on the front of the joystick unit or on the power base. Shine the flashlight into the socket. Look for dirt, grit, moisture, or a bent piece of metal around Pin 3. Spray a short burst of electrical contact cleaner into the socket. It washes out grit and moisture, then evaporates. Let it dry a minute before testing. If you saw a bent contact, ease it gently back into line with the non-metal tool (battery still disconnected). It only needs to line up with the plug pin again — bending it too far or too often can snap it. How you know it worked: With the charger unplugged, turn the chair ON: the inhibit fault is gone and the chair drives. It still refuses to drive with the charger plugged in — that is the safety feature working as designed. Procedure 3 — Battery pair load test & matched replacement Fixes: VR2 1 bar · R-net code 2C00 · LiNX 2 flashes. You need: A digital multimeter, a 100A battery load tester, eye protection, and an insulated wrench that fits your terminal bolts (M6 or M8). If a battery fails: a new matched pair in the same group size. Your chair runs on two 12V deep-cycle batteries wired in series (one after the other, so they add up to 24V). They are sealed VRLA batteries — AGM or Gel — in common group sizes: U1 (34–35 Ah), 22NF (55 Ah), Group 34 (60–65 Ah), Group 24 (75–85 Ah). A load tester pulls heavy current for a few seconds so you can watch whether the voltage holds up under real work. A worn-out ( sulfated ) battery can look fine at rest and still collapse under load. Turn the chair OFF. Disconnect the main battery harness, or trip the main circuit breaker if your chair has one. Block the drive wheels. Open the battery compartment so you can reach both batteries and their terminals. Remove rings, watches, and other metal jewelry. Work on one terminal at a time, and do not let the wrench touch another terminal or the frame. Before you disconnect anything else, take a photo of the wiring — which cable lands on which terminal. You will rewire from the photo, not from memory. Resting check, one battery at a time: multimeter on DC volts, one probe on each terminal, write the number down. A healthy, charged battery reads 12.7V or more , and the two should be within 0.1V of each other . Resting voltage alone can lie — do Step 3 before condemning either battery. Separate the pair first: disconnect the cable that joins the two batteries, so each battery stands completely alone. Then load-test each battery, following the tester’s own instructions. Clamp firmly onto clean posts before you start the test — a loose clamp can spark, and a battery that has failed internally deserves respect: no sparks near battery terminals. Watch the voltage while it pulls. A battery that reads 12.6–12.8V idle and then plummets below 9.0V under load has failed — and that collapse is exactly what triggers the chair’s sudden low-voltage cutout on a threshold or curb cut. If either battery failed, replace both with a new matched pair of the same group size — never just one; an old battery drags a new one down. Before bolting the cables back on, clean the cable ends until the metal is bright. Wire the new pair in series exactly as the old pair was wired, and tighten every terminal bolt securely — never finger-tight. Loose terminals cause over-voltage spikes and can melt the harness. Keep the inline fuse that was in the main cable. How you know it worked: Both batteries read 12.7V or more at rest, match within 0.1V, and hold under the load tester. The low-battery faults stop, and the chair climbs a threshold without cutting out. Procedure 4 — Bus cable inspection & contact restoration Fixes: VR2 7 bars + S light · R-net communication trips · LiNX 1 or 2 flashes. You need: Electrical contact cleaner/restorer (the source procedure specifies DeoxIT D5) and spiral cable wrap for Step 5. The bus cable is the round 4-pin cable running from the joystick on your armrest down to the power module in the base. It carries your driving instructions to the motors. Every time the armrest flips up or the seat tilts, this cable bends — thousands of bends over the chair’s life — and its connectors are where it fails first. Power down first. Turn the chair OFF and disconnect the battery harness or trip the main breaker. This cable carries battery voltage alongside its data wires — you do not unplug or clean it live. Then trace the cable from the back of the joystick down to the power base. There is a round connector at each end. Inspect both ends, one at a time. Grip the connector by its collar (the hard outer body) and pull it straight out. Never pull by the wire — that tears the conductors inside where you cannot see the damage. Look at the pins inside. Look for green oxidation (green crusty corrosion) and for any pin sitting pushed back lower than the others. Either one breaks the connection and shows up as a communication fault. Put one tiny drop of contact restorer on the pins. A drop is enough — this restores the contact surface; it is not a wash. Push the connector back in until the locking ring clicks. Repeat the inspection at the other end. Then wrap the cable in spiral wrap where it crosses a hinge, and leave a loose slack loop at every hinge, so the cable is never pulled tight when the seat moves. That is what stops the fault coming back. How you know it worked: The communication faults are gone and the chair answers the joystick normally in every direction. Procedure 5 — Caster bearing replacement Fixes: Mechanical drag — seized caster bearings that overheat the power module and kill batteries early. You need: Two sockets and a bench vise, and new sealed bearings in the size printed on the old ones. Casters are the small swivel wheels at the front (and sometimes the rear). Each spins on a bearing — a steel ring of small balls that lets it turn almost without friction. Chair casters use sealed bearings in size 608RS or 6001RS — standard industrial bearings, sold everywhere for about $3–$8 each . Hair and ca

title: Beyond Medicare: Medicaid, the VA, and Private Plans — PMD — BareBoard
headings: Beyond Medicare: Medicaid, the VA, and Private Plans
First: name your payer, not your chair
Medicaid: a federal floor, and your state at the wheel
How to find your state’s actual repair rule
Under 21: EPSDT is the strong protection
If Medicaid says no: the fair hearing
Veterans: the VA is a different building entirely
Private insurance: the contract is the rulebook
Which door is yours: the summary
text: Beyond Medicare: Medicaid, the VA, and Private Plans The companion page, Getting a Repair Paid For , teaches Medicare’s repair rules. Medicare is not the only payer. If your power wheelchair — a power mobility device (PMD) , meaning a power wheelchair or scooter you rely on to move around — was paid for by Medicaid, issued by the Department of Veterans Affairs (the VA), or covered by a private health plan, a different door, a different rulebook, and a different person to argue with apply. This page is those three doors, in plain language. Provenance: compiled from primary sources only — Medicaid.gov and the Code of Federal Regulations (42 CFR, the published federal rules) for Medicaid, and the VA’s own Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service pages for veterans. Private health plans publish no single public rulebook, and this page says so where that is the case instead of inventing one. This is documentation, not legal advice: if a claim is denied, the appeal and hearing steps named on this page are the road. First: name your payer, not your chair Repair arguments fail when they are made to the wrong payer, with the wrong payer’s rules. Before anything else, answer one question: who paid for this chair, or who covers you now? Medicare paid? Stop here and use Getting a Repair Paid For — that page is the Medicare rulebook, named and cited. Medicaid covers you? Read the Medicaid sections below. Your state’s rule, not a national one, decides most repair questions. The VA issued your chair? Read the VA section. VA repair runs through VA Prosthetics, not through an insurance claim. A private plan — through a job, a spouse’s job, or bought by you — covers you? Read the private-plan section. Your contract is the rulebook, and this page teaches what to ask for in it. You have two of these — for example Medicare and Medicaid together? Do not assume one door cancels the other. Name both when you talk to a supplier, and ask each payer what it will and will not do for this repair. Medicaid: a federal floor, and your state at the wheel Medicaid is health coverage for people with low income, run jointly by the federal government and each state. That joint structure is the whole lesson of this section, and Medicaid.gov’s Benefits page states it in one sentence: states establish and administer their own Medicaid programs and determine the type, amount, duration, and scope of services within broad federal guidelines . So there is a federal floor — things every state must do — and then there is your state’s own layer on top of it. Anyone who tells you “Medicaid’s repair rule is X” as a single national sentence is, at best, describing one state. Here is the floor, cited: Home health services are a mandatory benefit. Medicaid.gov’s Mandatory & Optional Medicaid Benefits list — the federal list of what states must provide and what they may choose to add — puts home health services on the mandatory side, under section 1905(a)(7) of the Social Security Act and 42 CFR §440.70 . Equipment lives inside that benefit. Section 440.70 defines home health services to include medical supplies, equipment, and appliances suitable for use in any setting in which normal life activities take place . Durable medical equipment (DME) — equipment that can be used again and again, serves a medical purpose, and is not useful to someone without a disability, illness, or injury — is the name suppliers and state programs use for this equipment category. A power wheelchair sits squarely in it. Medicaid is not capped by Medicare’s list. The same regulation says state Medicaid coverage of equipment and appliances is not restricted to the items covered as durable medical equipment in the Medicare program . A state may cover more than Medicare does. A state list cannot be a locked door. Section 440.70 lets a state keep a list of preapproved equipment for administrative ease, but it prohibits absolute exclusions: the state must have a process, with criteria it makes available, for requesting equipment that is not on its list. What the federal floor does not contain is a national Medicaid repair rule like Medicare’s. Whether a repair needs prior authorization — approval from the payer before the work is done, without which the payer may refuse to pay — which supplier may bill for it, on what form, and within what time limit: those are state rules. The next section teaches you to find yours instead of guessing it. How to find your state’s actual repair rule Two state documents decide most Medicaid repair questions. Learn their names, because a supplier’s front desk knows both: Your state Medicaid program’s DME fee schedule. A fee schedule is the payer’s published list of billing codes and the amount it pays for each. If a repair part or a labour code is on your state’s schedule, the state has a price for it — which is hard to square with a claim that the repair “isn’t covered.” Your state Medicaid program’s provider manual for DME. A provider manual is the rulebook the state gives suppliers: what is covered, what needs prior authorization, and what paperwork a claim must carry. It is written for suppliers, and it is public in state after state. As one concrete example — Texas only, not a national rule — the Texas Medicaid Provider Procedures Manual’s DME handbook is published by the Texas Medicaid & Healthcare Partnership, the claims administrator for Texas Medicaid. Your state’s equivalent has a different name and different rules. Search for it by your state’s name plus “Medicaid,” “provider manual,” and “durable medical equipment.” One more layer: many people get Medicaid through a managed care organization (MCO) — a private health plan company the state pays to run its members’ benefits. If your Medicaid card names a plan, that plan’s prior-authorization list sits on top of the state rule. Ask the plan and check the state manual; if they disagree, say so to both, in writing. Questions that cut through, whichever state you are in: “Which page of the provider manual, or which line of the fee schedule, covers — or excludes — this repair?” “Does this repair need prior authorization in this state, for this code? Show me where that is written.” “If this part is not on the state’s preapproved list, what is the state’s process for requesting it?” (Section 440.70 requires that process to exist.) “Is my Medicaid run by the state directly, or by a managed care plan — and which one is refusing?” Under 21: EPSDT is the strong protection If the chair’s rider is under 21 and enrolled in Medicaid, the strongest sentence in this whole page applies. EPSDT — Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment — is Medicaid’s federal benefit for children and young people under 21. Medicaid.gov’s EPSDT page states the rule plainly: states are required to provide any additional services that are coverable under the federal Medicaid program and found to be medically necessary — needed to treat, correct, or reduce an illness or condition — regardless of whether the service is covered in a state’s Medicaid plan . EPSDT is also on Medicaid.gov’s mandatory-benefits list, under sections 1905(a)(4)(B) and 1905(r) of the Social Security Act and 42 CFR Part 441, Subpart B. What that means at a supplier’s counter: for an adult, “our state plan doesn’t list it” can be a real answer that has to be worked around. For someone under 21, that sentence is not the end of the conversation. If the equipment or the repair is medically necessary to correct or reduce the rider’s condition, EPSDT requires the state to furnish it even when the state plan for adults does not cover it. Say the letters: E-P-S-D-T. Then ask for the denial, if there still is one, in writing — the hearing right in the next section is how a written denial gets tested. If Medicaid says no: the fair hearing A fair hearing is a formal review, run by the state, of a Medicaid decision you believe is wrong. It is a federal right, not a favour your state grants. Under 42 CFR §431.220 , the state agency must grant a hearing to a person who requests one because they believe the agency denied their claim for covered benefits or services, acted erroneously, or did not act on the claim with reasonable promptness. Get the denial in writing. The written notice names the action, the reason, and how to request a hearing. A verbal no cannot be appealed. Read the deadline on your notice and meet it. Do not guess it from a website — including this one. The notice in your hand is the document that controls your case. Bring the paper trail: the repair order, the fault evidence (see Fault Codes, Translated — write the code down, with the date), and, for under-21s, the EPSDT rule above. For the letters themselves — demanding the rule, the record, and a written answer — the templates are on the repair demand letter page . Veterans: the VA is a different building entirely The VA does not pay claims the way an insurer does. For equipment, it mostly provides — it issues the chair, and it repairs what it issued, through its own service: the Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service (PSAS) , the VA’s prosthetics service. On the VA’s own PSAS page , VA calls it the largest and most comprehensive provider of prosthetic devices and sensory aids in the world, and it uses the word “prosthetic” broadly: any device that supports or replaces a body part or function. The path, per VA’s own public pages: Be enrolled, and have a medical need. PSAS states its general eligibility in those two terms: veterans enrolled in the VA health care system who have a medical need for a prosthetic service or item. It also warns that additional eligibility criteria may apply for specific programs — ask, do not assume. A VA clinician starts it. VA’s PSAS pages describe veterans referred by a physical medicine and rehabilitation physician receiving a full range of services and durable medical equipment, including mobility aids such as walkers and wheelchairs — and, in the same list,

title: The Older PG Systems: Pilot+, Egis and S-Drive — PMD — BareBoard
headings: The Older PG Systems: Pilot+, Egis and S-Drive
How to read the gauge before you count
S-Drive — count the bars on the tiller
Egis — the same bars, and a hidden second layer
Trip codes: the number behind the bars
Owner checks first, whichever system you have
text: The Older PG Systems: Pilot+, Egis and S-Drive Before VR2 and R-net , PG Drives Technology — now part of Curtiss-Wright — put three other control systems on millions of chairs and scooters: Pilot+ on power chairs, and S-Drive and Egis on scooters. They are older, simpler, and still in daily use. When one stops, it already tells you why — in flashing bars on its battery gauge. This page translates those bars. A control system is the electronics that turn your joystick or throttle movement into motor power, apply the brakes, and watch for faults. A trip is the system stopping drive on purpose because it detected a fault. Counting the trip display costs nothing and needs no tools. Provenance: the bar tables below are Curtiss-Wright’s own published flash-code lists for Pilot+, S-Drive and Egis, checked against PG Drives Technology’s Mobility Diagnostic Guide and the S-Drive Technical Manual (SK76745/10) — whose Self-Help Guide Curtiss-Wright publishes as its S-Drive Flash Codes page. The four-digit trip codes are from that same Diagnostic Guide. Codes that could not be confirmed for the named system are not listed. Documentation, not bench measurement: if your vehicle disagrees with this page, the vehicle wins — write down what yours actually does. Before any check in these tables that touches a plug, cable, motor, brake, actuator, or battery terminal: put the chair on level ground, switch it OFF, and disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker. Do not do the check while seated in the chair. Connector pins can remain live after switch-off. Keep a disconnected cable from touching skin, jewelry, tools, or metal, and cover or restrain it so the pins cannot short. At a battery terminal, work on one terminal at a time with an insulated tool. If you cannot disconnect power, inspect visually only and stop. The manufacturer’s own warning, carried word for word from PG Drives Technology’s Mobility Diagnostic Guide : “Diagnostics should only be conducted by electronic service professionals with in-depth knowledge of PG Drives Technology electronic controllers. An incorrect or badly effected repair could result in an unsafe set-up of a vehicle.” And, from the same guide: “There are no serviceable parts in any of the PG Drives Technology control systems. Consequently, any defective units must be returned to PG Drives Technology or a PG Drives Technology approved service organization for repair.” True — for repairs inside the units. Reading a bar count needs no tools at all: the vehicle displays it for free, on purpose, where you can see it. That is the part this page uses. One more, word for word from the PG Drives VSI Technical Manual in the library — the sibling manual for this same gauge family: “Do not operate the controller if the battery is nearly discharged. Failure to comply with this condition may leave the user stranded in an unsafe position, such as in the middle of a road. PGDT accepts no liability for losses of any kind arising from failure to comply with this condition.” Which system do you have? Look at what you drive with, and how many motors the vehicle has. That separates the three faster than any label hunt — then confirm it on the controller’s own label in the base. System What it is Where it was fitted How it shows a fault Pilot+ A modular power-chair system: a separate Joystick Module (the unit in your hand) wired by a bus cable to a Power Module in the base that drives two motors, left and right. Some chairs add an actuator and lighting module (PG calls it the ALM ) for powered seating. The chair’s settings live in the Power Module. Power chairs of the generation before VR2. If your chair has two drive motors and a joystick with a 10-bar battery gauge, and it is not VR2 or R-net, Pilot+ is a likely fit — the label decides. Flashing bars on the TruCharge display — the 10-segment, red-yellow-green battery gauge. Count the flashing bars, 1 to 10. S-Drive A scooter controller family: one controller box driving a single motor through a transaxle (a combined gearbox and axle unit). You drive it from the tiller — the steering column — with a throttle lever (often called a wig-wag : push one way for forward, the other for reverse). The family covers several current ratings; the rating is printed on the controller label. Mobility scooters, across many makers. The S-Drive Technical Manual (SK76745/10) covers the Mark 2 range, identified by part number D51270 onwards. Flashing bars on the TruCharge gauge on the tiller, or flashes of the status indicator light. Count the bars or flashes, 1 to 10. Egis A compact single-motor scooter controller, in the same tiller-and-throttle layout as S-Drive. Curtiss-Wright’s own Egis Flash Codes support page gives its common ratings by the number in the square box on its label: 70 or 110 (amps — the most current it can deliver to the motor). Larger and heavier-duty scooters. Documented factory fits include the Handicare Trophy scooter and, in its owner’s manual specifications, the Golden Avenger (listed there as a 110 amp programmable PG Egis controller). Flashing bars on the battery gauge, 1 to 10 — the same pattern as S-Drive, because both drive one motor. Its deeper codes need a programmer: see the trip-code section below. One family habit explains all three tables: PG built them on the same 1-to-10 idea. Bars 1 and 10 are always the battery (too low, too high), the middle bars are the motor, brake and throttle wiring the system can see, and 5 is deliberately empty on the single-motor systems — on a two-motor chair that slot belongs to the second motor. Do not carry a Pilot+ meaning onto a scooter, or the other way round: same count, different vehicle. Not your system? Part one covers VR2, VSI (PG’s own VSI flash-code sheet ) and R-net, part two covers Shark, DX and MK6i, and Reading the Chair shows how to identify a system from its plugs and labels. How to read the gauge before you count The TruCharge display is PG’s name for the 10-bar battery gauge. Steady, it is just a fuel gauge: red, yellow and green bars lit means charged; just red and yellow means charge soon; just red means charge now. When something is wrong, the display changes its behaviour — and some behaviours are not faults at all: Flashing slowly: low battery. The controller is working correctly; charge as soon as you can. Stepping up (bars lighting one after another, upward): the batteries are charging — a charger is connected, and the vehicle will not drive until it is disconnected and you switch off and on again. Blinking on once every few seconds: sleep mode. The system has gone to sleep after a programmed idle time. It is not a trip. Switch off and on again to wake it. The Diagnostic Guide gives the Pilot+ family figure as once every 2.5 seconds; the S-Drive manual gives its figure as every 3.5 seconds. Rippling (the gauge pattern running up and down, or the speed indicator rippling): on chair systems this is the joystick having been pushed while switching on, or the system being locked. Centre the stick, or unlock the system, before you suspect a fault. Flashing rapidly, in a repeated count: this is the trip. Count how many bars flash before the pattern repeats. That count is your code — find it in your system’s table below. Count twice. The pattern repeats, so take your time, and write the number down with the date and what you were doing when it appeared. Pilot+ — count the flashing bars The manufacturer’s own list for this system is Curtiss-Wright’s Pilot+ Flash Codes page. Pilot+ drives two motors, so its table names a side. One warning from PG itself, carried in its flash-code list: if the programmable setting Motor Swap has been enabled on your chair, left and right swap places in this table — identify a motor by its plug at the Power Module, not only by side. Flashing bars What it means What you check first 1 bar Low battery voltage Charge the batteries overnight. Check the main battery plugs, terminal bolts and circuit breaker. If it keeps happening, load-test the pair (see Cheap Fixes ). The Diagnostic Guide puts the trip point plainly: the system trips when battery voltage has fallen below 16V (trip code 2C00). 2 bars Left motor disconnected The Power Module cannot see the left motor. Check its heavy plug at the Power Module and the cable run for pinches or cuts. 3 bars Left motor wiring trip (short) A left motor wire is shorting to a battery connection. Inspect the cable where it passes frame hinges and the battery box. This is a stop-and-inspect fault, not a keep-driving one. 4 bars Right motor disconnected Same checks as 2 bars, on the right motor: plug, then cable. 5 bars Right motor wiring trip (short) Same checks as 3 bars, on the right motor cable. 6 bars Charger connected / inhibit active The chair is being prevented from driving by an external signal. First: unplug the charger from the charging socket in the Joystick Module. If no charger is connected, an on-board charger or a seat-height switch can send the same inhibit signal — check what your chair’s manual lists for it. 7 bars Possible joystick trip Usually your own hand: the joystick was off centre at switch-on. Switch off, take everything off the stick, let it centre, switch on without touching it. If it returns with the stick centred, the Joystick Module itself is suspect. One Pilot+ tell the Diagnostic Guide adds: a communications fault between Joystick Module and Power Module is shown by the green lights below the TruCharge display flashing — check that bus cable first. 8 bars Possible control system trip The system failed its own check. Make sure every connection is secure, switch off for 30 seconds, and try again. If the code stays, the fault is inside a module. 9 bars Solenoid brake trip The electric parking brakes (one in each motor) have a bad connection. First: both freewheel levers firmly to DRIVE — a lever in PUSH gives this code. Then the small brake plugs and motor connections at the back of

title: Motors & Brakes on the Meter — PMD — BareBoard
headings: Safety first — every test on this page starts powered down
The drive unit is one assembly: motor, gearbox, brake
The owner’s reference standard: left against right
Procedure 1 — The brake coil test (“ohm out each brake coil”)
The click test — no meter needed
Procedure 2 — The motor winding test: continuity, and shorts to case
Brushes: the wear part inside the motor
Which designs let you change them
The gearbox: judged by sound, leaks and play
Freewheel levers: what they actually disconnect
Reading your results: what to replace, what to leave alone
text: Motors & Brakes on the Meter When a chair will not drive, veers, chatters, or shows a motor or brake code, the dealer’s next step is usually a quote for a whole motor. Your next step can be a multimeter. A multimeter is a handheld meter that can measure voltage, and — the setting used on this page — resistance : how hard it is for electricity to get through a part, measured in ohms (written Ω). Resistance tests need no power in the part at all. That is what makes them owner-safe, and it is also what the manufacturers’ own service manuals tell their technicians to do first. This page teaches three tests from those manuals: the motor winding test, the brake coil test, and the short-to-case test — plus brush inspection, gearbox noises, and freewheel levers. Every number printed here is tied to the manual that printed it first, for the model named next to it. There is no universal “good motor” number, and this page will not invent one: where your manual gives no number, the test is a comparison — left side against right side, on your own chair. Provenance: procedures and values are compiled from the manufacturers’ published service and owner manuals listed in Sources — Invacare, Sunrise Medical, Pride Mobility, PG Drives Technology and Dynamic Controls — and checked against them. Documentation, not bench measurement: if your chair disagrees with this page, the chair wins — write down what yours actually does. Safety first — every test on this page starts powered down Before any procedure here: put the chair on level ground, switch it OFF at the joystick, and disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker. Block the drive wheels so the chair cannot roll. Do not sit in the chair while testing. Take off rings, watches and other metal jewellery. A resistance test is done on a part with no power connected to it : never put a meter set to ohms on a live circuit — it can damage the meter and the reading is meaningless anyway. Unplug the motor connector from the power module (also called the controller — the electronics box in the base that sends battery power to the motors) and test on the motor side of that plug, so you are measuring the motor alone, not the electronics. One warning governs the whole page, from Invacare’s Pronto M71 service manual, word for word: “A shorted electro-mechanical brake will damage the brake output section in the controller. DO NOT connect a shorted electro-mechanical brake to a good controller module. A shorted brake MUST be replaced.” In plain words: if a test on this page shows a brake at or near 0 ohms, do not plug it back in “to see.” You have your answer, and plugging it in can kill the controller too. The drive unit is one assembly: motor, gearbox, brake Almost every power chair has two drive units , one per drive wheel, left and right. Each unit is three parts bolted together and usually sold — and quoted — as one assembly: The motor. On most chairs a brushed direct-current (DC) motor. Inside it: a winding (coils of copper wire; the winding on the spinning part is the armature ), a commutator (a ring of copper segments on the spinning shaft that the electricity passes through as it turns), and brushes (small blocks of carbon that press against the commutator and carry the current into the spinning part; because they rub, they slowly wear away — they are a wear part, like brake pads). The gearbox. A set of gears in a sealed, grease- or oil-filled case that trades the motor’s speed for turning force (torque) at the wheel. The wheel bolts to the gearbox output shaft, not to the motor shaft. The brake. An electric parking brake on the back of the motor, covered in its own section below . Permobil builds it the same way: the Permobil C300 service manual lists a magnetic wheel lock on each drive motor, wired separately from the motor itself. Why this matters for testing: a fault in any one of the three is quoted as a new “motor.” The meter separates them. The winding test accuses or clears the motor. The coil test accuses or clears the brake. The gearbox makes no electrical reading at all — it is judged by sound, leaks and play, in the gearbox section . Test first, and the quote has to name the part that actually failed. The plug is the test point. On the Invacare and Sunrise designs the manuals describe, motor and brake travel together in one 4-pin motor connector : two large pins for the motor, two small pins for the brake. Invacare’s Pronto M71 manual says to locate the two motor contacts in the red and black housings, and the two brake contacts side by side in the black housings. Sunrise’s Quickie Pulse 6 service manual says the same thing by size: small pins for the brake, large pins for the motor. Other chairs split them into two separate plugs — a heavy 2-wire plug for the motor and a small 2-wire plug for the brake. Either way: heavy pair = motor, light pair = brake. Identify the pair by the manual for your chair, not by guessing. The owner’s reference standard: left against right Your chair carries its own reference part: the other drive unit. It is the same make, same age, same mileage, and it has lived the same life. Before you judge any reading, take the same reading on both sides and write both down. Power down and disconnect the battery, as in Safety first . Unplug one motor connector at the power module. Touch the two meter probes together first and note what the meter shows: that small number is your leads’ own resistance. Subtract it from motor readings, or use the meter’s REL (relative) button if it has one, so you are not blaming the motor for your test leads. Take the motor reading and the brake reading on this side, exactly as in Procedure 2 and Procedure 1 . Write them down with the side: “left motor, left brake.” Reconnect that side, unplug the other side, and repeat, step for step, in the same order, with the chair in the same state. Compare. Two sides that read close to each other, and inside the range your model’s manual prints, are two healthy units — look elsewhere for the fault. One side open (the meter shows OL — “over limit,” no connection at all), shorted (at or near 0), or far from its twin is the faulty unit, and you can name it: side, part, and reading. Dynamic Controls makes the same point from the controller’s side in the SHARK power module technical manual : “It is important that both motors have approximately the same motor resistance and motor cable length.” The chair itself expects the two sides to match. So should your diagnosis. Procedure 1 — The brake coil test (“ohm out each brake coil”) Fixes the question behind: brake fault codes, including Invacare MK6i E09/E10 in Fault Codes, Translated: The Other Systems , where Invacare’s own service manual instruction is quoted word for word: “Check all connections. Ohm out each brake coil.” This procedure is that sentence, taught step by step. You need: A digital multimeter. What the brake is. The chair’s parking brake is spring-applied, power-released . Inside the brake housing, a spring presses a friction plate against the motor shaft whenever there is no power: brake ON. The brake coil is a coil of wire that works as an electromagnet (a magnet that only pulls while electricity flows through the coil — that kind of coil, used to move a mechanical part, is called a solenoid , and this brake is often called a solenoid brake). When you push the joystick, the controller sends power to the coil, the coil pulls the plate off the shaft against the spring, and the wheel is free to turn. When you let go, power stops and the spring clamps the brake again. That one design explains the stranded chair: a dead chair will not roll. No power means the springs hold both brakes on, on purpose — it is the fail-safe that stops a chair rolling away on a slope when its electronics die. It also means a brake coil that has failed open (a break in its wire) leaves that wheel clamped forever, and the controller, which checks the coil electrically, reports a brake fault and refuses to drive at all. Power down first. Chair OFF, battery disconnected or breaker tripped, wheels blocked, as in Safety first . Find the motor connector for one side at the power module and unplug it. Find the two brake contacts in that plug: the small pins, or the side-by-side pair in the black housings on Invacare’s 4-pin plug. Set the multimeter to ohms (the Ω setting; if the meter has ranges, choose the 200-ohm range). Put one probe on each brake contact, on clean metal. Polarity (which probe goes where) does not matter for resistance. Hold them still until the reading settles, and write the number down with the side. Read the result the way the manuals do. A steady reading inside your model’s printed range (table below) means the coil is whole. OL or a very high reading means an open connection: the coil wire is broken, or a pin is not making contact — check the plug pins first, then condemn the coil. 0 ohms, or near it, means a short circuit (the current has found a path with almost no resistance, usually damaged insulation inside the coil): the brake must be replaced, and per the warning in Safety first it must not be reconnected to the controller. Repeat on the other side and compare, as in left against right . Then reconnect everything firmly. There is no universal brake-coil number. The manuals disagree with each other by a factor of six — because brake coils genuinely differ by motor. Use the row for your chair, or compare sides: Manual Brake coil, normal Motor, normal (same manual) Sunrise Medical Quickie Pulse 6 service manual approximately 12 to 15 ohms (small pins) approximately 0.5 to 0.9 ohms (large pins) Invacare Pronto M71 service manual (part no. 1118377) 40–80 ohms, “depending on the motor” 0.5 to 5 ohms; OL or over 15 ohms indicates a problem Invacare Pronto M71, E09/E10 troubleshooting table (same manual) 45–50 ohms, for that fault 0–5 ohms, in the noise tables Invacare Pronto M61 service manual 45–100 ohms, “

title: What You Can Change From the Joystick Itself — PMD — BareBoard
headings: What You Can Change From the Joystick Itself
Curtiss-Wright R-net (CJSM2 colour-screen joystick): two doors
Door one: the Settings Menu (owner level)
Door two: OBP (only if it was left enabled)
Dynamic Controls DX2: there is no menu — and that is the finding
Dynamic Controls LiNX (REM400 / REM500 touchscreens): a real settings menu
Invacare MK6i (colour MPJ+ joystick): the 10-second menu
The summary: five systems, five doors
text: What You Can Change From the Joystick Itself Before the dealer’s laptop, before the dongle, there is a smaller door: the settings menus already built into the hand control you hold every day. Every major control system has one. None of them were ever walked through for owners. Here they are, system by system, exactly as the manufacturers printed them in their own manuals. First, the words. The hand control (also called the joystick module, or the remote ) is the unit in front of you: joystick, buttons, and screen. The drive screen is its home screen — the one that shows your speed, battery, and current profile . A profile is a saved set of drive behaviour — indoor, outdoor, attendant — built by whoever programmed the chair; you can switch between profiles, but on most systems you cannot edit what is inside one from the hand control. On-board programming , shortened to OBP , is a programming mode built into the hand control itself, as opposed to programming done from a separate tool. A mode is a job the hand control is doing right now — driving, seating, settings — and most hand controls step through modes with a Mode button. The stance of this page is narrow and deliberate: here is what the maker already left open to you. Every button sequence below is printed in a published owner manual or a published programming guide, and each section names its source. Where a menu exists but a dealer-set switch decides whether you may open it, this page says exactly that — it does not teach you to defeat the switch. And the safety line from the settings page stands in full: some settings can break hardware, including the seating actuator rule — on systems that sense the end of an actuator’s travel by motor current, actuator acceleration and deceleration must stay at 100%. That rule, and what each deep setting means, lives on the settings page ; this page does not re-teach deep settings. For the tools and permission tiers behind the locked doors, see the programmers page . Curtiss-Wright R-net (CJSM2 colour-screen joystick): two doors R-net chairs with the colour-screen CJSM2 joystick have two menus, and they are not the same door. The Settings Menu is the owner’s menu, printed in the chair’s user manual. OBP is the programming menu documented in Curtiss-Wright’s On-Board Programming manual SK78571 — and whether OBP opens at all was decided when the chair was programmed. Door one: the Settings Menu (owner level) Permobil’s CJSM2 user manual (order no. 341124) describes it this way: “The settings menu permits the user to change, for example the clock, the display brightness, and the background color.” On a Permobil-fitted panel: Press and hold the function button for hazard lights to open the Settings Menu. If your panel’s function buttons are programmed with seat functions instead, first press the Mode button one or more times until the settings icon appears on the screen, then press and hold the function button for hazard lights. Move the joystick to scroll through the menu. Push the joystick right to enter a submenu. To leave, select Exit at the bottom of the menu and push the joystick right. What is inside, per that manual: Time — Set Time sets the clock; Display Time chooses 12-hour, 24-hour, or off. Distance — the odometer (the chair’s mileage counter). Total Distance is stored in the power module and counts everything driven while that module has been fitted; Trip Distance counts since the last reset and can be cleared by you with a right joystick push; Display Distance chooses which of the two the screen shows. Backlight — screen brightness from 0% to 100%; Auto Backlight lets the panel’s light sensor adjust brightness for you (on or off); Backlight Time sets how long the backlight stays on after the last input, from 0 to 240 seconds. Bluetooth and Infrared setup (on panels fitted with them) — pairing devices, and learning or deleting infrared codes for controlling household devices. System — read-only: Diagnostics shows the control system’s diagnostic information, and Timers shows how many hours the chair has been driven. (What the diagnostic codes mean is on the fault codes page .) Panels differ between chair brands. PGDT’s own R-net CJSM2 user guide opens the same menu by pressing and holding the top left-hand screen button for 1 second. The menu contents are the same family; the button that opens it is the part your chair’s own manual decides. Door two: OBP (only if it was left enabled) The OBP manual SK78571 is blunt about the gate: “OBP in the field can be entered via two methods – connection of a hardware dongle or a keycode. The actual method required is set by the factory programming of the control system.” A dongle is a small hardware plug that carries programming permission (the tiers are mapped on the programmers page ). The manual also states: “OBP is not possible using an LED Joystick Module.” If your chair has the LED joystick, this door does not exist. If the dongle method is set, the published sequence is: Turn off the control system. Insert the R-net Dongle along the communication cables in the system configuration. Turn on the control system. After initialization, press the Mode key until the OBP screen is reached. If the keycode method is set, the published sequence is: Hold down the Horn button, then hold down the On/Off button until there is a short bleep. The normal power-up sound occurs before this bleep. Release the Horn button, but keep holding the On/Off button until there are two further short bleeps. Release the On/Off button. There is a longer bleep, and OBP mode is entered. (A dongle also opens OBP when the keycode method is set.) PGDT prints the consequence of that second method in its own manual, verbatim: “If the keycode method is set, then it may be possible for a wheelchair user to gain entry to the OBP function. PGDT accept no liability for losses of any kind if this method of OBP is set. PGDT also accept no liability for losses of any kind if OBP access is gained by unauthorised personnel obtaining a dongle.” Read that carefully: the maker knows the keycode door can be opened by the rider. Whether it is open on your chair was still someone else’s choice. Inside OBP, navigation is all joystick: forward and reverse deflections move up and down the parameter list; a left deflection on a highlighted parameter title shows its full name, and on the profiled screens a second left deflection goes back a screen. The Speed buttons change a value. The manual’s storage instruction matters: “To ensure all new values are stored correctly, exit OBP mode with a series of left hand joystick deflections.” There is no published “exit without saving” path — leaving any other way is exactly what that sentence warns against. What OBP contains is the deep parameter tree — speeds, acceleration, deceleration, torque, tremor damping, seating actuator speeds, profile enable, and more. That tree is translated setting by setting on the settings page , and the manual’s own warning, verbatim, is why this page does not walk you through changing them: “Programming should only be conducted by healthcare professionals with in-depth knowledge of PGDT control systems. Incorrect programming could result in an unsafe set-up of a wheelchair for a user. PGDT accept no responsibility for losses of any kind if the programming of the control system is altered from the factory pre-set values.” Knowing the door exists, knowing whether yours is set to dongle or keycode, and knowing the values you were fitted with — that is owner knowledge. The values themselves belong in a conversation with the clinician who fitted you. Dynamic Controls DX2: there is no menu — and that is the finding The DX2 hand controls covered by Dynamic’s DX2-REM42x manual (GBK65568) and DX2-ACS2 installation manual (GBK65548) are LED remotes: rows of lights and buttons, no screen, no settings menu, no clock to set. The ACS2 manual defines the system’s position in one sentence, verbatim: “The term ‘programming’ used in this manual refers to adjusting parameters and configuring options to suit an application. ‘Programming’ does not change or alter any software within the controller and is performed using a controlled programming tool available only to authorised personnel.” Every parameter change on DX2 goes through the Wizard PC software or the DX Hand Held Programmer, behind a dealer or OEM dongle — the full tier map is on the programmers page . What the REM42x buttons themselves do, per the manual, is operation, not programming: Choose a drive profile: press + or − on the Drive Profile Selection button. The remote supports 5 drive profiles, and the lit Drive Profile LEDs show which one is active. The manual’s own framing: a drive profile is “a specific drive setting (slow or fast, indoors or outdoors) that your therapist or dealer can adjust to suit your personal needs and preference.” You pick among them; you cannot edit inside one. Run the seating: press + or − on the Actuator Selection button to enter Seating Mode, press + / − or push the joystick left/right to choose among up to 4 seating functions, then push the joystick forward or reverse to move the selected function. Pressing the Drive Profile Selection button returns you to Driving Mode, in the profile you were in before. Lights (REM420 only): the side light button switches the side/positioning lights; the indicator buttons switch the turn indicators; the hazard button switches the hazard lights. Lock the chair: if the Lock Enable parameter has been set to Yes by the programmer, hold the On/Off button for more than 4 seconds while the system is on. The system turns off, and after 4 seconds all the Drive Profile LEDs and the Lock LED light. To unlock: press On/Off, then press the Horn button twice within 10 seconds while the Lock LED flashes; miss the 10 seconds and the system turns off again.
