title: Parts, Not Assemblies — PMD — BareBoard
headings: The parts that actually wear out
The warranty clock vs. the repair clock
text: Parts, Not Assemblies Dealers sell assemblies: the whole wheel, the whole module, the whole unit. Underneath every assembly is a part — a standard, buyable, nameable part. This page names them. A $6 inner tube became a $300 charge to Medicaid to replace both wheels, with a six-to-eight-week wait. The tube was the part. The wheels were the assembly. That gap is the business model. Inside the telematics box Fig. 1. The board inside a ConnectMe telematics unit (Permobil) — the box that, once activated, collects and transmits wheelchair data to the service provider. Nothing exotic: a standard Sierra Wireless cellular module does the talking, on an ordinary circuit board (marked ETRON 843000-01). Photo from the manufacturer’s own FCC internal-photos exhibit, FCC ID 2AKPO331495 . Fig. 2. The FLC-BTM805 Bluetooth module — photo cropped from Fujian Flaircomm Microelectronics, Inc.’s FCC internal-photos exhibit 1863218 (FCC ID P4IBTM805). The large chip is a CSR Bluetooth radio — the same family of radio sold for a few dollars as a component. The wireless inside chair electronics is standard parts, all the way down. The parts that actually wear out Caster bearings — 608RS or 6001RS sealed bearings, about $3–$8 each. Standard industrial bearings, sold everywhere bearings are sold. The size is printed on the old bearing’s seal. Replacing them is Procedure 5 . Batteries — sold in matched pairs, by group size. U1, 22NF, Group 34, Group 24. The chair does not care about the dealer’s brand; it cares about size, voltage, and a pair that matches. Testing them is Procedure 3 . Inner tubes and tires — sized like bicycle parts, because they are bicycle-class parts. A flat is a tube, not two wheels. Contact cleaner — one can covers the charger socket and every bus connector on the chair ( Procedures 2 and 4 ). The warranty clock vs. the repair clock Most manufacturers warranty the electronics for a year or two. Medicare will not replace the chair for five. (Ranges in the table are compiled from each maker’s published warranty inserts. Terms vary by model and insert revision, and makers revise them — treat every range below as approximate; your chair’s own insert is the authority.) The electronics’ real-world median life — 32.2 months, from 1,268 Group 2 chairs in the Wheelchair Repair Registry (Kim et al., 2025) — lands in the gap. Knowing which clock covers your failed part is the difference between a warranty repair and a bill. Maker Frame Electronics Motors / actuators Batteries Medicare’s clock (for comparison) — Electronics die at a 32.2-month median — Chair replacement locked for 5 years Permobil (Corpus line) 5-year frame 1–2 years Motors/gearboxes 2–3 years; actuators 1–2 years Batteries 12 months Quantum Rehab / Pride (standard insert INFINFB2779) Lifetime limited (frame) 1 year 1 year Batteries 12 months Pride Mobility / Quantum (Group 2/3 inserts INFINFB2781/2782) Lifetime limited (frame) 1–2 years 1 year–18 months Batteries 6–13 months Sunrise Medical (Quickie) 5-year frame 1 year, all electronics 1 year Batteries 6–12 months Invacare 5-year frame (seat frame 3) 1–2 years 1–2 years Batteries 6–12 months Full warranty terms are in each maker’s own published warranty insert — ask for it by name, and keep yours. ← Back to PMD · The settings →

title: The Keys: Programmers, Dongles and Access Tiers — PMD — BareBoard
headings: The Keys: Programmers, Dongles and Access Tiers
The map: five systems, five keys
Curtiss-Wright — the dongle is the level
Curtis Instruments — four versions of the same tool
Dynamic Controls LiNX — the free app and the paid key
Dynamic Controls DX, DX2 and Shark — the kit with no key in the box
Invacare MK6i — your settings live on a card
What to demand before anyone swaps a module
text: The Keys: Programmers, Dongles and Access Tiers The settings page showed you the numbers that make your chair yours. This page names the tools that read and write those numbers — and the tier system that decides who is allowed to hold them. Every control system has the same three-part lock: software (the program that talks to the chair), a key (a physical dongle — a small plug that carries the permission — or a card), and tiers (levels of access: the same tool shows more, or fewer, settings depending on which key is plugged in). The software is rarely the secret. The key is. Provenance: compiled from the manufacturers’ own published material — Curtiss-Wright’s programming support pages and R-net manuals , the Curtis Instruments 1313/1314 programming manual, Dynamic Controls’ LiNX Access documentation and SHARK / DX2 manuals , and Invacare’s MK6i Field Reference Guide (part no. 1141471). Where a fact comes from the owner community instead of a manual, it is not stated here. The map: five systems, five keys System The tools The key The tiers Curtiss-Wright R-net, VR2, VSI PP1A / PP1B hand-held programmers; R-net PC Programmer (PC software) A programming dongle for the PC tool; the hand-helds are level-built ‘A’ level (dealer) and ‘B’ level (engineering/OEM) — some parameters cannot be changed below ‘B’ Curtis Instruments (Quantum Q-Logic 3) 1313 hand-held programmer; 1314 PC Programming Station The programmer itself, sold in one of four versions User, Service, Dealer, OEM — each version works at its own level and every level below it Dynamic Controls LiNX LiNX Access app (iOS) and LiNX Access PC tool — the apps are free LiNX Access Key: DLX-HKEY01-A (Distributor) or DLX-HKEY02-A (Manufacturer) Default (no key: read files only), Distributor (basic parameters), Manufacturer (high-level parameters) Dynamic Controls DX, DX2, Shark (older systems) Wizard 5 PC software (DWIZ-SW); DX Hand Held Programmer (DX-HHP) Wizard Dongle, sold separately: DWD-OEM-U (OEM), DWD-EDL-U (Enhanced Dealer), DWD-DLR-U (Dealer) or DWD-FAC-U (Factory), plus system adapters Dealer, Enhanced Dealer, OEM and Factory dongles; the software kit is sold with no dongle in the box Invacare MK6i MK6i Easy Remote Programmer (hand-held); the older MK5 programmer also works A removable memory card in the programmer — a user card or a professional card The card is the tier: the fault log’s causes and fixes stay locked without a professional card Read the table once and the industry makes sense: the tool is never the product. The permission is the product. Curtiss-Wright — the dongle is the level For R-net, VR2 and VSI chairs, programming happens two ways. A hand-held programmer — Curtiss-Wright’s PP1A or PP1B — plugs into the chair and works through menus on its own small screen. Or a PC runs the R-net PC Programmer software, and the PC connects to the chair through the charging socket — the same round 3-pin socket the charger uses (Curtiss-Wright’s own support pages describe the programming cable landing in the charging socket of the controller). The PC software is one program. What it will show you is decided by the dongle. Curtiss-Wright’s support pages distinguish ‘A’ level tools (the dealer level) from ‘B’ level tools (the engineering level, held by chair manufacturers), and state plainly that some parameters — their examples include certain drive and profile settings — can only be changed with a ‘B’ level hand-held or PC programmer. If you do not have ‘B’ access, their answer is to send the controller back to them. One door is already in your hands: on-board programming . R-net chairs with a colour-screen joystick (CJSM2) carry a programming mode built into the joystick itself (documented in Curtiss-Wright’s On-Board Programming manual, SK78571 ). It covers a subset — display and user settings, and drive adjustments where the manufacturer has enabled them. Whether that door is open on your chair was decided by whoever programmed it. Curtis Instruments — four versions of the same tool Quantum’s Q-Logic 3 electronics are built by Curtis Instruments (PG Drives’ own fault-code listing names it: “Quantum Q-Logic 3 (Curtis Instruments)”). Curtis sells two programming tools that do the same job: the 1313 hand-held programmer and the 1314 PC Programming Station . Its manual states the rule in one breath: both programmers are available in User, Service, Dealer, and OEM versions , and each can perform the actions available at its own level and the levels below it — a User programmer works at User level only, while an OEM programmer has full access. Nothing about the hardware changes between versions. The version is the permission, sold as a different product at a different price to a different customer. Dynamic Controls LiNX — the free app and the paid key LiNX is programmed from the LiNX Access app (iPhone/iPad, or the PC tool). Dynamic Controls gives the app away free. The app is not the tool: it works through a LiNX Access Key , a hardware key that connects to the chair through its XLR (charger-style) port, and Dynamic’s own documentation defines three levels: Default (no key). You can receive a chair’s configuration file (a .lci file — the chair’s whole setup as one file) by email or file transfer, and view its distributor-level configuration and diagnostics, read-only. You cannot connect to a live chair. Distributor — key DLX-HKEY01-A . Connects to a live chair; reads and configures the basic performance parameters. This is the dealer/provider key. Manufacturer — key DLX-HKEY02-A . Connects and configures the high-level parameters. This is the chair-maker key. Dynamic defines the authorised users in its own listing: original equipment manufacturers and their approved distribution channels — dealers, providers, therapists and service technicians. The owner of the chair is not on the list. Note the one crack in the wall, though: the Default level means a dealer can email you your own .lci file and you can open it, read every setting in it, and keep it forever — free, with no key. Ask for that file by name. It is your backup, and the hub page explains what happens to owners who never got one. Dynamic Controls DX, DX2 and Shark — the kit with no key in the box The older Dynamic systems are programmed from a PC running Wizard 5 software, or with the DX Hand Held Programmer (DX-HHP) . Dynamic’s own SHARK installation manual lists the programming accessories by part number, and the list is the whole story: Wizard 5 Kit (DWIZ-KIT) — software, cables and DWIZ-ADAPT adapter. The manual notes, in parentheses: no dongle . Wizard 5 software only (DWIZ-SW) (the DX2 manual’s parts list). Wizard Dongle (USB) — OEM version ( DWD-OEM-U ), Enhanced Dealer ( DWD-EDL-U ), Dealer ( DWD-DLR-U ) or Factory ( DWD-FAC-U ), sold separately. SHARK Programming Adapter (DK-ADAPT) — the adapter a Shark system needs. You can buy the software, the cables and the adapter and still program nothing, because the dongle is a separate line item in four tiers — and the DX2 manual’s parts list says the same about its kit: software, cables and adapter (no dongle) . Invacare MK6i — your settings live on a card Invacare’s MK6i electronics (the TDX chairs) are programmed with the MK6i Easy Remote Programmer , a hand-held unit; Invacare’s Field Reference Guide also documents using the older MK5 programmer on MK6i electronics. What makes this system different is where the programming lives: on a removable memory card . The guide gives the memory card its own section — programs are saved to the card and restored from it. There are two kinds of card, and the difference is the tier. With a user card , settings can be saved and restored. But Invacare’s guide states that a professional memory card is required in the programmer to view the fault log’s error codes together with their causes and troubleshooting steps. Your chair records what went wrong, dates it, and timestamps it (on the colour MPJ+ joystick) — and the page that explains it is behind the professional card. The owner’s move on this system is real, though: because the whole setup is a file on a card, a copy of your card is a complete backup of your fit. If your chair is MK6i, ask for that copy before any module is swapped. What to demand before anyone swaps a module You may never hold the key. You can still hold the backup. Before a dealer replaces any electronic module on your chair, ask for four things — every one of them is a button-press in the tools above, and none of them costs the dealer anything but minutes: Your settings, exported, handed to you. The R-net program file, the LiNX .lci file, or a copy of the MK6i memory card — whichever your system uses. This is the fit your clinician built, in a file you own. The fault log, read before it is cleared. Codes and history first; erasing them destroys the evidence of what actually failed. Your settings restored after the swap — loaded from your backup, not factory defaults — and verified with a ride before the technician leaves. A swapped module at factory settings is how tremor dampening and torque silently vanish ( the settings page names what to check). The old module’s settings read before it goes back. If the replacement arrives wrong, the old module may be the only other copy of your fit. ← Back to PMD · The settings →

text: Quantum Q6 Edge 3, Opened — Every Part, Named This page takes the Quantum Q6 Edge 3 apart on paper — every assembly, every part, named. It is built from Quantum’s own Illustrated Parts Breakdown, callout by callout, with Quantum’s part numbers and a plain-language line for every part. If your chair is an Edge 3, this is the map of it. How to use this page: open the Q6 Edge 3 IPB to the page number given under each table. The IPB’s diagram shows the assembly pulled apart, each part marked with a callout letter and number. Find the callout in the table below it: that row gives you Quantum’s part number, the part’s name, how many the chair takes, and what it does, in one plain line. One warning before you start: this IPB is the Australian edition (serial JE7, September 2020). Part numbers for a US chair can differ. Check your chair’s serial number and confirm the part number with the dealer or on Quantum’s parts lookup before you order. What never differs is the shape of the chair: the assemblies, and what each part does, are the same. About this chair The Q6 Edge 3 is Quantum Rehab’s complex-rehabilitation power base — the chair underneath the seating that clinics fit to the rider. Its funding codes are K0848, K0849, K0856, K0857, and K0861 (Quantum’s code reference). It was sold with three electronics families: Q-Logic 3 (built by Curtis Instruments), and the simpler NE and NE+ families (built on Dynamic Controls’ LiNX system). The motors are rated for 6 miles per hour, standard or ACCU-TRAC. It runs on two NF-22 batteries. An iLevel seat lift was available. The source for this page is Quantum’s Illustrated Parts Breakdown for the chair, document INFMANU4994 Revision C, exported 8 September 2020. A parts breakdown — an IPB — is the manufacturer’s own list of every serviceable part, with a drawing of each assembly pulled apart and a table of callouts, part numbers, names, and quantities. How to read this exploded view Callout — the letter-and-number mark on the IPB’s drawing (A1, B1, J1). Find it on the drawing, find it in the table. Parent assembly — a callout range like A1–A3 means one part number buys the whole assembly: the part plus everything listed under it. The IPB says most parts live inside assemblies and may not be sold separately. No callout (—) — the IPB lists the part as “N/A”: paperwork and labels that have no place on a drawing. Qty — how many of that part one chair takes. What it is — Quantum’s own name for the part, word for word from the IPB. What it does — our plain-language line, written for this page. It says what the part type does, not which exact parts it joins to — the IPB does not say that, so neither do we. Left and right are from the rider’s point of view, sitting in the chair. Colors are Quantum’s names (Back in Black, Red Corvette, Cherry Bomb). The IPB’s color chart is not reproduced here; every color appears in the shroud and wheel-insert tables with its own part number. 1. Main frame The main frame is the chair’s steel skeleton. Everything else bolts to it. The IPB lists it as a single assembly — if the frame itself is damaged, the whole frame assembly is the part. Main Frame Assy, Edge 3 IPB p. 1–2 — diagram and parts list. Open the IPB to that page and match the callouts. Fig. 1. Main Frame Assy — exploded view reproduced from the manufacturer’s guide (source below). Callout Quantum part no. Drive motors The drive motors are the two motors that turn the big wheels. Each side has its own motor, its own mount, and its own suspension. title: Reading the Chair: The Bench Method — PMD — BareBoard
headings: Reading the Chair: The Bench Method
The parts you need — and how they connect
Procedure B1 — See what is plugged in
Procedure B2 — Listen without saying anything
Your phone: what it can and cannot do
text: Reading the Chair: The Bench Method Everything in this section was learned by listening. This page teaches the listening: how the parts of a power chair talk to each other on its control bus, how to hear that traffic with an ordinary computer, and how the chair’s configuration protocol was decoded from captured dealer-tool sessions. Education, step by step — the same way every finding on this site is made. The rule of the bench: listen first, transmit never. Every procedure on this page is read-only. The computer sends nothing onto the chair’s bus — not even the tiny acknowledgement bits a CAN device normally sends. The chair never knows you are there. The safety fact, first The chair’s 4-pin bus cable carries unregulated 24-volt battery power on the same connector as the data wires . That is the one way this work can hurt your equipment: bridge the battery line into a data line, or plug in a non-isolated adapter, and a wiring fault can travel straight up the USB cable into your computer. So: only ever connect through a galvanically isolated USB-to-CAN adapter (isolation rated 2500V or better) — an adapter with a built-in electrical barrier between the chair side and the computer side — and only in listen-only mode. No exceptions, including “just for a second.” The parts you need — and how they connect Three things. Each one is defined here, in the order you will touch them. A computer running Linux. Linux is a free operating system (the software that runs the computer, like Windows or macOS). It has CAN support built in, called SocketCAN : once the adapter below is plugged in, the computer treats it as an interface named can0 — can for the network, 0 because it is the first one. An isolated USB-to-CAN adapter (a gs_usb-compatible model with galvanic isolation; not every CANable-class board is isolated, so check the exact model). This small box translates between the computer’s USB port and the chair’s wiring. Isolated means it has a built-in electrical barrier between its two sides, so a fault on the chair’s 24 volts cannot travel into the computer. One end of the adapter is a USB plug, for the computer. The other end is where the chair’s wires land. The chair’s bus cable. The bus is the chair’s internal wiring network — the cables the joystick, the power module, and the seating module use to talk to each other. Its plugs are round, with 4 pins. The cable runs from the back of the joystick down to the power module in the base. How they connect, in plain words: computer → (USB cable) → adapter → (the adapter’s chair-side wires) → the chair’s bus cable. The adapter sits between the computer and the chair and only listens. Procedure B1 below connects only the computer half, first. Procedure B2 makes the chair connection, in listen-only mode. Open question, marked honestly: the R-net bus uses fault-tolerant CAN transceivers (a transceiver is the chip that speaks onto the wires). Which adapter transceivers are fully compatible with that bus must be confirmed on the bench before anything is connected to a live chair — the project’s own first bench session is pending hardware, and its results will be recorded here from the real session. Terminal output is never written in advance on this site. Procedure B1 — See what is plugged in Plug the isolated adapter into the computer. Nothing is connected to the chair yet. Ask the computer what it sees. You type commands into a terminal — a plain window that takes typed instructions and prints text answers. In the boxes on this page, lines starting with $ are lines you type exactly as shown (the $ itself is the computer’s prompt — do not type it), and you press Enter after each line. The first command lists every USB device; the second asks whether the CAN interface exists yet: $ lsusb -v | grep -E "idVendor|idProduct|iManufacturer|iProduct" $ ip -details link show can0 How you know it worked: the USB list shows the adapter as a named device, and the second command prints details for can0 instead of an error. Procedure B2 — Listen without saying anything STOP — do not connect to a live chair yet. The project has not confirmed which adapter transceivers are compatible with the R-net bus’s fault-tolerant CAN. Do not use this procedure on a live chair until this page names the confirmed adapter and its exact pin connections. (The steps below are the procedure as it will run, published for review.) Set the interface to the bus speed, listen-only, and bring it up. Every device on a CAN bus must agree on the speed or nothing can be read; the project’s captured dealer-tool sessions used 125000 (125 kbps): $ sudo ip link set can0 down $ sudo ip link set can0 type can bitrate 125000 listen-only on $ sudo ip link set can0 up Record the traffic while you trigger a fault you already understand — with the chair unoccupied, on level ground, and its drive wheels blocked — flip a freewheel lever, or unplug the charger (see the cheap fixes ). The log then contains a fault you can recognize, timestamped, next to the traffic that carried it: $ candump -tz -l can0 How you know it worked: the log fills with timestamped frames, including new traffic at the moment you triggered the fault — and the chair behaves completely normally the whole time, because the computer only listened. Your phone: what it can and cannot do Your phone is a documentation tool in this work — a camera, a light, and a notebook. It is not a bus tool. Here is the honest split, phone by phone, with every step spelled out. Both phones Photograph the fault before you touch anything. Open the Camera app, point it at the joystick screen or the flashing lights, tap the screen once to focus, and take the photo. On R-net chairs, photograph the screen showing the code. On VR2 and LiNX chairs, take a short video instead — a 10-second clip captures the flash count exactly, and you can count it as many times as you need. Use the flashlight to inspect. The charger-socket cleaning ( Procedure 2 ) and the connector inspection ( Procedure 4 ) both start with looking closely. iPhone: swipe down from the top of the screen to open Control Center, then tap the flashlight icon. Samsung: swipe down from the top to open Quick Settings, then tap the flashlight tile. Swipe or press Home to leave it on while you work. Photograph wiring before you disconnect it. Procedure 3 (batteries) depends on this: the photo is what you rewire from. Take it before the first bolt moves. Keep the record on the phone. The photos, the codes you wrote down, and a copy of your chair’s backup file belong together. iPhone: the Files app. Samsung: the My Files app. Name the folder with your chair’s model and the date. LiNX chairs: the manufacturer’s programming tool does not open the lock either. Dynamic Controls publishes the free LiNX Access tool for iOS and PC; it is not the Android app. (MyLiNX is the separate user diagnostics app — on Android and iOS.) Without an authorised LiNX Access Key — DLX-HKEY01-A (distributor/dealer) or DLX-HKEY02-A (manufacturer), plugged into the remote’s charger/programming (3-pin XLR) port — the tool cannot connect to a live chair to read the detailed fault log or the settings. Without the key, it can still open a stored configuration file at the default, read-only level. The lock reaches the phone too. iPhone: what it cannot do An iPhone cannot listen to the bus. There is no way to connect the CAN adapter to it that iOS will allow an app to use — this is a limit of the phone’s system, not a missing app. Reading the bus takes the computer. Samsung (Android): what it cannot do Android has a free terminal app called Termux that gives you the same kind of type-a-command window as the computer. But on a normal, unmodified Samsung phone, plugging the adapter in does not create the can0 interface — the phone’s system does not ship with that support turned on, and no app can add it. Any guide that tells you otherwise is skipping the part where it does not work. The phone documents; the computer listens. What the traffic taught us This is how the findings on the PMD page were made. Dealer programming sessions were captured on the bus and decoded offline. The chair’s configuration moves as data objects , each protected by a checksum — a number that proves the data arrived unchanged. Sixteen configuration objects were read straight off the bus in those captures. Decoding the read path showed there is no encryption on the bus, and no cryptographic authentication — the only authentication present is R-net’s documented XOR serial handshake, a simple fixed check between modules: the barrier is that the manufacturer’s software will not open its dealer settings unless its own dongle is plugged in. The project record contains incompatible accounts of what is inside that dongle, so its internal hardware is not stated as settled fact here. What this page does not teach, because it is not proven: writing a configuration back. The shortcut the community assumes — that a configuration file’s layout maps directly onto live bus addresses — is contradicted by the project’s own captures. A restore procedure will be published here when it has been proven on a live power module on the bench, and not before. That is this site’s standard, and it is not negotiable: proven today is reading captured dealer-tool sessions and understanding them; owner-adapter backup is not yet proven . ← Back to PMD · Fault codes →

title: Getting a Repair Paid For — PMD — BareBoard
headings: First question: do you own the chair, or is Medicare still renting it?
Repairs to a chair you own are covered
The paperwork myth: a repair does not need a new prescription
Why repairs are the whole game: the five-year clock
text: Getting a Repair Paid For Your chair broke. The supplier’s queue is measured in weeks, and somewhere in that queue is an approval step. For repairs, Medicare’s own rules say most of that queue should not exist. This page is those rules, in plain language, with the document names — so you can cite them, not just believe them. Provenance: compiled from CMS’s own publications — the Medicare Benefit Policy Manual (Publication 100-02, Chapter 15, §110.2), the Standard Documentation Requirements Policy Article A55426 as published by the DME MACs (the regional contractors that process Medicare equipment claims; this page cites Noridian’s publication), CMS’s prior-authorization documentation for power wheelchairs, and 42 CFR §414.210. This is documentation, not legal advice: if your claim is denied, the appeal steps at the end are the road, and your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) walks it with people for free. First question: do you own the chair, or is Medicare still renting it? Everything below splits on this. A capped rental is Medicare’s rent-to-own category: Medicare pays monthly, and after 13 months of payments the supplier must transfer ownership to you. Standard power wheelchairs (billing codes K0813–K0831 and K0898) must be rented — capped rental is the only route. During those 13 months, the chair is the supplier’s property on loan to you. Complex rehabilitative power wheelchairs — the Group 3 chairs most full-time users ride (codes K0835–K0843 and K0848–K0864) — can be rented or purchased , and the supplier must offer you the choice when the chair is first delivered. Most are purchased. A purchased chair is yours from day one. If your chair is still in its rental period: there is no separate Medicare payment for repairs at all — the DME MACs state it flatly: no payment for repair of rented items under any circumstances during a capped rental period. That is not a gap in your coverage. It means the repair is already paid for inside the rent: the supplier must service, repair, or replace the chair as part of the rental. A supplier who bills you for a rental-period repair, or parks your broken rental for a month, is failing an obligation — say so, in those words. If you own the chair — purchased outright, or past month 13 of a rental — read on. The rest of this page is yours. Repairs to a chair you own are covered Medicare’s definition of a repair (Benefit Policy Manual, Ch. 15, §110.2) covers work — parts and labour — needed to make equipment serviceable again after damage or wear. For equipment you own, the Standard Documentation Requirements (Policy Article A55426) say it in one line: repairs are covered when necessary to make the item serviceable . The limits, so nobody can inflate them later: Routine maintenance is not a repair. Testing, cleaning, regulating and checking are excluded. A covered repair fixes something that is broken or worn out. Warranty work is the maker’s bill, not Medicare’s — parts and labour covered by a manufacturer’s or supplier’s warranty are not separately payable. (Know which clock your failed part is on: Parts, Not Assemblies prints the makers’ warranty terms next to Medicare’s.) There is a cost ceiling: if a repair would cost more than replacing the chair for the remaining period of need, Medicare will not pay the excess. Your share is the standard Part B split: Medicare pays 80% of the approved amount for the repair; you owe 20% coinsurance (your percentage share) after the annual Part B deductible. A supplier quoting you 100% of a covered repair is not describing Medicare. The paperwork myth: a repair does not need a new prescription This is where weeks are manufactured. The rule, from Policy Article A55426: a new treating practitioner’s order is not needed for repairs. What a repair claim needs instead is documentation of two things: continued medical need (you still need the chair) and that the repair itself is reasonable and necessary (the chair is broken and this fixes it). And if Medicare paid for the chair in the first place, the chair’s medical necessity has already been established — it does not get re-proven because a motor died. Do not confuse this with prior authorization — Medicare’s pre-approval step. Prior authorization is real, but it belongs to delivery of a new chair : CMS requires it before delivery for specific new power wheelchairs (its own documentation checklist covers codes K0856 and K0861, the Group 3 single- and multiple-power-option chairs). It is a purchase gate. A supplier who sends a repair into the same queue — new evaluation, new face-to-face, new everything — is adding steps Medicare’s repair rules do not contain. Name the article: A55426. The loaner rule nobody mentions While your own chair is in the shop, Medicare pays for a temporary replacement : one month’s rental of a loaner chair, billed under code K0462 (the DME MACs publish this under Repairs, in so many words). One month will not cover a two-month repair — that gap is real, and it is the supplier’s delay, not a rule. But the loaner itself is a covered benefit with a code. Ask for it by the code. Why repairs are the whole game: the five-year clock Medicare will not replace your chair inside its five-year reasonable useful lifetime except for loss, theft, or irreparable damage (42 CFR §414.210(f) — the hub’s law section has the wider picture). Chair electronics die at a median of 32.2 months; batteries at 22.3 months. Do the arithmetic and the system’s design is plain: your chair is expected to break, more than once, in a window where replacement is barred — and repairs are the only bridge Medicare built across that window . The rules above are not fine print. They are the bridge. Use them like it. When a supplier says no Ask which rule. “Which Medicare rule requires a new evaluation for a repair? The Standard Documentation Requirements, Article A55426, say a new order is not needed for repairs.” A rule that cannot be named usually does not exist. Get the denial in writing. Verbal refusals evaporate. A written denial carries the reason — and the reason can be appealed. Use the free help. Your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) gives free, local Medicare counselling, including on equipment claims and appeals. 1-800-MEDICARE can also open a complaint against a supplier. Write the code down. Same as every page in this section: the fault code, the date, what was said, by whom. A repair you can document is a repair you can argue about — and win. ← Back to PMD · Your chair stopped: start here →

title: Scooters Are PMDs Too — PMD — BareBoard
headings: The parts, in the order your hands meet them
The electronics chain: tiller pod → controller → transaxle
Dynamic Controls Shark — the scooter system this site already translates
PG Drives S-Drive — the scooter-only controller family
PG Drives VSI — the chair system that crosses over
The failures that strand scooters — and the owner checks
Travel scooters: the ones that come apart
How the site’s fault tables apply to scooters
text: Scooters Are PMDs Too PMD stands for power mobility device — Medicare’s name for the whole family. It covers power wheelchairs and mobility scooters. Medicare’s own words for a scooter are power-operated vehicle , shortened to POV . This section of the site has taught chairs so far. This page teaches the other half of the family: the scooter — how it steers, how it drives, what its electronics are, and what strands it. If you already know the chair pages, almost everything transfers. The batteries, the brakes, the controllers and the dealer lock are the same ideas in a different shape. What changes is the shape: a scooter is steered like a bicycle and driven by one motor through one axle, where a chair is steered by a joystick and driven by two motors. Read the differences once and the rest of this section is yours too. Provenance: this page is compiled from the manufacturers’ own published documents — Dynamic Controls’ SHARK Power Module Installation Manual (GBK80262, Issue 7) , PG Drives Technology’s newVSI Technical Manual (SK80151-1) and Mobility Diagnostics guide , Pride Mobility’s Go-Go owner’s manuals and its Celebrity 2000 Illustrated Parts Breakdown , Drive Medical’s Scout owner’s manual, and Curtiss-Wright’s published S-Drive flash-code list — and checked against them. Where a manual named in this page is not yet in the site library, its name is left unlinked and it is listed as a collection target. Documentation, not bench measurement: if your scooter disagrees with this page, the scooter wins — write down what yours actually does. Before any check on this page that touches a plug, cable, motor, brake, or battery terminal: put the scooter on level ground, switch it OFF and take the key out, and disconnect the battery pack or trip the main circuit breaker (the resettable switch that cuts all power when the electrics are overloaded). Do not do the check while seated on the scooter. Never change the freewheel lever (defined below) on a slope, and never sit on a scooter that is in freewheel mode — in freewheel the brake is off and the scooter can roll. If you cannot disconnect power, inspect visually only and stop. The manufacturers’ own warnings, carried word for word. Pride Mobility, from the Go-Go ES2 owner’s manual: “Before placing your Travel Scooter into or taking it out of freewheel mode, turn the power switch to the “OFF” (center) position. Never sit on a Travel Scooter when it is in freewheel mode. Never put a Travel Scooter in freewheel mode on any incline.” “When your Travel Scooter is in freewheel mode, the braking system is disengaged. • Disengage the drive motors only on a level surface. • Ensure the power switch is in the “OFF” (center) position. • Stand to the side of the scooter to engage or disengage freewheel mode. Never sit on a scooter to do this. • After you have finished pushing your Travel Scooter, always return it to the drive mode to lock the brakes.” “Do not pull on electrical harness wires directly to detach them from the Travel Scooter. Always grasp the connector itself when disconnecting the harness to prevent wire damage.” Drive Medical, from the Scout owner’s manual: “Always make sure freewheel levers are in the drive position before getting in or out” and “Do not put the scooter in freewheel when on an incline or decline.” Dynamic Controls, from the SHARK manual ’s safety list: “Do not try to open or disassemble any case - there are no user-serviceable parts inside” and “Do not use the park brake release on a slope.” True — for repairs inside the cases. Everything on this page stays outside them: levers, plugs, batteries, and the codes the scooter shows you for free. One category, two machines Medicare Part B covers “wheelchairs and power-operated vehicles (scooters)” under the same benefit, on the same terms: medically necessary, a face-to-face examination and a written prescription first, and a supplier enrolled in Medicare. The site’s hub page says the same thing in one line: PMD is the official Medicare name for a power wheelchair or a power scooter. The repair rights are shared too — the state laws tracked on Repair Rights name mobility scooters alongside wheelchairs. So why did the chairs get eleven pages first? Because the gatekeeping is identical and the chairs were documented first. A scooter has the same lock in a simpler box: one controller, one motor, one brake, and a fault code standing between you and a dealer visit. Here is the whole difference, side by side: Power chair Mobility scooter You steer with A joystick. Push it left and the chair turns left. A tiller (defined below): handlebars on a steering column. Turn the bars and the front wheel turns, like a bicycle. How it turns Skid steering : two drive motors, one per side. To turn, the controller runs one side slower or backwards. The chair can spin in its own length. The front wheel steers mechanically. The scooter turns like a bicycle or a car, in an arc, and cannot spin on the spot. Drive motors Two — one on each drive wheel. One — inside the transaxle (defined below), driving both rear wheels through it on almost every model. Speed control How far you push the joystick. A wig-wag lever (defined below): one side for forward, one side for reverse. Brakes Two electric park brakes, one in each motor. Usually one electromagnetic brake on the transaxle. Seat Fixed to the chair; seating is part of the prescription. Usually lifts off its post, and swivels to help you get on and off. Taken apart for a car boot Rarely; chairs travel whole or by lift. Often by design — travel scooters split into sections with no tools (see Travel scooters below). Three wheels or four? Both exist in both sizes. A 3-wheel scooter has one front wheel: it turns tighter indoors and is easier to manoeuvre, and less steady on slopes and rough ground. A 4-wheel scooter has two front wheels: steadier, with a wider turning circle. Pride’s parts book for the Celebrity 2000 — a full-size scooter of the same era as the Jazzy chairs — lists both front ends for the same machine: “Front 3-Wheel” and “Front 4-Wheel” assemblies in one Illustrated Parts Breakdown . The parts, in the order your hands meet them Every term is defined where it first appears. Once you can name these parts, every other PMD page makes sense on a scooter too. Part What it is, in one line Tiller The steering column and handlebars in front of the seat. You turn it to steer, and it carries the controls. On many models it folds or tilts toward you, locked by a tiller adjustment knob . Delta tiller A tiller whose bar is a wraparound loop, roughly the shape of the Greek letter delta. You can rest your wrists on it and work the throttle with either hand — the standard bar on most full-size scooters, including Golden Technologies’ Buzzaround line. Tiller pod (also called the tiller console, or dash) The control box on top of the tiller: key switch, battery gauge, speed dial, horn, lights, and the throttle. Pride’s words: “The tiller console houses all controls needed to drive your Travel Scooter including the horn, the power switch, the battery condition meter and the throttle control lever.” Wig-wag (throttle control lever) One rocker lever across the tiller. Press or pull one side and the scooter goes forward; the other side reverses. Let go and it springs back to the middle — neutral — and the scooter stops. Either thumb or fingers can work it, from either side. Throttle potentiometer (throttle pot) The electrical part under the wig-wag. A potentiometer is a variable resistor — a knob or lever that turns a position into a voltage. The wig-wag turns this one: middle position means stop, and the further it moves each way, the faster the controller is told to go in that direction. It is a wear part, and its wear is the scooter fault chairs do not have (see Failures ). Speed potentiometer (speed pot, speed dial) A second, smaller potentiometer: the dial that caps your top speed before you set off. The wig-wag then controls speed up to that cap. Key switch The scooter’s ignition. Many scooters have no power button beyond this: key in and on, or off and out. Controller The sealed electronics box, usually under the seat or in the rear section, that takes the tiller’s signals and meters battery power to the motor. The scooter’s equivalent of a chair’s power module. The families are named in The electronics chain . Transaxle The combined gearbox and axle unit between the rear wheels: one sealed unit containing the gears and the axle the wheels bolt to. The motor mounts on it. Pride’s specification line for the Go-Go Ultra is the whole drive in nine words: “Rear-wheel drive, sealed transaxle, 24 volt DC motor.” Motor A 24-volt DC motor bolted to the transaxle. It drives both rear wheels through the transaxle’s gears and its built-in differential — the gear arrangement that lets the two rear wheels turn at different speeds in a corner, as on a car. Electromagnetic brake (park brake) A brake on the motor/transaxle that is held on by a spring and released by electricity . Power flows, the brake releases, the scooter can drive. Power stops — you let go of the wig-wag, switch off, or a fault trips — and the spring clamps the brake on. That is why a dead scooter will not roll, and why releasing it is a deliberate act (the freewheel lever, next). Freewheel lever (manual freewheel lever) A small lever on the transaxle, usually at the top right of the rear section. In DRIVE the transaxle is engaged and the brake works. In freewheel (also marked PUSH or N) the drive and brake are disengaged so a helper can push the scooter by hand for a short distance. Pride’s words: “Push forward on the manual freewheel lever to disable the drive system and the brake system. Push the manual freewheel lever rearward to reengage the drive and the brake systems.” Positions and markings vary by model — your manual’s picture is the authority for yours. Battery pack Two 12-volt deep-cycle batter

title: Power Seating, Part by Part — PMD — BareBoard
headings: First: the manufacturers’ own safety warnings, word for word
The five functions, one line each
The hardware chain: command → module → actuator
Procedure 1 — the manufacturer’s own actuator test (R-net, no meter)
Procedure 2 — voltage at the actuator connector (basic electrical check)
Procedure 3 — continuity and resistance, power off (basic electrical check)
Procedure 4 — endstop and inhibit check, before condemning anything
Drive inhibits, tilt limits and speed limits: the safety interlocks
The like-for-like swap: what has to match
text: Power Seating, Part by Part Tilt, recline, elevate, power legrests and standing are not five different machines. They are one idea repeated: a small electric pusher — an actuator (a motor-driven unit that pushes or pulls in a straight line) — moves one part of the seat, a seating module switches its power, and something tells it when to stop. Learn that one chain and you can follow every seating fault on the chair. This page names the parts, says how each one fails, gives the meter checks an owner can actually do, and sets out what has to match before one actuator can be swapped for another. It does not invent specifications: where a number appears, it comes from the manufacturer document named next to it. Where a check is a plain electrical check rather than a manufacturer procedure, it is labelled that way. Provenance: compiled from the manufacturers’ own published documents — Curtiss-Wright’s R-net On-Board Programming manual (SK78571) , Dynamic Controls / Invacare’s LiNX service manual (1605129-C) , the Permobil M3 Corpus owner’s manual , the Permobil F5 Corpus VS owner’s manual , the Invacare TDX SP2 owner’s manual and the Quantum Q6 Edge 2.0 owner’s manual — and checked against them. Warnings in quotation marks are carried word for word from those manuals. First: the manufacturers’ own safety warnings, word for word Before any check on this page that touches a plug, cable, actuator or battery terminal: put the chair on level ground, switch it OFF, and disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main circuit breaker, unless the step says to power the chair to run a function. Do not test a seating function while seated in the chair unless the step is simply operating it normally. Support any seat, backrest or legrest you unbolt before you remove its actuator — once the actuator is off, nothing else holds it up. Keep fingers, clothing, cables and tools out of the moving linkage at all times. Permobil, on pinch risk, in both the M3 Corpus and F5 Corpus VS owner’s manuals, under the heading “WARNING! Do not get pinched”: “The wheelchair is heavy and contains many moving parts, which means that you can be pinched when you adjust the wheelchair or if you use the wheelchair incorrectly. When you see this warning, be mindful of your body location to avoid being pinched. Do not put any part of your body between moving parts.” Permobil, on driving with the seat moved, under “WARNING! Drive extra carefully when lifted or tilted”: “If the seat or backrest is lifted or tilted on flat ground, drive at a low speed. If the seat or backrest is lifted or tilted, do not drive the wheelchair on slopes or over obstacles. If you do, the wheelchair can become less stable and injure you.” Permobil, on legrests, under “WARNING! Use leg rest tilt cautiously”: “Do not use the leg rest tilt when a knee support is in place. If you do, it can lead to bodily injury.” Permobil, on standing, in the F5 Corpus VS manual under “WARNING! Only use the standing function on level ground”: “Only use the standing function on level ground. If you do not, the wheelchair can lose traction or become less stable and injure you.” Invacare, on elevating legrests, in the TDX SP2 owner’s manual : “Risk of injury — If your power wheelchair has been fitted with elevating legrests, there is a risk of personal injury and damage to the power wheelchair if you drive the power wheelchair with the legrests raised. — To avoid unwanted displacement of the power wheelchair centre of gravity to the front (especially when travelling downhill) and in order to avoid damage to the power wheelchair, elevating legrests must always be lowered during normal travelling.” Quantum Rehab, on the power elevating seat, in the Q6 Edge 2.0 owner’s manual : “Do not allow the motor to run more than a few seconds after the mechanism reaches the top or bottom limit.” “The power elevating seat option is intended for use on a level surface only. Never raise the seat from its lowest position on an inclined surface. Failure to heed this warning can result in the power chair tipping over. Never raise the seat from its lowest position when operating your power chair on bumpy or uneven surfaces. Failure to heed this warning can result in the power chair tipping over. Never raise the power elevating seat while your power chair is in the freewheel mode. Always fasten the positioning belt when operating the power elevating seat.” The five functions, one line each A seating function is one named movement the rider can command. A seating motion is the programmed movement behind it — in the LiNX service manual’s words, a seating motion defines the icon shown, the overall speed, and the individual actuators and their speeds, and one motion can control one or more actuators at once. Function What moves, in one line Tilt (also called seat tilt, or tilt-in-space) The whole seat — seat, backrest and legrests together, at a fixed angle to each other — tips backwards and forwards as one unit. Recline (backrest tilt) Only the backrest leans back and returns upright, opening and closing the angle between backrest and seat. Elevate (seat lift, lifter) The whole seat rises straight up and lowers again, without changing any angle. Quantum calls its version with added stability control iLevel in the Q6 Edge 2.0 manual . Power legrests (leg rest tilt, elevating legrests, footplate lift) The legrest swings up toward horizontal and back down; on some chairs each legrest has its own actuator, on others one actuator moves both, and a separate short movement lengthens or shortens the legrest to lift the footplates. Standing A linked sequence — seat, backrest and legrests moving together through several actuators — brings the rider from seated to standing in the chair, as on the Permobil F5 Corpus VS . Anterior tilt (forward tilt) The seat tips forward by a small programmed amount — Permobil gives typical positions of 5°, 10° and 20° in the M3 Corpus manual — to extend reach; it is tilt in the other direction, not a sixth mechanism. Permobil’s manuals make the shared consequence plain: the wheelchair’s centre of gravity changes when you change the position of the seat or the backrest, and lifting, tilting or standing decreases the wheelchair’s stability. That is why the safety interlocks further down this page exist. The hardware chain: command → module → actuator Every seating movement, on every system on this page, follows the same three-link chain: You give a command. Through the joystick in seating mode, a separate switchbox or toggle, a button switch, or a special control. On LiNX, the manual separates this out as the seating function : the user input that defines how the motion is operated — proportional (it moves as far and as fast as you push), switched (it moves while you hold), latched (one push starts it, another stops it), or toggle. A seating module switches the power. The module is an electronic box that takes battery power and sends it, in the chosen direction and at the programmed speed, down one of its actuator channels (a channel is one actuator output). It also watches current, temperature and the safety inputs described below, and it is where the seating settings live. The actuator does the pushing. See the next section for what is inside one. The module names differ by maker. They are the same link in the chain: System Seating module(s) What the manufacturer document says R-net (Curtiss-Wright, formerly PG Drives Technology) ISM — Intelligent Seating/lighting Module The R-net programming manual covers ISM actuator channels 1 to 6, each set independently for up speed, down speed, acceleration and deceleration. Curtiss-Wright’s own ISM product page describes the current module as driving up to eight seat adjustment actuators, with up to twelve independent axes of motion (an axis is one named movement, which can combine several channels), at independently programmable speeds and with interlocking signals — and gives the maximum actuator current as 12A, increased to 15A at slower speeds. LiNX (Dynamic Controls, fitted by Invacare) DLX-PM75AL / DLX-PM120AL power modules with built-in actuator ports, plus DLX-ACT200 and DLX-ACT400 add-on actuator modules The LiNX service manual states that the “AL” power modules that feature actuators and lights have two actuator ports, and that if required the system is completed with the DLX-ACT200 (2 actuator channels) or DLX-ACT400 (4 actuator channels), with actuator power provided through the bus. Its factory port set-up assigns channels in order to tilt, recline, right leg, both legs / left leg or centre-mounted legrest, and lifter. Permobil ICS — Intelligent Control System Permobil’s seating system on the Corpus chairs: a master module, a switchbox the rider presses, and standard and position-sensing (“smart”) actuators. It manages the powered seat functions and supplies drive-inhibit information to the driving system. No copy of Permobil’s ICS technical manual is in this site’s library yet — it is listed as a collection target in the report that produced this page, so the ICS is described here only at the level the Permobil owner’s manuals in the library support. Invacare (older, pre-LiNX) ACS 2 actuator modules ACT2 and ACT4 Invacare’s ACS 2 sales document lists ACT2 for 2 actuators and ACT4 for 4 actuators, combinations controlling up to 12 actuators, with actuator speed proportional to the joystick and simultaneous movement of several actuators. Quantum Rehab / Pride Seating run through the chair’s controller, a toggle, or a single switch; TRU-Balance 3 power positioning on the Q6 Edge range The Q6 Edge 2.0 owner’s manual shows the power elevating seat operated through the controller, a toggle, or an optional single switch, with the seat plate interface bracket bolted onto the actuator — and refers readers to a separate TRU-Balance 3 manual for the full positioning system, a document not yet in this site’s library.
