title: The Settings, in Plain Language — PMD — BareBoard
headings: The one setting that can break hardware
text: The Settings, in Plain Language Your chair’s behavior — how fast it goes, how hard it launches, whether it filters out your tremor — is a list of numbers stored inside it. A dealer tool reads and writes that list. You were never shown it. Here are the core drive and seating settings, setting by setting. Today, changing these takes the dealer’s programmer. Knowing what each one means is the first half of taking it back: you cannot ask for a setting you cannot name, and you cannot tell when a swap has silently taken one away. Provenance: the parameter list and ranges are from Curtiss-Wright’s own R-net programming documentation ( On-Board Programming manual SK78571/4 and the R-NET Technical Manual), rewritten in plain language. Setting Range What it actually does What goes wrong Top speed (forward speed, max/min) 0–100% How fast the chair goes at the top speed setting, and at the lowest. The settings in between are spread evenly between the two. After a factory reset, top speed can come back clamped too slow for a crosswalk — or too fast for a hallway. Acceleration (forward accel, max/min) 0–100% How hard the chair launches when you push the stick. Higher = harder launch. Too high: the launch snaps your head back. Too low: the chair feels sluggish and cannot climb a door threshold from a stop. Deceleration (forward decel, max/min) 0–100% How hard the chair brakes when you let the stick go. Higher = shorter stop. Too high: letting go pitches you forward. Too low: the chair coasts into walls — or traffic. Turn speed / turn accel / turn decel 0–100% How fast the chair turns and how sharply it ramps into and out of a turn. Too high on a mid-wheel-drive chair: violent spinning and caster strikes. Tremor dampening (joystick filtering) 0–100% A filter that smooths out high-frequency hand tremor and spasm so the chair follows your intended push, not your shaking. Critical on a module swap: if a swapped module comes back at 0%, a rider with tremor or spasticity gets a chair that bucks with every shake — uncontrollable. This is the setting a wiped configuration takes with it. And the manual’s own warning cuts the other way: heavy dampening also increases stopping distance — it is a balance, not a maximum. Torque (low-speed power) 0–100% Extra power at low speed, for climbing ramps, door thresholds, and thick carpet. Too low: the chair stalls on a one-inch threshold. It is a working setting, not a comfort setting — a reset that loses it strands you at a curb cut. Sleep timer 0–30 min How long the chair sits idle before it powers itself down. At 0 (off), the battery drains overnight. Too short, and a switch or sip-and-puff user gets locked out mid-rest. Seating actuator accel / decel 1–100% How fast power tilt, recline, elevate, and legrests start and stop moving. Must stay at 100% on systems with automatic current-sensing endstops — see the warning below. The one setting that can break hardware Some power seating systems find the end of an actuator’s travel by sensing motor current (an automatic endstop ) instead of a physical switch. On those systems, the seating actuator acceleration and deceleration must be 100% . Set lower, the endstop detection does not work and the motor drives past its mechanical limit — destroying the actuator or bending the seat frame. (Curtiss-Wright R-NET Technical Manual, “Endstop Autodetect”: “This parameter must be set to 100% on systems that use automatic endstops, i.e. those that do not use micro-switches at the end of actuator travel. If the value is not set to 100%, then the automatic endstop function will not operate and damage to the actuator motor or the wheelchair frame may occur.”) This is the honest core of the dealer’s safety argument — real for a handful of settings. It is not an argument for locking all of them, including reading your own. ← Back to PMD · Fault codes →

title: Your Chair Stopped: Start Here — PMD — BareBoard
headings: Step 1 — Read what the chair is telling you
Step 2 — The four checks that fix most strandings
Step 3 — If it moves again, prove it before you trust it
Step 4 — If it still won’t move: what to say to the dealer
text: Your Chair Stopped: Start Here Your power wheelchair just stopped, and you have never fixed anything in your life. Good — this page was written for you. No tools. No experience. These checks use no tools and do not open the chair, but follow Step 0 and stop if anything feels forced, hot, damaged, or different from the words here. Most strandings end at Step 2. Work down the steps in order. Every word is explained where it is used. Where a step names a part, the picture and the full procedure are one click away. Step 0 — Be safe If you are somewhere unsafe — a road, a slope, weather — get yourself safe first; the chair can wait. If the chair is on a slope, do not do any step that asks you to release a brake or flip a lever until someone is with you. Step 1 — Read what the chair is telling you Your chair knows what is wrong, and it is already saying so. Find which of these three yours does: A row of battery lights is flashing. Count how many lights flash together. That count is the message. A color screen shows words and a number. The number is a 4-digit trip code — the chair’s name for the exact fault. Photograph the screen with your phone before you switch anything off. The light inside the round power button flashes red. Count the flashes between pauses. Take a 10-second video on your phone — you can count from the video as many times as you need. Write down the count or the code, and the date. Then look it up in Fault Codes, Translated — the codes covered here, in plain language, with what to check first. If your code’s first check is one of the Step 2 items below, do that now. Step 2 — The four checks that fix most strandings No tools. Do them in this order, and try the chair after each one. The freewheel levers. On each drive motor (the unit each big wheel attaches to) is a small lever. One position is DRIVE; the other is PUSH, which releases the motor so someone can push the chair by hand. If a lever is in PUSH — or stuck halfway — the chair reads it as a brake fault and refuses to drive. Push both levers firmly all the way to DRIVE until they click. ( Procedure 1 , with the safety steps.) The charger. Is the charger plugged into the chair? The chair will not drive while it is — that is a safety feature, not a fault. Unplug it. If it is already unplugged but the chair still acts plugged-in, the socket may be dirty: that check is Procedure 2 — read its safety step first. The thick cable. A round cable runs from the back of the joystick down to the base. Its plugs work loose. Grip each plug by its hard outer body — never pull the wire — push it firmly back in until it seats. (Full version, with power off first: Procedure 4 .) The battery plugs and the breaker. If your chair has a main plug or a circuit breaker (a small switch that cuts power, like the breakers in a house), check the plug is fully in and the breaker has not tripped. If it tripped, push it back once. If it trips again right away, stop — that is a real fault, and Step 4 is yours. Power rule for the thick-cable and battery checks: switch the chair OFF first. Pushing an insulated plug body back in is the check here. If a plug is partly out, exposes pins, or has to be pulled out, disconnect the main battery harness or trip the main breaker before touching it. Step 3 — If it moves again, prove it before you trust it Work on level ground, with the chair unoccupied for the push test. Drive slowly in an open space. Stop. Switch off and try to push the chair by hand — it must not roll. If you cannot safely move around the chair and stop it yourself, have another person beside it for this test. You just cleared a fault; a short, slow test is how you know the fix is real and the brakes hold. Then write down what the code was and which check fixed it. That note is gold the next time — and there is usually a next time. Step 4 — If it still won’t move: what to say to the dealer You have already done the most valuable thing: you know the code. When you call, you are not “a broken chair” — you are a specific fault with a date. Say these, in this order: “The chair shows code [your code] . Read me the trip text that goes with it.” “Before you replace any module, back up my configuration — and give me a copy.” (A module is one of the chair’s electronic boxes. Your settings live inside them; a swap without a backup erases how your chair was set up for your body.) “What is the part number of the part you say failed?” (Write it down. Parts have names and prices outside the dealer too — see Parts, Not Assemblies .) “Is this covered under the electronics warranty?” (The clocks are on the parts page. Ask before you agree to pay.) Nothing here is an argument. It is an owner reading their own chair’s message out loud — which is the whole of taking control back, at its most basic. Words we use, defined Module — one of the chair’s electronic boxes (joystick module, power module, seating module). Each does one job. Configuration — the list of settings stored inside the modules: how fast, how hard it launches, how it filters your hand’s tremor. Your chair’s setup, in numbers. Trip code — the number or light pattern the chair shows when something is wrong. Its name for the fault. Freewheel lever — the small lever on each motor: DRIVE to drive, PUSH to be pushed by hand. Inhibit — the chair’s “do not drive” signal, sent while the charger is plugged in. Bus — the wiring network the modules use to talk to each other. Dongle — a small plug-in device. The dealer’s programming dongle is the physical key their software demands. Firmware — the software built into a module, the instructions it runs. Actuator — a small electric pusher that moves part of the seat (tilt, recline, legrest). Endstop — the point where an actuator’s travel ends; some systems sense it by motor current instead of a switch. Where to go next Fault Codes, Translated — the codes covered here, what they mean, what to check first. The Cheap Fixes — the five repairs, step by step, with the safety steps in. The Settings, in Plain Language — what the dealer’s numbers mean for your body. Parts, Not Assemblies — the real parts, named and priced, and the warranty clocks. Reading the Chair — for when you want to go further: how to listen to the chair’s own wiring with a computer, and how every finding here was made. PMD, the whole picture — why the lock exists, the numbers behind it, and the law catching up.

title: What Your Chair Phones Home — PMD — BareBoard
headings: The hardware: what the FCC record documents
The other kind of pipe: a session you start (Quantum / Pride)
What you can switch off — and what you cannot
When the radio is the risk: the WHILL Bluetooth recall
text: What Your Chair Phones Home Some power wheelchairs carry a small radio box that reports on the chair — where it is, how its batteries are doing, how it has been driven and seated, and what has gone wrong with it. This page says what that box is, what the manufacturer’s own documents say it sends, where the data goes, and which parts of it you can switch off. Where the public record runs out, this page says so instead of guessing. Words used on this page, defined once: Telematics — a unit fitted to a vehicle or machine that collects information about it and sends that information away over a radio link. On a power chair, the telematics unit is the reporting box itself. Cellular modem — the radio that talks to mobile phone networks (the same networks phones use), so the chair can reach the internet without your phone or your home Wi-Fi. SIM (Subscriber Identity Module) — the small card, or built-in chip, that gives a cellular device its identity on a phone network. It is what lets the modem connect. GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) — positioning by satellite signals. GPS (Global Positioning System) is the American GNSS system and the word most documents use. A GNSS receiver works out where the chair is by listening to satellites; it does not transmit to them. Bluetooth — a short-range radio (metres, not kilometres) for talking to nearby devices such as a phone. BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) is its low-power version. The cloud — in these documents, the manufacturer’s computers on the internet. “Sent to the cloud” means sent to the maker, not stored on the chair. Fleet Management (Permobil’s name; shortened to Fleet in its documents) — the maker’s online system where dealers and service providers can see data from connected chairs. The board-level teardown of the reporting box — what the silicon actually is — lives on Parts, Not Assemblies . This page is about the data: what flows, and who controls the tap. The hardware: what the FCC record documents A maker cannot legally sell a radio device in the United States without filing test reports and photographs with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). Those filings are public. They prove what radios a unit contains. They do not, by themselves, prove what data the unit sends — for that, this page uses the makers’ own manuals and privacy documents, in the sections below. Permobil ConnectMe (FCC ID: 2AKPO331495) The ConnectMe user’s manual (Permobil, Edition 2, 2017-03) states the unit’s purpose in its own words: “ConnectMe is a cellular solution that provides communication between the Permobil wheelchair and Permobil cloud service. It is also used in near field communication for transfer of data between the wheelchair and a Bluetooth® device e.g. SmartPhone.” — Permobil, ConnectMe user’s manual The same manual’s technical specifications list: Cellular: GSM (quad-band 850/900/1800/1900 MHz) and UMTS (bands B1, B2, B5, B8), with an internal antenna. The manual’s label page says the unit contains a pre-qualified embedded GSM/UMTS module, FCC ID: N7NWP8, and the label carries an ICCID — the serial number of a SIM card — which is how the manual documents that the unit holds its own SIM and its own phone-network connection, independent of your phone. Bluetooth: Bluetooth® 4.1, internal antenna. Positioning: “GNSS: A-GPS L1, GLONASS, Galileo” — that is, the unit can work out its position from three satellite systems (the American GPS, the Russian GLONASS, and the European Galileo). A-GPS means the satellite fix is assisted by data from the cellular network, which makes the fix faster. Connections to the chair: a 6-pin connector and a 4-pin R-net connector — R-net is the chair’s control system, so the unit is wired into the same network that carries the chair’s fault codes and settings (see Fault Codes, Translated and Reading the Chair ). Supported chairs listed in the manual: M3, M5, F3, F5, M300, M400. The hardware itself is photographed in the FCC exhibits: internal photos and the test report are in the library, and Parts, Not Assemblies walks through the board. The newer Permobil module (FCC ID: 2AKPO338877) A second, newer Permobil filing covers module model 338877, hosted in what its SAR test report (a SAR report measures radio energy absorbed by the body) calls the “Permobil Power Platform.” The report describes the equipment under test, in its own words, as a “Module fixed on a wheelchair, supports Cellular, WLAN 2.4 GHz and BT 2.4 GHz technologies” — cellular, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth in one module. Its external photos exhibit labels the cellular module inside as an EG25-G module. The tested cellular technologies span GSM, WCDMA, and LTE across many bands. So the newer generation adds Wi-Fi and LTE to the radio set; the original ConnectMe was GSM/UMTS and Bluetooth. WHILL’s user-interface device (FCC ID: 2AN6F-4218000) WHILL’s FCC filing for its wheelchair user-interface device (the control unit the rider uses) documents Bluetooth, Bluetooth LE, Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz, and LTE cellular test data in its exhibits, including its user manual exhibit and internal photos . That documents radio capability in the hardware. This page found no WHILL-published document describing a telematics data flow — what, if anything, those radios report, and to whom — so it makes no claim about one. WHILL appears on this page again below, where the public record does speak: a Bluetooth safety vulnerability. What Permobil says is reported Everything in this section comes from Permobil’s own published documents: its MyPermobil privacy notice , its Fleet Management privacy notice , its MyPermobil FAQ (DOC0096-01) , and its Factory Connected Wheelchair FAQ for the newer factory-connected chairs. No other maker’s behaviour is described by these documents, and this page does not stretch them to cover anyone else. The MyPermobil privacy notice states the core list verbatim: “The wheelchair collects details about how you use our products. This includes seating and positioning regimen and history, mileage, battery status, maintenance information, diagnostic data and service data.” — Permobil, MyPermobil privacy notice (“Usage and Device Information”) What is reported What it means in plain words Stated in Seating and positioning regimen and history How the powered seat functions (tilt, recline, lift and the rest) have been used, and when MyPermobil and Fleet privacy notices Mileage Distance the chair has travelled MyPermobil and Fleet privacy notices Battery status Charge level and battery condition; the Factory FAQ adds battery health and charging status Privacy notices; Factory Connected FAQ Maintenance information Information about upkeep of the chair MyPermobil and Fleet privacy notices Diagnostic data and service data Fault and health information from the chair’s electronics, and records of service activity; the Factory FAQ names “system error codes” explicitly — the same fault codes translated on this page and its second part Privacy notices; Factory Connected FAQ Actuator metrics and motor performance How the seat actuators and drive motors are performing (an actuator is the powered mover that tilts, reclines or lifts the seat) Factory Connected FAQ, Level 2 telemetry list Real-time geographic location Where the chair is, from its GPS receiver — only under the consent rule in the next row’s document, see below MyPermobil and Fleet privacy notices (“Location Information”) Your name, email address and country; phone number if you choose to add it; and the chair’s serial number Collected only when you register a MyPermobil account and link it to the chair; the Fleet notice says this information “is visible in Fleet as long as the MyPermobil account is active” Fleet privacy notice; Factory Connected FAQ, Level 3 App technical and usage data From the phone app itself: IP address (the number that identifies a device on a network), device type and version, operating system; pages viewed, time spent in the app, and navigation paths MyPermobil privacy notice (“Data Collected from app users”) On location, the notice is specific about both the trigger and the recipients: “Permobil offers location-based services that require your explicit consent prior to activation. The information collected includes the real-time geographic location data of your wheelchair when the GPS device is activated. When you activate location data you share GPS information with Permobil and with your Service Provider.” — Permobil, MyPermobil privacy notice (“Location Information”) The MyPermobil FAQ adds two owner-facing details. First, the history the app builds when GPS is on: “places that have been visited for >30 minutes will appear as part of historical travel details.” Second, the one transmission rhythm any Permobil document states: battery range estimates in the app are “updated approximately every 5-10 minutes within the app.” No Permobil document found for this page states how often the chair itself transmits its telemetry — see “What is not publicly documented” below. Two generations, two defaults The ConnectMe generation (the aftermarket/earlier fitted unit): the MyPermobil FAQ says activation and consent come first, verbatim: “Permobil respects our users’ privacy therefore remote connectivity is turned off by default during the production process. Permobil does not collect any data without consent. During MyPermobil activation process user must provide consent and agree to the data privacy regulations.” — Permobil, MyPermobil FAQ (DOC0096-01) The same FAQ confirms whose network carries the ongoing traffic: data “transmission to the cloud relies on the internal SIM card in the ConnectMe module in the power wheelchair base” — the chair’s own cellular connection, not your phone’s. The factory-connected generation: the Factory Connected Wheelchair FAQ describes newer M and F-series chairs (it gives a shipping start of 1 December 2026 for the UK & Ireland) as sending three levels of data. Level 1, Core Con

title: Flying With Your Chair — PMD — BareBoard
headings: The battery split that decides everything
Before the flight: tell the airline, and paper the chair
At the gate: gate-check, the door, and the aisle chair
text: Flying With Your Chair A power wheelchair or scooter can fly. The chair itself is not luggage — the law treats it as an assistive device (a piece of equipment that helps you live with a disability). What decides how hard the trip is, almost every time, is one thing: the battery. This page is the battery split, the steps before and at the gate, and the claim path when an airline breaks the chair — in plain language, from the regulators’ own pages. Provenance: compiled from the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) aviation consumer protection pages, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) PackSafe pages, which state they are “Based on US DOT regulations (49 CFR, Sec. 175.10),” DOT’s Air Travel Consumer Report, and DOT’s Federal Register notices on the 2024 wheelchair rule. Airline policies can be stricter than the federal floor — the FAA says so itself — so confirm with your airline for your flight. This is documentation, not legal advice. The law in one paragraph The Air Carrier Access Act (ACAA) is the federal law that bans airlines from discriminating against passengers because of a disability. It is not the Americans with Disabilities Act — that law does not govern airlines. DOT enforces the ACAA through its rule at 14 CFR Part 382. DOT summarises the ACAA on its Wheelchair and Guided Assistance page this way: “The Air Carrier Access Act (ACAA) prohibits U.S. and foreign carriers from discriminating against an otherwise qualified individual because the individual has a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities.” An assistive device does not count toward your baggage limit, and if it cannot be stowed in the cabin, DOT says airlines must stow it in the cargo compartment at no extra cost — see DOT’s Assistive Device — Stowage, Damage, and Delay page. The battery split that decides everything Find your battery type first. It is printed on the battery label and in your owner manual. Watt-hours (Wh) measure how much energy a battery holds. The FAA explains how to work the number out when it is not printed: “To determine Wh, multiply the volts (V) by the amp hours (Ah). Example: A 12-volt battery rated to 8 Ah is rated at 96 Wh (12 x 8 = 96).” — FAA, Airline Passengers and Batteries (PackSafe, last updated October 2, 2026). For the battery types themselves — gel, AGM, lithium — and how each ages, see Batteries & Chargers . Sealed gel and AGM: “non-spillable” Non-spillable means the liquid inside the battery is absorbed or gelled, so it will not spill out if the case is cracked. Sealed gel and absorbed glass mat (AGM) wheelchair batteries are the common non-spillable types. For wheelchairs and mobility devices, the FAA PackSafe chart lists this row as checked only, with this instruction, verbatim: “For complete passenger instructions contact your airline as advanced arrangements and extra check-in time may be necessary” — FAA PackSafe, row “Wheelchairs and Mobility Devices with Spillable, Non-Spillable, or Dry Batteries.” The wheelchair-specific row sets no watt-hour limit . The battery flies with the chair in the cargo compartment, and DOT’s assistive-device page states the handling rule for airlines: “You must allow non-spillable batteries labeled as ‘non-spillable’ by a manufacturer to remain installed on a device when stowed onboard the aircraft; and you must not require separate packaging.” In plain words: a labelled non-spillable battery does not have to come off the chair. The separate FAA row for small non-spillable wet batteries used in portable electronic devices (12 volts and 100 watt hours) is a different row for a different thing — it is not the wheelchair row. The underlying federal rule is 49 CFR §175.10 , at paragraph (a)(15) for a wheelchair or mobility aid with a non-spillable battery carried as checked baggage: the battery must meet the non-spillable test in the regulations, show no obvious defects on inspection, be disconnected with terminals protected against short circuit unless the chair’s design prevents accidental starting, and be securely attached, or removed into strong, rigid packaging marked “NONSPILLABLE BATTERY.” Lithium-ion: different rules Lithium-ion means the rechargeable lithium chemistry used in most folding travel chairs and many scooters. It is judged by watt-hours, by whether it stays on the chair, and by whether it is a spare. Lithium metal (non-rechargeable lithium) batteries are, in the FAA’s words for these devices, forbidden with these devices — in every row below. How the lithium battery travels Where it goes Watt-hour rule (FAA PackSafe) What you must do Installed, and protected by the design of the chair Checked with the chair; not carried on No watt-hour figure is listed for this row in the FAA chart Tell the airline where the battery is on the device, in the FAA’s words: “The passenger must advise the airline of the battery location on the device.” Removed, or not adequately protected on the chair Carry-on baggage only; never checked “Lithium-ion battery size is limited to 300 watt hours (Wh).” Carry it in the cabin, protect its terminals, and advise the airline of the battery location Spare battery (an extra, or a removed battery carried as a spare) Carry-on only; never checked “A maximum of one spare battery not exceeding 300 watt hours (Wh) or two spare batteries not exceeding 160 Wh each carry-on only.” Carry it in the cabin and protect its terminals against short circuit That is the whole lithium table, exactly as the FAA publishes it. Note what it does not say: it does not cap a battery that stays installed and protected by the chair’s design at 300 Wh. The 300 Wh cap is for a battery that comes off, and for a single spare. Two spares are capped at 160 Wh each. International flights also follow the IATA Battery-Powered Wheelchair and Mobility Aid Guidance Document (revised for the 2026 regulations), which classifies chairs by the same three battery families — non-spillable, spillable, and lithium — and requires every chair to be prepared to prevent unintentional activation, with terminals protected from short circuits. Damaged batteries do not fly. FAA, verbatim: “Damaged or recalled batteries and battery-powered devices, which are likely to create sparks or generate a dangerous evolution of heat, must not be carried aboard an aircraft (e.g. carry-on or checked baggage) unless the damaged or recalled battery has been removed or otherwise made safe.” If a battery is swollen, cracked, hot, or recalled, do not take it to the airport as a surprise — contact the airline first, as the FAA advises. Before the flight: tell the airline, and paper the chair Tell the airline in advance. DOT’s tips say: “Provide notice that you will be traveling with a personal wheelchair in advance whenever possible so that the airline can best accommodate you,” and “Share information about your wheelchair such as the device’s size, weight, and battery type to help the airline safely and properly handle your assistive device.” Confirm the chair will fit the cargo hold, especially on a small commuter or regional aircraft. DOT also notes airlines may require 48 hours’ advance notice to carry an electric wheelchair on an aircraft with fewer than 60 seats. Arrive early. DOT, verbatim: “If you travel with a battery-powered wheelchair, you must arrive at the airport 1 hour prior to the normal check-in time.” Make a chair information card and tape it to the chair. This is the one-page card owners attach where handlers will see it. Write: chair make and model; total weight and dimensions (length, width, height, and folded height if it folds); battery type in plain words (non-spillable gel/AGM, or lithium-ion) plus its watt-hours if lithium; where the battery is; how to put the chair in freewheel (the manual-push mode: a lever or switch that disengages the motors so the chair can be pushed by hand without driving it — and how to put it back); how to disconnect power or remove the joystick cable if handlers must, including any small clip or circlip (a C-shaped spring clip that holds a pin or connector) that must not be lost; how to prevent accidental starting (key out, joystick off, or battery disconnected); safe lifting points; and what not to lift by — the joystick, armrests, and push handles on most chairs. DOT’s own instruction points the same way: “Attach clear assembly and disassembly instructions to your wheelchair before you head to the airport.” Read your own manual for the exact steps. The freewheel lever, battery disconnect, and folding steps are in the owner manual for your model — for example the Invacare TDX SP2 owner manual , the Permobil M3 Corpus owner manual , and the Pride Jazzy 600 ES owner manual , all in this site’s library. Copy the exact wording for your chair onto the card; do not guess a lever position. Photograph the chair’s condition. Before you leave home and again at the gate, take dated photos and a short video: all four sides, the joystick and screen lit and working, the wheels, armrests, footrests, and any existing scratches. Drive it in the video if you can. If the chair comes back damaged, those photos are the “before” that proves the airline received it working — see the damage section below. Keep what you can in the cabin. Removable cushions, headrests, and small detachable parts are less likely to be lost if they travel with you, and a removed lithium battery must travel with you (above). Protect battery terminals against short circuit — the battery’s own case or pouch, or covering the terminals — as the FAA chart requires for spares. Battery health and replacement are covered in Parts, Not Assemblies and fault behaviour in Fault Codes, Translated . At the gate: gate-check, the door, and the aisle chair Gate-check means you hand the chair over at the departure gate, not at the ticket counter, and it is tagged there and loaded from the jet bridge. title: PMD — Power Mobility Devices — BareBoard
headings: Why the lock can be beaten — our findings
text: PMD — Power Mobility Devices PMD is the official Medicare name for a power wheelchair or a power scooter. This section teaches you how to take back your own chair. Chair stopped right now? Start here — no tools, no experience: Your Chair Stopped . Your chair’s settings, its fault logs, and a backup of the fit that took your clinician years to build all sit behind programming tools ordinarily available only through the dealer channel, not by direct sale to owners. The industry’s power is that it holds the knowledge. We publish it, in plain language, free. Your legs shouldn’t need a dealer’s permission. The dealer lock Almost everything that makes your chair yours lives behind that lock: How fast the chair goes, and how hard it launches and stops. Whether your hand tremor is filtered out — or fed straight into the motors. Whether the seat still works after a part is swapped. The fault codes your chair already displays on its own screen — shown to you, explained to no one. And when a dealer swaps a module, your configuration goes with the old one. The clinical fit built over years reverts to factory defaults, and you were never given a backup. Settings like tremor dampening can vanish silently — and a chair set up for somebody else’s hands can be uncontrollable in yours. The numbers 63.8% of full-time wheelchair users need at least one repair within six months. (Toro 2016, spinal-cord-injury users, manual and power chairs.) The median repair takes 14 days — and 14% of users who needed repairs got none of them completed at all . (Worobey 2025.) 62% of users in U.S. PIRG’s “Stranded” survey estimated their average repair wait at four weeks or more ; 40% said seven weeks or more. A $6 inner tube became a $300 charge to Medicaid to replace both wheels — with a six-to-eight-week wait. (PIRG Colorado storybank.) A chair’s electronics have a median survival of 32.2 months (Kim 2025 — Group 2 power chairs in the Wheelchair Repair Registry) — against Medicare’s replacement clock, which will not replace a chair inside its five-year reasonable useful lifetime except for loss, theft, or irreparable damage (42 CFR §414.210(f)). The electronics die, on median, with more than two years left on the clock. What we publish Fault codes, translated . The owner-actionable codes for the systems covered here, in plain language: what it means, what to check first, and in what order. The settings, in plain language . The core dealer-menu settings rewritten for the person who rides the chair — what each one changes, what symptom it fixes, the programmer’s ranges. The few genuinely dangerous ones are flagged, not hidden: for example, seating actuator acceleration/deceleration must stay at 100% on current-sensing endstops, or the actuator destroys itself. The dealer’s safety argument is real for a handful of settings. The lock covers all of them — including just reading and backing up your own. The cheap fixes . Step-by-step repairs for the failures that strand people: freewheel/brake reset, charger-inhibit pin cleaning, battery-pair load testing, bus-cable contact restoration, caster bearing replacement. Parts, not assemblies . The service parts covered here, identified and published — what each is, what it does, where to get it — so you buy the $6 tube, not the $300 assembly. Exploded views . Each chair taken apart to the component level with the manufacturer’s own parts guide — every exploded diagram, every callout, every part number, laid out in build order with a plain-language line for every part. The keys: programmers, dongles and access tiers . Every system’s programming tools named — the hand-helds, the PC software, the dongles, keys and cards — and which tier opens which settings, so you know exactly what is being kept from you and what to demand before a module swap. Fault codes for the other systems . Dynamic Shark and DX flash codes and Invacare MK6i E-codes, translated the same way: what it means, what to check first, in what order. Getting a repair paid for . Medicare’s repair rules in plain language: repairs to a chair you own are covered, no new prescription is required for a repair, prior authorization belongs to new chairs — and the loaner rule most owners are never told. Q-Logic, translated . The fault lesson the Quantum chairs were missing: Q-Logic 3’s screen words and Q-Logic 2’s numbers in plain language, what you check first, and exactly which readings stay behind the dealer’s programmer. Batteries & chargers . The pair is a system: gel vs AGM, the real capacities by group size from the battery maker’s own sheets, the 15-to-20-cycle break-in, the charging habit that decides whether a pair lives two years or five, and the lithium question answered honestly. The older PG systems . Pilot+, Egis and S-Drive — the bar-count faults of the older chairs and scooters still running them, translated the same way, with the trip code behind the bars explained. Power seating, part by part . Tilt, recline, elevate and legrests: how actuators fail, how to test one with a meter, what a like-for-like swap really involves — and the endstop setting that must never be touched. Motors & brakes on the meter . Winding continuity, brake-coil resistance, brush inspection, gearbox noises decoded — the electrical tests an owner can run before a drive unit is condemned. Driving without a standard joystick . Sip-and-puff, head arrays, chin controls and switch scanners: how they talk to the same bus, and what an owner can check when they stop working. The attendant control . The second control a carer drives from behind: how dual controls decide who is in charge, the faults the attendant control itself causes, and safe setup for families. Scooters are PMDs too . Tillers, transaxles and the controllers scooters actually run — and how this site’s fault tables apply to the machines that use them most. What you can change from the joystick itself . The on-board menus every owner already owns, system by system — what the maker left open to you, and what stays locked even there. What your chair phones home . Connected chairs transmit — location, battery, usage. What the makers’ own documents say is reported, and what an owner can and cannot switch off. Beyond Medicare . Medicaid, the VA and private plans: where the repair rules differ, how to find your state’s actual rule, and what to cite. Flying with your chair . Battery rules in plain language — why sealed gel and AGM fly installed and lithium plays by different numbers — the gate-check procedure, and what to do when the airline breaks it. Quantum Q6 Edge 3, opened . The first full exploded view: every assembly of the highest-volume complex-rehab chair, callout by callout, with Quantum’s part numbers and a plain-language line for every part. Why the lock can be beaten — our findings There is no cryptography to break. The chair’s bus — the cable network its parts use to talk to each other — is standard CAN — the project’s captured dealer-tool sessions ran at 125 kbps — with no encryption. The only authentication anywhere on the bus is R-net’s documented XOR serial handshake — a simple fixed check between modules, not cryptographic authentication. The lock was never a cipher. It is a tool they won’t sell you. The gate is the software, not a cipher. The proven gate is the dealer software and its access tiers. The project record contains incompatible accounts of what is inside the manufacturer’s dongle, so this page does not state the dongle’s internal hardware as settled fact. We decoded the configuration protocol. A chair’s configuration moves as data objects, each with a checksum (a number that proves the data arrived unchanged). We read 16 configuration objects straight off the bus in captured dealer-tool sessions. A generic owner adapter that can make the same backup without the dealer tool is not yet proven. How these findings were made — and how to listen to your own chair the same way — is published as a bench procedure: Reading the Chair . The owner tool The owner tool is a goal, not a finished product: a proposed physical adapter that would plug into your chair’s own control bus and connect it to this website. Its intended first job would be to back up your chair’s configuration and show you the backup. Then it would read your fault codes and walk you through the repair for your model, step by step. Reading captured dealer-tool sessions is proven today. Backup through this proposed adapter is not yet proven, and the project’s first bench session with it is pending hardware. Nothing is written to your chair. The proposed adapter is deliberately dumb hardware. Everything intelligent would live here on the website, so the adapter would not need updating when a new model is supported. Version 1 of the software exists now: Chair Control runs in your phone’s browser — a practice chair with every feature working, fault codes translated from the same tables as this section, and your settings shown to you. On a real chair it listens and reads only, for exactly the reason this page gives: the write path is not proven yet, and it will not be guessed at. Honest limits Proven today: reading captured dealer-tool sessions and understanding them. Backup through the proposed owner adapter, and the write/restore path, are not proven . The shortcut the community assumes — that configuration-file byte offsets equal live bus addresses — is one our own captures contradict, so we do not ship a restore claim. It settles only with a live power module on the bench. The cheap fixes on this site run on a few dollars in parts — the $10 class of failures: lockouts, dirty contacts, worn bearings. Battery pairs, motors, and power modules are real money. Education does not fix Medicare’s replacement clock or suppliers’ repair economics. Those are policy fights. Ours works without permission: the knowledge stops being theirs alone. The law Colorado got it right. Its powered-wheelchair right-to-repair law ( HB22-1031 ) exp

title: Privacy Policy — BareBoard
text: Privacy Policy We collect almost nothing. Here is exactly what that means. Last updated: November 24, 2026. What we collect BareBoard is designed to minimize data collection. We do not require accounts, do not sell or share personal data — because we do not have it to sell. No analytics runs on this site as published: no page-view counting, no cookies, no tracking of individual visitors. Information you provide voluntarily Email correspondence: If you email contact@bareboard.org (for takedown requests, corrections, tips, or questions), we receive your email address and message content. We use this solely to respond. We do not add you to any mailing list. Donations: Donations are processed by third-party providers (Ko-fi, PayPal). We do not receive or store your payment details. Their privacy policies apply to those transactions. Information collected automatically Server logs: Our hosting provider may log standard web server data (IP address, requested URL, user agent, timestamp) for security and operational purposes. We do not use this data for tracking or profiling. No cookies: BareBoard does not set tracking cookies. No third-party advertising or social media scripts are loaded. Web analytics: None. No analytics script or beacon runs on this site as published, so no page views are counted and no visitor data is collected for measurement. No fingerprinting: We do not attempt to identify or track individual visitors across sessions. What we do not do We do not sell, rent, or share personal information with third parties. We do not use personal data for marketing. We do not run A/B tests or behavioral analytics on visitors. Data retention Email correspondence is retained only as long as needed to handle the inquiry. Server logs are subject to our hosting provider’s retention policy. Your rights If you have emailed us and wish to have your correspondence deleted, contact contact@bareboard.org and we will comply. Children BareBoard is a general-audience educational resource. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13. Changes We may update this policy to reflect changes in our practices. The “last updated” date above will be revised accordingly. Contact Privacy questions: contact@bareboard.org .

title: AI Crawler Defense — BareBoard
text: ← About BareBoard AI Crawler Defense How BareBoard keeps training scrapers off its work BareBoard publishes original hardware research — teardowns, measurements, photography — for humans learning hardware. AI training crawlers are not our audience, and we do not consent to feeding them. This page documents the layered defense we run: declared boundaries for the compliant, and active traps for the trespassers who ignore them. The problem Our content is expensive to produce — bench time, hardware, photography, careful documentation — and trivially cheap to scrape. Training crawlers ingest it into models that then compete with the free resource they learned from. We want search engines, because humans find us through search. We do not want training ingestion. Those are different crawlers with different purposes, and we treat them differently. Layer 1: robots.txt hardening The perimeter. Our robots.txt names 53 known AI training and scraping user-agents one by one — 54 groups in all — and denies each of them the whole site. The one wildcard group leaves the door open for everyone else, including Google and Bing, which is how humans discover us; the only path it closes to them is /tarpit/ . User-agent: GPTBot Disallow: / User-agent: ChatGPT-User Disallow: / User-agent: ClaudeBot Disallow: / User-agent: anthropic-ai Disallow: / User-agent: CCBot Disallow: / User-agent: Google-Extended Disallow: / User-agent: PerplexityBot Disallow: / # ... 53 named agents in total (54 groups with the wildcard) ... User-agent: * Disallow: /tarpit/ How the matching works (per RFC 9309): a crawler uses the most specific group that names it — the order of the groups in the file does not matter. A named training crawler matches its own group and is denied everything. Every other crawler falls to the wildcard group, which disallows only /tarpit/ : search crawlers are welcomed in everywhere else. Note what this does not do: robots.txt is a voluntary protocol. Respectful crawlers obey it; bad actors ignore it. This layer stops the compliant majority — which includes every major lab's documented training crawler — and draws a clear line for the rest: a crawler that ignores robots.txt is trespassing, and our footer says so in plain language. Layer 2: page-level opt-outs Every page carries <meta name="robots" content="noai, noimageai"> in its head. The noai and noimageai directives tell participating crawlers not to use the page's text or images for AI training. It is belt-and-suspenders alongside robots.txt : one operates at crawl time, the other at the page level. Every page also carries <meta name="tdm-reservation" content="1"> , the W3C TDM Reservation Protocol opt-out, backed by a site-wide /.well-known/tdmrep.json . This is the machine-readable form of the EU's text-and-data-mining reservation (CDSM Directive Article 4): a formal "no" to mining our content for model training, recognized in law even where crawler conventions are voluntary. Layer 3: strict Content Security Policy Every page ships a tight CSP in a meta tag. This page’s reads: default-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://translate.googleapis.com; img-src 'self' data:; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'none'; object-src 'none'; frame-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'none' No scripts at all on this page ( script-src 'none' ; pages that run the site’s own JavaScript use script-src 'self' ), no frames, no objects, no form submissions — and exactly one permitted network endpoint beyond the site itself: Google Translate, which powers the in-browser language translation. This keeps the page exactly what we published — nothing injected, nothing exfiltrated — which shrinks the surface that scraping and injection tooling can work with. Layer 4: the legal notice Every page's footer carries the declaration: all text, findings, and original photography are copyrighted; automated scraping for AI model training is prohibited; crawlers that ignore robots.txt are trespassing. The site operates as a non-commercial educational resource under 17 U.S.C. § 107 (fair use). This is the layer that turns a technical boundary into a stated one. Layer 5: clean publishing hygiene Before any photo goes public, tools/purge_metadata.sh strips EXIF data, GPS coordinates, macOS extended attributes, and resource forks from the image files. Scrapers and downloaders get pixels, not a map of where our bench is or what camera shot it. Privacy for us, nothing lost for the reader. Layer 6: honeypot links Every page footer carries an invisible link to /tarpit/ — 1×1 pixel, clipped offscreen, removed from keyboard tab order ( tabindex="-1" ) and hidden from assistive technology ( aria-hidden="true" ). No human will ever see it, focus it, or click it. It exists for exactly one audience: scrapers that extract and follow every href on the page. Compliant visitors never notice it; harvesters walk straight in. Layer 7: the tarpit /tarpit/ is a five-level maze of junk device indexes — plausible-looking but entirely fabricated model numbers, circular links between levels, and no real content. Every tarpit page carries <meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow"> so legitimate search engines never index the maze — the site’s normal pages carry only the noai / noimageai opt-out from Layer 2, never noindex — and robots.txt disallows it for all compliant crawlers. Only a bot that ignores robots.txt and follows invisible links ends up here — which is precisely the bot we want wasting its time instead of ours. A crawler that burns its crawl budget on five pages of nothing is a crawler not harvesting our teardowns. Layer 8: poisoned content The tarpit pages contain deliberately false technical claims — wrong pinouts, impossible voltages, fabricated chip part numbers — each labeled in the HTML source as poison for scrapers. This is the consequence layer: a training pipeline that ingests our tarpit learns confidently-stated nonsense about hardware that does not exist. We keep the poison strictly quarantined to pages no human ever visits (they are unlinked from all visible navigation and carry noindex ), so there is zero risk of a reader mistaking it for real findings. Our published research stays clean; the traps stay dirty. Layer 9 (planned): edge enforcement The next layer sits at the CDN, pending dashboard access: Cloudflare AI Labyrinth (tarpit content served at the edge to detected AI crawlers), Bot Fight Mode , and WAF rules keyed to the same training-crawler user-agents named in our robots.txt . The philosophy is the same as every layer below it — declare the boundary, then enforce it — moved one step closer to the attacker. Honest limitations No robots.txt setup stops a determined bad actor — it is a social contract, not a firewall. The traps do not stop one either; a sophisticated harvester can detect and avoid tarpits. What this stack does is raise the cost at every step: compliant crawlers are stopped cold at layer 1, lazy scrapers burn budget in the tarpit at layer 7, and bulk ingestion pipelines risk poisoned training data at layer 8. Defense in depth, not a guarantee. We document it here so other small publishers can copy the whole thing in an afternoon. Why the traps We used to run boundary-setting only: declare non-consent, hope for compliance. That stops the labs that publish crawler docs and honor opt-outs. It does nothing against the harvesters that ignore robots.txt , spoof user-agents, and strip our work at scale. Those operators have already opted out of the social contract — so we stopped extending it to them. The traps are strictly defensive and strictly quarantined. Honeypot links are invisible to humans. The tarpit is unlinked from visible navigation, noindex ’d, and labeled in its own source as junk. The poison never touches a page a reader might see. Nothing here attacks anyone’s infrastructure, exfiltrates anything, or harms a legitimate visitor. It wastes a trespasser’s time and corrupts a trespasser’s dataset — which is exactly what trespassers signed up for when they ignored the signs at the gate. “As a rule, software systems do not work well until they have been used, and have failed repeatedly, in real applications.” — Dave Parnas

TP-Link routers — the reset button is a recovery button
3.5mm headphone jack — a serial port in disguise
ESP8266/ESP32 devices — one button, one cable
Every way in: the firmware access playbook
1. Serial console — Sonoff Basic smart switch
2. Serial console on devices without a header — Amazon Echo Dot (3rd gen)
3. SWD debug port — Raspberry Pi Pico as the probe
4. JTAG on ESP32 — smart bulbs and plugs
6. Replace the firmware — Sonoff Basic with Tasmota
7. eMMC direct read — phones and tablets

13. Voltage glitching — when the chip refuses
text:
Community reverse engineering Protocol Reverse Engineering Closed protocols the community has pried open. What was reverse engineered, what’s still unknown, and the open-source projects that document it. Only public, community-driven work — no leaked confidential material. Raspberry Pi Pico — about $4. Flash it with Picoprobe firmware and it becomes a full debug probe for reading other devices’ firmware. Photo: Wikimedia Commons. Take control for under $10 You don’t need a $300 debugger. The cheapest way into a device’s firmware is a Raspberry Pi Pico (about $4), a USB-to-serial breakout board (about $2–3 — look for CH340 or CP2102), and a micro USB cable you already own. That’s the whole shopping list. Step 1: listen before you touch Many devices — routers, smart plugs, cameras — have a serial console (UART) that narrates everything the device does as it boots. Think of it as the device’s diary. It’s often exposed on small test pads you can reach without fully opening the case. Plug in your USB-to-serial adapter, then: $ ls /dev/ttyUSB* /dev/ttyUSB0 $ screen /dev/ttyUSB0 115200 /dev/ttyUSB0 is your adapter showing up. 115200 is the speed (baud rate) most devices use — if you see gibberish, try 9600 or 57600. screen just opens a window onto the serial line. Power the device on and watch: U-Boot 2021.04 (Jan 12 2022 - 09:14:22) DRAM: 128 MiB Loading kernel from NAND... Starting kernel ... [ 0.000000] Linux version 5.4.0 (builder@factory) [ 1.240000] console [ttyS0] enabled root@smartplug:/# That root@smartplug:/# prompt is a root shell on the device itself. From here the firmware can be copied off directly — no disassembly required. Step 2: turn a $4 Pico into a debug probe For chips with SWD (the debug port on ARM microcontrollers — two tiny pads usually labeled SWDIO and SWCLK), flash Picoprobe firmware onto a Raspberry Pi Pico. It becomes a proper debug probe: $ picotool load picoprobe.uf2 Loading picoprobe.uf2 into RP2040 device... The device was rebooted into application mode. $ openocd -f interface/picoprobe.cfg -f target/rp2040.cfg Open On-Chip Debugger 0.12.0 Info : RP2040 Flash Bank Command Info : Listening on port 3333 for gdb connections OpenOCD is free, open-source software that can now read and write the target chip’s flash through the Pico — the same job as a $100+ commercial probe. Step 3: back up, then take over (ESP32 example) ESP32-S2 DevKitC. Millions of smart bulbs and plugs run ESP chips — all flashable with free tools. Photo: Espressif. ESP-based smart-home devices are the friendliest starting point: the manufacturer’s own flashing tool is free. Always save a copy of the original firmware first — that’s your way back if anything goes wrong: $ esptool.py --port /dev/ttyUSB0 read_flash 0x0 0x400000 backup.bin esptool.py v4.7 Serial port /dev/ttyUSB0 Connecting... Chip is ESP32-D0WD-V3 (revision v3.0) 4194304 bytes read successfully. $ esptool.py --port /dev/ttyUSB0 write_flash 0x0 tasmota.bin Writing at 0x0003e800... (100 %) Wrote 598016 bytes at 0x00000000 in 5.6 seconds. Hard resetting via RTS pin... Tasmota replaces the vendor’s cloud-dependent firmware with local control — no account, no app, no internet required. Prefer config files over clicking? ESPHome does the same job. Either way, the device now answers to you — not a server that might shut down next year (see the obsolescence archive for why that matters). Simple entry points: everyday ports that open the door Sometimes the case never needs to open at all. Many devices respond to the ports and buttons you already use every day — if you know the right signal to send. The methods below use ordinary connectors: a Joy-Con rail, a charging port, an Ethernet jack, a headphone socket, a USB cable. No soldering, no clips, and usually no extra hardware beyond a cable or a paperclip. A note on scope: everything here is for hardware you own, for educational and repair purposes — understanding how your own devices boot, recovering a device that will not start, or installing community firmware that you choose. None of these methods bypass copy protection or digital rights management, and nothing here is intended to enable that. If a method does not apply to a device you own, treat it as a case study in how embedded hardware is designed. Nintendo Switch — RCM through the Joy-Con rail The Switch’s processor has a built-in recovery mode called RCM. To reach it, pin 10 inside the right Joy-Con rail must be connected to ground while the console powers on — this tells the console to behave as though the Home button is being held. A small jig that slides into the rail bridges pin 10 to a ground pin (pins 1, 2, or 7). Community guides recommend a proper jig (~$5, or 3D-printed) and warn that paperclips or tinfoil can damage the rail’s pads. You need: an RCM jig; a USB-C cable; a computer running free payload software. Steps: power the console fully off, slide the jig into the right Joy-Con rail, hold Volume Up and tap Power. A black screen means RCM is active — the screen stays dark because the console is waiting for instructions over USB. $ # connect the Switch by USB-C, then send a bootloader payload
 $ python3 fusee-launcher.py hekate.bin
Tegra X1 detected in RCM mode (0955:7321)
Uploading payload... complete.
 $ # the Switch wakes into the Hekate bootloader The Switch entry point is a case study in how recovery modes work at the hardware level: a boot ROM — code burned into the processor that cannot be changed — listens on USB for instructions whenever a specific pin is grounded at power-on. Researchers use this to study the Tegra X1’s boot process and to run alternative operating systems such as Linux on hardware they own. Note: payload delivery only works on unpatched launch-era consoles; later units can still enter RCM but will not accept payloads. Samsung phones — a resistor in the charging port Classic Samsung phones with micro-USB ports check the resistance between the port’s ID pin (pin 4) and ground (pin 5) at power-on. A 301 kΩ resistor across those two pins tells the phone to start directly in Download Mode — the firmware installation mode — with no buttons pressed. A few cents of resistor soldered into a spare micro-USB plug is the entire tool. You need: a spare micro-USB plug, one 301 kΩ resistor (three 100 kΩ in series works the same), basic soldering. Steps: solder the resistor between pins 4 and 5 of the plug, power the phone off, insert the jig. The phone enters Download Mode on its own — then swap in a normal USB cable and communicate with it over USB. $ # the phone now shows the Download Mode screen
 $ lsusb | grep -i samsung
Bus 001 Device 017: ID 04e8:685d Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd
 $ # the bootloader is communicating over USB TP-Link routers — the reset button is a recovery button Most TP-Link routers include a built-in recovery routine: if the reset button is held while the router powers on, the bootloader pauses and tries to download a firmware file over the network (TFTP) from a fixed address — 192.168.0.66. All you need is an Ethernet cable, a paperclip for the recessed button, and free TFTP software on your computer. You need: Ethernet cable, paperclip, free TFTP server software (tftpd64 on Windows; tftpd-hpa or dnsmasq on Linux). Steps: set your computer’s wired address to 192.168.0.66, place the correctly named firmware file for your exact model (for example ArcherC7v2_tp_recovery.bin — check your model’s documentation for the right name) in the TFTP folder, connect to a LAN port, hold reset, power on, and release after about five seconds. The router fetches the file and flashes it by itself. $ sudo ip addr add 192.168.0.66/24 dev eth0
 $ sudo dnsmasq --enable-tftp --tftp-root=/tftpboot --port=0
 $ cp ArcherC7v2_tp_recovery.bin /tftpboot/
 $ # hold reset, power on the router, watch the server log:
dnsmasq-tftp: sent /tftpboot/ArcherC7v2_tp_recovery.bin to 192.168.0.1
 $ # the router flashes the file and reboots on its own 3.5mm headphone jack — a serial port in disguise On some Android phones and media players, the 3.5 mm headphone jack doubles as a serial console. Community documentation describes the arrangement: the sleeve carries power while the tip and ring carry the transmit and receive lines. A simple adapter cable plus a USB-to-serial converter turns the headphone jack into the same boot-log window described in the playbook’s first technique — with zero disassembly. You need: a 4-pole 3.5 mm plug wired to a USB-to-serial breakout, and the pinout for your specific device — the postmarketOS serial debugging wiki and device forums track which models support this. Steps: connect the cable, open a terminal at 115200 baud, and power the device on. $ screen /dev/ttyUSB0 115200
[BL] Bootloader starting...
[BL] serial console active
Android boot log follows... This is device-specific — it only works where the manufacturer wired the jack this way — so verify against your model’s documentation first. ESP8266/ESP32 devices — one button, one cable Espressif chips enter flash mode when GPIO0 is held low during power-on. Manufacturers wire this to an onboard button (often labeled BOOT or FLASH). Hold the button, connect the USB cable, release the button — the chip is now waiting for firmware over the same cable it charges from. No probe, no clips, nothing beyond the charging cable. You need: the device’s own USB cable. That is all. Steps: hold the button while plugging in USB, then talk to the chip with the free esptool utility. Save a backup of the original firmware first — it is your only way back. $ # hold BOOT, plug in USB, release BOOT
 $ esptool.py --port /dev/ttyUSB0 chip_id
Detecting chip type... ESP32
Chip ID: 0x240ac0
 $ esptool.py --port /dev/ttyUSB0 read_flash 0x0 0x400000 backup.bin
4194304 bytes read successfully.
 $ # original firmware safely backed up, using only the charging cable Every way in: the firmware access playbook If a device runs code, that code is stored on a chip inside it

text: Rare Manuals 150 of the rarest lawfully-public hardware manuals, datasheets, and schematics — 1980 to today, ranked by how hard each one is to obtain. Public sources only: no leaked documents, no NDA material, no login-walled content. Preservation: every manual on this page is being archived to the BareBoard collection on the Internet Archive . Documentation links point to Internet Archive copies where one exists, and otherwise to the public source hosting the document. Search manuals 1980–1989 (20 entries) #1 Intellivision Keyboard Component Plans (June 2, 1982) only-known-copy Manufacturer: Mattel Electronics Internal planning documents for the infamous unreleased Intellivision keyboard add-on — the expansion module whose delays and high price became a running industry story. From the Dr. David P. Chandler collection. Why rare: Planning documents for a cancelled peripheral from a dead division of a defunct-era Mattel Electronics; survives as a single archive.org scan of a collector's copy. Public source #2 Intellivision Intellivoice Service Manual (Model 3330) few-mirrors Manufacturer: Mattel Electronics (Model 3330) Service manual for the Intellivoice voice-synthesis module: schematics, PCB layout, component-level repair procedures for the speech cartridge add-on. Why rare: Mattel Electronics-era Intellivision hardware documentation is thinly preserved; the Intellivoice service manual is found on one document aggregator. Public source #3 Osborne 1 Technical Manual (1982) few-mirrors Manufacturer: Osborne Computer Corporation Technical manual for the Osborne 1, the first mass-produced portable computer: theory of operation, full schematics (main logic board drawings IAI0063, sheets 1–9), disk electronics board schematics, bill of materials. Osborne folded in 1983. Why rare: Osborne Computer Corporation is long defunct and its documentation survives almost entirely through community preservation; this scan is the working reference for Osborne 1 repair. Public source #4 Kaypro Technical Manual (1984, 1484-C) few-mirrors Manufacturer: Non Linear Systems / Kaypro Corporation Kaypro technical manual covering the Kaypro 2/4/10 and 2/83–4/84 series: mainboard removal, scope-waveform troubleshooting, Dotronix and Elston video board adjustments, full schematics and parts lists. Kaypro is defunct. Why rare: Kaypro (Non Linear Systems) collapsed in the early 1990s; its technical manuals survive on a handful of retro-computing mirrors. Public source #5 Sinclair ZX Spectrum Servicing Manual (March 1984, Thorn EMI Datatech) few-mirrors Manufacturer: Sinclair Research Official dealer service manual for the ZX Spectrum: fault diagnosis procedures, Issue 2 and Issue 3 board schematics, power-supply and ULA test points. Produced by Thorn EMI Datatech. Why rare: Sinclair's dealer-only service documentation is far scarcer than its user manuals; this March 1984 Thorn EMI edition lives on obscure personal hosting rather than the big archives. Public source #6 Amiga 1000 Assembly Level Repair (1985) several-mirrors Manufacturer: Commodore-Amiga, Inc. Official 1985 assembly-level repair manual for the Amiga 1000: chassis disassembly, drive installation, RFI shield and bezel procedures, service diagnostics. Commodore is defunct. Why rare: The launch-era Amiga 1000 repair manual predates Commodore's later service program; the 1985 edition is preserved on archive.org but rarely mirrored elsewhere. Public source #7 Amiga 1000 Service Manual (Orval Bair Commodore Tech Topics Collection) several-mirrors Manufacturer: Commodore Business Machines Amiga 1000 component-level service manual: full schematics including the piggyback PCB assembly #327139, parts list for PCB assembly #327137 (Agnus 8361, Denise 8362, Paula 8364, 68000), resistor/capacitor tables. Why rare: Survives via the Orval Bair Commodore Tech Topics collection on archive.org — a collector-assembled set of Commodore service bulletins, not a current manufacturer archive. Public source #8 Commodore 64 Service Manual (February 1985, PN-314001-02) several-mirrors Manufacturer: Commodore Business Machines (PN-314001-02) Official C64 service manual: full schematics (#326106 board), parts lists, troubleshooting flowcharts, alignment procedures for the best-selling computer of the 1980s. Why rare: The definitive factory service manual; public copies cluster on archive.org with few independent mirrors of the complete February 1985 edition. Public source #9 Commodore 1541 Troubleshooting and Repair Guide several-mirrors Manufacturer: Commodore Business Machines VIC-1541/1540/1542 troubleshooting and repair guide: block diagrams, interconnect diagrams, schematics, parts layouts and parts lists for the 6502-based intelligent floppy drive, plus CMOS handling precautions and disk-controller IC descriptions. Why rare: The deep technical appendix (schematics, interconnect maps, parts lists) goes well beyond the user manual; the full guide is preserved on archive.org and a few community mirrors. Public source #10 1541 Single Drive Floppy Disk Maintenance Manual several-mirrors Manufacturer: Commodore Business Machines Maintenance manual for the 1541 single-drive floppy disk unit: frame assembly schematics (115/230 VAC), parts layouts, test-equipment specifications, timing-light fabrication appendix. Why rare: A maintenance-depot document rather than a retail manual; the complete scan with appendices A and B survives on archive.org. Public source #11 Atari 2600/2600A VCS Domestic Field Service Manual (FD100133, Rev.02) few-mirrors Manufacturer: Atari, Inc. (FD100133, Rev.02) Field service manual for the 2600/2600A Video Computer System: theory of operation, silkscreens and schematics (2600A motherboard revs 14–16+), testing and troubleshooting with diagnostic cartridge DTC 2.6, 2600 and 2600A diagnostic flowcharts, game-controller schematics, parts lists, service bulletins. Atari, Inc. is defunct. Why rare: The official field service manual (not the owner's manual) with full board silkscreens and schematics; the Rev.02 domestic edition is preserved on a handful of mirrors. Public source #12 Atari CX5200 Field Service Manual (Rev. June 1983) few-mirrors Manufacturer: Atari, Inc. Field service manual for the Atari 5200 SuperSystem: theory of operation, silkscreens and schematics for both 4-port and 2-port models, diagnostic tests, troubleshooting flowcharts, game-controller and trak-ball schematics, parts lists. Why rare: The 5200's short market life means its service documentation was printed in small numbers; the June 1983 revision survives on bitsavers mirrors and a few Atari community sites. Public source #13 Atari 400/800 Home Computer Field Service Manual (Updated) few-mirrors Manufacturer: Atari, Inc. Field service manual for the Atari 400 and 800: theory of operation, silkscreens and schematics, testing and troubleshooting, disassembly/assembly, diagnostic flowcharts, parts lists. Why rare: The updated edition of the 400/800 field service manual is preserved on community Atari sites rather than the major archives. Public source #14 Atari 800XL Field Service Manual several-mirrors Manufacturer: Atari, Inc. Field service manual for the Atari 800XL: system interfaces (SIO, PBI, cartridge, keyboard), bus protocol, SIO connector pin assignments, power-supply schematics, parts lists, service bulletins section. Why rare: The 800XL field service manual is widely mirrored on archive.org but original Atari, Inc. service documentation is otherwise thinly preserved. Public source #15 Atari 520 ST / 1040 ST Service Manual several-mirrors Manufacturer: Atari Corporation Computer field service manual for the Atari 520 ST and 1040 ST (1985-era 16/32-bit machines): service procedures, schematics, parts information. Why rare: Atari Corporation-era ST service documentation was never broadly distributed; this scan is one of the few public copies of the 520/1040 ST field service manual. Public source #16 BBC Microcomputer Service Manual (October 1985) few-mirrors Manufacturer: Acorn Computers Limited Official Acorn service manual for BBC Micro Models A & B: general and detailed circuit descriptions (processor, memory, video, Econet, 1 MHz bus, power supply), servicing and faultfinding with test programs and waveforms, interfacing survey, component location tables, main PCB circuit diagram and keyboard/power-supply diagrams. Why rare: The full Acorn-published service manual (not the user guide) with complete foldout schematics; the October 1985 edition survives on a computing-history mirror. Public source #17 Acorn BBC Micro Circuit Diagram (1983) several-mirrors Manufacturer: Acorn Computers Limited The complete circuit diagram for the BBC Model B, originally published as part of the Advanced User Guide for the BBC Micro. Why rare: Acorn's full board-level circuit diagram as a standalone document; preserved on archive.org but seldom mirrored independently of the user-guide bundles. Public source #18 TRS-80 Model 4P Service Manual several-mirrors Manufacturer: Tandy Corporation / Radio Shack Service manual for the TRS-80 Model 4P portable: full schematics including the switch-mode power supply (page 161), theory of operation, troubleshooting and adjustment procedures. Why rare: The 4P (portable) variant's service manual is scarcer than the desktop Model 4 documentation; the complete scan with power-supply schematics survives on archive.org. Public source #19 TRS-80 Model 4/4P Technical Reference Manual (1985) several-mirrors Manufacturer: Tandy Corporation (26-2110) Model 4/4P technical reference manual: theory of operation (CPU and timing, buffering, video), memory circuits, full hardware section with schematics. The hardware section is a page-for-page reprint of the NGA Model 4 service manual. Why rare: The 26-2110 edition carries the complete hardware/service section that later editions trimmed; preserved on a bitsavers mirror. title: The Registry — BareBoard
text: The Registry Every important document, ranked by honesty. A document's value to a repairer is not proportional to how hard a company guards it — so we say exactly what exists, what is public, and what is sealed. For the map of everything the site covers — all 163 topics in 20 domains, with coverage status — see the Domains Atlas . Status legend PUBLIC — the vendor publishes it. Collect, preserve, cite. PUBLIC-RESEARCH — no vendor doc, but public research exists. We compile originals from it. SEALED (NDA) — vendor-internal. Listed for awareness, with public-research pointers. No bounties. EXCLUDED — material that exists only to defeat hardware security. Never a target. Level legend ( The Foundry ) L0 — silicon (chips, secure elements) · L1 — interconnect (boards, power rails) L2 — controllers (storage, wireless, firmware) · L3 — systems (devices, human impact) The board (condensed) Target Level Status Legitimate resource Intel CSME register maps L0 SEALED me_cleaner · REcon 2014 · coreboot tooling → original doc in Library Intel DFX / JTAG lock-override procedures L0 EXCLUDED Excluded — circumvention material AMD PSP integration manual L0 SEALED coreboot PSP Integration Guide · PSPTool → original doc in Library Apple SEP register specs L0 SEALED Black Hat 2016 · MOSEC 2020 → original doc in Library Qualcomm QSEE fuse maps L0 SEALED Public academic TrustZone research Microsoft Pluton L0 PUBLIC Microsoft Learn documentation STMicro ST33 L0 PUBLIC st.com datasheets (security-target docs are NDA) NXP SE050 EdgeLock L0 PUBLIC nxp.com datasheet + user guides + open-source middleware Google Titan M/M2 L0 SEALED Google's published Titan M/M2 security material. (OpenTitan is a separate open-source root-of-trust reference design — related in spirit, but it is not documentation of the Titan chips.) Apple ANS NVMe controller L2 SEALED Asahi Linux m1n1 project documents it publicly Samsung / Phison / SMI controller registers L2 SEALED nvme-cli · smartmontools · vendor tools SK hynix H9-series memory/eMMC L2 PUBLIC SK hynix + distributor datasheets (one preserved in Library) Broadcom BCM43xx registers L2 SEALED / PUBLIC-RESEARCH Linux b43/brcmfmac · OpenFWWF · community register wiki Apple 339S/338S PMICs L1 SEALED Original identification guide in Library TI / Maxim-ADI / Dialog-Renesas power ICs L1 PUBLIC ti.com · analog.com · renesas.com Bounty rules Bounties for devices to teardown and document. Bounties for rare public documents — collect and preserve. Bounties for original documentation written from public research. No bounties for sealed documents — that is a market for stolen trade secrets. Never list circumvention material. Full registry: bareboard-registry-draft.md · Tracker (CSV): doc-targets-tracker.csv · Entry template: templates/registry-entry.md “The most effective debugging tool is still careful thought, coupled with judiciously placed print statements.” — Brian W. Kernighan, in the paper Unix for Beginners (1979)
