headings: Demand Letters That Cite the Law
Letter 1 — Wheelchair owner invoking a state powered-wheelchair law
Letter 2 — Independent repair provider invoking the same laws
text: Demand Letters That Cite the Law Three fill-in-the-blank letters: a wheelchair owner invoking a state powered-wheelchair repair law, an independent repairer invoking the same, and a rebuttal to a “your warranty is void” threat. Each one names the statute it stands on. Fill the [BRACKETED] fields, attach the evidence listed under the letter, and send it in a form you can prove was sent. This is education, not legal advice. These templates state what the cited laws say; they are not a lawyer’s review of your facts. If the amount in dispute is large, or anyone threatens you with legal action, get a consumer-protection attorney — several of the laws cited here let a winning consumer recover attorney’s fees, which is exactly the kind of case those attorneys take. How to use these Pick the letter that matches who you are — owner, repairer, or warranty holder. Do not blend them; each cites a different legal basis. Replace every [BRACKET] with your facts. Bracketed choices separated by slashes mean pick one and delete the others. If a field asks for a statute citation, copy it from the matching state entry on The Shield — never cite a law from memory. Attach what the letter lists. A demand without proof of ownership and the refusal in writing is an opinion. With them, it is a record. Send it so you can prove sending — email with the thread kept, or paper mail with a certificate of mailing. Keep your copy with the date. Then work the escalation ladder . Letter 1 — Wheelchair owner invoking a state powered-wheelchair law Legal basis: your state’s powered-wheelchair statute — Colorado Rev. Stat. §§ 6-1-1501 to 6-1-1505 ; Cal. Health & Safety Code §§ 21300–21303; Md. Code, Commercial Law §§ 14-5001 to 14-5004; Nev. Rev. Stat. §§ 597.2691 et seq.; Oregon SB 550 (2025) under the Right to Repair Act; R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 6-61; Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 47-18-5701 et seq.; Washington SB 5680 (2025), Title 19 RCW. Full text and limits per state: The Shield, layer two . [YOUR FULL NAME] [YOUR ADDRESS] [YOUR EMAIL] · [YOUR PHONE] [DATE] VIA [EMAIL / CERTIFIED MAIL] [MANUFACTURER LEGAL NAME] [MANUFACTURER ADDRESS OR SUPPORT EMAIL] Re: Demand for repair resources under [STATE] law — [CHAIR MAKE AND MODEL], serial number [SERIAL NUMBER] Dear [MANUFACTURER]: I own the powered wheelchair identified above, purchased on [PURCHASE DATE] from [SELLER]. I am writing to demand the repair resources that [STATE STATUTE CITATION, e.g., Colo. Rev. Stat. § 6-1-1503] requires you to provide to owners of your powered wheelchairs on fair and reasonable terms: - [PART NAME AND PART NUMBER, e.g., "motor/gearbox assembly, part no. ______"] - [DOCUMENTATION, e.g., "the service manual and fault-code table for this model"] - [SOFTWARE/TOOL, e.g., "the programming tool and access needed to calibrate the replacement part"] On [DATE OF REFUSAL], your [support line / dealer / email support] declined to provide these items, stating: "[THE REFUSAL, QUOTED AS CLOSELY AS YOU CAN]." A copy of that refusal [is attached / was made verbally by (NAME) on (DATE) and I ask you to confirm or correct it in writing]. [FOR CALIFORNIA: This letter is also notice of a first violation under Cal. Health & Safety Code § 21302; I note the statute's three-day cure provision and ask for compliance within it.] Please confirm in writing by [DATE — ALLOW AT LEAST 14 DAYS UNLESS A STATUTE GIVES A SHORTER CURE PERIOD] that the items above will be made available, the price and terms for each, and the ordering procedure. If you contend any item is exempt — for example, as a trade secret, or in California as a part requiring programming, calibration, or clinical involvement for seating and positioning — please identify the item and the specific exemption you rely on. If I do not have your written confirmation by that date, I will pursue the remedies the law provides, which [in this state include a complaint to the Attorney General / include suit under (CONSUMER PROTECTION ACT CITATION)]. This letter is written in good faith to obtain what the statute already requires. I would rather have the part than the argument. [YOUR SIGNATURE] [YOUR PRINTED NAME] Attach: proof of ownership (receipt, delivery paperwork, or Medicare/supplier record showing the chair is yours); a photo of the serial-number plate; the refusal in writing if you have it (if the refusal was verbal, say so in the letter, as the template does — and ask them to confirm or correct it in writing); any fault code or diagnosis you already have from the chair itself. Letter 2 — Independent repair provider invoking the same laws Legal basis: the same eight state statutes. Every one of them extends the manufacturer’s duty to independent repair providers — a repair business with no authorized-dealer arrangement — on the same fair and reasonable terms. Two practical differences from Letter 1: identify your business precisely, and expect the manufacturer’s trade-secret and (in California) clinical-parts carve-outs to be raised against you first. [BUSINESS LETTERHEAD — BUSINESS NAME, ADDRESS, PHONE, EMAIL] [DATE] VIA [EMAIL / CERTIFIED MAIL] [MANUFACTURER LEGAL NAME] [MANUFACTURER ADDRESS OR DEALER-SUPPORT EMAIL] Re: Independent repair provider demand under [STATE] law — [CHAIR MAKE AND MODEL], serial number [SERIAL NUMBER] Dear [MANUFACTURER]: [BUSINESS NAME] is an independent repair provider located in [CITY, STATE]. We are not an authorized dealer for your products and hold no arrangement with you. We are repairing the powered wheelchair identified above for its owner, [OWNER NAME], with the owner's authorization [attached]. Under [STATE STATUTE CITATION], you are required to make available to independent repair providers, on fair and reasonable terms, the documentation, parts, embedded software, firmware, and tools used to diagnose, maintain, and repair your powered wheelchairs. We demand: - [PART / DOCUMENTATION / TOOL, WITH PART NUMBERS WHERE KNOWN] - [ITEM] - [ITEM] On [DATE], [your parts desk / dealer channel / support line] [refused this request / quoted terms of (DESCRIBE — e.g., a price of $___ against a dealer price of $___ ) / stated that these items are dealer-only]. [A copy of that response is attached.] Please provide, in writing, by [DATE — AT LEAST 14 DAYS]: the price and terms for each item above on the same basis you offer your authorized providers, and the ordering procedure for independent providers under the statute. If you contend an item is exempt, identify it and the specific exemption. Unreasonable delay or dealer-only terms are a violation of [STATUTE CITATION] [and, in this state, an unfair or deceptive trade practice under (CONSUMER PROTECTION ACT CITATION)]. We will document any further refusal for the owner's complaint to the Attorney General and for our own remedies under the Act. We repair what you sell, in the open. We would rather do it with your parts desk than despite it. [BUSINESS OWNER NAME AND TITLE] [BUSINESS NAME] Attach: the owner’s written authorization naming your business and the chair’s serial number; your business license or registration if your state issues one; the refusal or discriminatory quote in writing. Send a copy to the chair’s owner the same day — in several states the owner’s own complaint to the Attorney General carries independent weight, and your file becomes their evidence. One disclosure note: some state frameworks (California’s and Nevada’s among them) expect an independent provider to tell the customer, in writing, that it is not an authorized repair provider for the product before repairing it. Do it on your invoice if not before; it protects you and costs nothing. Letter 3 — “Your warranty is void” rebuttal Legal basis: federal. The Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act, 15 U.S.C. § 2302(c) , bars a warrantor from conditioning warranty coverage on the use of branded parts or service unless they are provided free or the FTC has granted a waiver; the FTC’s interpretation at 16 C.F.R. § 700.10 treats void-for-aftermarket-parts terms as deceptive, and its 2022 orders against Harley-Davidson and MWE/Westinghouse required those companies to strike exactly these clauses. If coverage is ultimately refused, 15 U.S.C. § 2310(d) gives you a private right to sue, with attorney’s fees if you prevail. This letter works for any warranted product — chair, console, appliance — because the law is federal. [YOUR FULL NAME] [YOUR ADDRESS] [YOUR EMAIL] · [YOUR PHONE] [DATE] VIA [EMAIL / CERTIFIED MAIL] [WARRANTOR — MANUFACTURER OR SELLER WHO ISSUED THE WARRANTY] [ADDRESS OR WARRANTY-CLAIMS EMAIL] Re: Warranty claim [CLAIM/TICKET NUMBER] — unlawful void-for-repair condition; [PRODUCT, MODEL, SERIAL NUMBER] Dear [WARRANTOR]: On [DATE], your [representative / service center / warranty desk] [denied my warranty claim / stated that my warranty is void] because [the product was repaired by an independent provider / a non-branded replacement part was installed / the warranty seal was broken — DESCRIBE EXACTLY WHAT WAS SAID, AND BY WHOM]. That condition is unlawful. The Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act, 15 U.S.C. § 2302(c), provides that a warrantor may not condition warranty coverage on a consumer's use of an article or service identified by brand, trade, or corporate name, unless the article or service is provided without charge or the Federal Trade Commission has waived the prohibition. The FTC's interpretation, 16 C.F.R. § 700.10, is to the same effect, and in 2022 the FTC ordered Harley-Davidson and MWE Investments (Westinghouse) to remove identical void-if-repaired terms from their warranties. If you contend that a specific repair or part in fact caused the failure now claimed, the burden of demonstrating that is yours. Please provide, in writing, the specific causal finding and the evidence for it. title: Repair Economics: Why Fixing What You Have Is Now the Rational Move — BareBoard
headings: Repair economics: why fixing what you have is now the rational move
What this does to the repair-or-replace decision
text: Repair economics: why fixing what you have is now the rational move For years, the honest advice about a broken graphics card or an old laptop was often “buy a new one — it’s cheaper than the repair.” That advice is out of date. AI data centers have eaten the memory supply, and the prices of new hardware have moved so far that repair is now the economical choice in cases where it was not two years ago. This page lays out the numbers — all of them from November 2026 tracking and reporting — and what they mean for the decision to repair or replace. What happened: the “RAMpocalypse” AI data-center construction has diverted DRAM and HBM wafer capacity — the memory chips that go into both data-center accelerators and consumer devices — away from consumer memory. JP Morgan’s estimate: DRAM prices up 400% since 2024 by the end of 2026. TrendForce expects DRAM to stay tight through 2027; Intel points to 2028 for normalization. There is no relief in sight this year, and probably not next year either. The numbers, November 2026 Graphics cards: Tom’s Hardware tracking puts the RTX 5090 street price at about $4,920 to $4,999 against a $1,999 manufacturer’s suggested price — roughly 2.5 times. The RTX 5080 is at $1,899 against $999. NVIDIA removed the 5090 from its U.S. store in October. Chinese RTX 50 prices rose by up to 3,300 yuan (about $500) per card in the first week of November alone. Memory: a 2x16GB DDR5-6000 kit went from $59 in April 2025 to $429 on November 3, 2026 — more than seven times. GDDR6 spot prices went from about $2.50 per gigabyte in September 2025 to $12.45 on October 5, 2026 — about five times. Everything downstream: the Steam Deck OLED went from $549 to $789; the Raspberry Pi 5 16GB rose $80 to $385 on November 2, with the maker citing a “lack of alternative supply for 16GB DRAM”; Xbox, PlayStation 5, and Switch 2 prices have risen too. MSI told investors gaming hardware prices rise 15 to 30% across 2026; AMD confirmed a 10% or larger Radeon price increase effective August 2026. Amazon cancelled GPU orders — Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney said his were among them. What this does to the repair-or-replace decision Work the arithmetic on a concrete case. A graphics card with a melted 16-pin connector (see our failure analysis ) is a soldered-connector replacement at a board-level shop — a repair measured in tens or low hundreds of dollars. The replacement card, at street prices, is $1,899 for a 5080 or about $4,900 for a 5090. The repair was always cheaper; the gap is now so large that the repair is cheaper by an order of magnitude. The same logic reaches further down the stack: Fans, paste, and pads — the Level 1 service on our GPU Repair page — cost tens of dollars in parts and an afternoon. They restore a card that would cost thousands to replace. Memory-chip faults that once meant “scrap the card” are now worth a shop’s labor to isolate, because the card itself is worth so much more than the labor. Used cards are worth verifying, not fearing. At these prices, a secondhand card is a serious purchase — which is why our fake-GPU guide matters: the scams exist precisely because the prices make them profitable. Old hardware gains a second life. A machine that was marginal at 2024 prices is worth keeping at 2026 prices. The same logic applies beyond GPUs: a laptop with a failing fan or a dead battery is a repair, not a replacement, when its replacement costs 30% more than it did a year ago. The honest limits Repair is not always the answer, and the prices do not change the cases where it is not: Some failures are genuinely uneconomical — a dead GPU die, or heat damage spread across the board, can cost more to fix than the card is worth even now. Replacement parts have risen too: memory chips and modules cost more, and a repair that needs new RAM may cost more than the same repair did last year. Get a quote before committing. Prices are volatile. The figures on this page are November 2026 tracking; check current street prices before deciding. The direction of travel — tight supply through 2027 — is the part analysts agree on, not the exact price of any one card next month. Why this page is here This site’s mission is to put repair knowledge in everyone’s hands, free. For most of its life, that mission fought an economic headwind: new was cheap, repair was dear, and the rational consumer replaced. The memory shortage has reversed the headwind. Repair is now, for a large class of failures, the rational economic choice — not only the principled one. That is a window, and it will not stay open forever: if supply normalizes in 2028, the arithmetic shifts back. While it is open, the knowledge on this site is worth more than it has ever been. Learn it now. Sources “GPU supply problem: no end in sight” — Engadget, November 2026: engadget.com . “Why are RAM and GPU prices spiking?” — Capital & Compute, November 24, 2026: capitalandcompute.net . “GPU prices surging: what to do” — Tech Journal, November 2026: techjournal.org . “RAM shortage: gaming hardware prices 2026” — Tech Insider, November 2026: tech-insider.org . On this site: GPU Repair ; the 16-pin connector failure analysis ; spot a fake GPU before you pay . BareBoard — free hardware education. New is expensive. The card you already own is the cheapest card you will ever buy — if you can fix it.

title: The Shield: Right-to-Repair Law — BareBoard
headings: The Shield: Defending Yourself with Right-to-Repair Law
Your warranty cannot be voided for repairing your own device
Picking the lock on your own device is federally exempt
The FTC is actively enforcing against repair restrictions
Once it’s sold, patent law stops policing it
Layer two: the eight powered-wheelchair states
Colorado — the first, and the template
Layer three: the general electronics laws
When they say no: the escalation ladder
text: The Shield: Defending Yourself with Right-to-Repair Law When a manufacturer says “dealer only,” that is not the end of the conversation. In much of the United States it is the start of a legal one — and the law is increasingly on the owner’s side. This page is the layered defense: the federal floor, the eight powered-wheelchair states, the wider electronics laws, and the exact escalation ladder for when they say no anyway. Provenance: every law below is cited to its primary text — the U.S. Code, the Code of Federal Regulations, state session laws and codes, FTC orders, and court opinions. Several of those documents are collected in our own library and linked where they appear. This is education, not legal advice: we are a documentation project, not your lawyer. If money or mobility is on the line, a consumer-protection attorney or your state Attorney General’s office is the next call. Five words, defined once Statute — a law passed by a legislature (Congress or a state assembly). Everything below with a section number is a statute or a regulation made under one. Exemption — a written exception that takes specified conduct out of a ban. The DMCA repair rules below are exemptions: the ban still exists; the exempted repair is carved out of it. Preemption — when a higher level of law overrides a lower one. Federal law preempts conflicting state law; it is why the anti-trafficking limit in the DMCA section matters even in states with strong repair statutes. Standing — the legal right to bring a complaint or a lawsuit. Some laws below give standing to you personally; some give it only to the Attorney General. Knowing which one you are holding changes what you do. Parts pairing — software that ties a replacement part to one specific device by serial number or cryptographic check, so the device rejects or degrades a working part the manufacturer did not bless. Several newer laws ban or restrict it by name. Layer one: the federal floor Your warranty cannot be voided for repairing your own device The Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act (the federal warranty law, 15 U.S.C. §§ 2301–2312) contains the sentence manufacturers hope you never read, at 15 U.S.C. § 2302(c) : a warrantor may not condition warranty coverage on the customer using an article or service that carries a brand, trade, or corporate name — unless the article or service is provided free, or the Federal Trade Commission (FTC, the federal consumer-protection agency) has waived the rule for that product. That is the tie-in ban : “use our parts or lose your warranty” is unlawful as a blanket condition, and the FTC’s own interpretation ( 16 C.F.R. § 700.10 ) treats a warranty that purports to void coverage when the owner uses non-branded parts as deceptive. The burden runs the other way from what service desks claim: a maker that wants to deny a claim must show that your part or your repair caused the failure — it is not your job to prove it didn’t. This is enforced law, not theory. In 2022 the FTC ordered Harley-Davidson ( Decision and Order, File No. 2123140 ) and MWE Investments/Westinghouse ( Decision and Order, Docket No. C-4774 ) to strike their void-if-repaired terms and to tell customers their rights were restored; Weber settled the same charge the same summer. And the Act gives you standing of your own: 15 U.S.C. § 2310(d) lets a consumer sue a warrantor that fails to comply, with attorney’s fees recoverable if you win. Template 3 on the demand-letter page is built on this layer. Picking the lock on your own device is federally exempt The Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), § 1201 (17 U.S.C. § 1201) bans circumventing — bypassing — the digital locks on copyrighted software, which includes the firmware inside almost every modern device. Every three years the Librarian of Congress, on the Copyright Office’s recommendation, issues exemptions to that ban, codified at 37 C.F.R. § 201.40 . The repair exemptions now include: Medical devices — circumvention for diagnosis, maintenance, and repair of lawfully acquired medical devices, first exempted in the 2021 rule ( 86 Fed. Reg. 59627 ) and renewed in 2024 ( 89 Fed. Reg. 85437 , exemption at § 201.40(b)(17)). The device industry sued to kill it; the D.C. Circuit upheld the exemption in Medical Imaging & Technology Alliance v. Library of Congress , 189 F.4th 1150 (decided September 1, 2026) — the opinion is in our library . Under threat now: in the tenth triennial proceeding the Register intends to recommend renewal of every existing exemption except this one — first-round comments are due December 7, 2026. See our DMCA 1201 medical-device explainer . Video game consoles — circumvention solely to repair a console’s optical drive, exempt since 2021 and renewed in 2024, under the same § 201.40 list. Consumer devices generally — diagnosis, maintenance, and repair of lawfully acquired software-enabled devices is exempt, the provision the wheelchair and medical-device exemptions build on. The honest limit, and it matters: the exemptions free the act of circumventing for repair. They do not free the tools . § 1201’s separate anti-trafficking ban — no making or distributing circumvention tools — is not something the Librarian has statutory authority to exempt, so it stands. An owner may legally pick their own lock; selling them the pick remains banned. Our PMD law section states the same line. No state law can override this, because of preemption : federal copyright law wins where the two conflict. The FTC is actively enforcing against repair restrictions Three markers worth citing in any dispute. The FTC’s report to Congress Nixing the Fix (May 2021) found “scant evidence” justifying manufacturer repair restrictions. Its Policy Statement on Repair Restrictions (July 21, 2021) committed the Commission to prioritizing enforcement under the FTC Act, Magnuson-Moss, and the antitrust laws. And on July 8, 2026 the FTC and five states settled FTC v. Deere & Company : the stipulated order requires Deere, for ten years, to give owners and independent repairers repair resources equivalent to its dealers’, on fair and reasonable terms. A manufacturer refusing you in 2026 is refusing against the stated position of its federal regulator. Watch the defense bill. A military right-to-repair provision was in both the House and Senate versions of the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, but on November 24, 2026 the House Armed Services chair said it likely would not survive into the final bill. That is a statement of intent in an unfinished negotiation, not a final vote — check the enacted text before citing it either way. Our FY27 NDAA explainer carries the full story, the FY26-versus-FY27 distinction, and the record against the “zero examples” claim. Military.com, November 24, 2026 . Once it’s sold, patent law stops policing it Impression Products, Inc. v. Lexmark International, Inc. , 581 U.S. 360 (2017) — Supreme Court opinion in our library — held that a patent holder’s rights are exhausted (used up) at the first authorized sale, domestic or foreign: post-sale restrictions cannot be enforced through patent law. It is the doctrine under the whole refill-and-repair economy, and the reason “patent protected, no unauthorized parts” stickers mean less than they claim. Layer two: the eight powered-wheelchair states These statutes are specific to powered wheelchairs (some reach wider mobility equipment). Each one obliges the manufacturer to supply the means of repair to owners and independent repair providers. Read your state’s entry for the four facts that matter in a dispute: the citation , the effective date , exactly what you are entitled to , and who enforces it . Colorado — the first, and the template Citation: Consumer Wheelchair Repair Bill of Rights Act, Colo. Rev. Stat. §§ 6-1-1501 to 6-1-1505 (Part 15), enacted by HB22-1031 — signed act in our library . Effective: January 1, 2023. Entitles you to: documentation, parts, embedded software, firmware, and tools — expressly including the resources to reset or disable security functions — on fair and reasonable terms, for any chair. The only carve-out is genuine trade secrets. Enforcement: a violation is a deceptive trade practice under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act (§ 6-1-105(1)(qqq)), enforceable by the Attorney General and by private suit under that Act. California Citation: Consumer Wheelchair Right to Repair, Cal. Health & Safety Code §§ 21300–21303, enacted by SB 1384 (2024). Effective: January 1, 2025; applies to wheelchairs sold or in use on or after that date. Entitles you to: documentation, parts, embedded software, firmware, and tools on fair and reasonable terms and costs. For chairs under the Medi-Cal complex-rehabilitation rules, parts that require programming, calibration, or clinical involvement for seating and positioning are carved out — the statute names the covered ordinary parts (batteries, chargers, nonprogrammable joysticks, wheel assemblies, casters, armrests and similar). Enforcement: civil penalties — up to $2,500 per wheelchair for a first violation (with a three-day cure window for a non-knowing first violation), up to $10,000 per wheelchair for later ones — in actions by an injured person or by the Attorney General, a district attorney, county counsel, or a city prosecutor. Maryland Citation: Powered Wheelchairs Repair subtitle, Md. Code, Commercial Law §§ 14-5001 to 14-5004, enacted by HB 31 (Chapter 546, Acts of 2025; cross-filed as SB 382). Effective: October 1, 2025; applies prospectively. Entitles you to: documentation, parts, embedded software, firmware, and tools for the covered repairs. Maryland’s definition of a tool is the sharpest in the country: it expressly includes software or other mechanisms that provide, program, or pair a new part or calibrate functionality — pairing software is a repair tool by statute. Enforcement: a violatio

title: Repair Guides — BareBoard
text: Scores: iFixit Repair Guides The devices that fight back. Ranked worst-first by iFixit’s published repairability score (0 = unrepairable, 10 = easiest to repair). Scores are iFixit’s, not ours — devices are ranked here by documented repair hostility. Score bands: 0–3 effectively destructive to open · 4–6 repairable in theory, blocked by locks or design · 7+ doable with care and the right tools. “Parts pairing” means replacement parts are cryptographically tied to the original logic board. The consequences vary: many paired parts still work after a swap but show warnings or lose features (a battery-health readout, True Tone, Face ID in some generations); only some are rejected outright. An iPhone 6s opened up — battery, logic board, and cameras laid bare. Newer phones glue all of this down far more aggressively. Photo: Wikimedia Commons. Loading… Open it without destroying it Most “unrepairable” devices are just glued shut. Adhesive softens with heat — a hair dryer on medium works if you don’t own a heat gun. Warm the edges for a minute or two, then work a thin plastic pick (an old guitar pick does the job) around the seam. Never use a metal screwdriver as a pry tool: it scratches boards and can puncture batteries. The basic kit is inexpensive: Plastic spudger and picks — for prying without scratching (a few dollars, or cut up an old credit card) Suction cup — lifts screens and back glass once the adhesive is warm Precision screwdrivers — phones use tiny pentalobe and tri-point screws; one $8 driver set covers all of them Tweezers — for the tiny ribbon-cable connectors inside Golden rule: if something won’t budge, add more heat — not more force. Cracked screens happen when people pry cold adhesive. A note on smart-home gear Smart bulbs and plugs are usually sonic-welded shut — opening them destroys the shell. For IoT, the software route is the better first move: many of these devices expose a serial console you can talk to without opening the case at all. See Protocol Reverse Engineering for how to do it with under $10 in parts. “OAuth is the best that the wrong way of doing things can provide.” — Mike Stay [http://blog.360.yahoo.com/blog-TBPekxc1dLNy5DOloPfzVvFIVOWMB0li?p=1006]

title: Start Here — BareBoard
headings: What do I need to buy?
Your first project: update the firmware on your Pico
Step 1 — Put the Pico in bootloader mode
Step 2 — Install MicroPython (this is a firmware update)
Step 3 — Find the Pico’s serial port
A note on staying safe and legal
text: Start Here Never opened a device? Never typed a command? Perfect — this page was written for you. You will not open, break, or damage anything. By the end, you will have updated the software on a tiny computer with your own hands — and you will understand what is inside your gadgets. The Raspberry Pi Pico — a $4 computer the size of a stick of gum, and the best first tool you can own. What is this site? BareBoard is a free school for hardware. Every device you own — your phone, your smart plug, your game console — is a small computer. The companies that sold them to you would prefer you never look inside. We disagree. Here is the principle this site is built on: this is your device. You have the right to update it, fix it, and remove software you don’t want on it. When a manufacturer stops updating your gadget, or bundles in software you never asked for, you should be able to do something about it — because it is yours. On this page, everything is non-destructive : no enclosures opened, nothing pried apart, nothing broken. You will learn what firmware is, how to replace it on hardware designed to let you, and how to talk to a device over a cable. Everything here is about hardware you own , documented for learning and repair. Nothing here is for sale, and nothing here is about anyone else’s property. You do not need to be an engineer. You do not need to know how to code. You just need curiosity and about fifteen dollars. What do I need to buy? Everything on this list is cheap, and most of it you will use for years. Total cost to get started: about $7 — the Pico and the adapter; the cable you probably already own. The whole list, including the for-later items, comes to about $18. Item 1 — about $4 Raspberry Pi Pico A Raspberry Pi Pico. Photo: Wikimedia Commons. A tiny computer on a circuit board — and your first project subject. It is designed to be reprogrammed over USB with no tools at all. Buy the plain Pico (not the Pico W) to start — it is the cheapest. Item 2 — about $3 USB-to-serial adapter A CH340 USB-to-serial adapter. Photo: Quartz Components. A translator between your computer and gadgets: one end plugs into USB, the other end speaks the simple serial language that device firmware understands. Search for CH340 USB to TTL or CP2102 USB to TTL . Either works. Make sure it has a 3.3V / 5V switch and set it to 3.3V . Item 3 — you probably own one Micro USB cable A micro USB cable. Photo: Adafruit. The small, trapezoid-shaped plug — the kind older Android phones used. It carries both power and data. If you have a drawer of old cables, you already own this. Make sure it is a data cable, not a charge-only cable (charge-only cables have no data wires inside). Item 4 — about $5, for later Small screwdriver set A precision bit set, like the iFixit Mako. Photo: iFixit. You will not need this today — nothing on this page requires opening anything. But when you are ready for the Repair Guides , gadgets use tiny screws, and a precision bit set (Phillips, Torx, pentalobe, tri-point) will last you years. Item 5 — about $6, your second patient ESP32 development board An ESP32 development board. Photo: Espressif. The chip inside most smart plugs, bulbs, and sensors — on a board you can reprogram over USB, with no mains voltage and nothing to open. Once you finish the Pico project below, this is your next step: the same skills, applied to the chip that runs the smart home. Your first project: update the firmware on your Pico Goal: replace the software on your Raspberry Pi Pico with MicroPython, then talk to it. No screwdriver. No opened enclosures. Nothing gets broken. About 30 minutes. Why this matters: manufacturers update — or abandon — the software on your devices all the time. Here you will do it yourself, on hardware you own, and see exactly what “firmware” means. If software you don’t want ever ships on your device, this is the skill that lets you remove it. Step 0 — What is a terminal? A terminal is a window where you type text commands instead of clicking icons. It looks old-fashioned, but it is the most direct way to talk to hardware. Windows: press the Windows key, type PowerShell , press Enter. Mac: press Cmd + Space , type Terminal , press Enter. Linux: press Ctrl + Alt + T . A window opens with a blinking cursor. That cursor is waiting for you. Everything in the gray boxes below is typed there — lines starting with $ are what you type, and the lines after are what the computer prints back. Step 1 — Put the Pico in bootloader mode Hold down the small white BOOTSEL button on the Pico, and while holding it, plug the micro USB cable into the Pico and your computer. Then let go of the button. A new drive appears on your computer called RPI-RP2 — the Pico is pretending to be a USB flash drive. That is the bootloader : a tiny built-in program whose only job is to accept new firmware. You have just met the first piece of software on the chip, and you didn’t open anything to reach it. Step 2 — Install MicroPython (this is a firmware update) Go to micropython.org/download/rp2-pico in your browser and download the latest .uf2 file. Drag it onto the RPI-RP2 drive — the same way you’d copy a photo onto a USB stick. The drive disappears and the Pico reboots. Congratulations: you just updated firmware . The old software is gone, replaced by MicroPython — your choice, on your hardware. If a manufacturer ever ships software you don’t want, this is the same class of operation that removes it. Step 3 — Find the Pico’s serial port MicroPython is now running, and the Pico is listening on a serial port. Ask your computer where it is: $ ls /dev/ttyACM* /dev/ttyACM0 /dev/ttyACM0 appearing means your computer sees the Pico. (On a Mac, look for /dev/tty.usbmodem* . On Windows, open Device Manager, look under “Ports” for a COM number like COM4 , and use PuTTY instead of the next command.) Step 4 — Talk to it Open a serial window onto the Pico: $ screen /dev/ttyACM0 115200 MicroPython v1.24.0 on 2024-10-25; Raspberry Pi Pico with RP2040 Type "help()" for more information. >>> screen opens the window; 115200 is the speed (baud rate). If you see gibberish, try unplugging and replugging the Pico. (To quit screen later: hold Ctrl , press A , then press K .) The >>> prompt is MicroPython waiting for instructions. Type these lines one at a time and press Enter after each: >>> from machine import Pin >>> led = Pin(25, Pin.OUT) >>> led.on() The tiny green LED on the Pico lights up. You just controlled hardware with three lines of typed text. Try led.off() to turn it off, and led.toggle() to flip it. Now ask the Pico what software it is running — this is how you check firmware on any device: >>> import sys >>> sys.implementation (name='micropython', version=(1, 24, 0), mpy=6543) That version string is the firmware identifying itself. When you want to know whether your devices are running current — or trustworthy — software, this is the question you ask. Step 5 — What you just learned Bootloader: the BOOTSEL button woke a built-in program that accepts new firmware. Every smart device has one. Firmware: the MicroPython file you dragged over is firmware — the device’s entire operating personality in one file, replaceable by you. Flashing: installing firmware is called flashing. You did it by drag-and-drop; professionals use cables, but it is the same operation. Serial terminal: the >>> prompt is a direct line to the chip. This skill works on routers, cameras, and thousands of other devices. You updated a device, verified what it runs, and controlled its hardware — with $4 of parts and no disassembly. That is the whole game. Everything else on this site is the same ideas, applied to bigger devices. Glossary Every field has jargon. Here is ours, in one sentence each. Firmware The software stored inside a device that tells its chip what to do — replaceable, if you know how. Microcontroller A tiny, complete computer on one chip — processor, memory, and inputs/outputs together. The Pico’s RP2040 is one. SoC (System on a Chip) A microcontroller’s bigger sibling: a whole computer system — CPU, graphics, Wi-Fi — on a single chip, like in your phone. PCB (Printed Circuit Board) The flat board that chips and components are soldered onto. Bootloader The first program that runs when a device powers on — it can also accept new firmware, like the Pico’s BOOTSEL mode. Flashing Installing firmware onto a device — what you did by dragging the .uf2 file onto the Pico. Flash memory The chip where firmware is stored. It keeps its contents when power is off, and it can be rewritten. UART / serial A simple two-wire conversation between chips — one wire talks, one listens. The “direct line” to a device’s firmware. TX / RX Transmit and Receive — the two wires of a serial conversation. TX on one side connects to RX on the other. GND (Ground) The shared electrical reference point. Both sides of a serial connection must share ground, or nothing makes sense. Baud rate How fast the serial conversation goes, in bits per second. 115200 is the most common speed. Terminal A text window where you type commands directly to your computer instead of clicking icons. REPL “Read, Evaluate, Print, Loop” — the >>> prompt that runs each line you type immediately. A conversation with the chip. Datasheet The manufacturer’s official manual for a chip — what every pin does, how to power it, how to talk to it. Teardown Opening a device to document what is inside: which chips, how it is built, how hard it is to repair. FCC ID A code the U.S. government requires on wireless devices. You can look it up to find official test photos of a device’s insides — without opening it yourself. What can I do next? You have the basics — and you did it without opening a single enclosure. Here is where each part of BareBoard takes you: Protocol Reverse Engineering Fourteen documented, non-destructive ways to read a device’s firmware — simple entry points using everyday ports, and community tools that work wit

title: How BareBoard Stays Up — BareBoard
headings: What we post, and why we may
text: How BareBoard Stays Up No single company can switch this site off — because no single company holds all of it. The name, the signpost, the host, and the preserved library are four separate layers, run by four separate organizations, and every layer keeps a copy somewhere else. The four layers 1. The name. bareboard.org is registered through Porkbun, an independent registrar. The registration is locked against transfer and deletion, the contact details are private, and the renewal rules are set by ICANN policy, not by any host: if a renewal ever failed, ICANN’s recovery policy guarantees notice beforehand and a 30-day window to restore the name afterward. 2. The signpost. Cloudflare runs the directory that tells your browser where the name points, and stands in front of the site absorbing junk traffic. Cloudflare does not hold the site itself — in its own words, through these services it does not host the content and cannot remove it. If this layer ever failed, the signpost can be rebuilt at any other directory service; the building stays where it is. 3. The building. The pages live on GitHub Pages as plain, hand-written HTML files in a public repository. There is no database, no server code, nothing proprietary in the format: any basic web host on earth can serve these exact files, unchanged. 4. The preserved library. The document collection — the manuals, filings, and records in the Library Hub — is mirrored at the Internet Archive, a nonprofit library that has been keeping the web since 1996: the BareBoard Manufacturer Documentation Archive , free for anyone to download. And a complete copy of the site and library also sits on the maintainer’s own machine, off every platform. If a layer fails anyway Providers can change terms, suspend accounts, or disappear — the arrangement above assumes they might. A host action costs hours, not the site: the same files go up on another host and the signpost is pointed at them. A takedown aimed at one document is answered through the host’s own counter-notice process, with the document’s source on record (see below), and the library keeps its local copy and a link to the public source either way. The layer that would hurt most is the name itself — which is why it is the layer with locks on it and a recovery policy behind it. What we post, and why we may Staying up also means never posting what we have no right to post. Every item here falls in a named class, with the basis recorded next to it in the library index: our own lessons and findings; public records — FCC equipment filings, FDA records, court filings, and laws, which belong to the public; manufacturer manuals and parts catalogs that the manufacturers themselves published, carried with attribution for owners repairing their own equipment; and everything else linked, not copied . Nothing is taken from behind a login or a paywall, nothing marked confidential is published, and the site hosts no firmware binaries, keys, or exploits. The full declarations are on the Copyright and DMCA pages. Mirror it yourself Preservation works better with more copies. Anyone can download the whole documentation archive from the Internet Archive item and keep it, share it, or re-host it — that is what it is there for. If this site ever goes quiet, the library is already out in the world, and the lessons are plain files that anyone can serve. BareBoard — free hardware education, built to outlast its hosts.

title: Support — BareBoard
text: Support BareBoard Our mission BareBoard exists so that anyone, anywhere, can learn how the hardware in their life actually works — for free, forever. The modern device is a locked box. The schematic is a trade secret. The datasheet sits behind a non-disclosure agreement. The battery is glued in, the parts are serialized, the bootloader is signed — and you’re told that opening your own property voids your right to understand it. This is the world as manufactured. We open the box anyway — legally, carefully, and in public. Every device on this bench gets the full treatment: chip-level identification, boot-log forensics, board mapping, protocol analysis. UART headers, JTAG pads, hidden radios, silent telemetry — if it’s on the board, it goes in the report, written so a curious student can follow along and a seasoned engineer can verify every claim. This work stands on principles we don’t negotiate: Learning is a birthright, not a product. Nobody grants you the right to understand the world — you’re born with it. But the knowledge that runs modern life keeps getting fenced off: paywalled manuals, NDA’d datasheets, tuition-gated engineering programs. We publish everything — every trace, every decode, every identification — openly, free, forever, for anyone with curiosity and a connection. No one gets to decide who’s worthy of knowing how things work. What you bought is yours. Ownership used to mean something. Now it means a license agreement, a subscription for features the hardware already has, and a repair manual you’re not allowed to read. We document devices so owners can actually own them: real board maps, real component IDs, real procedures — the information that repair monopolies depend on you never seeing. Fixing things is a right. A working device shouldn’t become landfill because a manufacturer moved on. Serialized parts, software-locked components, and “authorized service” gatekeepers aren’t engineering — they’re rent extraction. Documentation is the antidote. Secrecy serves the seller, not you. The hidden radio broadcasting in your bedroom, the telemetry phoning home at 3 AM, the backdoor nobody documented — if it’s in your house and on your network, you deserve to know it’s there. The balance of power is wrong, and knowledge corrects it. Right now, corporations decide what your devices do, what they report, and when they die — and you get a terms-of-service checkbox. Every teardown here hands a piece of that power back to the person holding the screwdriver. No paywall. No ads. No sponsored findings. No selling your data. No investor deciding what gets covered. Just the truth about the circuit boards, published for the people who believe a device you can’t open isn’t really yours. That’s the mission. Your support keeps the bench powered. Chip in Any amount, one-time or monthly, entirely your call. Pick whichever way is easiest: Donate with Ko-fi Donate with PayPal Ko-fi accepts cards and PayPal — no account needed. The PayPal button goes straight to PayPal. Donate Hardware Contribute devices for teardown analysis. Phones, tablets, IoT hardware, development boards — functional or non-functional. To donate: Contact contact@bareboard.org with a description of the hardware. Shipping instructions will be provided upon review. Donor is responsible for shipping costs. All donated hardware is subject to full teardown documentation published on BareBoard. Where every dollar goes Bench devices. Teardowns need hardware — the rarer the device, the more it costs to rescue one from a landfill or an auction listing and get it onto the bench. Test equipment. Logic analyzers, UART adapters, soldering gear, microscopes — the instruments that turn a pile of chips into documented knowledge. Domain & hosting. The unglamorous cost of staying online and staying independent. A donation buys no influence. Findings are published on the evidence — never on who’s paying. No sponsored teardowns, no embargoed results, no pay-to-play coverage. Ever. Other ways to help Money isn’t the only currency here: Spread the word. Send one teardown to one curious person. That does as much as a donation. Donate hardware. Got a dead or retired device gathering dust? It might be our next autopsy. (Contact details on the About page.) Correct us. Found an error in a report? Tell us. Accuracy is the whole product. Send us a target. Know a device with undocumented hardware, a locked bootloader begging for analysis, or a board nobody’s mapped? Point us at it. Link us. Writing about hardware? Cite our findings. Open knowledge grows by being referenced. We started BareBoard on a simple belief: education should be a human right — free and free to access. Everything here will always be free to read. No paywall, no premium tier, no exceptions. Thank you for keeping it that way. Allies & further reading We’re one bench in a much bigger movement. These are the organizations and communities fighting the same fight: Open Source Hardware Association (OSHWA) — the home of the open-hardware definition, community certification, and the annual Open Hardware Summit. Electronic Frontier Foundation — Right to Repair — legal advocacy against DRM, software locks, and anti-circumvention abuse. iFixit — the repair community’s workshop: free teardowns, repair guides, and parts for thousands of devices. Repair.org / The Repair Association — the coalition pushing right-to-repair legislation across the US. Free Software Foundation — defending users’ freedom to run, study, share, and modify software since 1985. Open Source Initiative — stewards of the Open Source Definition and license review. Creative Commons — the licensing infrastructure that makes sharing knowledge legally simple. What is Free Software? — the GNU Project’s foundational essay on user freedom. Required reading. “There’s nothing in computing that can’t be broken by another level of indirection.” — Rob Pike

title: Texas Right-to-Repair Law: What It Does, and What It Does Not — BareBoard
headings: Texas right-to-repair law: what it does, and what it does not
The loopholes: where the law does not bite yet
What it does not cover: wheelchairs and medical devices
text: Texas right-to-repair law: what it does, and what it does not Texas has a right-to-repair law now. It took effect September 1, 2026, and it is the largest state consumer-electronics repair law yet — and the first led by a Republican legislature. If you live in Texas, it changes what a manufacturer must give you when your electronics break. But read the fine print: the law has a one-year grace period, it can require you to get remote permission or an internet connection, and — said plainly, because it matters most to this site’s readers — it does not cover wheelchairs or medical devices at all. What the law is HB 2963 , the Texas consumer-electronics right-to-repair law, applies to consumer electronic products costing $50 or more, first sold after September 1, 2026. Manufacturers must make available, on fair and reasonable terms, the parts, tools, and documentation (manuals, schematics, diagnostics) needed to repair the product — to owners and to independent repair shops, not only to authorized dealers. Texas joins six other states with active consumer-electronics repair laws: New York, Minnesota, California, Colorado, Washington, Oregon, and Connecticut (effective July 1, 2026). Kansas has enacted its own law, applying only to equipment made for sale in Kansas from July 1, 2027. The loopholes: where the law does not bite yet The live debate about the Texas law is whether its exceptions swallow it. Three matter: The one-year grace period. Manufacturers get up to a year after a product’s first sale before they have to provide the parts, tools, and documentation. A product that breaks in its first year — when failures are most common — may have no repair material available at all, legally. Remote authorization. The law allows a manufacturer to require remote authorization or an internet connection before a repair can proceed. That is the software-lock problem in legal form: the repair still depends on the manufacturer’s server saying yes. If the server is down, or the product line is discontinued, the authorization may never come. The product window. The law reaches products first sold after September 1, 2026. Everything already in people’s homes — the phone, laptop, or television bought in August — is outside it. What it does not cover: wheelchairs and medical devices This is the part that must be said plainly, because it is the part most likely to be misunderstood. HB 2963 is a general electronics law. Like the consumer-electronics repair laws in other states, it expressly excludes medical devices . A powered wheelchair is a medical device. So: A Texas wheelchair owner gains nothing from HB 2963 for their chair. The dealer-only programmers, the locked firmware, and the parts restrictions on power mobility devices are untouched by this law. Texas has no wheelchair right-to-repair law . Eight states do — Colorado, California, Maryland, Nevada, Oregon, Rhode Island, Tennessee, and Washington — but Texas is not one of them. The full list, with the statutes and their enforcers, is on our Shield page , and the Texas carve-out is noted in the law section of our PMD section . What does protect a Texas wheelchair owner today is federal law: the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act, and the DMCA §1201 repair exemptions — including the medical-device exemption that is under threat right now (see our DMCA 1201 explainer ). The same exclusion applies to the other state electronics laws: they are written for phones, laptops, and appliances, not for medical devices. Do not let a headline about “right to repair in Texas” tell you your chair is covered. It is not. What to do with it For electronics: if a product first sold after September 1, 2026 breaks and the maker refuses parts, tools, or documentation, ask in writing, cite HB 2963, and keep the refusal. If the maker claims the one-year grace period, note the date the product was first sold and the date the grace period ends. For wheelchairs: use the federal ground and the demand-letter templates on our repair demand letter page, and the escalation ladder on The Shield . Sources “Right to Repair 2026 Fall Update” — Tech Care Association, November 4, 2026: techcareassociation.org . On this site: The Shield: right-to-repair law (Layer three: the general electronics laws, including Texas HB 2963, Connecticut, and Kansas); the PMD law section ; the DMCA 1201 medical-device exemption . BareBoard — free hardware education. A repair law that excludes your chair is not your repair law. Know which law covers you, and which one does not.

title: “Hello Again”: the TPM Attack That Breaks Your PIN Lockout — BareBoard
headings: “Hello Again”: the attack that breaks your laptop’s PIN lockout
What was tested, and what was not
text: “Hello Again”: the attack that breaks your laptop’s PIN lockout Your laptop’s short PIN — the four digits you type to unlock Windows Hello, or to unlock BitLocker disk encryption — is protected by a lockout: guess wrong too many times, and the chip refuses to try again. Researchers at Technische Universität Berlin have shown how to defeat that lockout with a small board, a voltage glitch, and physical access to the machine. A 4-digit PIN that should have taken 69 days to guess now takes 40 hours at worst. A 6-digit BitLocker PIN that should have taken 19 years now takes 20 days at worst. There are no reported attacks outside the lab. But the fix is yours to make now: a longer PIN, and a firmware update when your maker ships one. First, the pieces, defined TPM (Trusted Platform Module): a security chip (or, on modern machines, a piece of firmware running inside the processor — a firmware TPM , or fTPM ) that stores secrets such as the keys that protect your disk encryption, and that counts wrong PIN guesses. Windows Hello: Microsoft’s sign-in system — face, fingerprint, or PIN — that uses the TPM to protect your credentials. BitLocker: Windows’ built-in disk encryption. A BitLocker PIN unlocks the key that decrypts the drive. Lockout (anti-hammering): after a set number of wrong guesses, the TPM refuses further guesses for a long time. This is what makes a 4-digit PIN safe: there are only 10,000 possible 4-digit PINs, so without a lockout an attacker could try them all in minutes. With a working lockout, trying them all takes 69 days. SPI flash: a small memory chip on the motherboard that holds firmware, including the fTPM’s saved state — among other things, its wrong-guess counter. RPMC (replay-protected monotonic counter): a counter stored in the flash chip that only ever goes up, and whose value is protected by a cryptographic signature (an HMAC — a keyed checksum that proves a value is genuine). Its job is to stop rollback : an attacker copying an old saved state of the fTPM back onto the flash to reset the wrong-guess counter to zero. How the attack works The attack, presented at the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS ’26) in The Hague in November 2026 and covered by The Hacker News on November 18, 2026, is called “Hello Again.” It breaks the RPMC protection in two ways: The counter is never checked (AMD). AMD’s Secure Processor firmware — the code that runs the fTPM on AMD machines — never verifies that the RPMC counter actually increased. So an attacker can put a small interposer board (a thin circuit board fitted between the processor and the flash chip) in the way, block the counter update, and report success. The fTPM believes the counter moved forward; it did not. The attacker can then replay an old fTPM state with a fresh wrong-guess counter, as many times as they like. This flaw is CVE-2026-43613 (a CVE number is the standard public ID for a security flaw; CVSS 5.1, AMD bulletin AMD-SN-7079). The counter’s signing key can be stolen (Winbond flash). A brief voltage glitch — a precisely timed dip in the power supplied to the flash chip — makes Winbond RPMC flash leak its HMAC signing key in about a second. With the key, an attacker can forge any counter value they want, so the counter’s signature proves nothing. With the lockout defeated, the attacker simply tries PINs until one works. In the lab, a 4-digit Windows Hello PIN was cracked in 57 minutes; the worst case, trying every combination, is 40 hours instead of 69 days. A 6-digit BitLocker PIN was cracked in under 7 minutes in the lab; the worst case is 20 days instead of 19 years. What was tested, and what was not The researchers tested an HP OmniBook 3 (Ryzen AI 5 330) and a Framework Laptop 13 (Core Ultra 5 125H). AMD has confirmed the flaw and plans firmware fixes for most affected chips between November 2026 and February 2027. The physical-access caveat, stated plainly. This is not a remote attack. Nobody can do this to your laptop over the internet. The attacker needs the machine in their hands, needs to open it, and needs to fit hardware to it (or glitch its power supply). If your laptop is stolen, that is exactly the scenario that matters — a thief has physical access. If your laptop never leaves your sight, this attack does not reach you. And no attacks outside the lab have been reported. The point of this page is not panic; it is that the lockout you were relying on is weaker than advertised, so your PIN needs to be longer than you thought. What to do Make your PIN longer — today. This is the fix that works regardless of firmware. A 4-digit PIN has 10,000 possibilities; a 6-digit PIN has a million; an 8-digit PIN has a hundred million. The researchers’ own numbers show the difference: even with the lockout broken, a 6-digit BitLocker PIN takes up to 20 days to brute-force, and longer PINs scale far beyond that. Use at least 8 digits for a BitLocker PIN, and at least 6 for Windows Hello — longer if you will remember it. A passphrase (words, not just digits) is stronger still where the system allows it. Install the firmware update when it arrives. AMD plans fixes for most affected chips between November 2026 and February 2027. Your laptop maker (HP, Framework, Lenovo, and others) will ship them as BIOS/UEFI updates — install them the way you would any other firmware update. Check your maker’s support page for your exact model rather than assuming you are covered. Keep treating a stolen laptop as compromised. Physical access has always been the boundary of laptop security: a thief with time and tools can read a drive that is not encrypted, and can now also attack a short PIN faster than before. Full-disk encryption (BitLocker, with a long PIN) plus a long PIN is the honest defense. If a laptop is stolen, change your passwords and treat the data as exposed. Why this matters beyond laptops The lesson is general, and it is why this page is on a repair site. The TPM’s lockout depended on a counter stored in a separate flash chip, protected by a signature — and the protection failed in two different places at once: the firmware never checked the counter, and the flash chip leaked the signing key. Security that lives in firmware is only as good as the firmware’s handling of its own state, and no software scan or parts list (no SBOM) can catch a flaw like this, because the flaw is in how the platform security processor treats a counter. The people who find these flaws do it the same way repair people work: by reading the hardware, probing the bus between two chips, and testing what the documentation claims. SPI flash, interposer boards, and voltage glitching are bench skills — and they cut both ways. Sources “Flash Chip Attack Bypasses TPM Lockout, Cracks Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs” — The Hacker News, November 18, 2026: thehackernews.com . “‘Hello’ Attack Bypasses Windows Hello and BitLocker” — Cyber Security News, November 18, 2026: cybersecuritynews.com . CVE-2026-43613 — AMD bulletin AMD-SN-7079 (via the sources above). AMD firmware fixes planned November 2026 to February 2027. On this site: GPU Repair (the same bench skills, applied to graphics cards). BareBoard — free hardware education. A 4-digit PIN was safe because the lockout worked. The lockout does not work. Make the PIN longer.

title: W³ — Who Watches the Watchmen — BareBoard
headings: Run your own W³ audit — seven basic steps
text: W³ Who Watches the Watchmen? “WHO WATCHES THE WATCHMEN?” — Alan Moore, Watchmen (1986–1987). The phrase appears as graffiti throughout the graphic novel, adapted from Juvenal’s Latin “Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?” ( Satires VI, circa 100 AD). Every instrument on the BareBoard bench exists to answer one question: what is really inside this hardware? This page turns that question around. The logic analyzers, debug probes, and programmers we trust with our examinations — do we know what is inside them ? A tool that sits between you and a target can shape everything you observe. A closed chip, an unverifiable firmware blob, a driver you cannot inspect: each one is a place where trust replaces evidence. That is acceptable only when it is a conscious choice. Below, each tool on our bench is examined the same way we examine everything else — chip by chip, license by license. Trust, but verify — starting at home. The examinations For each tool: what is on the board, how open the design and firmware are, whether an independent person can verify its behavior, and anything worth watching. Glasgow Interface Explorer Raspberry Pi Pico Bus Pirate v3 Tigard Shikra Saleae-compatible logic analyzers (FX2-based) CH341A programmers Saleae Logic 8 / Logic Pro 8 Rigol DS1054Z Siglent SDS1104X-E Hantek 6022BE Fluke 87V UNI-T UT61E Aneng AN8008 Hakko FX-888D Pinecil Quick 861DW Segger J-Link ST-Link V2 (genuine vs. clone) Black Magic Probe FTDI FT232RL WCH CH340 / CH341A Flipper Zero Glasgow Interface Explorer Links: Docs & site · Source & hardware (GitHub) What it is: a reconfigurable USB multitool for communicating with digital hardware — UART, SPI, I²C, JTAG, and many other protocols, defined in software and synthesized onto an FPGA. What is on the board: a Lattice iCE40HX8K FPGA (supported by a fully open-source FPGA toolchain) and a Cypress FX2 high-speed USB interface, with 16 level-shifted GPIO channels. How open is it: the gateware is written in Amaranth (a Python-based hardware description language) and released under permissive terms (0BSD / Apache-2.0); the host software is Python. The board design is open. It is built with Project IceStorm, the community reverse-engineered open toolchain for iCE40 — no vendor license, no account, no closed synthesizer required. Can you verify it: yes, completely. Every layer from gateware source to bitstream can be rebuilt with open tools and compared. Anything to watch: very little. Glasgow is the reference example of a fully verifiable instrument. The main practical note is that the FPGA bitstream is generated on demand, so reproducing an exact historical bitstream requires the same toolchain versions. Raspberry Pi Pico Photo: Ogidya, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons . Links: Product page · RP2040 datasheet (PDF) · Pico SDK (GitHub) · UF2 spec (GitHub) What it is: a $4 microcontroller board, widely used on this bench as a USB-to-serial adapter and as a debug probe (running Picoprobe firmware) for SWD targets. What is on the board: the RP2040 microcontroller (dual Arm Cortex-M0+, 264 KB SRAM) plus 2 MB of external flash. The RP2040 contains a mask-ROM bootloader that presents the board as a USB drive — firmware is installed by dragging a file onto it. How open is it: Raspberry Pi publishes the board design files, the RP2040 datasheet is unusually thorough for the industry, and the Picoprobe firmware is open source. The mask-ROM bootloader itself is fixed in silicon and cannot be independently rebuilt, but its behavior (USB mass storage + UF2 flashing) is documented and observable. Can you verify it: largely yes. The firmware you run is firmware you can build from source; the ROM bootloader’s behavior is simple and well documented. Anything to watch: the ROM is the one closed corner — small, documented, and fixed, but closed. For a $4 probe, this is an acceptable and conscious trade. Bus Pirate v3 Photo: Tylerl (talk), CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons . Pictured: the Bus Pirate v3a. Links: Bus Pirate site · Firmware (GitHub) What it is: a USB multitool for UART, SPI, I²C, 1-Wire, and more, controlled from a serial terminal. A long-standing community instrument. What is on the board: a Microchip PIC24FJ64GA002 microcontroller, an FTDI FT232RL USB-to-serial chip, and a 4066 analog switch array, with an ICSP header for programming the PIC directly. How open is it: the hardware design is released under CC-0 and the firmware under CC-0, with a GPL v3 bootloader. Schematics, part lists, and firmware source are published by Dangerous Prototypes. Can you verify it: yes. The firmware can be rebuilt and re-flashed over USB via the bootloader, or through the ICSP header with an external programmer. Anything to watch: the FTDI FT232RL is a closed chip (as with all FTDI parts) — it handles USB only, not protocol logic, so its closed nature has limited bearing on measurement integrity. Note that FTDI’s drivers have a history of aggressive counterfeit-chip handling; genuine boards avoid the issue. Tigard Links: Hardware & docs (GitHub) · Crowd Supply page What it is: an open-source FTDI FT2232H-based multi-protocol tool (UART, JTAG, SPI, I²C, SWD) with on-board level shifting from 1.8 V to 5.5 V, designed for attaching to low-speed interfaces on examined hardware. What is on the board: an FTDI FT2232HQ dual high-speed USB interface chip, bi-directional level shifters, and dedicated headers for UART, SWD, JTAG, SPI, and I²C, plus a logic-analyzer tap header. How open is it: the board design is released under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0, with design files on GitHub. It works with standard open tools (OpenOCD, Flashrom, PyFtdi). Can you verify it: the board design, yes. The FTDI chip’s internal firmware is closed, but the chip is used as a standard USB interface whose behavior is defined by FTDI’s public drivers and the open host-side tools. Anything to watch: same FTDI note as the Bus Pirate: the closed USB interface chip is a transport, not the measurement logic. Verify the level-shifter voltage selection before connecting to a target — wrong voltage is a hardware risk, not a trust issue. Shikra Links: Community docs & pinouts (GitHub) What it is: an FTDI-based USB adapter for JTAG, SPI, I²C, UART, and GPIO, from Xipiter. What is on the board: an FTDI interface chip (USB to the low-level protocols listed above). How open is it: less documented than the others here. Public design files and firmware sources are limited, which is itself the finding. Can you verify it: partially. It works with standard FTDI-compatible host tools, so its observable behavior can be checked, but the board-level design is not as openly published as the tools above. Anything to watch: this is the weakest link on the bench from a verifiability standpoint. It remains useful, but it is used with that limitation in mind — and it is a candidate for replacement by a fully open equivalent. Saleae-compatible logic analyzers (FX2-based) Photo: Molivio, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons . Pictured: the Cypress FX2LP (CY7C68013A) — the chip inside these analyzers. Links: sigrok wiki: Saleae Logic & the FX2 clones · Saleae support What it is: inexpensive 8-channel, 24 MHz USB logic analyzers, widely sold as low-cost alternatives to the original Saleae Logic. What is on the board: a Cypress CY7C68013A (FX2LP) USB controller, an NXP LVC245A transceiver, a 24C02N I²C EEPROM, and a 24 MHz crystal. (Documented by the sigrok project’s hardware notes.) How open is it: the hardware is an unlicensed copy of the original design — not open, and not authorized. The redeeming factor is the firmware: sigrok’s fx2lafw is fully open-source firmware that these boards can run, replacing the factory-installed firmware. Can you verify it: yes, when running fx2lafw under sigrok/PulseView. The firmware is built from source and loaded onto the FX2LP at each session. Anything to watch: two things. First, the hardware’s provenance is a copy — buy it for the price, not the brand story. Second, always run the open firmware; the firmware a clone ships with is of unknown origin. With fx2lafw loaded, the instrument is verifiable. CH341A programmers Photo: RAIL P (RAIL.PHOTOGRAPHY), CC0, via Wikimedia Commons . Links: WCH CH341 product page · flashrom What it is: ~$3 USB programmers for SPI flash and I²C EEPROM (25-series / 24-series), used with a SOIC-8 test clip to read chips without desoldering. What is on the board: the WCH (Nanjing Qinheng) CH341A USB interface chip, a voltage regulator, and a ZIF socket or pin header. The CH341A itself is closed silicon. How open is it: the chip is closed, and the bundled vendor software is of uncertain provenance. The community answer is open host software: AsProgrammer (MIT-licensed) and flashrom both support the CH341A. Can you verify it: behaviorally, yes — read-back verification (read the chip, compare against what was written) is standard practice and catches misbehavior. Use the open host tools, not the bundled software. Anything to watch: voltage. Some inexpensive boards have jumpers or design quirks around 3.3 V vs 5 V selection — always verify the output voltage with a multimeter before connecting to a 3.3 V target. A wrong voltage damages the target; this is the most common real-world failure with these boards. The Amassed Bench Who watches the watchmen? You do. The amassed bench: 28 devices , 21 examined in full below and 7 summarized in the table, awaiting full examination. Each full examination carries the same fields — pictures (public, including the internal photos inside FCC filings), FCC ID , datasheets , documentation , a litigation & controversy check , and a basic-as-basic, do-it-yourself audit that anyone can run without any education. The goal is for the people: understand your tools, verify them yourself, fix what you rightfully own. The rules of the bench. Public sources only: FCC filings, datasheets, court and regulatory records, vendor statem

title: Watchmen — Auditing the Tools — BareBoard
text: Watchmen — Auditing the Tools Your tools are the most privileged devices in the lab. This section audits them. The watchmen rules Your tool is the most privileged device in the lab. Open beats closed — if you cannot read the design, you cannot trust the tool. Verify, don't trust — build from source, hash the firmware, scan the tool itself. Air-gap for sensitive targets. title: Watchmen — Audit Checklist — BareBoard
text: Watchmen — Audit Checklist Seven steps to audit any lab tool before trusting it with a sensitive target. The checklist Design openness — Are schematics and PCB layout public? (Glasgow: yes. Saleae: no.) Firmware openness — Is the firmware source available and buildable? (Pico: yes. J-Link: no.) Host software — Is the host-side code open? Can you read what it sends? Nmap the tool — If it has a network interface, scan it. If it phones home, air-gap it. USB descriptors — Dump them. Unexpected interfaces are a red flag. Supply chain — Who makes it? What's their history? (FTDI's driver-bricking incident is instructive.) Operational hygiene — Dedicated bench machine, no cloud sync, hashed firmware. Quick reference Check Open tool (Glasgow) Closed tool (Saleae) Schematics public Yes No Firmware rebuild Yes No Host code readable Yes Partial Phone-home risk None Low (check) Verdict Trusted Sandboxed If you can't complete steps 1–3, treat the tool as untrusted and sandbox it.
